title: Default by Tenant
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due and does not cure the failure within the time period specified by applicable law after receiving written notice from Landlord. Tenant will also be in default if Tenant fails to comply with any other obligation under this Lease and does not cure the failure after receiving written notice, except where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure. Except as required by applicable law, Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate this Lease or pursue eviction. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may exercise all rights and remedies available under applicable law, including terminating this Lease, regaining possession of the property, and recovering unpaid Rent, late fees, and reasonable costs and expenses, less amounts obtained from the Security Deposit. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to mitigate damages resulting from Tenant's default to the extent required by applicable law. To the extent permitted under applicable law, the prevailing party may recover from the other party court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees and expenses incurred in connection with any legal proceedings related to this Lease.
notes: CO added - verified this session (statute walk + full-library audit; content itself EDITED this session | CORRECTED 2026-08-20 (caught by Claude CLI review): added explicit carve-out that an unpaid late fee alone cannot trigger termination/eviction, consistent with CO law that a late fee is distinct from rent and cannot be grounds for eviction on its own. WY added 2026-08-21 (full-library cross-check pass): generic mechanics, no CO-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with WY findings from this project. | MN extended (Minnesota session, CO;WY-scoping resolution): cure-period language defers to 'applicable law' rather than hardcoding a number, so it doesn't shorten any MN statutory cure right (MN has no general statutory cure period for lease violations, confirmed absent this session). Fee-shifting sentence is already mutual ('prevailing party') — compatible with MN's automatic-mutuality rule (§504B.172), no conflict. | Cross-state plain-language cleanup (Minnesota session, follow-up to MN's plain-language audit): long compound sentence split into shorter ones, no substantive change. Not a legal requirement for this clause's other tagged states (only MN's Plain Language Contract Act, Minn. Stat. §325G.31, was confirmed to apply this project) — done as a general readability improvement since the pattern was found library-wide, not MN-specific. | ND extended (North Dakota session 1, CO;WY-maintenance-scoping review resolved by reading the full CO and MN decision logs directly): defers to 'applicable law' for cure timing, no ND-specific conflict. Fee-shifting language ('prevailing party') matches N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.6 exactly, which awards attorney's fees 'to the prevailing party' -- mutual, not one-way. This resolves ND's piece of the standing fee-shifting-mutuality question (though the broader cross-state consolidation across CO/WY/KS/NE/MN remains a separate open item). | 5a.1 RETROACTIVE CLASSIFICATION 2026-08-28: the prevailing-party attorney-fee rewrite here was STATE-DRIVEN (forced by C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(II)), not uniform, and was inherited by WY/MN/ND/SD without classification - the exact failure mode 5a.1 exists to prevent. Checked for WY 2026-08-28: WY has NO reciprocity statute (see edu-no-fee-reciprocity-wy), so a landlord-only clause would be enforceable there and the mutual language is a voluntary giveaway. Taylor's decision 2026-08-28: KEEP mutual language for WY. MN, ND, and SD remain unclassified for this edit. | CROSS-STATE FEE-SHIFTING CONSOLIDATION COMPLETED 2026-09-06 (ND re-audit). The standing open item -- 'is this clause's fee language genuinely mutual, and does it work in every tagged state?' -- is resolved. Operative sentence: 'To the extent permitted under applicable law, the prevailing party may recover from the other party court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees and expenses incurred in connection with any legal proceedings related to this Lease.' FIVE DISTINCT STATE ARCHITECTURES, not one question: (1) CO -- a landlord-only fee clause is VOID and the lease must be drafted mutual; 'prevailing party' SATISFIES this. (2) MN -- fee clauses are made mutual BY OPERATION OF LAW regardless of lease text; consistent, no conflict. (3) KS (K.S.A. 58-2547) and NE (§ 76-1415(1)(c)) -- attorney-fee clauses are BANNED OUTRIGHT in either direction; this clause is correctly NOT tagged to either, and a library-wide check confirmed ZERO LEASE_CLAUSE rows tagged KS or NE contain attorney-fee language. (4) ND -- § 47-16-13.6 awards fees to 'the prevailing party' by statute; clause language matches exactly. (5) WY -- American Rule, no reciprocity statute, contract governs. OPEN FLAG FOR WYOMING, surfaced not resolved: per edu-no-fee-reciprocity-wy the Wyoming Supreme Court requires a contract to 'unequivocally provide' for fee recovery before fees may be awarded. This clause hedges twice -- 'TO THE EXTENT PERMITTED UNDER APPLICABLE LAW' makes the entitlement conditional on an external referent, and 'MAY recover' is permissive rather than mandatory. Under a strict unequivocal-provision standard that phrasing may not suffice, which would leave a WY landlord with NO fee recovery in a state whose default is that each side bears its own. No Wyoming case applying the standard to comparable hedged language was located, and no edit is made on that basis -- flagged for Taylor. Note the hedge exists for a reason: it is what makes the clause safe to share with CO and MN. Any WY fix should be a WY-specific override, NOT an edit to the shared text. | WYOMING FLAG RETRACTED 2026-09-06 after reading the actual case law rather than this library's characterisation of it. NO WY-SPECIFIC OVERRIDE IS NEEDED. The Wyoming standard is EXPRESS CONTRACTUAL AUTHORISATION, not a heightened magic-words test: Cowardin v. Finnerty (Wyo. 1999) -- 'absent statutory or contract language expressly authorizing recovery of attorney fees, parties are responsible for payment of their own attorney fees'; Emken, 2006 WY 112, ¶ 8 -- 'a prevailing party may be reimbursed for its attorney fees when express statutory or contractual authorization exists'; Thorkildsen v. Belden, 2012 WY 8; Circle Resources v. Hassler, 2023 WY 22, ¶ 8 -- 'A prevailing party may, however, be reimbursed for attorneys' fees when provided for by contract or statute.' The Wyoming failure cases are ones where the contract said NOTHING about fees. Cowardin is explicit: 'Given the absence of any reference to attorney fees in the purchase agreement, Sellers were not entitled to recover attorney fees.' THIS CLAUSE EXPRESSLY REFERS TO ATTORNEY FEES, NAMES THE PREVAILING PARTY, AND USES THE COURT'S OWN FORMULATION. The supposed defect -- 'may recover' being permissive -- is the verb the Wyoming Supreme Court itself uses in stating the rule. 'To the extent permitted under applicable law' is a savings clause; no Wyoming authority was located suggesting a savings clause defeats otherwise-express authorisation, and the circularity concern raised earlier in this session was speculative. PROCESS NOTE: the flag originated from this library's own edu-no-fee-reciprocity-wy row, which characterises the standard as requiring a contract to 'unequivocally provide' for fees. The cases say 'expressly authorizing' / 'express... authorization'. Raising a structural change to a four-state shared clause on a secondary characterisation, without reading the cases, was the Addendum L.5 failure committed in the same session that wrote L.5. CA: extended to California 2026-09-19 after re-screen against the full CA pass (the extend manifest had deferred tagging until the blocked set was resolved, and the step was then missed). No CA conflict found. | NV: Read in full 2026-09-24 against NRS 118A (revisor text Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated). Applies as written: promises a cure opportunity for every non-rent breach, more generous than 118A.430 (5 days for remediable breach; none for a breach that cannot be remedied) - lawful. Prevailing-party fee sentence is the form 118A.220(1)(c) permits. PROVISIONAL pending NRS Ch. 40 read. | NV (text batch 2, 2026-09-24): PROVISIONAL CLEARED. NRS 40.2516: 5-day perform-or-quit, lease saved by performing within 5 days, no notice if the breach cannot be cured; NRS 40.2514: 3-day notice to surrender with NO cure for unauthorized assignment/sublet, waste, unlawful business, nuisance, or controlled-substance violations (other than simple possession). The clause promises a cure for every non-rent breach - more than NV requires for 40.2514 grounds; lawful, but a product choice worth knowing. NRS 40.252: a landlord may not shorten statutory notice periods by contract - the clause defers to law, so no conflict. | TX: Read in full 2026-09-25 against Tex. Prop. Code chs. 24, 54, 91, 92 and 301 (official statutes.capitol.texas.gov text for chs. 24/54/91/301). Applies as written. Tex. Prop. Code s24.005(a) as amended by S.B. 38 (89th Leg., R.S., eff. Jan. 1, 2026): 3 days' written notice to vacate unless the lease sets a shorter or longer period; for a tenant NOT previously late before the month of the notice, a nonpayment notice must be a NOTICE TO PAY RENT OR VACATE - so 'the time period specified by applicable law' for a rent cure has a Texas referent. Cure for non-rent defaults is voluntary (Texas requires none). Prevailing-party fee sentence matches s24.006(b)-(c): a lease fee clause entitles the prevailing landlord AND makes fees reciprocal for a prevailing tenant. Mitigation sentence: s91.006. Base chosen over -ks-ne because it carries the fee sentence. | NJ: 2026-09-26 tag REMOVED same session (research pass): its attorney-fee sentence triggers N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.66/-61.67 (implied reciprocal tenant fee covenant; mandatory bold reciprocity sentence in any lease fee clause). NJ override default-by-tenant-nj pending primary text of 2A:18-61.66/-61.67. s5a.1: states-only change. | CURE CARVE-OUT ADDED 2026-09-26 (Taylor's decision, targeted fix at the FL sync; checklist instruction 33): the non-rent cure promise now ends 'except where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure.' Before, promising a cure for every breach could contractually give up a state's no-cure termination grounds (the logs record such grounds for at least NV §40.2514, ND ch. 47-32, MN §504B.171, CA CCP §1161(4) and NE). UNIFORM: self-limiting, adds no landlord right where no such law exists. Propagation notes appended to every tagged state's log. | AZ: Applies as written, instruction 33 checked. Rent: A.R.S. §33-1368(B), 5 days after written notice. Non-rent: 10-day cure notice, or 5 days for a §33-1341 breach materially affecting health and safety (§33-1368(A)). No-cure grounds the carve-out ("except where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure") must and does cover: (1) immediate termination for a material and irreparable breach on the premises (§33-1368(A), trial within 3 days under §33-1377(E)); (2) a second noncompliance of the same or similar nature, 10 days after a notice with no cure; (3) material falsification of criminal record, eviction record or current criminal activity on the application ("not curable"). Attorney fees: §33-1315(A)(2) allows only a prevailing-party clause in writing, which is what this row has; §33-1368(C) lets the landlord recover reasonable fees anyway. Mitigation: §§33-1305(A), 33-1370(C). Late-fee sentence: Arizona reinstatement before filing requires past-due rent plus a reasonable late fee set forth in a written lease (§33-1368(B)); the row's promise not to evict over a late fee alone is the library default (NJ decision), recorded as a judgment call in AZ log s6. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | GA: Applies as written. Nonpayment: 3-business-day written notice to vacate or pay all past-due rent, late fees, utilities and other charges before filing (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50(c), leases entered or renewed on or after 2024-07-01), posted in a sealed envelope on the door plus any delivery method the lease adds (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50(d)); tender of all rent plus warrant costs within 7 days of service is a complete defense once per 12 months (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-52). INSTRUCTION 33: Georgia has no statutory cure period for non-rent breaches and no enumerated no-cure grounds, so there is no statutory no-cure right to forfeit; the clause's contractual cure promise is the library default, kept for GA by Taylor's decision 2026-09-28 (GA log §6.3): the shared carve-out covers the state-specific case, as it did for the earlier state that raised it. INSTRUCTION 32: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-2(c) voids a tenant-pays-landlord's-fees clause unless it also makes the landlord pay the tenant's fees on the landlord's breach; the mutual prevailing-party sentence satisfies it, and no forced wording exists. The late-fee sentence gives up O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50(c)'s late-fee ground (library default). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | SC: Tagged (Taylor decision 2, 2026-09-28: keep the shared clause). Nonpayment: 5 days after the due date plus written notice, which the lease itself can give (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-710(B); `nonpayment-notice-sc` states it is that notice). Other breaches: 14-day written notice and cure for remediable breaches (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-710(A)); instruction 33: non-remediable breaches and illegal activity (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-540, reached by S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-710(B)) need no cure, and the carve-out preserves that. Fee sentence: self-limited; landlord fees need an attorney and wilful noncompliance or nonpayment not in good faith (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-710(C)); after termination (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-750). Mitigation: the aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-50(a); S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-730(c)). No reciprocity or bold-text rule (instruction 32). Late-fee sentence gives up a small right (late charges are rent, S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-210(11)); kept by decision. | TN: Tagged 2026-09-28 (section text read 2026-09-28 in the built-in browser (Justia host copy of the 2025 Tennessee Code with history lines; 2025-2026 public chapters screened; TN log §1)). KEPT FOR TN (instructions 32, 33, 48 checked). Cure language is self-limited and satisfies both regimes: Act counties 14-day cure for remediable breaches and non-remediable 14-day and 3-day routes (Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 66-28-505(a), 66-28-517); other counties 14 days for rent or damage with cure, 30 days for other defaults, 3 days for violence or drugs (§ 66-7-109) - the carve-out 'except where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure' preserves the no-cure routes. Fees: § 66-28-505(d) lets the landlord recover reasonable attorney's fees 'as provided in the rental agreement'; no bold or reciprocity rule (contrast NC, NJ). Late-fee sentence: 'rents' includes all payments (§ 66-28-104(13)), so the sentence gives up a small right, as Taylor accepted for SC. Instruction 48: the Act-only nonpayment-notice-waiver-tn expressly overrides this clause's 'after receiving written notice'. TN-SCOPE: STATEWIDE. | VA: Tagged 2026-09-28. VA-SCOPE: STATEWIDE. Read against the official Code of Virginia section-open (law.lis.virginia.gov; VA log §1). Basis: KEPT FOR VA (instructions 32, 33, 48 checked). Nonpayment cure 'within the time period specified by applicable law after receiving written notice' matches the 14-day notice (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1245(F), 2026 Acts ch. 353/354). The 'except where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure' carve-out preserves non-remediable breaches, repeat breaches and immediate termination for criminal or willful acts (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1245(C), (E)). No statute forces text into the fee clause; landlord fees are recoverable 'as contracted for in the rental agreement or as provided by law' (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1245(H)-(I)), and 'to the extent permitted' preserves the reasonable-failure exception. Mitigation and no accelerated rent: Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1251. Library policy that a late fee alone is not grounds for termination is narrower than Virginia law (late charges are 'rent', Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1200) and lawful. | PA: Tagged. No statutory cure period in Pennsylvania: rent default triggers a ten-day notice to quit after demand; breach triggers a fifteen- or thirty-day notice (68 P.S. § 250.501(a)-(b), Act § 501). The base's written-notice-and-cure promise is more generous than the statute; 'except where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure' covers the drug grounds (68 P.S. § 250.505-A, Act § 505-A; ten-day notice 68 P.S. § 250.501(d)) - instruction 33 checked. Prevailing-party fees: Pennsylvania has no lease fee ban (contrast `default-by-tenant-al`); contractual fee shifting is case law, not read. No penalty for using prohibited terms (instruction 49; AZ1.4 analog not located). If `notice-to-quit-waiver-pa` is used, it expressly keeps this Section's written notice of default (instruction 48). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | UT: Nonpayment: 3 business days pay-or-quit (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-802(1)(c)); other breach: 3 calendar days perform-or-quit ((1)(h)); no-cure 3-calendar-day notices for unauthorized sublet or waste, unlawful business, nuisance and criminal acts ((1)(d)-(g)), preserved by the carve-out (rule 43 checked). The court must award reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party in an unlawful-detainer action (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-811(5)(a)); reciprocity statute Utah Code Ann. § 78B-5-826. Mitigation: Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-811(1)(d)(ii). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | IL: Tagged. Step D rule 43: the cure promise for other breaches carves out cases where 'applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure', which covers the 10-day notice to quit (735 ILCS 5/9-210) and voiding for crimes or drugs (735 ILCS 5/9-120; 740 ILCS 40/11), so the landlord keeps its no-cure rights; the nonpayment cure follows the 5-day demand (735 ILCS 5/9-209). Mitigation: 735 ILCS 5/9-213.1. No Illinois statute bars a prevailing-party fee clause (edu-attorney-fees-il); an eviction-notice fee is banned (765 ILCS 705/35(c)(4)) and the clause's 'reasonable costs and expenses' is limited by 'applicable law' (Step D rule 49). Read section-open 2026-09-30 (IL log §1). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | ID: Idaho Code § 6-303(2) (3-day written notice to pay or quit) and Idaho Code § 6-303(3) (3-day written notice to perform or quit; no notice where the breach 'cannot afterward be performed') are the 'time period specified by applicable law'; assignment, subletting or waste contrary to the lease ends it on a 3-day notice to quit (Idaho Code § 6-303(4)) and drug activity is a ground with no notice stated (Idaho Code § 6-303(5)); the clause's carve-out covers these. Idaho Code § 6-324 awards the prevailing party attorney fees in an unlawful-detainer action (not where treble damages are awarded), and, in cases requiring the Idaho Code § 6-303(2) nonpayment notice, only if that notice told the tenant fees would be awarded; the clause's fee sentence is consistent. Idaho Code § 55-305(1): fees, including late fees, must be reasonable. Read section-open 2026-09-30 from legislature.idaho.gov (ID log s1). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | MO: Applies as written. Nonpayment: Missouri requires a demand for the rent before a rent-and-possession action (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.020; a demand is good any time after the rent is due, Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.060) and sets no cure period, so the clause's written-notice step is a landlord practice, not a statutory period. Other breaches: violating a condition of a written lease lets the landlord re-enter after 10 days' notice to vacate, with no cure right (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.030, Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.040), which the clause's exception for proceeding without an opportunity to cure preserves (rule 43). Fee-shifting: no Missouri statute bars a reciprocal attorney-fee term (MO battery 89); enforceability of lease fee terms is case law, not read. A lease clause declaring a forfeiture for nonpayment 'for a specified time' delays process until that time runs (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.050); this clause sets no such time. Read section-open 2026-09-30 (MO log §1). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | IN: Applies as written. Rent: a landlord may terminate for nonpayment on not less than 10 days' notice unless the parties otherwise agreed or the tenant pays in full first (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-6); no notice is needed where the lease requires rent in advance and it is not paid (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-8(5)). This clause still requires written notice and the statutory cure time, so it gives up the Ind. Code § 32-31-1-8(5) no-notice route; kept on purpose (Taylor declined a notice waiver, IN log §6.2). Non-rent duties: an action to enforce the statutory tenant obligations needs notice and a reasonable time to remedy unless occupancy has ended, and the prevailing landlord may recover attorney's fees (Ind. Code § 32-31-7-7). Emergency possessory orders for waste, crime or a materially false application need no cure (Ind. Code §§ 32-31-6-3, 32-31-6-7.1), which the clause's no-cure exception covers. No mitigation statute (IN battery 97); case law not read. Read section-open 2026-09-30 from iga.in.gov (IN log §1). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed.

title: Surrender at End of Term
bodyText: Upon the expiration or earlier termination of this Lease, Tenant will surrender possession of the property and return all keys to Landlord immediately. The property will be left in the same condition as at the start of the Term, except for ordinary wear and tear, and free of all personal property of Tenant and any occupants. Personal property left at the property after Tenant vacates may, to the extent permitted by applicable law, be treated as abandoned and disposed of at Tenant's cost.
notes: SD extended (South Dakota session 1, Title 21-16 review): no SD-specific surrender/move-out statute found beyond the security-deposit-return mechanics (handled separately by security-deposit-return-sd); generic mechanics compatible as-is. | OH: Ohio has NO abandoned-property disposal procedure for conventional tenancies (§§1923.12-.14 are manufactured-home-park only) and §5321.15(B) bars seizing a tenant's possessions for rent except by court order. Any disposal language must be reviewed before OH ships. CA: extended to California 2026-09-19 after re-screen against the full CA pass (the extend manifest had deferred tagging until the blocked set was resolved, and the step was then missed). The 'to the extent permitted by applicable law' hedge is doing real work in CA: disposal must follow Civ. Code ss1980-1991 to keep the s1989 liability shield, removing belongings outside that procedure is barred by s789.3(b)(3), no storage cost may be charged if reclaimed within two days (s1990(c)), and service members' property needs a court order (Mil. & Vet. s409.1(b)). See edu-abandoned-property-ca. | NV: Read in full 2026-09-24 against NRS 118A (revisor text Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated). Applies as written on its hedge; NV disposal mechanics (118A.460) in abandoned-property-nv. Base chosen over -mn-nd/-ks-ne, which cross-reference sections that do not exist in an NV lease. | TX: Read in full 2026-09-25 against Tex. Prop. Code chs. 24, 54, 91, 92 and 301 (official statutes.capitol.texas.gov text for chs. 24/54/91/301). Applies as written. Self-limit ('to the extent permitted by applicable law') is necessary in Texas: s54.044(d) lets a landlord remove the contents of abandoned premises and s92.0081(b)(2) permits exclusion for that purpose, but no Texas statute read prescribes a notice/storage/disposal procedure for abandoned (non-lien) property. Seizure/sale for unpaid rent is a separate, lease-authorized lien process (landlord-lien-tx). Post-writ property is handled by the officer under s24.0061. Variants not used - they cross-reference sections absent from a Texas lease. | FL: Applies as written (tag-first screen). Instruction 31: Florida has no good-cause renewal; expiration ends the tenancy (Fla. Stat. §§83.57, 83.575, 83.58). The self-limit 'to the extent permitted by applicable law' is load-bearing: Fla. Stat. §§715.10-715.111 is an OPTIONAL procedure (§715.101(2)) giving the landlord nonliability (§715.11) after notice (§§715.104-.106), storage with reasonable care (§715.107), and public sale or, under $500, retention or disposal (§715.109); reasonable storage costs are chargeable (§715.111) and sale costs come out of proceeds. §83.67(5) allows removing property only after surrender, abandonment, death of the last tenant or lawful eviction. 'At Tenant's cost' is within those limits. Opt-out legend: abandoned-property-release-fl. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | AZ: Applies as written. A.R.S. §33-1370(I): if the tenant returns the keys and leaves property, the landlord may remove and dispose of it immediately without liability unless the parties agreed otherwise in writing; otherwise §33-1370(D)-(H) storage and sale procedure. "To the extent permitted by applicable law" carries the load. Instruction 31: Arizona has no just-cause or good-cause renewal rule in ch. 10. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | GA: Applies as written. No Georgia procedure for property left after a voluntary move-out: confirmed absent statute-wide (official full-text search 2026-09-28; `edu-abandoned-property-ga`); after a writ is executed the property 'shall be regarded as abandoned' (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-55(c)). 'To the extent permitted by applicable law' carries the load. Instruction 31: no just-cause rule in Georgia. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | SC: Removed 2026-09-30 (SC retro, SOP 1.9 rule 53): the last sentence lets property be treated as abandoned 'after Tenant vacates', 'to the extent permitted by applicable law'; South Carolina allows disposal only of property worth $500 or less, and only after abandonment or the end of the agreement where the tenant has removed a substantial portion of the property or permanently ended the utilities, with everything else removed only through the court (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-730(d)-(e)), a figure and trigger the self-limiting wording hides. SC now tagged on `surrender-end-of-term-mn-nd`, which points to the lease's abandoned-property provision (`abandoned-property-sc`). Text unchanged; states-only change, no propagation owed. | TN: Tagged 2026-09-28 (section text read 2026-09-28 in the built-in browser (Justia host copy of the 2025 Tennessee Code with history lines; 2025-2026 public chapters screened; TN log §1)). No just-cause or good-cause renewal law in Tennessee (instruction 31 checked); left property 'to the extent permitted by applicable law' is governed by abandoned-property-tn (Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-405) or, after a detainer judgment, § 29-18-127(b). TN-SCOPE: STATEWIDE. | VA: Tagged 2026-09-28. VA-SCOPE: STATEWIDE. Read against the official Code of Virginia section-open (law.lis.virginia.gov; VA log §1). Basis: No just-cause or good-cause renewal law in Virginia (instruction 31 checked); Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1233 (vacate, remove property, good and clean order less reasonable wear and tear); left property 'to the extent permitted by applicable law' is governed by abandoned-property-va (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1254). | AL: removed 2026-09-30 (AL retro, SOP 1.8 rule 53): the last sentence lets property be treated as abandoned "after Tenant vacates", "to the extent permitted by applicable law"; Alabama allows disposal only of property left "more than 14 days after termination pursuant to this chapter" (Ala. Code § 35-9A-423(d)), a different trigger the self-limiting wording hides. AL now tagged on `surrender-end-of-term-mn-nd`, which points to the lease's abandoned-property provision (`abandoned-property-al`). Text unchanged; states-only change, no propagation owed. | CO added - verified this session (statute walk + full-library audit; content itself unchanged WY added 2026-08-21 (full-library cross-check pass): generic mechanics, no CO-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with WY findings from this project. | CO: CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 41. CO REMOVED from states and superseded by surrender-end-of-term-co. Shared text unchanged. Reason: C.R.S. § 38-12-1303(1) bars a landlord from serving a notice to terminate, demanding possession or proceeding under article 40 of title 13 "unless there is cause for the eviction", and § 38-12-1303(2)(c) gives the hold-over-after-expiration ground (§ 13-40-104(1)(c)) ONLY for nonresidential property and for residential premises exempt under § 38-12-1302(1)(a), (1)(b), (1)(d), (1)(e) or (1)(f). For a covered Colorado tenancy the expiration of the Term therefore does not end the right to possession, and § 38-12-1305 makes void "a provision of a rental agreement ... that purports to authorize or effectuate a waiver or modification of any provision of this part 13". An unqualified promise to surrender on expiration is that kind of provision. Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). Other tagged states unaffected (rule 62: no shared text edit proposed). | NC: Applies as written. North Carolina bars distress and distraint and lets a landlord deal with a residential tenant's belongings only under N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 42-25.9(d), (g), (h), 42-36.2, 28A-25-2 and 28A-25-7 (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-25.7); a contrary lease provision is void (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-25.8). 'To the extent permitted by applicable law' keeps the last sentence inside those procedures (edu-abandoned-property-nc). A promise to return the property in move-in condition is also the kind of contract that can make a tenant liable for accidental damage (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-10: not liable 'unless he so contract'); recorded, not a forfeiture of a landlord right. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | NC: RETRO 2026-10-02 (SOP 1.21, rule 22): a doubled citation prefix in this row's NC notes (a section sign followed by a second 'N.C. Gen. Stat.' prefix, left by the 2026-09-28 citation-format pass) now reads as a plain double section sign. Notes only; no claim changed.

title: Early Termination
bodyText: Tenant may terminate this Lease before the end of the Term by providing Landlord at least 30 days' written notice. Tenant will pay an early termination fee equal to one month's Rent ({{monthly_rent}}) or 30% of the remaining Rent due under the Term, whichever is greater, and remains responsible for Rent and other obligations up to the termination date. Landlord may terminate this Lease early by providing Tenant at least 30 days' written notice if Tenant breaches a material term of this Lease and fails to cure the breach within 10 days of receiving written notice, or if Tenant vacates or abandons the property without notifying Landlord. Nothing in this Section limits any right either party has under applicable law. This includes a Tenant's right to terminate without penalty due to active military service under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, due to the property becoming uninhabitable through no fault of Tenant, or — except as prohibited by law in the case of a Tenant's death — any other termination right or limitation provided by applicable law.
notes: CO added - verified this session (statute walk + full-library audit; content itself EDITED this session WY added 2026-08-21 (full-library cross-check pass): generic mechanics, no CO-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with WY findings from this project. | MN extended (Minnesota session, CO;WY-scoping resolution): the clause's '10 days to cure' for landlord-initiated termination is more generous than Minnesota law requires (MN has no general statutory cure period for material lease violations, confirmed absent this session) — unlike KS/NE, where a real statutory cure period (14 days) made this clause's shorter figure a rights-shortening conflict. No conflict for MN. | Cross-state plain-language cleanup (Minnesota session, follow-up to MN's plain-language audit): long compound sentence split into shorter ones, no substantive change. Not a legal requirement for this clause's other tagged states (only MN's Plain Language Contract Act, Minn. Stat. §325G.31, was confirmed to apply this project) — done as a general readability improvement since the pattern was found library-wide, not MN-specific. | ND extended (North Dakota session 1, same scoping review): no numeric conflict with N.D.C.C. §§ 47-16-16/17's landlord/tenant termination rights, neither of which specifies a notice period or cure timeline that would contradict this clause's 30-day/10-day figures. | SD extended (South Dakota session 1, Title 21-16 review): generic mechanics (30-day notice + 1 month's rent fee) are not statutorily mandated for SD but not prohibited either; no conflicting SD statute found (SDCL 43-32-19's tenant-termination causes are different grounds, not a fee framework). | OH: no Ohio conflict, but the greater-of-one-month-or-30% fee carries real §5321.14 unconscionability exposure, and Ohio's mitigation duty (Lemstone, commercial holding) is waivable — do NOT stack a waiver with this fee. CROSS-STATE FLAG RAISED AND NOT RESOLVED 2026-09-19 - it is wider than first recorded. The fee of 'one month's Rent or 30% OF THE REMAINING RENT, whichever is greater' appears IDENTICALLY in this row and its KS and NE variants, i.e. across EIGHT states (CO, WY, KS, NE, MN, ND, SD, OH). California is the only state where it was removed, because Civ. Code s1671(d) makes a liquidated-damages provision in a DWELLING lease void unless fixing actual damages would be impracticable, with s1951.5 confirming s1671 reaches leases of real property. Every state applies some liquidated-damages or penalty doctrine, and a percentage-of-remaining-rent charge is its classic target. The identical figure in all eight suggests it was INHERITED rather than verified state by state. UNLIKE the setoff flag, this CANNOT be fixed by a savings clause - where such a term is void it is the AMOUNT that offends, and 'as permitted by law' does not cure it. Needs a per-state read of liquidated-damages law before the next lease goes out. CA: early-termination-ca. FLAG DOWNGRADED AND CLOSED 2026-09-19 — MY ESCALATION WAS OVERSTATED. I recorded the 30%-of-remaining-rent fee as an unresolved eight-state risk needing a fresh per-state read. The library already answered it: each state's own session screened this clause (MN Plain Language Act check; ND - no conflict with N.D.C.C. ss47-16-16/17; SD - not mandated but not prohibited, no conflicting statute; OH - no conflict but real s5321.14 unconscionability exposure and do NOT stack with a mitigation waiver; KS and NE - the cure-period figure was corrected and the tenant's voluntary 30-day-plus-fee right expressly left intact). THE ACTUAL POSITION: CALIFORNIA IS THE OUTLIER, not the other eight. Civ. Code s1671(d) is a PER SE statutory bar on liquidated damages in a dwelling lease; no other state in the library has one. Everywhere else the ceiling is CASE-BY-CASE UNCONSCIONABILITY - statutory in KS, NE and OH (s5321.14), general doctrine in SD (53-9-3) and by common law in WY and MN, with CO's express liquidated-damages prohibition confined to the death-of-tenant context (edu-death-of-tenant-co). So the fee is NOT void per se outside CA; it is lawful-but-exposed, and the exposure rises with the size of the figure. PRODUCT GUIDANCE: keep the fee configurable, set it defensibly against actual re-letting loss, and in OH never combine it with a waiver of the mitigation duty. No further statute reading is required. | NV: Read in full 2026-09-24 against NRS 118A (revisor text Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated). Applies as written. Equal 30-day notice both ways satisfies 118A.220(1)(e). Fee is lawful-but-exposed under NRS 118A.230 unconscionability (same posture as KS/NE/OH, CA s5.41); no per se liquidated-damages bar located in 118A. Savings sentence preserves 118A.340 and 118A.345 rights. | NV (text batch 2, 2026-09-24): NRS 118.175 (read): on abandonment the landlord must make reasonable efforts to re-rent at fair rental, and the former tenant owes actual damages. The contractual early-termination fee is an agreed option, not abandonment; OH's warning applies - never pair the fee with a waiver of that mitigation duty. | TX: Read in full 2026-09-25 against Tex. Prop. Code chs. 24, 54, 91, 92 and 301 (official statutes.capitol.texas.gov text for chs. 24/54/91/301). Applies as written. Contractual option. Tex. Prop. Code s91.006: landlord's duty to mitigate on abandonment is non-waivable, and the clause does not purport to waive it. Fee is lawful-but-exposed (no per se liquidated-damages bar in chs. 24/91/92) - same posture recorded for KS/NE/OH/NV. Statutory termination rights (ss92.016, .0161, .017, .0162) preserved by the clause's savings sentence; the REQUIRED Texas statement is early-termination-rights-statement-tx. s92.1031 (failure to occupy + replacement tenant) caps retention at an agreed cancellation fee or actual re-letting costs in that narrow case. | NJ: added 2026-09-26 (tag-first screen, instruction 26). Tagged as lawful-but-exposed (same posture as KS/NE/OH/NV/TX): fee enforceability against a mitigation duty is case law, not read. Statutory tenant terminations it preserves: death (N.J.S.A. 46:8-9.1 - note it yields to a lease that 'explicitly provide[s] otherwise'; this clause does not), disability/assisted living/low-income housing (46:8-9.2), domestic violence (46:8-9.6, non-waivable 46:8-9.9), flood non-disclosure (46:8-50(e)). Landlord early termination for breach still requires an Anti-Eviction ground and court process. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | NJ: REMOVED 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12 retro, rules 37 and 43). Two defects in NJ: (1) its landlord-termination sentence promises a 10-day cure for any material breach, which can give away New Jersey's no-cure grounds (willful or grossly negligent damage and the criminal-activity grounds, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(c), (n)-(r), on three days' notice, 2A:18-61.2(a)), and its 30-day notice does not track the one month's notice 2A:18-61.2(b) sets for lease-breach removal; (2) the fee measured on "the remaining Rent due under the Term" assumes a fixed Term. NJ now uses early-termination-ks. Not a re-audit. | AZ: Applies as written. No early-termination fee statute in ch. 10 (full read). "Nothing in this Section limits any right" preserves the A.R.S. §33-1318 domestic-violence and sexual-assault termination (no early termination penalties or fees) and §33-1318.01 law-enforcement officer release. The landlord's 10-day cure tracks §33-1368(A); the statutory no-cure grounds remain available. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | AZ: REMOVED 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.13 retro, rules 37 and 43). Two defects in AZ: (1) the fee measured on 'the remaining Rent due under the Term' and the option to end 'before the end of the Term' read as reaching a month-to-month tenancy, which either party may end on 30 days' written notice under A.R.S. §33-1375(B) with no fee (a fee on that statutory right risks §33-1315(A)(1) and the (B) penalty); (2) its landlord-termination sentence promises a 10-day cure for any material breach, which can give away §33-1368(A)'s no-cure grounds (material and irreparable breach; a second breach of the same or similar nature; falsified criminal or eviction record). AZ now uses early-termination-ks. Not a re-audit. | GA: Applies as written. No Georgia cap on early-termination fees located; a fee is liquidated damages, binding 'unless the agreement violates some principle of law' (O.C.G.A. § 13-6-7; penalty case law not relied on). 'Any other termination right' preserves the non-waivable military (O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-22, 44-7-37) and family-violence (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-23) rights. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | GA: REMOVED 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 37; rule 43 and fix 23 screened). The fee measured on 'the remaining Rent due under the Term' and the option to end 'before the end of the Term' read as reaching a Georgia tenancy at will (any tenancy with no time set for it to end, O.C.G.A. § 44-7-6), which the tenant may end on 30 days' notice with no fee (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-7). GA now uses `early-termination-ks`, whose fixed-Term limb answers this and whose landlord limb defers to the default provisions. Rule 43: the landlord limb's 30-day notice plus 10-day cure was lawful in Georgia (no statutory cure or no-cure grounds; O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50(a) and (c)), so no defect there. Not a re-audit. s5a.1: states-only change. | NC: Applies as written. No North Carolina statute regulates contractual early-termination fees (the N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-46 fee list governs late fees, eviction administrative fees, litigation costs and insurance, not early termination); enforceability as liquidated damages is case law, not relied on. The savings sentence preserves the military-technician (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-45), N.C. Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (Chapter 127B, Article 4), domestic-violence (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-45.1) and foreclosure (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-45.2) termination rights. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | NC: REMOVED 2026-10-02 (SOP 1.21 retro, rule 37; rule 43 and fix 25 screened). The fee measured on 'the remaining Rent due under the Term' and the option to end 'before the end of the Term' read as reaching a North Carolina periodic tenancy, including the month-to-month tenancy `holdover-ca` creates 'on the same terms', which either party may end on seven days' notice (two days week to week) with no fee (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-14). NC now uses `early-termination-ks`, whose fixed-Term limb answers this and whose landlord limb defers to the default provisions. Rule 43: the landlord limb's 30-day notice and 10-day cure gave up no statutory North Carolina route (none exists for non-rent breaches; Article 7 and N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-3 were preserved by the savings sentence). Not a re-audit. s5a.1: states-only change.

title: Holdover Tenancy
bodyText: If Tenant does not vacate the property by the end of the Term, Landlord may pursue any remedy allowed by applicable law to recover possession. Landlord will also be entitled to recover from Tenant holdover damages in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law for each day Tenant remains in possession after the end of the Term. Alternatively, Landlord may accept Tenant's continued payment of Rent, in which case this Lease will be deemed to continue on a month-to-month basis on the same terms and conditions, terminable by either party upon the written notice required by applicable law or, where applicable law sets no notice period, by this Lease.
notes: CO added - verified this session (statute walk + full-library audit; content itself unchanged WY added 2026-08-21 (full-library cross-check pass): generic mechanics, no CO-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with WY findings from this project. | NE added (session 1): Neb. Rev. Stat. §76-1437(3) allows up to 3x periodic rent or 3x actual damages for willful bad-faith holdover — higher than this clause's double-rent figure, so the clause still holds up in NE without an override (per Taylor's read, Flag 6). See edu-holdover-ne for the full NE figure and a note to revisit the double-rent baseline once more states are surveyed. | MN extended (Minnesota session, whole-library audit): generic mechanics, already vetted against KS/NE's prohibited-lease-provisions statutes (the strictest bar found in this project to date) since this clause was already tagged KS;NE; no MN-specific statutory language or number identified in this session's statute walk that conflicts. No exculpatory/liability-waiver language present. | Cross-state plain-language cleanup (Minnesota session, follow-up to MN's plain-language audit): long compound sentence split into shorter ones, no substantive change. Not a legal requirement for this clause's other tagged states (only MN's Plain Language Contract Act, Minn. Stat. §325G.31, was confirmed to apply this project) — done as a general readability improvement since the pattern was found library-wide, not MN-specific. | SHARED-CLAUSE PASS 2026-09-03 (§5a.1). EDIT: removed the hardcoded 'double the Monthly Rent ... or the maximum amount allowed under applicable law, if less' and replaced it with a pure deferral to the statutory maximum. §5a.1 JUDGMENT: **STATE-DRIVEN** — the holdover figure genuinely differs per state — but the EDIT itself is uniform-safe and no per-state override is required, because each state's figure is already carried by its own education row. WHY THE OLD TEXT WAS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, which is why leaving it was not an option: (1) OVER-PROMISED in MN — Minnesota has NO holdover multiplier at all (§504B.141 and the eviction chapter, confirmed at MN re-audit), so 'double the Monthly Rent' described a remedy that does not exist; the self-limiting tail made it lawful but misleading. (2) UNDER-CLAIMED in NE — Nebraska allows three months' periodic rent or threefold actual damages, whichever is greater, PLUS statutory attorney fees (§76-1437(3)), all of which EXCEED double monthly rent. The old 'or the maximum allowed ... if less' language could only ever cap DOWNWARD, so a Nebraska landlord relying on the clause would recover materially less than the statute allows. A ceiling-only formulation silently forfeits recovery in any state whose statutory figure is higher than the hardcoded one. KS is unaffected either way (1.5x cap under K.S.A. 58-2570(c), already below double, per edu-holdover-ks). GAP SURFACED, NOT CLOSED: CO and WY have NO holdover-damages education row and their statutory figures have never been verified in this project. The 'double' figure appears to have originated as Colorado's, but that has not been confirmed against C.R.S. Recommend verifying CO and WY holdover figures and adding edu-holdover-co / edu-holdover-wy, matching KS/NE/MN. | FOLLOW-UP 2026-09-03: the gap flagged in the shared-clause pass is now closed, and the answer is worse than expected. THE 'DOUBLE THE MONTHLY RENT' FIGURE HAD NO STATUTORY BASIS IN ANY OF THE FIVE TAGGED STATES. CO: no multiplier, damages = reasonable rental value (§13-40-123, Behr v. Burge). WY: no multiplier, actual damages plus 10% interest (§1-21-1211(b), provisional). KS: 1.5x cap, BELOW double (K.S.A. 58-2570(c)). NE: three months' periodic rent or threefold actual plus attorney fees, ABOVE double (§76-1437(3)). MN: no multiplier at all. So the number was wrong in every direction simultaneously — too high in three states, too low in one, and baseless in the two where it was assumed to have originated. The shared-clause pass hypothesized it 'appears to have originated as Colorado's'; that hypothesis is now DISPROVED. It appears to be generic template boilerplate that entered the library before any state research and was never questioned, and it survived four state re-audits. Removing it was correct. Recording the provenance because it is the clearest example in the project of an unsourced number propagating through a shared clause: nothing in the library ever asserted where 'double' came from, and every state's own research quietly contradicted it. | FL: Applies as written (tag-first screen, instruction 26). The referent exists: Fla. Stat. §83.58 lets the landlord recover double the rent for the period a tenant holds over without permission (last amended s. 10, ch. 2013-136). holdover-ca NOT tagged: it would give up the double-rent recovery (K.3, ceiling-only). §83.575(3): a tenant who stays with permission after termination without §83.57(3) notice owes one additional month's rent; statutory, no lease text needed. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. |  SHARED EDIT 2026-09-28 (Taylor's decision, gap-discovery backfill): the month-to-month notice now falls back to this Lease where the law sets no period. Wyoming has none, and `periodic-tenancy-notice-wy` supplies it. Raised by the WY backfill. Uniform under §5a.1: the words are self-limiting, so no state needs an override. | AZ: Applies as written. The referent exists: A.R.S. §33-1375(C) - if the holdover is willful and not in good faith, the landlord may recover up to the greater of two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages; if the landlord consents in writing to continued occupancy, §33-1314(D) makes it month-to-month. holdover-ca NOT tagged: its actual-damages measure would give up the statutory recovery (K.3). The "for each day" wording does not match Arizona's lump-sum measure but does not cap it. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | AZ: REMOVED 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.13 retro, rules 53 and 37); superseded for AZ by holdover-az. A.R.S. §33-1375(C) gives a one-time measure ('an amount equal to not more than two months' periodic rent or twice the actual damages sustained by the landlord, whichever is greater') only for a holdover that is willful and not in good faith, triggered by remaining in possession after expiration of the term or its termination (so also after a notice ending a periodic tenancy). This row's 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law for each day ... after the end of the Term' misstates that shape and trigger, and its acceptance-of-Rent month-to-month sentence differs from §33-1375(C), which applies §33-1314(D) on the landlord's written consent (acceptance of rent with knowledge of a default also waives termination for that breach, §33-1371(C)). Not a re-audit.

title: Month-to-Month Termination Notice
bodyText: Either party may end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice served as provided in Code of Civil Procedure section 1162 or by certified or registered mail. Tenant will give at least [state the notice period: at least 30] days' notice. Landlord will give at least [state the notice period] days' notice, or any longer notice California law requires, together with any statement California law requires in the notice.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 from primary text of Civ. Code s1946.1. The pre-existing dormant row was defective in four ways: (1) it applied the 30/60 split to BOTH parties - s1946.1(b) imposes 60 days on the OWNER only; a tenant's notice is one tenancy period regardless of occupancy length, so the old text bound a long-term tenant to a 60-day duty CA law does not impose, while reciting 'as required by California law'; (2) it omitted the s1946.1(d) bona-fide-purchaser 30-day path entirely; (3) it omitted the s1946.1(h) abandoned-property statement the owner's notice must contain; (4) it was silent on the s1946.2 just-cause overlay, so for a covered unit it told the tenant the tenancy could be ended on notice alone, which is false. Same error shape as the CO entry-notice 'as required by Colorado law' correction. | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): Taylor's pattern 2: notice periods are the chosen periods; the statutory 30/60-day rules, the 1946.1(d) sale exception, the abandoned-property statement and just cause moved to edu-termination-notice-periods-ca.

title: Notices
bodyText: Any notice of termination, notice of default, or other notice required to be given in writing under this Lease or applicable law will be delivered to the addresses specified in this Lease, or to any updated address either party provides in writing to the other. Where applicable law requires a particular method, form, timing, or content for a notice, that requirement will control over this Section, and nothing in this Lease designates an alternative method of delivery for any notice governed by law.

Code Ann. § 66-28-106(b) (Act counties): written notice to 'the last known or designated address contained in the lease agreement' - the clause names the lease addresses and designates no alternative method (instruction 44 checked); Tennessee's UETA has no eviction-notice exclusion (instruction 47; edu-electronic-notices-tn). UETA scope has no landlord-tenant exclusion (Va. Code Ann. § 59.1-481; instruction 47). | AL: Tagged. Alabama's notice definitions (Ala. Code § 35-9A-144) do not apply to notices to terminate or evict (Ala. Code § 35-9A-144(e)); the electronic-transactions act does not apply to default, eviction or cure notices under a rental agreement for a primary residence (Ala. Code § 8-1A-3(c)(2)b.). Stat. § 441.065) and how an unlawful detainer demand is delivered (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 534.050); the clause defers to each (edu-notice-service-mo). Read section-open 2026-09-30 (MO log §1). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | NJ: Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12), rules 44, 45, 47. 2A:18-61.2 re-read: delivery methods are fixed by statute ("served either personally... at his usual place of abode... or by certified mail"), with no "as agreed in the lease" wording, so the lease adds no binding method. Code § 32-31-1-9); the clause defers to that method. No electronic-transactions exclusion for notices (Ind. Code § 26-2-8-103). Read section-open 2026-09-30 from iga.in.gov (IN log §1). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | OK: Okla. Comp. Laws § 554.634(1); lessor-notice-address-mi); demands for possession are served as Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5718 provides. Read section-open 2026-10-01 from legislature.mi.gov (MI log §1). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | IA: Applies as written. Iowa Code § 562A.8 sets the methods for notices under ch. 562A (hand delivery, signed acknowledgment, personal service under Iowa R. Civ. P. 1.305, regular plus certified mail, posting on the primary entrance door, or any method resulting in actual receipt; mail complete four days after mailing); termination notices and notices to quit must use Iowa Code § 562A.29A or Iowa Code § 648.3(2). The clause yields to both.

title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord. Tenant will pay Landlord a pet deposit, if applicable, and pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor, and disturbance caused by a pet, and will indemnify Landlord from claims arising from Tenant's pet(s). Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern, and may enter the property and remove a pet, without liability to Tenant to the extent applicable law permits, if the pet becomes vicious or displays symptoms of severe illness, or if Tenant dies, becomes incapacitated, or is otherwise unable to care for the pet and Landlord believes in good faith that the pet is being abused or neglected.

bodyText: Only operable, currently registered passenger vehicles may be parked at the property; commercial vehicles, recreational vehicles, trailers, and oversized vehicles are not permitted without Landlord's prior written consent. Landlord may require Tenant to provide vehicle registration information and may issue parking tags, decals, or access cards, the cost of which may be charged to Tenant. Landlord may, in accordance with applicable law, have a vehicle towed at the vehicle owner's expense if it is illegally parked, abandoned, inoperable, or has expired registration. Vehicle repairs are not permitted at the property except minor emergency repairs necessary to move the vehicle, and vehicles may be washed only in areas Landlord designates, if any.

Wrongful towing liability: §715.07(4). No lease-content rule (contrast TX Occ. Code §2308.253(e)); the clause's 'in accordance with applicable law' suffices because the vehicle rules define what parking is permitted. Local tow-rate caps: Fla. Stat. §§125.0103(1)(b)-(d), 166.043(1)(b)-(d); §715.07(2)(b) lets counties and cities add rules (municipal layer, flagged). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | AZ: Applies as written. title: Keys
bodyText: At the start of the Term, Tenant will receive the keys specified by Landlord and will sign a receipt acknowledging the number and type of keys provided. Tenant will return all keys to Landlord at the end of the Term. If Tenant fails to return all keys or requires a replacement, Landlord may re-key the applicable locks and charge the cost to Tenant. Tenant may not duplicate keys without Landlord's consent.

title: Use of Property & Common Areas
bodyText: Tenant will not, without Landlord's written consent, drill holes, use nails, hooks, or screws on the property, or fasten anything to its fixtures, appliances, or interior or exterior surfaces. Tenant will comply with any weight restrictions on balconies or porches and will not use them to store personal belongings without Landlord's consent. Tenant will not keep a waterbed or other water-filled furniture at the property, or any item (such as a piano or safe) whose weight Landlord has not agreed is reasonable for the floor, without Landlord's prior written consent. Tenant will not burn wax candles at the property. Tenant will not post or display any sign, banner, or advertisement visible from outside the property without Landlord's consent. Nothing in this Section restricts any display that applicable law entitles Tenant to make, such as the display of the flag of the United States or of religious or cultural items, subject to any lawful limits on its size, placement, and manner.

title: Landscaping & Irrigation

title: Lead-Based Paint Disclosure
bodyText: LEAD WARNING STATEMENT. Housing built before 1978 may contain lead-based paint. Lead from paint, paint chips, and dust can pose health hazards if not managed properly. Lead exposure is especially harmful to young children and pregnant women. Before renting pre-1978 housing, lessors must disclose the presence of known lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards in the dwelling. Lessees must also receive a federally approved pamphlet on lead poisoning prevention. Landlord's disclosure: [state either that Landlord has no knowledge of lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards in the dwelling, or describe all known lead-based paint and lead-based paint hazards]. Records and reports: [state either that Landlord has no reports or records pertaining to lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards in the dwelling, or list all available records and reports and confirm they have been provided to Tenant]. Tenant acknowledges receipt of the information above and of the federally approved pamphlet Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home. Landlord and Tenant each certify, to the best of their knowledge, that the information they have provided is true and accurate.

title: Bed Bug Disclosure
bodyText: Information about Bed Bugs. Bed bug Appearance: Bed bugs have six legs. Adult bed bugs have flat bodies about 1/4 of an inch in length. Their color can vary from red and brown to copper colored. Young bed bugs are very small. Their bodies are about 1/16 of an inch in length. They have almost no color. When a bed bug feeds, its body swells, may lengthen, and becomes bright red, sometimes making it appear to be a different insect. Bed bugs do not fly. They can either crawl or be carried from place to place on objects, people, or animals. Bed bugs can be hard to find and identify because they are tiny and try to stay hidden. Life Cycle and Reproduction: An average bed bug lives for about 10 months. Female bed bugs lay one to five eggs per day. Bed bugs grow to full adulthood in about 21 days. Bed bugs can survive for months without feeding. Bed bug Bites: Because bed bugs usually feed at night, most people are bitten in their sleep and do not realize they were bitten. A person's reaction to insect bites is an immune response and so varies from person to person. Sometimes the red welts caused by the bites will not be noticed until many days after a person was bitten, if at all. Common signs and symptoms of a possible bed bug infestation: • Small red to reddish brown fecal spots on mattresses, box springs, bed frames, mattresses, linens, upholstery, or walls. • Molted bed bug skins, white, sticky eggs, or empty eggshells. • Very heavily infested areas may have a characteristically sweet odor. • Red, itchy bite marks, especially on the legs, arms, and other body parts exposed while sleeping. However, some people do not show bed bug lesions on their bodies even though bed bugs may have fed on them. For more information, see the Internet Web sites of the United States Environmental Protection Agency and the National Pest Management Association. Tenant shall report any suspected bed bug infestation to Landlord promptly and in writing, using the following procedure: {{bed_bug_reporting_procedure}}.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 against Civ. Code s1954.603 (primary text supplied by Taylor). Statute requires the information 'in substantially the following form' and in AT LEAST 10-POINT TYPE - shipped effectively verbatim because 'substantially' is not a licence to compress. THIRD type-size floor found in CA (8-point at s2079.10a, 10-point here, 12-point at s1946.2(f)(3)); the schema still cannot express any of them. The prior dormant row was a four-line paraphrase and had two substantive defects beyond omitting the entire prescribed block: (1) it promised 'Landlord's process for investigating a suspected infestation' - s1954.603(b) requires the opposite, the procedure for the TENANT TO REPORT to the landlord, which is why this row now carries a landlord-supplied {{bed_bug_reporting_procedure}} field; (2) it asserted the notice covers 'the danger of self-treating with pesticides' - NO SUCH ELEMENT EXISTS in s1954.603. That element appears in other states' bed-bug statutes, so this is the Instruction 18 error shape (another state's architecture imported as fact) sitting inside a shipped CA row. Timing: duty attaches on and after 2017-07-01 prior to creating a NEW tenancy. The separate one-time catch-up duty to notify all existing tenants by 2018-01-01 is spent and is deliberately not modelled. s1954.601 defines 'pest control operator' as a Branch 2 licensee of the Structural Pest Control Board. notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 against H&S s25400.28 (primary text supplied by Taylor; Chapter 6.9.1, amended by Stats. 2019 ch. 691 (AB 1596), eff. 2020-01-01). The chapter is 6.9.1, not 6.9.2 as I guessed. Five defects in the prior dormant row. (1) TRIGGER WRONG: the row keyed off 'an order prohibiting occupancy due to methamphetamine contamination that has not been satisfied'. The statute keys off a REMEDIATION ORDER under ss25400.22/25400.25, and the duty runs until the owner receives a s25400.27 notice that the property requires NO FURTHER ACTION. An occupancy prohibition is not the trigger. (2) FENTANYL OMITTED: the chapter has covered methamphetamine OR FENTANYL since AB 1596 took effect 2020-01-01. The row was meth-only and is retitled - six years stale. (3) TIMING: s25400.28(b) attaches the duty to all prospective tenants WHO HAVE COMPLETED A RENTAL APPLICATION, earlier than lease signing. The row modelled it purely as a lease disclosure, so the duty could be missed entirely for an applicant who never reaches signature. (4) FREE TEXT IS NOT COMPLIANCE: the statute requires four mechanical things - written notice, A COPY OF THE ORDER provided, the tenant's WRITTEN ACKNOWLEDGMENT before signing, and the notice ATTACHED to the rental agreement. The old '[describe any known contamination order]' bracket satisfies none of them. This is document assembly, not clause text - same class of problem as the s1632 translation duty. (5) REMEDY OMITTED: if the owner does not comply with (b), THE PROSPECTIVE TENANT MAY VOID THE RENTAL AGREEMENT. Severe, and absent from the old row. OUT OF SCOPE, flagged not resolved: s25400.28(c) is a separate stricter regime for a mobilehome, manufactured home or recreational vehicle subject to an order - it may not be sold, rented OR OCCUPIED until notice of all meth or fentanyl laboratory activities and any remediation is given, with notice and order attached to the rental agreement, and (c)(4) gives the same void right. Consistent with the standing mobilehome-park deprioritization. Subdivision (a) is the sale-side duty and is not our concern. | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): optional (Taylor's pattern 3): the disclosure is owed before signing; the clause records it. title: Mold Disclosure
bodyText: If Landlord knows, or has reasonable cause to believe, that mold is present at the property in an amount that may exceed exposure limits recommended by a health authority, Landlord must disclose that condition to Tenant in writing, as required by California law. Landlord discloses: [describe any known mold condition, or state 'none known'].
notes: CA: STILL INACTIVE after reading H&S s26147 (primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19). The row asserts a live disclosure duty; the statute's own commencement clause may mean no such duty has ever taken effect. s26147(e): 'The requirements of this section shall not apply until the first January 1 or July 1 that occurs at least six months after the department adopts standards pursuant to Sections 26103 and 26105 AND develops guidelines pursuant to Section 26130.' The operative trigger in (a) is likewise defined by reference to the s26103 permissible exposure limits or the s26105 health-threat guidelines. VERIFIED FROM TEXT: the duty is contingent and self-suspending. NOT VERIFIED: whether the department ever adopted those standards and guidelines - that is a factual question outside the section text and is the single thing needed to close this row. It is widely reported that the PELs were never adopted, but this project has been burned by widely reported, so it stays open. This is a NEW ERROR SHAPE for the checklist, adjacent to the s2924.85 repeal: a statute that is on the books, correctly cited, and still not in force. Other limbs read and captured for whenever it does commence: (b) no duty to conduct air or surface testing; (c)(1) disclosure to prospective tenants before entering the agreement and (c)(2) to current tenants in affected units as soon as reasonably practical; (d) exemption where the mold was remediated per the s26130 guidelines. NOTE the (a) trigger reaches mold 'both visible and invisible or hidden'. SEPARATE AND UNREAD: Civ. Code s1941.1(a)(7) is reported to place visible mold in the habitability list, which would make mold actionable in CA regardless of s26147's status. Not read this pass - pull it before concluding CA has no mold obligation. CORRECTION 2026-09-19: my earlier pointer to Civ. Code s1941.1(a)(7) as the mold limb was WRONG - (a)(7) is garbage and rubbish receptacles. The real route is the OPENING WORDS of s1941.1(a), read section-open: a dwelling is untenantable if it substantially lacks the listed characteristics OR IS A RESIDENTIAL UNIT DESCRIBED IN H&S s17920.3 OR s17920.10. That incorporation is confirmed from the text. Whether s17920.3 actually lists visible mold growth as a substandard condition is NOT confirmed - s17920.3 has not been read. NEEDED: H&S s17920.3. The supplied s1941.1 text also stopped at (a)(7), so (a)(8) onward is unread. RESOLVED 2026-09-19 on the habitability limb: H&S s17920.3(a)(13) (read section-open; amended by Stats. 2024 ch. 487 (SB 1465), eff. 2025-01-01) DOES list 'Visible mold growth' as a substandard condition, and Civ. Code s1941.1(a) incorporates s17920.3 by reference. So California DOES have a live mold obligation - it is a HABITABILITY duty, not a disclosure duty. This row is a disclosure clause and stays INACTIVE: the s26147 disclosure duty remains contingent under s26147(e) and the only question left on it is factual, whether the department ever adopted the s26103/s26105 standards and s26130 guidelines. Two limits on the habitability route that matter and are easy to overstate: (1) visible mold growth must be 'as determined by a health officer or a code enforcement officer, as defined in Section 829.5 of the Penal Code' - it is NOT self-executing on a tenant's or landlord's own assessment; (2) it EXCLUDES mold that is minor and found on surfaces that can accumulate moisture as part of their properly functioning and intended use (shower surrounds and the like). The s17920.3 preamble adds a further threshold: the condition must exist to an extent that endangers life, limb, health, property, safety or welfare. s17920.10, the OTHER s1941.1(a) incorporation, READ 2026-09-19 - it governs lead hazards, not mold, so it does not affect this row. See edu-lead-hazards-ca. FACTUAL QUESTION RESOLVED 2026-09-19: the s26147(e) predicate standards were NEVER ADOPTED. Primary source: CDPH's own 2005 Report to the Legislature on implementing the Toxic Mold Protection Act concluded that science-based permissible exposure limits for indoor mold could not be established, and CDPH's 2017 Statement on Indoor Dampness and Mold confirms the scientific basis for that conclusion had not changed as of 2015 and that no federal or state policy sets safe exposure limits. The SB 655 (2015) Senate floor analysis quotes the same CDPH position. Consistent secondary sources through 2026 report no PELs adopted. So s26147 has NEVER COMMENCED and this row correctly stays INACTIVE - now VERIFIED as not in force, the same posture as foreclosure-disclosure-ca. WORTH NOTING: at least one 2026 secondary source describes s26147 as operative with a 'practical trigger' of visible mold - the exact misreading s26147(e) forecloses. Another secondary-source error of the kind this project was built to catch. Residual limit: CDPH's primary statements run to 2017; post-2017 status rests on consistent secondary reporting and the absence of any contrary source.

title: Mold Disclosure in the Move-In Report
bodyText: As part of the move-in inspection report, Landlord will state in writing whether there is any visible evidence of mold in areas readily accessible within the interior of the property. A statement that there is no visible evidence of mold will be considered correct unless Tenant objects in writing within five days after receiving the report. If the report states that there is visible evidence of mold, Tenant may choose to terminate this Lease and not take possession or not remain in possession. If Tenant chooses to take or remain in possession, Landlord will promptly remediate the mold condition, no later than five business days after Tenant's choice, reinspect the property, and give Tenant a new report stating that there is no visible evidence of mold.
notes: VA: VA-SCOPE: STATEWIDE. Read section-open 2026-09-28 in the built-in browser on the official Code of Virginia (law.lis.virginia.gov; Title 55.1 Chapter 12 read whole from the vacodefull page, which prints the 2026-session amendments and every delayed-effective version with its history line); 2024-2026 amending chapters read in enrolled text on lis.virginia.gov with their effective-date clauses (VA log §1). Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1215 (history ends 2019, c. 712), read with the § 55.1-1200 definitions of 'visible evidence of mold', 'readily accessible' and 'interior of the dwelling unit'. Continuing duties: prevent moisture and mold, remediate per Va. Code Ann. § 8.01-226.12(E), give the tenant a summary of remediation information (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1220(A)(5)); tenant's moisture and mold duties (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1227(A)(10)); relocation for remediation up to 30 days (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1231) - edu-mold-rules-va. DORMANT ROW REWRITTEN AND ACTIVATED (kickoff): the pre-project text had the landlord 'disclose any visible evidence of mold observed' in the lease itself ('[describe ... or state none observed]'), which is the wrong document and the wrong time: the statute puts the statement in the written move-in report delivered within five days after occupancy, gives it deemed-correct effect only after a five-day objection window, and attaches the tenant's termination or five-business-day remediation option. Now REQUIRED (the statute uses 'shall'), verified and active.

title: Flood Disclosure
bodyText: Flood Hazard Disclosure. [If Landlord has actual knowledge that the property is located in a special flood hazard area or an area of potential flooding, state that fact here; otherwise state 'Landlord has no actual knowledge that the property is located in a special flood hazard area or an area of potential flooding.'] Tenant may obtain information about hazards, including flood hazards, that may affect the property from the Internet Web site of the Office of Emergency Services, including the MyHazards tool at {{myhazards_url}}. Landlord's insurance does not cover the loss of Tenant's personal possessions, and it is recommended that Tenant consider purchasing renter's insurance and flood insurance to insure Tenant's possessions from loss due to fire, flood, or other risk of loss. Landlord is not required to provide additional information concerning the flood hazards to the property, and the information provided pursuant to Government Code section 8589.45 is deemed adequate to inform Tenant.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 against Gov. Code s8589.45 (primary text supplied by Taylor, current as of 2026-01-01). STRUCTURAL DEFECT CORRECTED - rule_type moved CONDITIONAL -> REQUIRED. The prior dormant row treated the WHOLE disclosure as conditional on the property being in a flood zone. It is not: s8589.45(a) requires the disclosure in EVERY residential lease entered into on or after 2018-07-01, and only element (a)(1) carries the 'if the owner has actual knowledge' qualifier. Elements (a)(2), (3) and (4) are unconditional. As previously modelled, a non-flood-zone CA property would have received NO disclosure at all. Four further defects in the old text: (1) it omitted element (a)(2) entirely, including the statutory requirement that the disclosure CONTAIN the MyHazards Internet Web site address; (2) it omitted element (a)(4), the landlord safe harbour; (3) it narrowed element (a)(3) to 'renter's insurance covering flood damage' - the statute requires stating that the owner's insurance does not cover the tenant's possessions AND recommending both renter's and flood insurance against fire, flood or other risk of loss; (4) it glossed the trigger as a 'special flood hazard area as designated by the Federal Emergency Management Agency' - the statute says 'special flood hazard area OR AN AREA OF POTENTIAL FLOODING' and never mentions FEMA, so the row imported a narrower federal definition the statute does not use. ACTUAL KNOWLEDGE is defined, not left at large - s8589.45(a)(1)(A)-(C): written notice from any public agency, the mortgage holder requiring flood insurance, or THE OWNER CURRENTLY CARRYING FLOOD INSURANCE. The third is the one landlords overlook: carrying the policy is itself actual knowledge. This belongs in the builder as a question, not as landlord free text. Prescribed floor: NO SMALLER THAN EIGHT-POINT TYPE. s8589.45(b) subjects the disclosure to Civ. Code s1632 - SECOND statute in CA carrying the translation duty after s1946.2(f)(3). OPEN: {{myhazards_url}} is an app-config value, not landlord input. The statute requires the address to appear; the current CalOES MyHazards address has NOT been verified from primary source this pass and must be confirmed and maintained at sync - a hardcoded URL is exactly the kind of value that rots silently.

title: Flood Disclosure
bodyText:
[Separate document. Required for a rental agreement with a term of 1 year or longer; give it to the prospective tenant at or before execution of the rental agreement.]

FLOOD DISCLOSURE

Flood Insurance: Renters' insurance policies do not include coverage for damage resulting from floods. Tenant is encouraged to discuss the need to purchase separate flood insurance coverage with Tenant's insurance agent.

1. Landlord has ☐ has no ☐ knowledge of any flooding that has damaged the dwelling unit during Landlord's ownership of the dwelling unit.

2. Landlord has ☐ has not ☐ filed a claim with an insurance provider relating to flood damage in the dwelling unit, including, but not limited to, a claim with the National Flood Insurance Program.

3. Landlord has ☐ has not ☐ received assistance for flood damage to the dwelling unit, including, but not limited to, assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

4. For the purposes of this disclosure, the term "flooding" means a general or temporary condition of partial or complete inundation of the dwelling unit caused by any of the following:
a. The overflow of inland or tidal waters.
b. The unusual and rapid accumulation of runoff or surface waters from any established water source, such as a river, stream, or drainage ditch.
c. Sustained periods of standing water resulting from rainfall.
notes: FL: DORMANT ROW REWRITTEN AND ACTIVATED 2026-09-26 (instruction 21). Primary text read section-open 2026-09-26 from the official 2026 Florida Statutes (flsenate.gov / leg.state.fl.us), with per-section history lines. Controlling text: Fla. Stat. §83.512 (s. 1, ch. 2025-166; Laws of Fla. ch. 2025-166 (CS/SB 948), effective 2025-10-01). What the pre-rigor row got right: a separate written flood disclosure, and a tenant termination right on violation. What it got wrong: (1) Florida's form asks about flood DAMAGE during the landlord's ownership, flood insurance CLAIMS and federal ASSISTANCE, not flood-zone designation; (2) the duty applies only to rental agreements of 1 year or longer, so the row is CONDITIONAL, not REQUIRED; (3) the remedy needs a 'substantial loss or damage' to the tenant's personal property (repair or replacement cost of 50% or more of market value) and termination by written notice and surrender within 30 days after the damage; termination is effective on surrender; the landlord refunds rent paid in advance for any period after termination; delinquent rent owed before termination remains owed (§83.512(2)-(4)); (4) the statutory form must be used in substance. Body is the statutory form verbatim. Layout (instruction 28): SEPARATE document; at or before execution. Builder: show when term >= 12 months. Kickoff lead said '2024 flood-disclosure law'; the 2024 law (s. 689.302) covers sales; the landlord duty is 2025 (ch. 2025-166 amended 689.302 too).
