Landlord's entry to inspect shall comply with Civil Code section 1954.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1954.604, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. Note the statute deems entry to inspect a unit selected by the pest control operator, and followup inspections of SURROUNDING units, a 'necessary service' for s1954 purposes - so a neighbour's infestation supplies lawful grounds to enter an uninfested tenant's unit. The tenant cooperation duty is statutory, so this clause restates rather than creates it. s1954 READ 2026-09-19 - see landlord-entry-ca. The s1954.604 'necessary service' characterisation maps onto s1954(a)(2) (necessary or agreed services), so the entry right is real and the 24-hour written-notice presumption in s1954(d)(1) applies to it.

title: Bed bug duties beyond the move-in disclosure
bodyText: California imposes three bed bug duties on landlords beyond the written disclosure given before a new tenancy. A landlord may not show, rent or lease a vacant unit the landlord knows has a current bed bug infestation. There is no duty to inspect for bed bugs absent notice of a suspected or actual infestation, but an infestation evident on visual inspection counts as notice. And where a pest control operator inspects units, the landlord must notify the tenants of those units of the operator's findings in writing within two business days of receiving them; for a confirmed infestation in a common area, all tenants must be notified. The information-about-bed-bugs notice is owed to prospective tenants before a new tenancy begins (Civ. Code 1954.603); the lease's optional clause carries the text and the reporting procedure, but give it before signing.
notes: CA: Civ. Code ss1954.602 and 1954.605, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. The two-business-day written notice clock runs from the landlord's RECEIPT of the operator's findings, not from the inspection, and it is an affirmative duty with no tenant-request trigger - the kind of operational habitability duty the CO re-audit found the library systematically missed. s1954.602(b) is the landlord-protective limb worth knowing: no affirmative inspection duty absent notice, but visual evidence IS notice, so 'I never looked' is not a defence. No penalty appears in the chapter as supplied; enforcement route not researched. | CA: Pattern-3 sentence added by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29) for bed-bug-disclosure-ca.

title: California mold: a habitability duty, and a booklet disclosure duty since 2022
bodyText: California treats mold primarily as a habitability matter, but it does also carry one live disclosure duty. Visible mold growth is listed as a substandard condition under Health and Safety Code section 17920.3(a)(13), and Civil Code section 1941.1(a) makes a dwelling untenantable if it is a residential unit described in section 17920.3. Two limits apply: the visible mold growth must be determined by a health officer or a code enforcement officer, and mold that is minor and found on surfaces that accumulate moisture as part of their properly functioning and intended use is excluded. The mold article contains two separate disclosure sections with different triggers, and only one of them operates. The general mold disclosure at Health and Safety Code section 26147 is suspended by section 26147(e) until six months after the department adopts permissible exposure limits and health guidelines and develops remediation guidelines, and it has never adopted them. But section 26148 requires a residential landlord to give prospective tenants a consumer-oriented booklet on the health risks of mold before entering the rental agreement, and section 26148(c) makes that duty operative six months after the department approves a booklet rather than after any standards are adopted. The department published its renters' booklet and states that landlords have been required to provide it since January 1, 2022. A landlord is never required to conduct air or surface testing for mold. The Department of Public Health's dampness-and-mold booklet must be given before the lease is signed; the lease's optional clause records that it was, and the tenant's duty to report dampness or mold.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 once H&S s17920.3 was read section-open. The earlier version of this row framed CA as possibly having NO mold obligation, which would have been the wrong conclusion - the duty exists, it just sits in habitability rather than disclosure. Both limbs now verified from primary text: s17920.3(a)(13) (mold listed, officer-determination required, minor-moisture-surface carve-out) and s26147(e) (disclosure duty contingent). The one thing still NOT verified is whether the s26103/s26105/s26130 standards were ever adopted - a factual question about departmental rulemaking, not a text question. It is widely reported they were not, and this row is drafted so that it stays accurate either way. CROSS-REFERENCE for the base habitability clause screen: s1941.1(a)'s incorporation of s17920.3 pulls a 16-item inadequate-sanitation list plus structural, wiring, plumbing, mechanical, weather-protection and fire limbs into CA's tenantability standard - far broader than the seven affirmative characteristics in s1941.1(a)(1)-(7) that a reader stopping at the enumerated list would see. Note s17920.3(a)(12) subjects insect, vermin and rodent infestation to the same officer-determination requirement as mold. ADDED 2026-09-19: Civ. Code s1941.7(a) - no s1941 or s1942 duty to repair a mold dilapidation under H&S s17920.3(a)(13) arises until the lessor HAS NOTICE of it, or if the tenant is in violation of s1941.2. s1941.7(b) permits entry to repair mold subject to s1954. So CA's mold duty is notice-triggered as well as officer-determined. RESOLVED 2026-09-19: CDPH never adopted the s26103 PELs (2005 Report to the Legislature; 2017 Statement on Indoor Dampness and Mold). The contingency has never been satisfied. The row's drafting - accurate either way - no longer needs to hedge. || CORRECTED 2026-09-28, gap-discovery source 2 (real-lease comparison). THIS ROW WAS WRONG. It said California treats mold 'as a habitability matter rather than a disclosure matter' and that 'the mold disclosure statute at H&S s26147 does not operate on its own terms', full stop. H&S s26148 - the very next section, in the same Article 4 (Disclosures) of Chapter 18 - imposes a SEPARATE booklet disclosure duty with a SEPARATE contingency, and it has been operative since 2022-01-01. s26148 was never read in the CA pass. Both sections read section-open on leginfo 2026-09-28. s26147(e) waits on s26103/s26105 standards and s26130 guidelines (never adopted); s26148(c) waits only on the department APPROVING A BOOKLET (done). CDPH's Indoor Air Quality mold page: 'As of Jan. 1, 2022, California rental housing providers are required to provide this mold booklet to prospective tenants.' New row mold-booklet-disclosure-ca carries the lease-side acknowledgment and the delivery duty; this row keeps the habitability analysis and now states both disclosure sections correctly. HOW IT WAS FOUND: not by statute search but by the professional-lease comparison - the CAA CA-041 12/24 form cites H&S s26148 and the C.A.R. RLMM 12/24 form delivers the booklet at paragraph 38A. A landlord form caught what a statute sweep missed. ERROR SHAPE, now recorded for the fourth time in this state: answering from the provision in hand rather than the one that governs, and concluding an absence from an adjacent section - the same cause as the s1932/s1934 corrections and the lead-paint canvass miss. The specific trap here is that the row treated 'the mold disclosure statute' as ONE section when the article has two, with different triggers, one live and one dead. LESSON: when a section's operation is contingent, read the whole article before asserting the topic is absent, because a sibling section may carry the same duty on a different condition. | CA: Pattern-3 sentence added by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29) for mold-booklet-disclosure-ca.

title: Returned-check service charge and treble damages are alternatives
bodyText: California gives the payee of a bad check two separate remedies, and a landlord cannot have both. The service charge is capped at $25 for a first check and $35 for each subsequent one. Alternatively, the landlord may pursue treble damages, but only after mailing a written demand by certified mail that states the provisions of the statute, the amount of the check, and the amount of the service charge, and then waiting 30 days for payment. Treble damages are not less than $100 and not more than $1,500. Once a tenant becomes liable for treble damages on a check, the tenant is no longer liable for the service charge or the mailing costs on that check. A tenant is liable only once per check. No service charge is owed if the tenant stopped payment to resolve a good-faith dispute with you, or shows written confirmation from their bank that the instrument was returned because of the bank's error, or that the account was short because a regularly scheduled social security or government benefit deposit was delayed (Civ. Code 1719(a)).
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1719(a)(2), together with (h)-(k) from the partial text supplied earlier. The election point is the trap: s1719(a)(2)'s closing sentence extinguishes the service charge once treble liability attaches, so a landlord demanding both is overreaching. Three MANDATORY contents in the certified-mail demand - miss one and the treble claim fails. Partial payments within the 30 days reduce the base before trebling. s1719(h) makes the remedies mandatory upon a court; (i) lets an assignee or holder enforce them; (j)(2) caps exposure at once per check; (k) preserves Commercial Code Division 3 rights and defences including holder-in-due-course status. Routed to LANDLORD_EDUCATION rather than lease text because it is an enforcement procedure, consistent with the project's notice-and-cure routing decision. | CA: Defenses sentence added by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29) from nsf-fee-limit-ca; content unchanged: Civ. Code § 1719(a).

title: Methamphetamine or fentanyl remediation order: disclosure mechanics
bodyText: Where a local health officer has issued a methamphetamine or fentanyl remediation order affecting a property, the owner's disclosure duty to prospective tenants continues until the owner receives written notice from the health officer that the property requires no further action. During that period the owner must give written notice of the order to every prospective tenant who has completed a rental application, provide a copy of the order, obtain the tenant's written acknowledgment of receipt before the rental agreement is signed, and attach the notice to the rental agreement. A prospective tenant may void the rental agreement if the owner does not do all of this. The lease's optional clause records the notice and acknowledgment; the duty itself is owed before the rental agreement is signed.
notes: CA: H&S s25400.28(b), read section-open 2026-09-19. Routed to education because three of the four obligations are procedural and occur before signature - the lease clause alone cannot discharge them. The application-stage trigger is the one most likely to be missed by a product that only generates documents at lease time. Void-the-agreement is the remedy; no damages provision appears in the subdivision. | CA: Pattern-3 sentence added by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29) for meth-disclosure-ca.

title: Assistance Animal Accommodation
bodyText: Landlord will make reasonable accommodations for assistance animals, which include both service animals and support animals and are not pets. Tenant will not be charged any pet fee, additional rent, additional security deposit, liability insurance requirement or other additional fee in connection with an assistance animal. No breed, size or weight limitation applies to an assistance animal. Tenant remains responsible for the cost of repairing damage the animal causes to the premises, excluding ordinary wear and tear, and for keeping the animal under control, including reasonable conditions on waste disposal and on behavior that would constitute a nuisance, provided those conditions are no more restrictive than those applied to other animals on the property and do not interfere with the animal's work. An assistance animal need not be allowed if that specific animal poses a direct threat to the health or safety of others, or would cause substantial physical damage to the property of others, and the threat cannot be sufficiently mitigated by another reasonable accommodation.
notes: CA: Written 2026-09-19 against 2 CCR ss12185 and 12005(d) (Civil Rights Council fair housing regulations, Subchapter 7 Art. 18; new section filed 1979-09-16, operative 2020-01-01). RESOLVES the Instruction 24 REQUIRED-family gap - the base assistance-animal-accommodation row is tagged KS only and was invisible to the 2+ state extend screen, exactly as it was for Ohio. CLASSIFICATION for the CO re-audit's four-way ESA test: California is INDEPENDENT AND ANIMAL-SPECIFIC, but the animal-specific layer is REGULATORY rather than statutory - arguably a fifth category the checklist does not yet have. s12005(d) expressly defines assistance animals to include SUPPORT ANIMALS providing emotional, cognitive or similar support, and s12185(c) gives them a reasonable-accommodation route in dwellings. Authority is Gov. Code s12935(a), referencing ss12920, 12921, 12926, 12926.1, 12927, 12955 and 12955.3 and Auburn Woods I HOA v. FEHC (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th 1578 - state authority throughout. This is the STRONGEST answer in the project to the ESA row the HUD withdrawal threatens: CA's support-animal coverage does not rest on HUD guidance at all and survives its withdrawal intact. INSTRUCTION 16 FLAG: this is an ADMINISTRATIVE-CODE citation, not a statute. Agency rulemaking is invisible to legislative bill-tracking, so the legal-watch workflow needs a separate Civil Rights Council rulemaking watch - same treatment as KS's K.A.R., ND's Admin. Code, SD's ARSD. SCOPE TRAP, the WY/MN pattern: 2 CCR s14331 is a near-identical assistance-animal regulation but sits in the state-programs/covered-entities article, NOT housing. Do not cite s14331 for a lease. s12185 is the housing rule. Not carried into body text, see edu-assistance-animal-documentation-ca: the s12185(b) two-permissible-questions rule, the s12185(c)(2) online-certification presumption (see the sub-cite correction below), s12185(d)(4) multiple animals, s12185(d)(7) vests and ID cards, and the s12185(d)(9)(B)-(D) individualized-assessment standard. ss12176-12180 (the general reasonable-accommodation standards and defences) and s12178(f) have NOT been read. SUB-CITE RESOLVED 2026-09-19, AND I WAS WRONG TO 'CORRECT' IT: s12185(c)(2) was read section-open and it does say, in terms, that an online certification without an individualized assessment is 'presumptively considered not to be information from a reliable third party UNDER SECTION 12178(f)'. My original note faithfully reproduced the regulation's own cross-reference; my intervening 'correction' second-guessed a correct note against an inference and should not have been made. THE MIS-CITE IS THE REGULATION'S, NOT OURS. s12178(f) is the SELF-CERTIFICATION provision; the reliable-third-party list is s12178(g) and the reliability test is s12178(h), so s12185(c)(2)'s pointer does not land where its own sentence says it does. LIKELY CAUSE, recorded as a hypothesis and not verified: s12185 was filed 9-16-2019 and has NEVER been amended, while s12178 was amended 11-19-2021 operative 1-1-2022 - a re-lettering in that amendment would leave s12185 pointing at the pre-2022 subdivision. The pre-2022 text of s12178 has NOT been seen. Do not silently repair the cite when quoting the regulation; quote it as written and footnote the discrepancy. ss12176-12180 now READ section-open 2026-09-19; s12181 (modifications, restoration, escrow) remains unread. Pen. Code s365.5 READ 2026-09-19: s365.5(c) makes it a MISDEMEANOR, fine up to $2,500, to prevent or interfere with a disabled person's rights under the section - but those rights, at (b), are admittance to 'accommodations, advantages, facilities... hotels, lodging places, places of public accommodation... and other places to which the GENERAL PUBLIC IS INVITED'. A private residential tenancy is not a place to which the general public is invited, so on its text s365.5 reaches HOTELS AND LODGING but NOT ordinary rental housing. It is also CANINE-ONLY and reaches only guide, signal and service dogs - never support animals. So California has NO criminal penalty for a landlord denying an assistance animal in a residential tenancy; the remedy runs through FEHA and 2 CCR s12176 et seq. Textual conclusion; Civ. Code s54.1, the housing-access provision s365.7 cross-refers to, remains unread. Civ. Code s54.1 READ 2026-09-19 (Disabled Persons Act). s54.1(b)(6)(A): refusing to rent to, or to let a tenant keep, a GUIDE, SIGNAL OR SERVICE DOG is a denial of equal access to housing - even where the landlord bars dogs generally (s54.1(b)(5)). s54.1(b)(6)(B): the lease MAY reasonably regulate the dog's presence outside its duties, and the tenant stays liable for proven damage. Like the Penal Code sections, s54.1 is DOG-ONLY; SUPPORT animals rest on FEHA and 2 CCR s12185 alone. s54.1(b)(3)(A): modifications at the tenant's expense may be conditioned on RESTORATION, and NO ADDITIONAL SECURITY may be required - though an escrow for restoration costs may be negotiated. s54.1(d): any ADA violation is also a s54.1 violation. Remedies are in s54.3, NOT READ.

title: Assistance animals: what a landlord may ask and require
bodyText: California limits how a housing provider may verify an assistance animal. For a service animal, only two questions may be asked: whether the person is an individual with a disability, and what disability-related task the animal has been trained to perform. The person may not be asked to demonstrate the task. Service animals need not be professionally trained or certified. Animal vests, identification cards and certificates are not by themselves documentation of a disability or of the need for an accommodation. A support animal certification bought from an online service, without an individualized assessment by a medical professional, is presumptively not reliable third-party information - but before denying the request the housing provider must give the individual an opportunity to supply information that does meet the standard. A denial for direct threat must rest on an individualized assessment of objective evidence about that specific animal's actual conduct, not on speculation, fear, or what other animals have done.
notes: CA: 2 CCR s12185(b), (c)(2), (d)(7) and (d)(9)(B)-(D), plus s12005(d)(1), read section-open 2026-09-19. The online-certification presumption at (c)(2) is the landlord-favourable limb most likely to be misapplied - it is a presumption about the RELIABILITY of one document, not a licence to deny, and the regulation expressly requires giving the tenant a chance to cure the documentation first. An individualized assessment must show the disability, describe the accommodation INCLUDING THE SPECIES, and connect the two. s12185(d)(9)(D): a dog finally determined by a court to be a 'potentially dangerous dog' or 'vicious dog' under Food & Agric. Code s31601 et seq. is PRESUMPTIVELY a direct threat - the one bright line in an otherwise individualized standard.

title: Landlord Entry
bodyText: Landlord may enter the dwelling unit only in an emergency; to make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, exhibit the unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors, or make an initial inspection under Civil Code section 1950.5(f); when Tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises; or pursuant to court order. Except in an emergency or after abandonment or surrender, Landlord will give Tenant reasonable written notice stating the date, approximate time and purpose of entry, and will enter only during normal business hours unless Tenant consents at the time of entry to a different time. Twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable notice; notice mailed at least six days before entry is presumed reasonable. No notice is required to respond to an emergency, where Tenant is present and consents at the time of entry, or after Tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit. Landlord will not abuse the right of access or use it to harass Tenant.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1954, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (amended by Stats. 2018 ch. 445 (SB 721), eff. 2019-01-01). Core Obligations canvass row, now answerable for CA. Details that distinguish CA from the prior eight states: the notice must state DATE, APPROXIMATE TIME AND PURPOSE - not merely 'reasonable notice'; 24 hours is a PRESUMPTION rebuttable by evidence, not a fixed period; and s1954(d)(1) supplies a second presumption for MAILED notice at six days. s1954(c)'s no-abuse/no-harass rule is a standalone duty with no prior-state analogue in the library. NOT carried into body text, deliberately: s1954(d)(2) permits ORAL notice to show the unit to purchasers if the landlord gave written notice within 120 days that the property is for sale, and then requires written evidence of entry to be left inside the unit - a conditional landlord right worth its own row; s1954(d)(3) permits an oral agreement for agreed repairs or services with entry within one week. Two entry grounds in s1954(a) are cross-references not yet read: (a)(5) Chapter 2.5 (s1954.201 et seq.) and (a)(6) H&S s17973 (Art. 2.2 inspections). Both should be screened before this row is called complete. EXTEND SCREEN 2026-09-19: now supersedes the base row `landlords-access`, which is blocked for CA. ENTRY GROUNDS CLOSED 2026-09-19: s1954(a)(5) refers to Chapter 2.5 (commencing with s1954.201), which s1954.201 states is the WATER SUBMETERING chapter for multifamily residential rental buildings - so that ground is entry for submetering purposes. s1954(a)(6) refers to H&S Art. 2.2 (s17973), the EXTERIOR ELEVATED ELEMENT (balcony) inspection regime - see edu-balcony-inspection-ca. Both were flagged unread and are now identified. SEPARATE ENTRY AUTHORITY OUTSIDE s1954: H&S s13113.7(d)(2)(A) independently authorises entry to install, repair, test and maintain smoke alarms, with its own reasonable-written-notice requirement and 24-hour presumption. A CA landlord therefore has at least two statutory entry regimes with parallel but separately worded notice rules - see alarm-duties-ca. The remaining s1954.201 et seq. sections beyond the intent provision are NOT READ. || CHAPTER 2.5 NOW PARTLY READ, 2026-09-28. These notes said 'The remaining s1954.201 et seq. sections beyond the intent provision are NOT READ', and that unread chapter turned out to contain a REQUIRED prescribed lease disclosure the library had no row for. ss1954.202, 1954.204, 1954.205, 1954.206, 1954.213, 1954.214 and 1954.218 are now read section-open - see water-submeter-disclosure-ca and edu-water-submeter-billing-ca. Still not read: ss1954.203, 1954.207 to 1954.212, 1954.215 to 1954.217 and 1954.219. ALSO CLOSED: s1954(d)(2), the oral-notice-for-showings right that these notes flagged as 'a conditional landlord right worth its own row', now has one - edu-selling-rented-property-ca.

title: Lease translation duty (five languages)
bodyText: California requires a landlord who negotiates a lease primarily in Spanish, Chinese, Tagalog, Vietnamese or Korean to deliver the tenant a full translation of the lease, including every term and condition, before the lease is signed, and to provide a notice in that language at the time and place of signing. The duty applies only to a tenancy for a period longer than one month. It does not apply where the tenant negotiated through the tenant's own interpreter, meaning an adult fluent in both languages who is not employed by or supplied through the landlord. House rules and furnishing inventories ordinarily incorporated by reference do not have to be translated, but a later document making substantial changes to the parties' rights does. The English lease governs the parties' rights; the translation is admissible only to show that no contract was formed because of a substantial difference in material terms. A tenant may rescind the lease if the landlord does not comply, and any waiver of these requirements is void.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1632, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (amended by SB 1103, Stats. 2024 ch. 1015, eff. 2025-01-01). This is the duty s1946.2(f)(3) and Gov. Code s8589.45(b) both invoke, now read at source. Findings that change how the app must treat it: (1) SCOPE LIMIT - s1632(b)(3) reaches a tenancy 'for a period of longer than one month' only, so a pure month-to-month tenancy is OUTSIDE the duty. That is a large carve-out nobody would guess from the cross-references in s1946.2 or s8589.45. (2) The trigger is negotiating PRIMARILY in the language, orally OR in writing - not the tenant's stated preference. (3) REMEDY IS RESCISSION of the lease, s1632(k)(1); waiver void, s1632(l). (4) s1632(g)(3) excludes matters ordinarily incorporated by reference - tenancy rules and regulations and furnishing inventories - from the 'contract' to be translated. s1632(g)(1) INCLUDES any later document making substantial changes, so a material amendment re-triggers the duty. (5) s1632(h) own-interpreter exception, with the interpreter defined as a non-minor fluent in both languages and NOT employed by or made available through the landlord. (6) s1632(i) permits retaining names, addresses, brand names, numerals, dollar amounts and dates untranslated; s1632(j) makes the ENGLISH text controlling. PRODUCT IMPLICATION, escalated not solved: for a covered lease the app must generate a complete translated lease, not a translated disclosure. That is a capability the schema and builder do not have, and it is the second half of the type-size/translation schema gap recorded in the CA decision log.

title: Lease provisions void as contrary to public policy, and the before-possession rule
bodyText: California voids two categories of lease provision outright. First, any provision by which a tenant agrees to modify or waive rights or remedies under the security deposit statute or the landlord entry statute, the right to assert a future cause of action against the landlord, the right to a notice or hearing required by law, procedural rights in litigation over the tenancy, or the right to have the landlord exercise a duty of care imposed by law to prevent personal injury or personal property damage. Second, any provision modifying or waiving any other statutory right is void unless the lease was presented to the tenant before the tenant took actual possession of the premises. That second rule does not apply to a renewal that carries forward the same provision from the agreement being renewed. Both rules apply to leases executed on or after January 1, 1976.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1953 (Hiring of Real Property chapter), primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. NOTE this is CIVIL CODE s1953, not CCP s1953 - see the cross-body citation ambiguity topic. s1953(a)(5) is the operative bar for the library's exculpation rows and it is MUCH CLOSER TO OHIO s5321.13(D) than s1668 is: it voids any waiver of the tenant's right to have the landlord exercise a duty of care imposed by law to prevent PERSONAL PROPERTY DAMAGE, which is exactly what a blanket 'Landlord is not liable for loss or damage to Tenant's personal property' clause does. s1953(a)(2) is broader still - it voids waiver of the right to assert ANY future cause of action against the lessor, which reaches blanket not-liable and landlord-indemnity limbs generally. See the CA extend manifest: this supersedes my earlier read that s1668 alone might permit a merely narrowed clause. s1953(a)(1) bars contracting around s1950.5 or s1954 at all, which is why security-deposit-cap-ca, security-deposit-return-ca and landlord-entry-ca must track the statutes rather than vary them. s1953(b) IS THE SLEEPER and has no analogue anywhere in the library: a provision modifying or waiving any OTHER statutory right is void UNLESS THE LEASE WAS PRESENTED TO THE TENANT BEFORE THE TENANT TOOK ACTUAL POSSESSION. A lease signed after move-in loses every statutory-right modification it contains. Carve-out: renewals carrying forward the same provision. This is a document-TIMING rule, not a drafting rule, and the app is the only thing that can enforce it. s1953(c): applies to leases executed on or after 1976-01-01. NOT RESOLVED: s1953(a)(4) 'procedural rights in litigation' plainly reaches some jury-waiver, venue and fee-shifting limbs, but how far is case law, not text - not researched. ss1942.1 and 1942.5, cross-referenced in s1953(b), remain unread. CONFESSION OF JUDGMENT, added 2026-09-19: CCP s1132(a) - 'a judgment by confession is unenforceable and may not be entered in any superior court', for judgments obtained or entered on or after 2023-01-01 (s1132(b)). So a confession-of-judgment or cognovit clause is dead in CA by a flat statutory bar, not merely void as a s1953(a)(4) waiver of procedural rights. Screen the base library for any such clause.

title: Disability Accommodation Requests
bodyText: Tenant, a family member, or anyone Tenant authorizes to act on Tenant's behalf may request a reasonable accommodation or reasonable modification because of a disability at any time, orally or in writing, and need not use any particular words, form or procedure. Landlord will not charge any fee, deposit or other financial contribution as a condition of receiving, processing or granting such a request. Nothing in this Lease requires Tenant to give up the right to request a reasonable accommodation or modification in the future.
notes: CA: 2 CCR ss12176(f)(1)-(3), 12176(f)(5) and 12180(a)(1), (a)(3), read section-open 2026-09-19. Three rules here bind LEASE DRAFTING directly, which is why this is a clause and not only education. s12180(a)(1): unlawful to charge a fee, additional deposit or financial contribution as a condition of receiving, PROCESSING, or granting an accommodation or modification - broader than the s12185(d)(2) animal fee ban because it reaches every accommodation, not just animals. s12180(a)(3): unlawful to request or require that an individual WAIVE THE RIGHT TO REQUEST A FUTURE accommodation or modification - a prohibited lease term, and it pairs with Civ. Code s1953(a)(2), which voids waiver of the right to assert a future cause of action. s12176(f)(5): a landlord MAY ask a tenant to use a form or follow a procedure, but MAY NOT refuse the request or refuse to engage in the interactive process because the tenant did not use it. Any library clause conditioning an accommodation on a written request on the landlord's form is unenforceable as written in CA - screen the base library for that pattern. s12176(f)(3): a request may be made at any point, including during the inquiry or application process, during the tenancy, during litigation, at or after trial, and after judgment. | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-accommodation-process-ca). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: Disability accommodations: the interactive process and inquiry limits
bodyText: When a landlord cannot immediately grant a requested accommodation or modification, California requires the landlord to engage in a timely, good-faith interactive process with the tenant. A request may not be denied for lack of information without first asking for the missing information and giving the tenant a reasonable opportunity to supply it, and undue delay in responding can itself amount to a denial. What the landlord may ask depends on what is already apparent: if the disability and the need are apparent or known, no further information may be requested at all; if only the need is unclear, the landlord may ask only for a description of the accommodation and how it relates to the disability. A landlord may never ask about the tenant's diagnosis, the severity of the disability, medical records, or medical history. A tenant can often establish disability by self-certification, such as proof of receipt of disability benefits or a credible statement. All information about a disability or a request must be kept confidential. Where the need for an accommodation arises from the landlord's own failure to maintain or repair the property as required by law, the undue-burden and fundamental-alteration defenses do not apply. A tenant, a family member or anyone the tenant authorizes may request a reasonable accommodation or modification at any time, orally or in writing, without particular words, forms or procedures; you may not charge any fee, deposit or other financial contribution for receiving, processing or granting one, and a lease can't make the tenant give up the right to ask in future (2 CCR 12176(f)(1)). Reasonable modifications: a tenant may make reasonable modifications at their own expense where a disability makes them necessary. You may ask for a reasonable description of the work and reasonable assurances it will be done competently with any required permits, but not require a particular contractor; you may not raise a customary security deposit, require a liability waiver or insurance, or require a move to another unit as a condition. Where reasonable, you may require the interior restored at the end of the tenancy, reasonable wear and tear excepted, but not exterior or common-area modifications (2 CCR 12181).
notes: CA: 2 CCR ss12176(e), 12177, 12178 and 12179, read section-open 2026-09-19. Far more operationally detailed than any prior state's accommodation rules. Items with no analogue anywhere in the library: s12176(e) CONFIDENTIALITY - disability and request information may not be shared with anyone not directly involved in the interactive process or decision, save four exceptions (needed to decide, needed to implement, written authorization, required by law). A standalone landlord duty. s12177(b) - may NOT deny for lack of information without first requesting it and allowing a reasonable opportunity to respond; s12177(e) - undue delay MAY ITSELF CONSTITUTE DENIAL; s12177(c) - must look for an equally effective alternative and must grant one that works, with the tenant's preference given significant weight; s12177(g) - a later request for the same accommodation must be considered independently of an earlier denial. s12178 tiered inquiry (a)-(e), with s12178(e)(1) barring any inquiry into diagnosis, severity, medical records or medical history; s12178(f) SELF-CERTIFICATION; s12178(g) five categories of reliable third party including peer support groups and non-medical service agencies; s12178(h) case-by-case reliability test. s12179(d)(6) - where the need arises from the owner's failure to maintain or repair as required by law, the undue-burden and fundamental-alteration defenses ARE UNAVAILABLE. s12176(f)(8) - failure to accommodate is an AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE to an unlawful detainer, and a request may be made during the eviction, at trial, or after judgment. This belongs in the legal tracker's eviction workflow, not only in the lease. s12181 (modifications: restoration, escrow, who pays) NOT READ. | CA: Content from accommodation-request-rights-ca (switched off) added by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); unchanged: 2 CCR §12176(f)(1); Civ. Code §1953(a)(2). | CA: Content from reasonable-modification-ca (switched off) added by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); unchanged: 2 CCR §12181; H&S §17959.6.

title: Reasonable Modifications
bodyText: Tenant may make reasonable modifications to the premises at Tenant's expense where necessary because of a disability. Landlord may ask Tenant for a reasonable description of the proposed work and reasonable assurances that it will be done competently and that any required building permits will be obtained, but will not require that the work be done by any particular contractor. Landlord will not increase any customarily required security deposit, require a liability waiver or insurance, or require Tenant to move to a different unit, as a condition of a modification. Where it is reasonable to do so, Landlord may require Tenant to restore the interior of the premises to its prior condition at the end of the tenancy, reasonable wear and tear excepted; Landlord will not require restoration of exterior modifications or modifications to common or public use areas.
notes: CA: 2 CCR s12181, read section-open 2026-09-19 (filed 11-19-2021, operative 2022-01-01; amended 2024-01-01). Four landlord-side prohibitions in this section are lease-drafting rules, which is why this is a clause: s12181(b) - MAY NOT increase a customarily required security deposit for an individual with a disability, and may not AUTOMATICALLY require an escrow account; s12181(c) - may not require a particular contractor or builder, and it is unlawful to deny a type of modification except for undue burden or fundamental alteration; s12181(f) - MAY NOT impose liability waivers or insurance requirements as conditions on a modification (a SECOND insurance-condition ban in CA after s12185(d)(2), and this one is not animal-specific); s12181(j) - may not require the tenant to move to a different unit in lieu of allowing a modification. Restoration, s12181(a): interiors only, only where reasonable, wear and tear excepted - never exteriors, common or public use areas. Where escrow IS justified it must be negotiated, capped at the cost of restoration, paid over a reasonable period, with INTEREST ACCRUING TO THE TENANT, and the full restoration cost may never be demanded up front (six factors at s12181(b)(1)-(6)). NOT in body text: s12181(h) - where the owner is a government entity or receives federal or state affordable-housing funding, the OWNER pays and the request is handled as an accommodation; s12181(i) upkeep allocation between owner and tenant; s12181(k)-(l) alternative-design rules, where the owner pays any extra cost of its own aesthetic or workmanship preference; s12181(d)-(e) common interest developments, which override conflicting Davis-Stirling governing documents; s12181(m) not-yet-constructed purchases and H&S s17959.6. s12181(g): applies to ALL housing regardless of building age and is independent of architectural accessibility compliance. | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-accommodation-process-ca). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: Repair and Deduct
bodyText: If Tenant gives Landlord or Landlord's agent written or oral notice of dilapidations rendering the premises untenantable that Landlord ought to repair, and Landlord neglects to repair them within a reasonable time, Tenant may either repair them and deduct the cost from rent when due, so long as the cost does not exceed one month's rent, or vacate the premises, in which case Tenant is discharged from further rent and other conditions as of the date of vacating. Tenant may use this remedy no more than twice in any 12-month period. This remedy is not available where the condition was caused by Tenant's own violation of Civil Code section 1929 or 1941.2. Nothing in this Lease limits any other remedy available to Tenant.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1942, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. Two features that cut against how repair clauses are normally drafted: (1) ORAL NOTICE SUFFICES - s1942(a) says 'written or oral notice to the landlord or his agent, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 1962'. Any lease clause conditioning the repair-and-deduct remedy on WRITTEN notice modifies a statutory right and is therefore exposed under Civ. Code s1953(b), which voids such a modification unless the lease was presented before the tenant took possession. SCREEN RESULT: the base library was searched for active rows tagged to 2+ core states that require written notice for repairs or maintenance - ZERO hits. Clean negative, recorded so a future canvass does not redo it. (2) s1942(b) makes 30 days a REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTION of reasonableness affecting the burden of producing evidence - not a waiting period. A shorter notice is permitted where circumstances require, so a lease stating a flat 30-day rule would overstate the landlord's protection. Caps: cost not more than one month's rent, and not more than TWICE in any 12-month period. s1942(d) makes the remedy cumulative. ss1929 and 1941.2 READ 2026-09-19 - see tenant-maintenance-obligations-ca. s1962(a) also READ - the agent who may receive s1942 notice is the person disclosed under owner-identity-disclosure-ca, which makes that disclosure load-bearing for this remedy: if no agent is validly disclosed, s1962(d) deems the signing party the owner's agent for receiving notices. GROUP NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Maintenance & Repairs' -> 'Landlord Responsibilities' (session drift; 12 canonical groups are used by all nine states). | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-repair-and-deduct-ca). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: Retaliation: the 180-day window and what counts
bodyText: California bars a landlord from recovering possession, causing a tenant to quit involuntarily, increasing rent, or decreasing services within 180 days of a tenant exercising rights relating to tenantability, where the tenant is not in default on rent. The triggering events include the tenant giving repair notice, giving notice of a suspected bed bug infestation, making an oral complaint about tenantability, filing a complaint with an agency, an inspection or citation resulting from such a complaint, commencing a proceeding involving tenantability, and a judgment on tenantability against the landlord; where more than one applies, the 180 days run from the latest. A tenant may invoke this protection only once in any 12-month period. Separately, and without that time limit, it is unlawful to retaliate because a tenant organized or participated in a tenants' association or lawfully exercised any legal right. Threatening to report a tenant, or anyone the landlord knows to be associated with the tenant, to immigration authorities is retaliatory conduct under both rules. A landlord may still act within the 180 days for a lawful reason if the notice states the good-faith ground relied on, and must prove that ground if it is challenged. A landlord who violates the section is liable for actual damages plus punitive damages of $100 to $2,000 for each retaliatory act involving fraud, oppression or malice, and the court awards attorney's fees to the prevailing party if either party requests them when the action begins. Any waiver of these protections is void.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1942.5, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (operative 2021-10-01 per s1942.5(l); amended by AB 832, Stats. 2021 ch. 27). Points the library has no analogue for: s1942.5(c) and (e) - THREATENING TO REPORT THE TENANT OR ANYONE ASSOCIATED WITH THE TENANT TO IMMIGRATION AUTHORITIES is expressly retaliatory under both the (a) and (d) prohibitions. No prior state has an immigration-based retaliation provision. s1942.5(k) carves out compliance with federal rent-limitation or rental-assistance program obligations. s1942.5(a)(1) expressly lists NOTICE OF A SUSPECTED BED BUG INFESTATION as a trigger, which ties this directly to bed-bug-disclosure-ca and edu-bed-bug-landlord-duties-ca - a tenant report under that chapter starts a 180-day retaliation clock. TWO DISTINCT PROHIBITIONS, easily collapsed: (a) is the 180-day tenantability window, limited to a tenant not in default on rent and invokable once per 12 months (s1942.5(b)); (d) is a separate, untimed ban on retaliation for tenant organizing or lawfully exercising ANY right, with the burden of producing evidence on the TENANT. Do not merge them. s1942.5(g) is the landlord's safe harbour and it is a DRAFTING duty: the notice must state the good-faith ground relied on, and the landlord must establish its truth if controverted - which dovetails with the s1946.2 just-cause statement requirement. s1942.5(i) is a RECIPROCAL FEE PROVISION triggered by either party requesting fees at initiation - relevant to the default-by-tenant / attorney-fee reciprocity question flagged in the CA extend manifest. s1942.5(f): waiver void as contrary to public policy, independent of s1953. ADDED 2026-09-19: Civ. Code s1942.6 - a person entering on an occupant's invitation, during reasonable hours or in an emergency, to provide information on tenants' rights or to participate in a tenants' association is NOT LIABLE FOR TRESPASS. Complements the s1942.5(d) protection of tenant organising.

title: Owner and Manager Identification
bodyText: Person authorized to manage the premises: {{manager_name}}, {{manager_phone}}, {{manager_street_address}}. Owner, or person authorized to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving and receipting all notices and demands: {{owner_agent_name}}, {{owner_agent_phone}}, {{owner_agent_street_address}}. Rent is payable to {{rent_payee_name}} at {{rent_payee_address}}, {{rent_payee_phone}}, in the following form or forms: {{rent_payment_forms}}. If rent may be paid personally, it may be paid on {{rent_payment_days_hours}}. Landlord will give Tenant a copy of this Lease within 15 days after Tenant signs it, and, once each calendar year on Tenant's request, an additional copy within 15 days.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1962, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (amended Stats. 2012 ch. 695 (AB 1953)). Sits in CHAPTER 4, Identification of Property Owners - outside the Chapter 2 landlord-tenant provisions. Instruction 7 cross-chapter pattern, fifth confirmation in CA. s1962(a) says 'Disclose THEREIN', so this is content the statute requires IN THE LEASE ITSELF - not a separate notice. The street address must be one 'at which personal service may be effected', so a PO box will not do. s1962(a)(2)(B) gives the owner an ALTERNATIVE to naming a payee: disclose either the financial-institution account number plus the institution's name and street address, PROVIDED THE INSTITUTION IS WITHIN FIVE MILES of the rental property, or the information needed to set up an electronic funds transfer. The five-mile limit is a real constraint the builder must express. ENFORCEMENT TEETH, s1962(c): the duty runs to a SUCCESSOR owner or manager, who must comply within 15 days of succeeding, and a successor who has not complied MAY NOT serve a CCP s1161(2) notice or otherwise evict for nonpayment of rent that accrued during the noncompliance period - though the tenant remains liable for the rent. A missing disclosure therefore disarms the eviction remedy for a period. s1962(d): a party who signs on behalf of a non-complying owner is DEEMED THE OWNER'S AGENT for service of process, for performing the owner's obligations, and for receiving rent - and (d)(3) then allows rent in cash, check, money order or any previously accepted form unless the agreement specifies a form or the tenant was notified in writing. s1962(f): where the disclosed address does not allow personal delivery, mailed rent or notice is CONCLUSIVELY presumed received on the date posted if the tenant proves mailing. s1961 READ 2026-09-19 and the scope gap is CLOSED: Chapter 4 'shall apply to every dwelling structure containing ONE OR MORE UNITS offered to the public for rent or for lease for residential purposes'. No unit-count threshold, no owner-type exemption, no small-landlord carve-out - unlike s1950.5(c)(5) or s1947.12(d). A single rented house is covered. The one boundary in the text is 'offered to the public', which is not defined in s1961 and has not been researched. s1962(b) oral-agreement variant not modelled. RECEIPTS, Civ. Code s1499 read 2026-09-19: 'A debtor has a right to require from his creditor a written receipt for any property delivered in performance of his obligation.' General and ON REQUEST - it covers every rent payment in any form, but it is not an automatic cash-receipt duty of the Minnesota kind.

title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText: For a tenancy from week to week, month to month, or any period less than a month, Landlord may increase the rent only on written notice delivered to Tenant personally or served by mail under Code of Civil Procedure section 1013. If the increase, by itself or combined with any other increases in the 12 months before its effective date, is 10 percent or less of the rent charged at any time during those 12 months, the notice will be delivered at least 30 days before the increase takes effect. If it is greater than 10 percent, the notice will be delivered at least 90 days before the increase takes effect. Where any other statute, regulation, recorded regulatory agreement or contract requires a longer notice period, that longer period applies.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s827, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (amended by SB 1103, Stats. 2024 ch. 1015, eff. 2025-01-01). Sits in DIVISION 2 (Property), Title 3 - a third code location for CA landlord-tenant law after Chapter 2 and Chapter 4. CRITICAL INTERACTION: this notice rule is INDEPENDENT of s1947.12 and applies even to units EXEMPT from the Tenant Protection Act. A landlord on an exempt single-family home has no rent cap but still owes 30 or 90 days' notice. Do not condition this row on TPA coverage. The 10 percent threshold is CUMULATIVE over the 12 months before the effective date, measured against the rent charged at any time in that window - so two 6 percent increases in a year push the second into the 90-day tier. s827(b)(3)(B) carves out increases caused by a change in income or family composition determined by a statutory or regulatory recertification: those revert to 30 days. SERVICE: personal delivery or mail under CCP s1013, READ 2026-09-19. The extension is FIVE CALENDAR DAYS where address and mailing place are both in California, 10 days if either is outside CA but within the US, 12 days for a Secretary of State address-confidentiality-program address, and 20 days if either is outside the US. A mailed increase within CA is therefore effectively 35 days at the 10-percent-or-less tier and 95 days above it, and the app must compute from the service method, not the tier alone. CCP s1013(c): two COURT days for Express Mail or overnight; s1013(e): two court days for fax, only where both parties agreed in writing; s1013(g) routes electronic service to CCP s1010.6 and the Rules of Court, NOT READ. s827(a) governs changing OTHER lease terms (30 days for month-to-month), and permits the parties to agree in writing that a terms-change notice may be given not less than seven days before expiration of a term - an opt-in landlord right of the s1946.2(b)(2)(A)(ii) family, not yet drafted as a row. s827(a)(2): a served notice itself establishes the new terms as part of the lease if the tenant holds over. Commercial/qualified-commercial-tenant limbs at s827(b)(1),(4)-(7) are out of scope. GROUP NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Rent & Fees' -> 'Rent & Payment' (session drift; 12 canonical groups are used by all nine states). | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-rent-increase-notice-ca). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: Tenant Care of Premises
bodyText: Tenant shall keep the part of the premises Tenant occupies and uses clean and sanitary as the condition of the premises permits; dispose of all rubbish, garbage and other waste from the dwelling unit in a clean and sanitary manner; properly use and operate all electrical, gas and plumbing fixtures and keep them as clean and sanitary as their condition permits; neither do, nor permit any person on the premises with Tenant's permission to do, anything that willfully or wantonly destroys, defaces, damages, impairs or removes any part of the structure or dwelling unit or its facilities, equipment or appurtenances; and use the premises as Tenant's abode, using portions of it for living, sleeping, cooking or dining only as those portions were designed or intended to be used. Tenant shall repair deteriorations or injuries to the premises caused by Tenant's want of ordinary care.
notes: CA: Civ. Code ss1941.2 and 1929, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. These are the two provisions cross-referenced by s1942(c) as disqualifying a tenant from repair-and-deduct, so they are the other half of repair-and-deduct-ca. s1941.2(a) is NOT a free-standing tenant duty clause - it is a CONDITION ON THE LANDLORD'S DUTY: the landlord's s1941/s1942 repair obligation does not arise where the tenant is in SUBSTANTIAL violation AND the violation CONTRIBUTES SUBSTANTIALLY to the dilapidation or substantially interferes with the landlord's ability to repair. Both qualifiers matter; a clause that recites the five duties without them overstates the landlord's position. rule_type RECOMMENDED rather than REQUIRED for that reason - the statute does not require these terms in a lease, it defines when the landlord is excused. TRAP AT s1941.2(b): paragraphs (a)(1) and (a)(2) - cleanliness and waste disposal - DO NOT APPLY where the landlord has EXPRESSLY AGREED IN WRITING to perform them. So a lease in which the landlord undertakes cleaning or waste removal silently disables those two limbs as an excuse. Screen any CA lease that bundles janitorial or trash service. s1929 is the general hiring rule (want of ordinary care) and sits in Chapter 1, not Chapter 2. SUPERSEDES tenant-maintenance for CA as of 2026-09-19: the overlap check found both rows stating the same tenant care duties, which would have put them in a CA lease twice. This row tracks s1941.2 and governs.

title: Application screening fees
bodyText: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only to cover the actual cost of screening, capped at a statutory amount that is adjusted annually for inflation, and may not charge one at all when the landlord knows or should know that no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must also operate one of two processes: either consider completed applications in the order received against written screening criteria given to the applicant with the application form and approve the first applicant who meets them, or return the entire fee to every applicant not selected within seven days of selecting a tenant or thirty days of the application, whichever comes first. The landlord must give the applicant an itemized receipt, refund any part of the fee not actually used, and give the applicant a copy of any consumer credit report obtained within seven days of receiving it.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1950.6, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. AMENDED BY AB 1170, Stats. 2025 ch. 67, EFFECTIVE 2026-01-01 - one of the most recently changed provisions in the CA set, and squarely in the legal-watch zone. DO NOT HARDCODE $30. s1950.6(b) caps the fee at the lesser of actual out-of-pocket cost plus the reasonable value of time spent, or $30 per applicant, BUT the $30 'may be adjusted annually by the landlord or their agent commensurate with an increase in the Consumer Price Index, beginning on January 1, 1998'. The operative figure today is therefore a CPI-indexed number well above $30, computed from a 1998 base, and it is landlord-computed rather than published. Body text deliberately says 'a statutory amount adjusted annually for inflation' rather than stating a number. The app should not assert a figure it cannot derive. s1950.6(c)(2) is the structural obligation and it is new to this project: the landlord must OFFER one of two defined processes - (A) first-come-first-considered against written criteria supplied WITH THE APPLICATION FORM, first qualifying applicant approved, no fee until the application is actually considered, with a 7-day refund for inadvertent duplicate collection (or, at the applicant's option, transfer to another unit); or (B) full refund to every non-selected applicant within 7 days of selection or 30 days of application, whichever is first. This is product workflow, not lease text. s1950.6(c)(1): no fee where the landlord knows or should know no unit is or will soon be available. s1950.6(d) itemized receipt; (e) refund of the unused portion where no reference check or credit report was obtained; (f) copy of the consumer credit report to the applicant within 7 days of receipt. s1950.6(k): the fee is NOT 'security' under s1950.5 and not an 'advance fee' - so it sits outside the AB 12 deposit cap entirely. s1950.6(j) includes GUARANTORS AND COSIGNERS in 'applicant'. s1950.1 READ 2026-09-19 - see edu-reusable-screening-report-ca. The interaction matters: s1950.1(d) applies 'notwithstanding Section 1950.6', so a landlord who elects to accept reusable reports may charge an applicant who supplies one NEITHER an access fee NOR an application screening fee at all.

title: Three-day notice content and service
bodyText: California's three-day notices are governed by statute rather than by the lease. The three days exclude Saturdays, Sundays and judicial holidays. A notice demanding rent must state the amount due and the name, telephone number and address of the person to whom rent is to be paid, with the usual days and hours that person is available if payment may be made personally; alternatively it may give a financial institution account number with the institution's name and street address, provided the institution is within five miles of the rental property, or refer to an electronic funds transfer procedure already established. It must be served on the tenant and on any subtenant in actual occupation, and may be served at any time within one year after the rent becomes due. A notice to perform other covenants gives the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee or another interested person three days to perform and save the lease from forfeiture, and no such notice is required where the violated covenant can no longer be performed. Assigning or subletting contrary to the lease, committing waste, maintaining a nuisance or using the premises for an unlawful purpose terminates the lease and supports a three-day notice to quit with no opportunity to cure. Notices may be served by personal delivery; by leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at the tenant's residence or usual place of business and mailing a copy to the residence; or, where neither can be ascertained and no suitable person is found, by posting conspicuously on the property, delivering to a person residing there if one can be found, and mailing to the property. A landlord may not charge any fee for serving, posting or delivering these notices. You also may not charge the tenant any fee for serving, posting or otherwise delivering any notice about the tenancy, including a notice ending a periodic tenancy or a three-day notice (Civ. Code 1946.1(i); CCP 1161(6)).
notes: CA: CCP ss1161 and 1162, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. s1161 amended by SB 611 (Stats. 2024 ch. 287), OPERATIVE 2025-02-01. Routed to LANDLORD_EDUCATION per the standing decision to send notice-and-cure mechanics to the legal tracker rather than into lease text. The s1161(2) content list MIRRORS Civ. Code s1962 almost exactly, INCLUDING THE FIVE-MILE FINANCIAL-INSTITUTION LIMIT and the conclusive-presumption-on-mailing proviso. The two must stay consistent: the lease disclosure under owner-identity-disclosure-ca supplies the same facts the pay-or-quit notice must recite, and s1962(c) separately bars a non-compliant SUCCESSOR owner from serving a s1161(2) notice for rent accrued during noncompliance. Getting the lease disclosure wrong therefore breaks the eviction notice too. The three days EXCLUDE Saturdays, Sundays and judicial holidays, in both s1161(2) and the s1161(3) cure window. A one-year outer limit applies to serving a rent notice. s1161(3): the cure right runs to the tenant, a subtenant in actual occupation, a MORTGAGEE OF THE TERM, or another person interested in its continuance - broader than the tenant alone. No notice is required where the violated covenant cannot afterward be performed. s1161(4): assignment or subletting contrary to the lease, waste, nuisance or unlawful purpose TERMINATES the lease by operation of the statute and supports a three-day notice to quit with NO cure right. Cross-references Civ. Code ss3482.8, 3485(c) and 3486(c), ALL READ 2026-09-19 - see edu-nuisance-eviction-assignment-ca. Only s3482.8 (dogfighting/cockfighting) is statewide. s3486 applies ONLY in the City of Los Angeles. s3485 APPEARS TO BE REPEALED as of 2024-01-01 by its own s3485(j), which means s1161(4) carries a cross-reference to a section that no longer exists - and s1161 was itself amended by SB 611 in 2024 and made operative 2025-02-01 without fixing it. Do not treat the s1161(4) deemed-nuisance list as three live statewide grounds; as read, it is one statewide ground, one city-specific ground, and one dead pointer. s1161(7): 'tenant' excludes occupancies described in Civ. Code s1940(b), READ 2026-09-19 - see edu-tenancy-scope-ca. Two exclusions: transient occupancy subject to transient occupancy tax under R&T s7280, and hotel/motel occupancy where the innkeeper retains a right of access AND all five listed services are offered. Anyone outside those exclusions is a 'tenant' for s1161 purposes. s1162(a) gives the three residential service methods; s1162(b)-(c) are commercial and out of scope. Note s1946.1(f) permits certified or registered mail as an ALTERNATIVE to s1162 service for a periodic-tenancy termination, whereas s1162 does not list mail alone as a method - the two regimes differ and must not be merged in the tracker. INTERACTION NOT RESOLVED: s1946.2(c) requires a cure opportunity 'pursuant to paragraph (3) of Section 1161' before a just-cause termination for a curable breach; how that sequences against a s1161(4) no-cure ground has not been worked through. | CA: Content from notice-service-fee-ban-ca (switched off) added by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); unchanged: Civ. Code §1946.1(i); CCP §1161(6); CCP §1161; Civ. Code §1946(b).

title: Who counts as a tenant, and which occupancies fall outside the chapter
bodyText: California's residential landlord-tenant chapter applies to everyone who hires a dwelling unit in the state, including tenants, lessees, boarders and lodgers, however they are described in the agreement. A dwelling unit means a structure or part of a structure used as a home, residence or sleeping place by one person maintaining a household or by two or more people maintaining a common household. Two occupancies are outside the chapter: transient occupancy in a hotel, motel, residence club or similar facility where the stay is subject to transient occupancy tax, and occupancy at a hotel or motel where the innkeeper keeps a right of access to and control of the unit and the establishment offers all of five services to every resident - personal property safekeeping, central telephone service under filed tariffs, maid, mail and room services, occupancy for periods of less than seven days, and food service from an establishment on or next to the premises connected to the innkeeper. Unless a particular provision says otherwise by its own terms, the chapter's provisions apply to a tenancy in a dwelling unit.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1940, read section-open 2026-09-19, together with s1961 for the separate Chapter 4 disclosure scope. Matters for a property-management product because it decides whether the whole CA clause set applies at all. s1940(a) reaches 'boarders, lodgers, and others, HOWEVER DENOMINATED', so calling an agreement a licence, a room-share or a lodging arrangement does not move it out of the chapter. s1940(b)(2): the hotel/motel exclusion is CONJUNCTIVE - the innkeeper must retain a right of access AND ALL FIVE services must be offered to all residents. A short-stay operator missing any one of the five is inside the chapter and owes the full CA clause set. This is the provision a short-term-rental operator is most likely to assume protects them. s1940(d) is a construction rule worth keeping: nothing limits the application of any Chapter 2 provision to a tenancy in a dwelling unit UNLESS the provision is so limited by its specific terms - i.e. read the chapter broadly by default. READING FLAGGED, NOT ASSERTED: s1940(b)(1) contains a double negative - the transient exclusion does not apply to 'a person to whom this paragraph pertains if the person has not made valid payment for all room and other related charges owing as of the last day on which his or her occupancy is or would be subject to tax'. On its face that keeps a non-paying transient OUTSIDE the chapter, but the sentence is genuinely awkward and the practical question - when a hotel guest who overstays becomes a tenant entitled to unlawful-detainer process - is the kind of thing that turns on case law. NOT researched. Do not build occupancy-type logic on this subdivision without confirming it. s1940(c)'s 'dwelling unit' definition is also the hinge for CCP s1162(c)'s commercial-tenant carve-out, so the two travel together. R&T s7280 READ 2026-09-19 and it supplies the operative line: s7280(a) authorises the tax on occupancy of a hotel, inn, tourist home, motel or other lodging 'UNLESS THE OCCUPANCY IS FOR A PERIOD OF MORE THAN 30 DAYS'. Because s1940(b)(1) excludes occupancy that IS OR WOULD BE subject to that tax, the 30-day line governs even in a jurisdiction that never levied one. So a stay of MORE THAN 30 DAYS is outside the transient exclusion and inside Chapter 2, subject still to the separate s1940(b)(2) five-service hotel exclusion. That is the concrete boundary a short-stay operator needs. s7280(c) also sweeps campground and RV-park spaces into 'other lodging', while excluding local-government facilities, time-share owner occupancy and s7282 campsites. The s1940(b)(1) non-payment double negative flagged above is a SEPARATE question and is still unresolved. EXCEPTION ADDED 2026-09-19: Civ. Code s1940.1 bars requiring a residential hotel occupant to move or check out and re-register before 30 days for the purpose of preserving transient status, with a rebuttable presumption of that purpose from any required check-out ($500 civil penalty). And Civ. Code s1954.071 moves the line from 30 days to 270 for DISASTER-DISPLACED guests until 2031-01-01 - see edu-disaster-displaced-guests-ca.

title: Reusable tenant screening reports
bodyText: California lets a rental applicant supply a reusable tenant screening report - a consumer report prepared within the previous 30 days at the applicant's own request and expense, made available to the landlord at no cost either directly or through a third-party service. Such a report must include the applicant's name and contact information, verification of employment, last known address, and the results of an eviction history check, and must state prominently the date through which its information is current. A landlord is not required to accept these reports. A landlord who does accept them may ask the applicant to confirm that nothing in the report has materially changed, but may not charge that applicant any fee to access the report and may not charge an application screening fee at all. Where a local ordinance conflicts with these rules, whichever gives applicants greater protection applies.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1950.1, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (added by AB 2559, Stats. 2022 ch. 288, eff. 2023-01-01). Closes the s1950.6(g) dependency. THE DECISION POINT IS BINARY AND HAS A PRICE: s1950.1(h) says a landlord need not accept reusable reports, but s1950.1(d) provides that IF the landlord accepts them and an applicant supplies one, the landlord may charge NEITHER an access fee NOR an application screening fee - 'notwithstanding Section 1950.6'. So electing to accept them forfeits screening-fee revenue from every applicant who brings one. The app should surface this as a landlord-level setting, not a per-application choice. s1950.1(e)(6): the report must have been prepared WITHIN THE PREVIOUS 30 DAYS, at the applicant's request AND EXPENSE, and be available to the landlord AT NO COST - a report the landlord must pay to access is not a reusable screening report and does not trigger the fee ban. s1950.1(g) is a one-way local-preemption rule: where a local policy conflicts, whichever gives APPLICANTS GREATER PROTECTION applies. Third CA provision found deferring to the municipal layer, after s1946.2(i) and s1947.12(d)(3), and it reinforces edu-municipal-layer-ca. UNREAD AREA SURFACED BY s1950.1(f): criminal-history consideration in housing is governed by 2 CCR Art. 24, s12264 et seq. (Civil Rights Council again) plus local ordinances. That is an entire tenant-screening regulatory area this pass has NOT touched and it is not in the canvass. Flagging it as a gap-discovery find, not resolving it.

title: Nuisance-based eviction and the city-prosecutor assignment
bodyText: California deems certain conduct a nuisance for the purpose of a three-day notice to quit, but the provisions are narrower than they appear. Using a building or property for dogfighting or cockfighting is a public nuisance statewide. A separate controlled-substance eviction procedure lets a city prosecutor or city attorney bring an unlawful detainer action, but it operates only in the City of Los Angeles. Under that procedure the prosecutor must first give the owner 30 calendar days' written notice requiring the owner to act, and the owner must within 30 days either supply all relevant information or give a written safety-related explanation together with an assignment of the right to bring the action. Accepting the assignment can cost the owner up to $600 in investigation, discovery and attorney's fees. If the owner does not act, or does not prosecute the action diligently and in good faith, the prosecutor may file and join the owner as a defendant, and on a finding of unlawful detainer the prosecutor's costs may be assessed against the owner and recorded as a lien on the property. The court may order a partial eviction removing only the person involved and barring their return, rather than ending the whole tenancy.
notes: CA: Civ. Code ss3482.8, 3485 and 3486, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. These are the three sections CCP s1161(4) incorporates as deemed nuisances. Reading them changes what that limb is worth. s3482.8 (added SB 426, eff. 2012-01-01): dogfighting under Pen. Code s597.5 or cockfighting under s597b(b) - STATEWIDE, and the only one of the three that is. s3486: controlled-substance purpose, defined at s3486(c) by a long list of H&S Code offences. s3486(g): 'This section applies ONLY IN THE COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES to a court having jurisdiction over unlawful detainer cases involving real property situated in the CITY OF LOS ANGELES.' s3486(h) further conditioned its 2014 operativity on the City of LA's reporting compliance. s3485 (unlawful weapons or ammunition): APPEARS REPEALED. s3485(j) reads 'This section shall remain in effect only until January 1, 2024, and as of that date is repealed', and the codifier's annotation says 'Repealed as of January 1, 2024, by its own provisions.' Corroborating but not conclusive: the text supplied is served as the 2022 California Code while ss3482.8 and 3486 came as 2025, which is what a publisher does when a section has left the current code. Same evidentiary posture as s2924.85 - strong, one notch below CITED. CONFIRM against the current Civil Code index at sync. SECOND INSTANCE OF CROSS-REFERENCE ROT IN CA, and worse than the 2 CCR s12178(f) case: there the target existed but had been re-lettered; here the target is GONE, and CCP s1161(4) was amended by SB 611 in 2024 and made operative 2025-02-01 while still citing it. LANDLORD EXPOSURE is the reason this is an education row rather than a footnote: s3486(a)(1)(E) puts up to $600 of the prosecutor's costs on the owner upon acceptance of an assignment, and s3486(a)(3) assesses the prosecutor's costs against the DEFENDANT OWNER with an abstract of judgment becoming A LIEN ON THE PROPERTY. An owner who ignores a 30-day notice can be joined as a defendant in an action against their own tenant. s3486(b) partial eviction: the court may remove and permanently bar an individual, including a household member, without terminating the tenancy, and may condition the remaining tenancy on the others not inviting that person back. s3486(f)(2)(B) gives the tenant an extreme-hardship stay on clear and convincing evidence, expressly NOT available on economic hardship alone. s3486(a)(5) preserves CCP s1179 relief from forfeiture - NOT READ. TYPE SIZE AND TRANSLATION AGAIN: s3486(a)(1)(C) requires the tenant notice in at least 14-POINT BOLD TYPE and in English plus all the s1632 languages. Fifth type-size floor found in CA and a third s1632 linkage - though this notice is the prosecutor's to serve, not the landlord's, so it is not lease content. s3485 EVIDENCE UPGRADED 2026-09-19, WITH A CAVEAT THE s2924.85 REPEAL DOES NOT CARRY: AB 2930 (Stats. 2018 ch. 880) as enacted on leginfo sunsets s3485 on 2024-01-01; the federal OJP National Gang Center legislation index, citing LexisNexis, lists it 'Repealed effective January 1, 2024'; Justia's latest version is 2022. BUT s3485 HAS BEEN REPEALED AND REVIVED BEFORE - AB 1013 (2007), AB 530 (2009), AB 2310 (2014, re-adding it after a lapse) and AB 2930 (2018). The 2014 revival came AFTER a lapse, so a post-2024 revival is plausible on the section's own history. Two targeted searches found every prior revival and NONE after 2018; per the two-attempt rule the search stopped there. Treat as repealed, but this is the one row in the CA set where a legal-watch hit is genuinely likely: watch for any bill adding s3485 to the Civil Code. FULL s3485 TEXT READ 2026-09-19 (2022 version, the last published): s3485(j) confirms the 2024-01-01 sunset from the section's own words, not just the enacting bill. SCOPE WHILE IN FORCE, s3485(f): only courts with unlawful detainer jurisdiction over property in the CITIES OF LOS ANGELES, LONG BEACH, SACRAMENTO AND OAKLAND - four cities, against s3486's one. So the named-locality pattern is stronger than recorded: both sibling sections were city-confined, to different city lists. While operative it also required a tenant notice in at least 14-POINT BOLD type, translated into every s1632(b) language, and conditioned the prosecutor's standing on annual reporting to the California Research Bureau (s3485(g)-(i)). This text does NOT resolve the revival caveat: a 2022 version shows what was repealed, not whether anything was re-added after 2024. The legal-watch item stands. REVIVAL CAVEAT NARROWED 2026-09-19: Justia's code pages are published by code year, and the s3485 page Taylor supplied is headed '2022 California Code' while every current section in this pass is headed '2025 California Code'. A section re-added by any 2023-2025 enactment would carry a later-year page. So no revival through the 2025 code year; only the CURRENT (2026) legislative session remains unchecked. Treated as repealed.

title: Permitted Payment Methods
bodyText: Tenant may pay Rent and the Security Deposit by the following methods: [list the accepted methods, including at least one that is neither cash nor electronic funds transfer]. If Tenant attempts to pay with a check drawn on insufficient funds or instructs the drawee to stop payment, Landlord may require cash as the only form of payment for up to three months, after giving Tenant written notice that the instrument was dishonored, stating the length of the cash-only period, and attaching a copy of the dishonored instrument.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1947.3, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (amended by SB 611, Stats. 2024 ch. 287, eff. 2025-01-01). Blocks two base rows - see the CA extend manifest. s1947.3(a)(1): at least one form of payment that is NEITHER CASH NOR ELECTRONIC FUNDS TRANSFER must be allowed, so an electronic-only or cash-only rent policy is unlawful from the outset. s1947.3(d) defines EFT broadly enough to catch ACH, card, telephone and recurring transfers, and even 'transfers initiated electronically that deliver a paper instrument'. s1947.3(a)(2): cash-exclusive is permitted ONLY after a dishonored check or a stop-payment instruction, ONLY for up to THREE MONTHS, and only with a written notice that states the dishonour, states the period, and ATTACHES A COPY of the instrument - and it must comply with s827 if it changes the lease terms. s1947.3(a)(3): third-party rent payment must be allowed, subject to a signed acknowledgment; the statute supplies a substantially-prescribed form, and failure to supply it voids the landlord's obligation to accept. s1947.3(a)(3)(E) preserves the landlord's freedom not to enter a Section 8 contract. s1947.3(b): NO FEE for payment by check, for rent or security deposit. Distinct from the s1719 returned-instrument service charge - do not conflate. s1947.3(f): waiver void. SUPERSEDES acceptable-payment-methods (link set 2026-09-19; the manifest recorded the replacement but the field was never populated - the only broken link of the 19 base-to-CA replacements). | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): kept the landlord's accepted methods and cash-only right; the statutory method rule is now a bracket prompt, and the third-party payment and no-check-fee duties moved to edu-payment-methods-ca.

title: Political Signs
bodyText: Tenant may post or display political signs relating to an election or legislative vote, the initiative, referendum or recall process, or issues before a public commission, board or elected local body. In a multifamily dwelling such signs may be posted in the window or on the door of the premises; in a single-family dwelling they may also be posted from the yard, window, door, balcony or outside wall. Landlord may prohibit a political sign only if it is more than six square feet in size, if posting it would violate a local, state or federal law, or if it would violate a lawful provision of a common interest development governing document. Tenant will post and remove political signs within the time limits set by any local ordinance, or otherwise within the period Landlord reasonably establishes, which will begin at least 90 days before the election or vote and end at least 15 days after it.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1940.4, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (added SB 337, eff. 2012-01-01). CONFIRMS the suspicion raised on the extend screen's eyeball pass: the base row common-area-use bars 'any sign, banner, or advertisement visible from outside the property without Landlord's consent', which s1940.4(a) makes unlawful as applied to political signs. common-area-use is BLOCKED for CA.
