The permitted display locations differ by dwelling type - window or door only in multifamily, but also yard, balcony and outside wall for a single-family dwelling - so the builder needs the property type to render this correctly. Only three grounds for prohibition, and size is a hard number: SIX SQUARE FEET. s1940.4(d) makes the TENANT solely responsible for any local-ordinance violation. s1940.4(e): a change of terms made to implement this section, noticed under s827, is NOT a diminution in housing services - which matters under a local just-cause ordinance. s1353.6, cross-referenced at s1940.4(c)(3), NOT READ. | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-tenant-display-and-use-rights-ca). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: Waterbeds and Liquid-Filled Bedding
bodyText: If the structure received its valid certificate of occupancy after January 1, 1973, Landlord will not refuse to rent to Tenant, or refuse to continue renting to Tenant, solely because Tenant has a waterbed or other liquid-filled bedding, provided Tenant meets the requirements of Civil Code section 1940.5. Those include furnishing Landlord, before installation, a waterbed insurance policy for property damage of at least $100,000 written by a carrier licensed in California and maintained until the bedding is removed; conforming to the floor load capacity and distributing the weight on a pedestal or frame substantially the dimensions of the mattress; installing, maintaining and removing the bedding per manufacturer, retailer or state standards, whichever is safest; and giving Landlord 24 hours' written notice before installing, removing or moving it. Landlord may inspect the installation on notice under Civil Code section 1954, may increase the security deposit by one-half of one month's rent, and may charge a reasonable administration fee.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1940.5, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. CONFIRMS the second suspicion from the extend screen's eyeball pass: common-area-use bans waterbeds outright, which s1940.5 forbids for any structure whose valid certificate of occupancy issued AFTER 1973-01-01. common-area-use is BLOCKED for CA on this ground as well as the political-sign ground. s1940.5(g) is a DEPOSIT-CAP EXCEPTION and is cross-noted at security-deposit-cap-ca: 'notwithstanding Section 1950.5' the owner may increase the deposit by one-half of one month's rent, plus a reasonable administration fee. A third exception to the AB 12 cap. s1940.5(f): the inspection right is expressly SUBJECT TO s1954 NOTICE, and non-conforming installation gets a three-day notice to conform or remove unless there is immediate danger to the structure. The insurance limb cross-references s1962 and s1962.5 for application content; s1962.5 NOT READ. Pre-1973 structures are outside the section entirely, so a ban there is unaffected - the builder needs the certificate-of-occupancy date, which the app does not currently capture.

title: Holdover
bodyText: If Tenant does not vacate the property by the end of the Term, Landlord may pursue any remedy allowed by law to recover possession and may recover the actual damages caused by Tenant's continued possession, including the reasonable rental value of the property for the period Tenant remains. Alternatively, Landlord may accept Tenant's continued payment of Rent, in which case this Lease will continue on a month-to-month basis on the same terms, terminable only as provided by law.
notes: CA: written 2026-09-19 to replace the base holdover row for California. CCP s1174 read section-open. CALIFORNIA SUPPLIES NO HOLDOVER MULTIPLIER, so the base row's 'holdover damages in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law for each day' resolves to NOTHING in CA - the same empty-referent defect that forced holdover-oh and holdover-sd. s1174(b) awards ACTUAL damages including rent found due, plus STATUTORY DAMAGES OF UP TO $600 only where MALICE IS SHOWN. That $600 is a court-awarded figure on a malice finding, NOT a per-day amount a lease can stipulate, and it must not be drafted as one. A stipulated per-day holdover charge would itself be liquidated damages under s1671(d) and void absent the impracticability showing, so California is doubly constrained here: no statute to point at, and a stated figure faces s1671(d). Body text therefore claims actual damages and reasonable rental value only. The month-to-month limb is deliberately 'terminable only as provided by law' rather than 'on written notice', because s1946.1 and s1946.2 both govern once the tenancy converts. s1951.5 RESOLVED 2026-09-19 (primary text supplied): it reads in its entirety 'Section 1671, relating to liquidated damages, applies to a lease of real property.' CONFIRMATORY, NOT CORRECTIVE, as predicted - s1671(c)(2) already reached a lease of real property for use as a dwelling on its own terms, and s1951.5 removes any argument that s1671 is confined to contracts for goods and services. No change to this row's analysis; the earlier flag is cleared. MALICIOUS HOLDOVER, added 2026-09-19: CCP s1174(b) - where the defendant is found guilty of unlawful detainer and MALICE is shown, the landlord may be awarded STATUTORY DAMAGES UP TO $600 in addition to actual damages including rent found due. The trier of fact decides which. A landlord remedy, not lease text. | NV: Read in full 2026-09-24 against NRS 118A (revisor text Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated). Applies as written: tracks NRS 118A.470 (actual damages; landlord-consented holdover is month to month on the same terms). Chosen over base holdover, whose "maximum amount permitted by law" figure has no located NV referent - the empty-referent defect this row was written to cure in CA. PROVISIONAL pending NRS Ch. 40 (any holdover multiplier there would add to, not contradict, this text). | NV (text batch 2, 2026-09-24): PROVISIONAL CLEARED. NRS 40.250: a fixed term ends without notice. NRS 40.360(2): in an unlawful-detainer judgment the court awards rent plus THREE TIMES the damages assessed. As in CA, that is a court-awarded measure, not a per-day figure a lease can stipulate; the clause's "any remedy allowed by law" preserves it. | TX: Read in full 2026-09-25 against Tex. Prop. Code chs. 24, 54, 91, 92 and 301 (official statutes.capitol.texas.gov text for chs. 24/54/91/301). Applies as written. No Texas holdover multiplier in chs. 24, 91 or 92 (full read), so the base 'holdover' row's 'maximum amount permitted by law' has no referent (K.3) - not tagged. This row's actual-damages / reasonable-rental-value measure and month-to-month conversion fit Texas; month-to-month termination is s91.001 (one month's notice, or as the parties agree in a signed instrument). | GA: Tagged instead of the base `holdover` (K.3). Georgia has no statutory holdover multiplier: confirmed absent statute-wide (official full-text search 2026-09-28: holdover, 'holding over', 'at sufferance' near rent, damages, double or mesne profits), so the base's 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law' has no referent. A tenancy continued without a set term is a tenancy at will: 60 days' notice from the landlord, 30 from the tenant (O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-6, 44-7-7), which 'terminable only as provided by law' picks up. A stipulated daily holdover rate (as in the Georgia REALTORS lease) would be liquidated damages under O.C.G.A. § 13-6-7; offered as the opt-in `holdover-rate-ga` (Taylor decision 2026-09-28, GA log §6.2). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | NC: Tagged instead of the base `holdover` (K.3). North Carolina has no statutory holdover multiplier (confirmed absent, full-text search 2026-09-28; edu-no-holdover-multiplier-nc): a holdover is removed by summary ejectment (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-26(a)(1)) and the landlord may claim 'damages for the occupation of the premises since the cessation of the estate' (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-28); occupation by permission without agreed rent yields 'reasonable compensation' (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-4). The base's 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law' therefore has no referent. A month-to-month tenancy ends on 7 days' notice (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-14), which 'terminable only as provided by law' picks up; the opt-in periodic-tenancy-notice-nc lets the parties agree a longer period. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | SC: Tagged instead of the base `holdover` (K.3): South Carolina's holdover recovery is statutory, not a per-day figure: attorney's fees if the holdover is not in good faith; if wilful, up to the greater of three months' periodic rent or twice actual damages (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-770(c)); see `edu-holdover-remedies-sc`. Month-to-month continuation ends on 30 days' written notice (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-770(b)). Opt-in daily rate `holdover-rate-sc` (decision 1). | TN: Tagged 2026-09-28 (section text read 2026-09-28 in the built-in browser (Justia host copy of the 2025 Tennessee Code with history lines; 2025-2026 public chapters screened; TN log §1)). Tagged in place of the base holdover (K.3: the base's 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law' has no Tennessee figure). Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-512(c) (Act counties): possession, back rent, fees and other lease damages; actual damages if willful. Pairs with holdover-rate-tn. TN-SCOPE: STATEWIDE. | VA: Tagged 2026-09-28. VA-SCOPE: STATEWIDE. Read against the official Code of Virginia section-open (law.lis.virginia.gov; VA log §1). Basis: Tagged in place of the base holdover (K.3: the base's 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law' has no Virginia figure unless the lease adopts the § 55.1-1253(C) liquidated amount). Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1253(C)-(D): possession plus actual damages, fees and costs; holdover with consent continues on the lease terms with rent change on 30 days' written notice. Opt-in liquidated damages: holdover-rate-va. | AL: Tagged instead of `holdover` (K.3). Alabama's statutory holdover recovery is lump-sum, not per-day: possession, and if the holdover is willful and not in good faith the greater of three months' periodic rent or actual damages, plus reasonable attorney's fees (Ala. Code § 35-9A-441(c)); if the landlord consents, the tenancy becomes periodic (Ala. Code § 35-9A-161(d)). Older double-rent sections (Ala. Code § 6-6-314; Ala. Code § 35-9-100(3)) and their interplay with the Act (Ala. Code § 35-9A-121) are case-law questions, not relied on: `edu-holdover-remedies-al`. Opt-in daily charge: `holdover-rate-al` (Taylor decision 2). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | PA: Tagged. K.3: Pennsylvania has no holdover multiplier; judgment is for 'damages, if any, for the unjust detention' plus rent (68 P.S. § 250.503(a)(2)-(3), Act § 503), matching actual damages / reasonable rental value. Opt-in `holdover-rate-pa`. 'Terminable only as provided by law': Pennsylvania sets only the landlord's notice to quit (68 P.S. § 250.501(b), Act § 501(b): fifteen days for a term of one year or less or an indeterminate term); the tenant's notice comes from `periodic-tenancy-notice-pa` (lease term). The base `holdover` was not tagged because its 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law' has no Pennsylvania measure. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | UT: A fixed term ends without notice (Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-802(1)(a)); 'terminable only as provided by law' reads with periodic-tenancy-notice-ut. The base holdover is not tagged: 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law' would point at the Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-811(3) treble-damages judgment (K.3). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | IL: Tagged. holdover not tagged: its 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law' states only a ceiling (rule 53). Illinois sets its own measures (double yearly value after written demand for a willful holdover, 735 ILCS 5/9-202; double rent after the tenant's own notice, 735 ILCS 5/9-203); this clause does not waive them (edu-holdover-damages-il), and no opt-in holdover rate is offered. Month-to-month notice: periodic-tenancy-notice-il. Read section-open 2026-09-30 (IL log §1). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | ID: Used instead of the base holdover row: the base's 'holdover damages in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' would point at Idaho Code § 6-317, under which a court may enter judgment for three times the actual damages in an unlawful-detainer action (rule 53). This variant claims actual damages and reasonable rental value only. The month-to-month limb is 'terminable only as provided by law' (Idaho Code § 55-208, one month's written notice). Read section-open 2026-09-30 from legislature.idaho.gov (ID log s1). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | MO: Tagged instead of the base holdover, whose 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law' would point at Missouri's double measures (double the yearly value after demand and written notice, Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.080; double rent after the tenant's own notice to quit, Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.100; double damages and double monthly rents in an unlawful detainer judgment, Mo. Rev. Stat. § 534.330), each with its own trigger, which the base clause's 'after the end of the Term' wording does not match (rule 53). The statutory measures remain available by statute (edu-holdover-damages-mo). Accepting Rent creates a month-to-month tenancy ended only on Missouri's notice (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.060(4)(1)). Read section-open 2026-09-30 (MO log §1). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | IN: Applies as written. No Indiana holdover statute or double-rent measure (IN battery 34: 19 sections, none a residential holdover rule); a general tenancy by the landlord's consent is month to month (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-2). Optional companion: holdover-rate-in. Read section-open 2026-09-30 from iga.in.gov (IN log §1). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | OK: Used instead of the base: the base claims holdover damages 'in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law for each day', but Oklahoma's statutory extra measure applies only to a willful holdover not in good faith (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 111(D): not more than twice the average monthly rental, prorated daily), so the base states an amount and trigger the statute does not give (rule 53). holdover-ca claims actual damages including rental value, matching Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 111(D) ('an action for possession and damages'); its month-to-month sentence is the parties' agreement that Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 111(D) allows ('unless the parties otherwise agree') and displaces the older presumption of renewal for up to a year on acceptance of rent (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 35). edu-holdover-ok. Read section-open 2026-09-30 to 2026-10-01 from oklegislature.gov (OK log §1). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | MI: Applies as written in place of the base. Michigan sets no statutory holdover multiplier (MI battery 63); a landlord who wins possession may recover damages from the notice to quit or demand for possession (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5750). Its month-to-month sentence is the parties' agreement; a month-to-month tenancy ends on the notice Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.134(1) sets. edu-holdover-mi. Read section-open 2026-10-01 from legislature.mi.gov (MI log §1). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed.

title: Forfeiture election and the five-day redemption window
bodyText: In California a judgment in an unlawful detainer action declares the lease forfeited only if the three-day notice stated the landlord's election to declare a forfeiture. If the notice did not say so, the lease is not forfeited. Separately, where the action is for nonpayment of rent, the lease has not expired by its own terms and the notice did not elect forfeiture, the court may delay the writ for five days after judgment so that the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee or another interested party can pay the rent, damages and costs and be restored to the tenancy. That five-day delay is mandatory rather than discretionary where the lease is in writing, is for a term of more than one year, and contains no forfeiture clause.
notes: CA: CCP s1174(a) and (c), read section-open 2026-09-19. Routed to education because it governs notice drafting and post-judgment procedure rather than lease text. s1174(a) is a NOTICE-DRAFTING TRAP: omit the election to declare forfeiture from the s1161 notice and the lease survives the judgment. Belongs in the legal tracker's notice generator. s1174(c) IS A FOURTH INSTANCE OF THE OPT-IN PATTERN, and this time the opt-in runs the landlord's way: the five-day mandatory redemption window applies only where the written lease of more than one year 'DOES NOT CONTAIN A FORFEITURE CLAUSE'. Including a forfeiture clause removes the mandatory stay and leaves it discretionary. That is a real drafting decision the library currently does not surface, and it should be weighed against s1174(a)'s requirement that the notice elect forfeiture. NOT drafted as a clause here - flagged for Taylor's decision. s1174(e)-(m) carry an entire abandoned-personal-property regime cross-referencing Civ. Code ss1980-1991, with landlord non-liability safe harbours at (j)-(l). NONE OF THOSE SECTIONS READ - this is an unexplored area and the library has no CA abandoned-property row.

title: Rent Payment
bodyText: Tenant shall pay Landlord monthly rent of {{monthly_rent}} (Monthly Rent) in advance on the due date specified in this Lease, without demand. If the due date falls on a weekend or legal holiday, rent is due on the next business day. Nothing in this Lease limits Tenant's rights under Civil Code sections 1941 and 1942, including Tenant's right to repair and deduct the cost from rent.
notes: CA: overrides the base rent-payment row. The base text requires rent 'without demand, DEDUCTION, OR SETOFF'. Civ. Code s1942.1 makes any agreement waiving or modifying s1941 or s1942 rights VOID as contrary to public policy with respect to any condition rendering the premises untenantable, and s1942 is the repair-and-deduct remedy - so the deduction waiver is void as written. Removed rather than narrowed, and replaced with an express preservation, because a clause that is void in its most important application should not be shipped to tenants as though it bound them. 'Without demand' is retained and is unaffected. Note also that CCP s1161(2) requires a rent notice to state the amount due, which a disputed setoff complicates - see edu-three-day-notice-ca. ALSO relevant, read 2026-09-19: Civ. Code s1942.4 bars a landlord from demanding or collecting rent at all, or issuing a rent increase or a three-day pay-or-quit notice, while the four conditions in s1942.4(a) coexist. See edu-rent-demand-bar-ca.

title: Existing Condition
bodyText: Tenant has examined the property and, by signing this Lease, acknowledges its condition as of the Start Date (Existing Condition), except as otherwise noted in this Lease or in any move-in inspection record. This acknowledgment does not waive or modify Landlord's obligations under Civil Code sections 1941 and 1941.1, does not apply to any condition rendering the premises untenantable, and does not affect Tenant's rights regarding any condition that existed before the tenancy began. Landlord will deliver possession of the property to Tenant on the Start Date in the same or better condition as the Existing Condition, except for ordinary wear and tear.
notes: CA: overrides the base existing-condition row. The base text has the tenant acknowledge the property is 'in good order and repair and satisfactory condition'. Under Civ. Code s1942.1 that is void as a modification of s1941 rights to the extent it reaches any condition rendering the premises untenantable. It also works against the tenant on deposits: s1950.5(e)(2)(B) bars deducting for preexisting conditions, and a blanket good-condition recital is exactly the evidence a landlord would use to defeat that bar. Rewritten to acknowledge CONDITION rather than GOOD condition, with express carve-outs. Pairs with the s1950.5(g) move-in photograph duty at edu-deposit-photo-duty-ca, which for tenancies beginning on or after 2025-07-01 gives both parties a better record than a recital. GROUP NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Property Condition' -> 'Tenant Responsibilities' (session drift; 12 canonical groups are used by all nine states).

title: Services and Utilities Provided
bodyText: Landlord will provide only the services and utilities expressly specified in this Lease, and as otherwise required by applicable law. Except as to any condition that renders the premises untenantable, Landlord is not liable for an interruption or insufficiency of a service or utility resulting from causes beyond Landlord's reasonable control. Nothing in this Lease waives or modifies Landlord's obligations under Civil Code sections 1941 and 1941.1 or Tenant's rights under Civil Code section 1942.
notes: CA: overrides the base services-utilities-provided row. This is the row where I first read CA as diverging from Ohio and was wrong. The base disclaimer is limited to causes beyond the landlord's reasonable control, which Civ. Code s1953(a)(5) may not reach - but s1942.1 does: an agreement modifying s1941 or s1942 rights is void with respect to any condition rendering the premises untenantable, and water, heat and electrical service are s1941.1(a)(3)-(5) tenantability items. Ohio blocked the same row outright under s5321.13(D). CA permits the NARROWER fix rather than removal, because outside tenantability the disclaimer waives no statutory right - so the clause survives with an express tenantability carve-out. This is a genuine drafting difference between the two states on identical base text. GROUP NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Utilities & Services' -> 'Landlord Responsibilities' (session drift; 12 canonical groups are used by all nine states).

title: Property and Common Area Use
bodyText: Tenant will not, without Landlord's written consent, drill holes, use nails, hooks, or screws on the property, or fasten anything to its fixtures, appliances, or interior or exterior surfaces. Tenant will comply with any weight restrictions on balconies or porches and will not use them to store personal belongings without Landlord's consent. Tenant will not keep any item (such as a piano or safe) whose weight Landlord has not agreed is reasonable for the floor without Landlord's prior written consent. Tenant will not burn wax candles at the property. Except for political signs Tenant may display under Civil Code section 1940.4, Tenant will not post or display any sign, banner, or advertisement visible from outside the property without Landlord's consent.
notes: CA: overrides the base common-area-use row, which carried two CA-unlawful limbs. (1) Its blanket ban on any sign visible from outside is unlawful as applied to political signs - Civ. Code s1940.4(a); carved out and cross-referenced to political-signs-ca. (2) Its flat waterbed ban is barred by s1940.5 for any structure whose valid certificate of occupancy issued after 1973-01-01; the waterbed sentence is REMOVED entirely and handled by waterbed-ca, which carries the statutory conditions. The general floor-load sentence is retained because s1940.5(b) and (d) themselves make weight and placement a condition of the waterbed right. Both limbs were caught on the extend screen's eyeball pass, not by the pattern screen. GROUP NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Property Use' -> 'Rules & Regulations' (session drift; 12 canonical groups are used by all nine states). | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): reference to the political-signs clause (now education) repointed to the statute.

title: Pet Policy
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord. Tenant will pay Landlord a pet deposit, if applicable, and pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor, and disturbance caused by a pet. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern. This Section does not apply to an assistance animal, meaning a service animal or a support animal that Tenant or an occupant needs as a reasonable accommodation for a disability: no pet deposit, pet rent, additional security deposit, liability insurance or other additional fee may be charged in connection with an assistance animal, and no breed, size or weight limitation applies to one. Tenant remains responsible for the cost of repairing damage an assistance animal causes, excluding ordinary wear and tear.
notes: CA: overrides the base pet-policy row, which failed for CA on four grounds. (1) 2 CCR s12185(d)(2) bars any pet deposit, pet rent, additional security deposit, liability insurance or other fee for an assistance animal, and s12185(d)(5) bars breed, size and weight limits - carve-out added, mirroring the Ohio OAC 4112-5-07(C) fix. (2) Its indemnity limb waived future claims against the landlord contrary to Civ. Code s1953(a)(2) - REMOVED. (3) Its 'without liability to Tenant' limb was exculpatory under s1953(a)(5) - REMOVED. (4) Its right to 'enter the property and remove a pet' is not among the permitted entry purposes in Civ. Code s1954(a) - REMOVED; any entry must fit s1954 and landlord-entry-ca. Pet deposits remain subject to the s1950.5(c) cap, since a pet deposit is security however denominated. ADDITIONAL CA CONSTRAINT, read 2026-09-19: Civ. Code s1942.7 makes it unlawful to advertise in a manner designed to discourage applicants whose animal is not declawed or devocalized, to refuse or deny occupancy because of a refusal to declaw or devocalize, or to REQUIRE a tenant to declaw or devocalize any animal. 'Animal' covers any mammal, bird, reptile or amphibian - not just cats. Civil penalty up to $1,000 per advertisement or per animal, enforced by a city attorney, district attorney or other prosecutor. Screen any CA pet clause or listing for a declaw requirement.

title: Amounts Due at Signing
bodyText: Tenant will pay Landlord the following amounts, at the time specified for each: first month's Monthly Rent ({{monthly_rent}}) due at signing, and the Security Deposit ({{security_deposit}}) due at signing. These amounts are due in addition to, and are not credited against, Rent due for any other month of the Term.
notes: CA: overrides the base due-at-signing row, whose worked example collected a PET DEPOSIT and LAST MONTH'S RENT alongside the security deposit. Civ. Code s1950.5(b) defines security as any payment to secure performance 'however denominated', so both count toward the one-month cap in s1950.5(c)(1) - the base example invites an unlawful overcollection at the moment of signing, which is also the moment s1950.5(c)(6) fixes as the operative date. Prepaid last month's rent removed from the example entirely; landlords wanting advance rent should use the s1950.5(c)(2) route (six or more months' rent on a lease of at least six months), which is a different mechanism with a different test. Exceptions to the cap that the builder must still handle: s1950.5(c)(5) two-month small-landlord exception (disapplied for service members), and s1940.5(g) half-month waterbed increase. | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): removed the restated deposit-cap sentence (edu-security-deposit-cap-ca).

title: Early Termination
bodyText: Tenant may terminate this Lease before the end of the Term by giving Landlord at least 30 days' written notice. Tenant remains responsible for Rent and other obligations up to the termination date. If this Lease terminates because Tenant breaches it and abandons the property, or because Landlord terminates Tenant's right to possession for breach, Landlord may recover the damages provided by Civil Code section 1951.2. Those damages include the worth at the time of award of the amount by which the unpaid rent for the balance of the Term after the time of award exceeds the amount of the rental loss that Tenant proves could be reasonably avoided. Unpaid rent earned before termination, and rent that would have been earned between termination and the award, shall bear interest at {{judgment_interest_rate}} or, if no rate is stated, at the legal rate. Landlord may terminate this Lease early only as permitted by law, including, where this property is subject to Civil Code section 1946.2, only for a just cause stated in the notice of termination, and only after giving Tenant an opportunity to cure where the law requires one. Nothing in this Section limits any right either party has under applicable law, including Tenant's right to terminate without penalty due to active military service, or due to the property becoming uninhabitable through no fault of Tenant.
notes: CA: overrides the base early-termination row, which failed for CA on two grounds. (1) Its early termination fee - 'one month's Rent or 30% of the remaining Rent, WHICHEVER IS GREATER' - is a liquidated damages provision in a residential lease. Civ. Code s1671(c)(2) routes it to s1671(d), where it is VOID unless actual damage would have been impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, and a whichever-is-greater formula is a penalty on its face. Replaced with an actual-damages-less-mitigation measure. (2) Its landlord limb let Landlord terminate on 30 days' notice for a material breach cured within 10 days, which ignores s1946.2 just cause, the s1946.2(c) cure requirement keyed to CCP s1161(3), and the s1946.1 notice periods. Rewritten to defer to law rather than state its own timetable. The death-of-tenant clause in the base row was dropped as unverified for CA rather than carried over. Civ. Code s1951.2 (landlord's damages on abandonment and the duty to mitigate) has NOT been read and is the section that would confirm the actual-damages measure - flag before this row is relied on. UPDATED 2026-09-19 after reading Civ. Code s1951.2, which the earlier flag said was needed - and the flag was right. s1951.2(c)(1) makes the (a)(3) measure - future rent for the BALANCE OF THE TERM AFTER AWARD, less avoidable loss - available ONLY IF THE LEASE SO PROVIDES, or (c)(2) only if the lessor relet before award and proves good-faith mitigation. My first draft said 'actual damages reduced by reasonable efforts to re-rent', which tracks (a)(2) but SILENTLY FORFEITED (a)(3). The statutory recital is now in the body text. FIFTH INSTANCE of the opt-in landlord right pattern in CA, after s1946.2(b)(2)(A)(ii) owner move-in, CCP s1174(c) forfeiture clause, s827(a) seven-day terms-change notice and s1942.1's arbitration limb. s1951.2(b) adds a second drafting opportunity: interest on the (a)(1) and (a)(2) amounts runs at the rate SPECIFIED IN THE LEASE if lawful, else the legal rate - so a silent lease takes the legal rate by default. The (a)(3) amount is discounted at the FRB San Francisco discount rate plus 1 percent and is not lease-adjustable. Burden note: under (a)(2) and (a)(3) it is the LESSEE who must prove the loss could reasonably have been avoided. s1951.5 RESOLVED 2026-09-19 (primary text supplied): it reads in its entirety 'Section 1671, relating to liquidated damages, applies to a lease of real property.' CONFIRMATORY, NOT CORRECTIVE, as predicted - s1671(c)(2) already reached a lease of real property for use as a dwelling on its own terms, and s1951.5 removes any argument that s1671 is confined to contracts for goods and services. No change to this row's analysis; the earlier flag is cleared. STATE MILITARY RIGHT, added 2026-09-19: California has its own non-waivable military termination right, Mil. & Vet. Code s409 - no early-termination charge, prorated rent, advance rent refunded within 30 days. See military-lease-termination-ca. This row's preservation language already accommodates it.

title: No general right of periodic inspection
bodyText: California limits landlord entry to the purposes listed in Civil Code section 1954. A general right to conduct periodic inspections of an occupied dwelling is not among them. The only inspection the statute provides for is the initial inspection a tenant may request before the end of the tenancy under Civil Code section 1950.5(f). Entry to make necessary or agreed repairs, to supply agreed services, or to show the unit is permitted, but a lease term reserving periodic inspections has no statutory basis and any waiver of section 1954 rights is void under Civil Code section 1953(a)(1).
notes: CA: CONFIRMED ABSENT 2026-09-19 from Civ. Code s1954(a) read section-open. Exists because the base row inspection-rights grants exactly this and is BLOCKED for CA with no replacement - per the proof-of-absence standard an absence recorded only in a prose manifest is invisible to future canvasses. Caught on the extend screen's eyeball pass, not by the pattern screen. Note the practical consequence: a CA landlord wanting a mid-tenancy condition check must fit it to a s1954(a) purpose, and s1953(a)(1) means the tenant cannot agree otherwise.

title: Damages when a tenant breaches and abandons
bodyText: When a tenant breaches the lease and abandons, or the landlord ends the tenant's right to possession for breach, California lets the landlord recover unpaid rent earned before termination, the rent that would have been earned between termination and the award less whatever loss the tenant proves could reasonably have been avoided, and any other detriment proximately caused by the breach. Recovering rent for the balance of the term after the award is different: it is available only if the lease expressly provides for it, or if the landlord re-rented the property before the award and proves the re-rental was reasonable and in good faith. Interest on the pre-award amounts runs at the rate stated in the lease if lawful, otherwise at the legal rate. Making efforts to re-rent does not waive the landlord's right to damages.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1951.2, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. Routed to education alongside the lease clause because the mechanics are litigation measures rather than lease terms. s1951.2(c)(1) is the OPT-IN: without the recital the landlord loses the post-award balance-of-term measure entirely unless it relet before award under (c)(2) - and (c)(2) recovery is itself 'subject to any limitations specified in the lease', so a badly drafted cap can bind the landlord on that route too. s1951.2(b): interest on (a)(1) and (a)(2) at the lease rate if lawful, else the legal rate; the (a)(3) amount is discounted at the FRB San Francisco discount rate PLUS 1 PERCENT and is not lease-adjustable. s1951.2(a)(2)-(3): the burden of proving avoidable loss is on the LESSEE, which is more landlord-favourable than a general duty-to-mitigate framing suggests. s1951.2(d): mitigation efforts do not waive damages. s1951.2(e) preserves the lessor's right to INDEMNIFICATION for pre-termination personal injury or property damage liability 'where the lease provides for such indemnification' - a sixth opt-in, but it sits in tension with s1953(a)(2) (waiver of future causes of action void) depending on whether the indemnity runs to third-party liability or to the tenant's own claims. NOT RESOLVED; flag before drafting an indemnity. s1951.4, cross-referenced at s1951.2(a) as the alternative remedy that keeps the lease in effect, has NOT BEEN READ - it is reported to depend on the lease permitting assignment and subletting subject to reasonable limitations, which would be a seventh opt-in. Read it before relying on either remedy.

title: Continuation of Lease After Abandonment
bodyText: The lessor has the remedy described in California Civil Code Section 1951.4 (lessor may continue lease in effect after lessee's breach and abandonment and recover rent as it becomes due, if lessee has right to sublet or assign, subject only to reasonable limitations).
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1951.4, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. VERBATIM SAFE-HARBOUR TEXT - s1951.4(a) states the remedy 'is available ONLY IF THE LEASE PROVIDES FOR THIS REMEDY' and then supplies this exact wording as a form that 'satisfies this subdivision'. Other wording is permitted, but there is no reason to invent any. SEVENTH CONFIRMED OPT-IN LANDLORD RIGHT IN CALIFORNIA. THIS ROW ALONE IS NOT ENOUGH, and that is the trap: s1951.4(b) makes the remedy operate only if the lease ALSO satisfies one of three sublet/assignment conditions - (1) it permits, or does not prohibit or restrict, subletting or assignment; (2) it permits them subject to express standards reasonable at execution (express standards are PRESUMED reasonable, a presumption affecting the burden of proof), with the landlord not enforcing a standard that has since become unreasonable; or (3) it permits them with landlord consent AND provides that consent shall not be unreasonably withheld, or a standard to that effect is implied by law. A lease reciting s1951.4(a) while forbidding assignment in the landlord's SOLE DISCRETION satisfies none of the three and gets nothing. See no-sublet-assign-ca. s1951.4(c): acts of maintenance or preservation, efforts to relet, appointment of a receiver at the lessor's initiative, and lawfully withholding or terminating consent to a sublet do NOT constitute terminating the lessee's right to possession - so none of them forfeits the remedy.

title: Subletting and Assignment (Reasonable Consent)
bodyText: Tenant will not sublease or assign all or any portion of the property or this Lease without Landlord's prior written consent, which Landlord will not unreasonably withhold. Tenant will not rent the property, or any portion of it, on any short-term rental or home-sharing platform.
notes: CA: overrides the base no-sublet-assign row, and this one is a JUDGMENT CALL FOR TAYLOR RATHER THAN A DEFECT FIX - the base clause is not unlawful in California, it is self-defeating. I marked no-sublet-assign 'provisionally clear' on the extend screen because a sole-discretion consent requirement is permissible in a CA residential lease. That was right as far as it went and WRONG in consequence. Civ. Code s1951.4(b) makes the continue-the-lease-and-collect-rent remedy available only if the lease (1) permits or does not restrict sublet/assignment, (2) permits it subject to express standards reasonable at execution, or (3) permits it with consent NOT UNREASONABLY WITHHELD. 'Sole discretion' satisfies none of the three, so a landlord using the base clause forfeits the s1951.4 remedy entirely - even if the lease also carries continue-lease-remedy-ca. THE TRADE-OFF, stated plainly for Taylor's decision: keep SOLE DISCRETION and retain maximum control over who occupies the property, but lose the s1951.4 remedy and be left with s1951.2 damages after termination; or adopt NOT UNREASONABLY WITHHELD, as drafted here, and keep both remedies at the cost of having to justify a refusal. Most landlords want the remedy. I have drafted the reasonableness version because s1951.4(b)(3) is the cheapest of the three routes and because s1951.4(c)(3) confirms that lawfully withholding consent does not itself forfeit the remedy - but this is reversible on request. s1951.4(b)(2) is the alternative worth considering if control matters more: express standards are PRESUMED reasonable, with the burden on the tenant. The short-term-rental sentence is carried over unchanged and is unaffected by s1951.4. CHOICE GROUP 'ca-sublet-consent' (2026-09-19): this row and no-sublet-assign-discretion-ca are ALTERNATIVES - a CA lease must contain EXACTLY ONE. This is the DEFAULT. The builder has no choice-group field yet; see the log. GROUP NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Property Use' -> 'Tenant Responsibilities' (session drift; 12 canonical groups are used by all nine states).

title: Termination by a Victim of Abuse or Violence
bodyText: Tenant may terminate this Lease if Tenant, a household member, or an immediate family member was the victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking, abuse of an elder or dependent adult, a crime that caused bodily injury or death, a crime involving a firearm or other deadly weapon, or a crime involving the use or threat of force. Tenant must give Landlord written notice with one of the following attached: a copy of a qualifying restraining or protective order; a copy of a written report by a peace officer stating that a report has been filed; documentation from a qualified third party in the form set out in Civil Code section 1946.7; or any other documentation that reasonably verifies the act or crime occurred. Notice must be given within 180 days of the order, the report, or the act or crime. Tenant is responsible for rent for no more than 14 calendar days after giving notice, prorated if the property is re-rented sooner, and is released without penalty from any further obligation. Tenant will not forfeit any security deposit or advance rent because of the termination, and the termination is not a breach of this Lease. Any other tenant remains bound by this Lease.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1946.7, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (SB 1017, Stats. 2022 ch. 558, eff. 2023-01-01). MUCH BROADER THAN 'DOMESTIC VIOLENCE' - s1946.7(a)(6)-(8) reach ANY crime causing bodily injury or death, any crime involving a firearm or other deadly weapon, and any crime involving force or the threat of force. A lease or a canvass row labelled 'domestic violence' understates it. s1946.7(b)(4) is a CATCH-ALL: 'any other form of documentation that reasonably verifies' the act occurred. But s1946.7(k)(2)(B) removes STATUTORY damages against the landlord where the tenant relied on (b)(4) alone - so the catch-all is easier for the tenant to use and weaker to enforce. s1946.7(f): the landlord may NOT require forfeiture of the deposit or advance rent, and the termination is not a breach for any purpose. s1946.7(g): co-tenants stay bound. s1946.7(i): the landlord MAY NOT DISCLOSE the tenant's information to third parties except on written consent or court order - a confidentiality duty. s1946.7(j): may not refuse to rent to someone who previously exercised this right. s1946.7(k): actual damages plus STATUTORY DAMAGES of $100-$5,000. s1946.7(c) is an easily-missed limb: where the victim is an immediate family member who did NOT live with the tenant and no part of the crime occurred in or within 1,000 FEET of the unit, the tenant must attach a further written statement of intent to relocate and why. CROSS-REFERENCE ERROR IN THE STATUTE'S OWN FORM, found 2026-09-19: the verbatim Qualified Third Party Statement in s1946.7(b)(3)(B) says a victim of violent crime advocate is defined 'in Section 1947.6 of the Civil Code'. s1947.6 is the ELECTRIC VEHICLE CHARGING section. The definition is actually at s1946.7(h)(5). The parallel forms in CCP s1161.3(a)(2)(C) and Civ. Code s1941.5(d)(3) both cite s1946.7 correctly, which confirms s1947.6 is a drafting slip rather than an intended cross-reference. If the app ever reproduces the s1946.7 form, reproduce it VERBATIM, error included - the statute says 'substantially the same form', and a silently 'corrected' form is no longer the statutory text - but add a builder-facing note. A third instance of cross-reference rot in CA, after 2 CCR s12185(c)(2) and CCP s1161(4). | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-abuse-violence-protections-ca). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: Right to Summon Emergency Assistance
bodyText: Nothing in this Lease prohibits or limits Tenant, any resident, or any other person from summoning law enforcement assistance or emergency assistance on behalf of a victim of abuse, a victim of crime, or an individual in an emergency. Landlord will not impose or threaten any fee, fine, penalty, termination, non-renewal, or inferior terms of tenancy because such assistance was summoned.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1946.8, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (AB 1171, eff. 2022-01-01). s1946.8(b): ANY lease provision prohibiting or limiting - or THREATENING to prohibit or limit - the right to summon assistance is VOID as contrary to public policy. s1946.8(e): waiver void. This row states the rule affirmatively rather than relying on silence, because a 'nuisance' or 'excessive police calls' clause elsewhere in a lease is the usual way the prohibition creeps in - SCREEN any CA lease for one. s1946.8(d): NO DOCUMENTATION is required to establish the person's belief that assistance was necessary. s1946.8(f)(2): REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTION that the affirmative defence is established if the landlord files an unlawful detainer WITHIN 30 DAYS of assistance being summoned and the notice alleges the summoning was a lease violation or nuisance. The landlord rebuts by showing another substantial motivating factor. 'Penalties' is defined broadly at s1946.8(a)(3) to include inferior terms and conditions of tenancy, not just fees and eviction. | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-emergency-assistance-right-ca). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: Abuse and violence: eviction bar, lock changes, confidentiality
bodyText: A landlord may not terminate or refuse to renew a tenancy based on an act of abuse or violence against the tenant, the tenant's immediate family member, or a household member once the landlord has received qualifying documentation. There are two exceptions: where the perpetrator is a tenant in residence of the same unit, and where the perpetrator's words or actions have threatened the physical safety of other tenants, guests or invitees and the tenant continues to permit the perpetrator on the premises after a three-day notice requiring them not to. Where a person restrained by court order is a tenant of the same unit, the landlord must change the locks at the landlord's own expense within 24 hours of a written request accompanied by the order, and give the protected tenant a key; if the landlord does not, the tenant may change the locks and the landlord must reimburse the cost within 21 days. Information a tenant provides under these protections may not be disclosed to third parties without written consent or a court order. A landlord is not liable to other tenants for complying. Ending the lease (Civ. Code 1946.7): a tenant may terminate if the tenant, a household member or an immediate family member was the victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking, elder or dependent-adult abuse, a crime that caused bodily injury or death, a crime involving a firearm or other deadly weapon, or a crime involving force or its threat. The tenant gives you written notice, within 180 days of the order, report or act, attaching a qualifying restraining or protective order, a peace officer's written report that a report was filed, qualified third-party documentation in the statutory form, or other documentation reasonably verifying the act. The tenant owes rent for no more than 14 days after the notice (prorated if you re-rent sooner), is released without penalty, forfeits no deposit or advance rent, and isn't in breach; any other tenant stays bound. Keep the tenant's information confidential. Where the person who committed or allegedly committed the abuse or violence is not a tenant of the same unit, change the locks at your own expense within 24 hours of the tenant's written request with any documentation listed in Civ. Code 1941.5(d), and give the tenant a key. If you don't, the tenant may change the locks without your permission and you must reimburse them within 21 days, provided they use locks of similar or better quality, tell you within 24 hours and give you a key.
notes: CA: CCP s1161.3 (amended AB 1756, eff. 2024-01-01) and Civ. Code s1941.6 (amended SB 1051, eff. 2025-01-01), primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. s1161.3(b)(2)(B) is the operative landlord route and it is procedural: the three-day notice requires the TENANT not to voluntarily permit or consent to the perpetrator's presence - it is not a notice to the perpetrator, and it only works if the perpetrator's conduct threatened others' physical safety. s1161.3(c) protects the landlord from other tenants' claims arising from compliance. s1161.3(d)(2) routes same-unit-perpetrator cases to CCP s1174.27, NOT READ. s1941.6 applies ONLY where the restrained person is a TENANT OF THE SAME UNIT - a different and narrower trigger than s1161.3. The 24-hour clock runs from the written request plus the order. s1941.6(c)(3) limits the self-help lock change to leases executed on or after 2011-01-01. s1941.6(e): the excluded person remains liable for rent under the lease. s1941.6(d) disapplies s789.3 liability - s789.3 READ 2026-09-19, see edu-self-help-eviction-ban-ca. The carve-out is necessary because excluding the restrained co-tenant by a lock change would otherwise be a willful lockout within s789.3(b)(1). Confidentiality duties sit in both s1161.3(e) and Civ. Code s1946.7(i). CCP s1174.27 READ 2026-09-19 (the same-unit-perpetrator procedure s1161.3(d)(2) routes to): where the court finds documentation of abuse or violence, the defendant raising the defence and other occupants not otherwise at fault are NOT guilty and owe NOTHING - no holdover damages, costs, termination fees or attorney's fees. Where another defendant is shown to be the perpetrator and guilty, the court MUST order a PARTIAL EVICTION of that person only, WITHOUT terminating the tenancy, and MUST order the landlord to change the locks; it may bar the perpetrator permanently, taking custody and visitation arrangements into account. A s1174.27 finding is inadmissible in any other proceeding. | CA: Content from dv-lease-termination-ca (switched off) added by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); unchanged: Civ. Code §1946.7; CCP §1161.3(a)(2)(C); Civ. Code §1941.5(d)(3); 2 CCR §12185(c)(2); CCP §1161(4). | CA: Content from lock-change-non-cotenant-ca (switched off) added by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); unchanged: Civ. Code §1941.5; CCP §1161.3(a)(1).

title: Protected classes and source-of-income rules
bodyText: California prohibits housing discrimination on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information, including a perception that a person has any of those characteristics or is associated with someone who does. Source of income includes federal, state and local public assistance and housing subsidies, expressly including Section 8 vouchers and HUD-VASH vouchers, so refusing to rent because an applicant holds a voucher is unlawful. Where there is a government rent subsidy, any financial or income standard must be based only on the portion of rent the tenant actually pays, and an applicant must be offered the option of supplying alternative evidence of ability to pay instead of a credit history. A landlord must also count the aggregate income of people residing together on the same basis as it would for married people.
notes: CA: Gov. Code ss12955 (amended SB 267, eff. 2024-01-01) and 12927 (SB 222, eff. 2020-01-01), primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. Answers two canvass rows at once. THREE OPERATIONAL RULES most likely to be breached by a screening workflow rather than by lease text: s12955(n) aggregate-income rule; s12955(o)(1)(A) subsidy income standard keyed only to the TENANT'S PORTION - a 3x-the-rent rule applied to full contract rent is unlawful for a voucher holder; and s12955(o)(1)(B) the credit-history alternative, which requires giving reasonable time AND reasonably considering the alternative evidence. These bind the app's screening logic, not the lease. s12955(b) bars INQUIRY into most protected characteristics - note source of income is deliberately absent from the (b) list and s12955(p)(2) confirms asking about level or source of income is not itself discrimination. s12927(c)(2)(A): narrow exception for renting a portion of an OWNER-OCCUPIED single-family house to ONE roomer or boarder, and even then the s12955(c) advertising ban still applies. s12927(d): 'housing accommodation' expressly includes units offered through a HOSTING PLATFORM. s12927(c)(1) is the statutory basis for the reasonable accommodation and modification duties implemented by 2 CCR ss12176-12181. ENFORCEMENT, Gov. Code ss12980-12989.3 read 2026-09-19: administrative complaint within ONE YEAR (s12980(b)); a private civil action within TWO YEARS, tolled while the complaint is pending, and available whether or not a complaint was filed (s12989.1); actual AND PUNITIVE damages, injunctions and discretionary prevailing-party fees (s12989.2); Attorney General pattern-or-practice suits with civil penalties up to $50,000 for a first violation and $100,000 for each subsequent one (s12989.3). NEW from 2026-01-01 (SB 477): s12981(a)(2) requires ALL PARTIES to take part in the department's MANDATORY DISPUTE RESOLUTION, free of charge, before the department sues. Candidate 572.7: NO RESPONDENT ELECTION RIGHT - because CA housing cases are not heard administratively at all. The department prosecutes by CIVIL ACTION in superior court (s12981(a)(1)), so there is no administrative forum for a landlord to elect out of, unlike Ohio's s4112.055(A)(2).

title: Tenant harassment and immigration-status disclosure
bodyText: California makes it unlawful for a landlord, for the purpose of influencing a tenant to vacate, to engage in conduct amounting to theft or extortion, to use or threaten force or menacing conduct interfering with the tenant's quiet enjoyment, to commit a significant and intentional violation of the entry statute, or to threaten to disclose information about the immigration or citizenship status of a tenant, occupant or anyone associated with them. A tenant who prevails may recover a civil penalty of up to $2,000 for each violation. Separately, it is unlawful to disclose such immigration or citizenship information to any immigration authority, law enforcement agency or government agency for the purpose of harassing or retaliating against a tenant, influencing them to vacate, or recovering possession. A court that finds such a disclosure must order statutory damages of between 6 and 12 times the monthly rent for each person whose status was disclosed, issue injunctive relief, and notify the district attorney. Separately, you may not ask about the immigration or citizenship status of a tenant, prospective tenant, occupant or prospective occupant, or require them to disclose or certify it (Civ. Code 1940.3(b)). You may still request information or documentation needed to verify financial qualifications or identity, and comply with federal law, a subpoena, warrant or court order.
notes: CA: Civ. Code ss1940.2 and 1940.35 (both AB 291, eff. 2018-01-01), primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. s1940.2(a)(4) is the one that connects to the rest of this state's work: a SIGNIFICANT AND INTENTIONAL VIOLATION OF s1954 is statutory harassment, so misuse of the entry right is not merely a s1954 problem - it carries the s1940.2(b) $2,000-per-violation penalty. Cross-reference landlord-entry-ca and edu-no-periodic-inspection-ca. s1940.35 damages are MANDATORY and formula-based - 6 to 12 times monthly rent PER PERSON - plus attorney's fees to the prevailing party (s1940.35(e)) and waiver void (s1940.35(g)). s1940.35(h) lets a 501(c)(3) bring the injunctive action as a party. Among the most severe landlord penalties found in any state in this project. s1940.2(c) safe harbour: a good-faith oral or written warning about conduct that violates the lease, and ordinary explanation of the lease in the normal course of business, are not violations. Also relevant to retaliation: Civ. Code s1942.5(c)/(e) separately make threatening immigration reporting retaliatory conduct - three overlapping provisions on the same subject. | CA: Content from immigration-status-inquiry-ca (switched off) added by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); unchanged: Civ. Code §1940.3(b).

title: Disposing of personal property left after a tenancy
bodyText: California provides an optional procedure for personal property a tenant leaves behind after the tenancy ends and the premises are vacated. The landlord gives written notice to the former tenant and anyone else reasonably believed to own the property, describing it well enough to be identified, stating where it may be claimed, that reasonable storage costs may be charged, and a claim deadline at least 15 days after personal delivery or 18 days after mailing. The statute supplies notice forms that satisfy the requirement. Property must be left on the premises or stored safely with reasonable care. If it is not claimed, it must be sold at public sale after published notice, unless the landlord reasonably believes the total resale value is under $700, in which case the landlord may keep or dispose of it. Sale proceeds left over go to the county within 30 days and may be claimed by the former tenant for a year. A landlord who follows the procedure is protected from liability. No storage cost may be charged if the tenant reclaims property within two days of vacating.
notes: CA: Civ. Code ss1980-1991 (Chapter 5, Disposition of Personal Property Remaining on Premises), primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. CLOSES A GAP THE PROJECT HAD NO ROW FOR IN ANY STATE. s1981(a): the procedure is OPTIONAL, but s1981(e) is the sting - if its requirements are not satisfied, the chapter does not protect the landlord at all and ordinary liability rules apply. The s1989 non-liability shield is the whole point of using it. PRESCRIBED FORMS at s1984 (former tenant) and s1985 (other owner), each 'in substantially the following form'; s1984(b) requires ONE OF TWO alternative closing statements depending on whether the property will be publicly sold or is believed worth under $700. Getting the wrong one in loses the shield. s1982: property the landlord reasonably believes to be LOST goes to police or sheriff first under ss2080 et seq., not through this chapter - and only if they refuse does this chapter apply. s1988(a) $700 threshold; s1988(c) surplus to the county within 30 days, claimable for one year. s1990(c): if stored on the premises, the storage cost is the FAIR RENTAL VALUE of the space; no cost at all if reclaimed within two days. s1983(a): records are presumed to be the TENANT'S. s1981(c) excludes manufactured homes, mobilehomes and commercial coaches; s1981(d) excludes animals; s1980.5 excludes commercial property but NOT self-storage units. s1991 permits combining this notice with a s1951.3 notice of belief of abandonment - s1951.3 since READ (2026-09-19), see edu-abandonment-belief-notice-ca. Note the two notices run on the SAME 15-day personal / 18-day mailed clock, which is what makes combining them practical. CCP s1174(e)-(m) is the post-writ route into this chapter. SERVICE MEMBERS, added 2026-09-19: Mil. & Vet. Code s409.1(b) bars foreclosing or enforcing ANY lien on a service member's property or personal effects - EXPRESSLY INCLUDING LIENS FOR STORAGE - during service and 120 days after, except on a prior court order. So recovering storage costs against a service member's left-behind property needs a court order first. Misdemeanor plus damages and fees.

title: Death on the premises: the three-year rule
bodyText: California law occupies the field on disclosing deaths that occurred on a property. An owner or agent is not required to disclose the occurrence of an occupant's death, or the manner of death, where the death occurred more than three years before the prospective tenant offers to rent, and is never required to disclose that an occupant was living with HIV or died of AIDS-related complications. The implication is that a death within the previous three years is treated as a material fact. An owner or agent is also not immunized for an intentional misrepresentation made in response to a direct question about deaths on the property.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1710.2, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. NOTE it sits in Part 3, Obligations Imposed by Law - outside the landlord-tenant title. Sixth cross-chapter confirmation in CA. The section is drafted as a NON-disclosure safe harbour, not as a disclosure duty, so it states no affirmative requirement and the three-year duty is an inference from s1710.2(a)(1)(A)'s carve-out plus the general materiality standard. FLAGGED AS AN INFERENCE, NOT A HOLDING - the row is written as education and no lease clause is shipped. Confirm against case law before the app prompts for it. s1710.2(b): express field preemption over death and HIV-status disclosure. s1710.2(d): no immunity for an intentional misrepresentation in response to a DIRECT INQUIRY - so 'has anyone died here?' must be answered honestly even outside the three years. s1710.2(c) preserves all other physical-condition disclosure duties. 'Transferee' expressly includes a lessee or renter.

title: Eviction court records are masked for 60 days
bodyText: An unlawful detainer court file in California is not publicly accessible for the first 60 days after the complaint is filed. During that period the clerk may release records only to a party or their attorney, to someone who supplies the names of a plaintiff and a defendant plus the address including any unit number, to a resident of the premises who identifies a party or the case number and proves residency, or by court order on a showing of good cause. After 60 days the file opens if judgment has been entered for the plaintiff, and in a residential case based on a post-foreclosure claim only if judgment was entered for the plaintiff after a trial. The parties may also stipulate to bar access entirely. The clerk mails every named defendant a notice within 24 to 48 hours of filing, with legal-aid and lawyer-referral information.
notes: CA: CCP s1161.2, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (amended AB 2304, eff. 2025-01-01). Answers the eviction-record-sealing canvass row - but the mechanism is MASKING AT FILING, not sealing after the fact, which is a materially different design from the sealing statutes found in ND and elsewhere. The default is CLOSED and access opens only on the s1161.2(a)(1)(E)-(G) conditions; a landlord who loses, or who settles, leaves a permanently non-public file. s1161.2(a)(2) also permits the parties to stipulate to bar access - a settlement lever worth knowing. s1161.2(d): an extra $15 filing fee on the plaintiff's first appearance. s1161.2(c) prescribes the clerk's notice content including a verbatim State Bar referral statement; that is the clerk's duty, not the landlord's, and no lease row is needed.

title: Balcony and exterior elevated element inspections
bodyText: Buildings with three or more multifamily dwelling units must have their exterior elevated elements - balconies, decks, porches, stairways, walkways and entry structures more than six feet above ground that rely on wood for support - inspected by a licensed architect, engineer, qualified contractor or certified building inspector hired by the owner. At least 15 percent of each type must be examined. The inspector delivers a written report within 45 days. Inspections were due by January 1, 2026 and are required every six years after that. Elements needing repair must be corrected by the owner under permit, within 120 days of permit approval, and anything posing an immediate threat requires immediate action including blocking access. An owner who does not comply within 180 days faces a civil penalty of $100 to $500 per day and a recordable building safety lien.
notes: CA: H&S s17973, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (amended AB 130, eff. 2025-06-30). This is one of the two previously-unread entry grounds in Civ. Code s1954(a)(6) - now closed. Entry to comply with this article is a permitted purpose, so a landlord scheduling these inspections has a s1954 basis, subject to the notice requirements in landlord-entry-ca. THE DEADLINE HAS PASSED: first inspections were due 2026-01-01, so any CA landlord with 3+ units who has not done one is already exposed to the s17973(i)(2) penalty of $100-$500 PER DAY plus a building safety lien with judgment-lien priority. That makes this a live compliance item, not a future one. s17973(d)(1): reports kept for two inspection cycles and DISCLOSED AND DELIVERED TO THE BUYER on sale. s17973(n): does not apply to a common interest development. s17973(o): local governments may impose greater requirements - another municipal-layer deferral. s17973(e): buildings permitted on or after 2019-01-01 are inspected within six years of the certificate of occupancy.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText: Landlord has installed smoke alarms approved and listed by the State Fire Marshal, and, if the property has a fossil fuel burning heater or appliance, a fireplace, or an attached garage, a carbon monoxide device. Landlord has ensured that the smoke alarms are operable as of the start of this tenancy. Tenant shall notify Landlord or the manager if Tenant becomes aware that any alarm is inoperable, and Tenant shall not disable, remove or obstruct any alarm. Landlord will correct any reported deficiency. Landlord or Landlord's agent may enter the property to install, repair, test and maintain alarms on reasonable written notice, during normal business hours, except in an emergency.
notes: CA: H&S ss13113.7 and 17926, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. s13113.7(d)(2)(B) is the lease-relevant duty and it is time-specific: AT THE TIME A NEW TENANCY IS CREATED the owner must ensure smoke alarms are OPERABLE - not merely installed. Thereafter the tenant must notify the owner of an inoperable alarm, and the owner IS NOT IN VIOLATION for a deficient alarm of which it has received no notice. That allocation is why this ships as a lease clause rather than education. s13113.7(d)(2) extended the owner's testing and maintenance duty to RENTED SINGLE-FAMILY DWELLINGS from 2014-01-01. s13113.7(a)(4): battery-operated alarms suffice unless a local rule prohibits them. s13113.7(b) excludes manufactured homes, mobilehomes and commercial coaches. Violation is an infraction, max $200 per offence (s13113.7(e)). CO devices are CONDITIONAL, not universal: s17926(a) requires one only in a unit having a FOSSIL FUEL BURNING HEATER OR APPLIANCE, A FIREPLACE, OR AN ATTACHED GARAGE. All compliance deadlines have long passed. s17926(c)(2) gives a 30-DAY NOTICE TO CORRECT before any fine, and s17926(d) caps the civil remedy at ACTUAL DAMAGES NOT EXCEEDING $100 - a remarkably limited remedy next to the rest of CA's landlord penalties, and worth not overstating to landlords. SEPARATE ENTRY AUTHORITY: s13113.7(d)(2)(A) grants its own right of entry to install, repair, test and maintain alarms, with its own reasonable-written-notice and 24-hour presumption, sitting in the Health and Safety Code rather than Civ. Code s1954. Cross-noted at landlord-entry-ca. H&S s17926.1 (referenced at s17926(g)) NOT READ. GROUP NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Property Condition' -> 'Landlord Responsibilities' (session drift; 12 canonical groups are used by all nine states).

title: Electric Vehicle Charging Station
bodyText: If Tenant has an allotted parking space, Landlord will approve Tenant's written request to install an electric vehicle charging station at that space where the request meets the requirements of Civil Code section 1947.6 and complies with Landlord's procedural approval process for modifications to the property. Tenant's request must include Tenant's consent to a written agreement covering Landlord's requirements for installation, use, maintenance and removal, a complete financial analysis and scope of work, a written description of the proposed modifications, Tenant's obligation to pay all costs associated with the installation and its infrastructure before any work is done, and Tenant's obligation to pay as part of rent the cost of electricity used and of any damage, maintenance, repair, removal and replacement. Tenant and any successor must maintain personal liability coverage in an amount not exceeding ten times the annual rent, covering property damage and personal injury caused by the installation or operation of the station, unless the station is certified by an OSHA-approved Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory and the work is performed by a licensed electrician. Landlord is not required to provide an additional parking space, and may charge monthly rent for a space that becomes reserved as a result.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1947.6, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (amended SB 638, eff. 2020-01-01). Applies to any lease EXECUTED, EXTENDED OR RENEWED on or after 2015-07-01, so it reaches long-standing tenancies at renewal. FOUR EXEMPTIONS the builder must evaluate, s1947.6(b): EV stations already available to lessees at 10 PERCENT OR MORE of designated spaces; parking not provided as part of the lease; FEWER THAN FIVE PARKING SPACES; or the dwelling is subject to a residential rent control ordinance - BUT that last exemption was itself switched off for any lease executed, extended or renewed on or after 2019-01-01, so it is now spent except in the narrow s1947.6(b)(5) case (rent control PLUS a local ordinance adopted on or before 2018-01-01 requiring approval). Do not code (b)(4) as a live exemption. s1947.6(i) is the insurance off-ramp: NO insurance may be required where the station is NRTL-certified AND a licensed electrician did the work. TENSION TO WATCH: s1947.6(h) authorises an insurance requirement, while 2 CCR s12181(f) bars imposing insurance as a condition on a DISABILITY-RELATED modification - different contexts, but a request framed as both would need care. Not resolved. s1947.6(g)(3) points at the OPR 'Zero-Emission Vehicles in California: Community Readiness Guidebook' Permitting Checklist - a non-statutory document the app cannot validate against. GROUP NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Property Use' -> 'Rules & Regulations' (session drift; 12 canonical groups are used by all nine states).

title: Criminal history in tenant screening
bodyText: California regulates how criminal history may be used in tenant screening. Blanket bans are unlawful: a policy excluding everyone with a criminal record, or with any prior conviction, misdemeanor or felony, is prohibited outright. A landlord may not seek, consider, use, or take adverse action based on an arrest that did not lead to conviction, on being questioned or detained, on participation in a diversion or deferred entry of judgment program, on an infraction, on a conviction that has been sealed, dismissed, vacated, expunged, pardoned or otherwise rendered inoperative, on a conviction for which a certificate of rehabilitation was granted, or on juvenile adjudications. Only convictions directly related to a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest may be considered, judged by the nature and severity of the offense and how much time has passed. Whether a screening practice is defensible turns partly on whether it gives the applicant written notice of an opportunity to present mitigating information and actually considers it, checks the accuracy of the record, and delays the criminal history inquiry until after financial and other qualifications are verified. Mitigating information includes youth at the time of the offense, time elapsed, good tenant history, rehabilitation, and conduct arising from the applicant's status as a survivor of abuse or from a disability.
notes: CA: 2 CCR ss12264-12271 (Civil Rights Council, Article 24, operative 2020-01-01), primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. CLOSES the tenant-screening gap flagged from s1950.1(f) - an area the canvass had no row for in ANY state. s12269(a)(5) bans BLANKET BANS by name and gives four examples, so the most common screening policy in the industry is per se unlawful in CA. s12269(a)(1)-(4) list categories that may not be sought OR considered at all - note 'SEEK' is prohibited, so merely running a report that surfaces them is exposure, not just acting on them. Narrow proviso: if the APPLICANT volunteers such information as mitigating evidence, it may be considered. s12266(d)(4) is the structural one for the product: delaying criminal history inquiry until AFTER financial and other qualifications are verified is a factor in whether a less discriminatory alternative was feasible. That is a workflow-ordering rule, not a lease term, and it interacts with the s1950.6(c)(2) screening-process choice and the s1950.1 reusable-report regime. s12266(e) mitigating information expressly includes conduct arising from SURVIVOR STATUS (DV, sexual assault, dating violence, stalking) and conduct arising from a DISABILITY that could be mitigated by a reasonable accommodation - linking this article to dv-lease-termination-ca and to ss12176-12181. s12269(b): the seven-year look-back permitted by Civ. Code s1785.13(a)(6) is a ceiling, not a safe harbour - a court may find a SHORTER look-back was the feasible alternative. s12270(a): complying with a federal law that REQUIRES consideration (sex offender public housing ineligibility, meth manufacture) is an affirmative defence. s12271: local ordinances may be more protective and are not displaced. s12268(b): advertising a lawful screening policy is not itself unlawful. ss12005(f), 12005(k), 12062(c)-(d) and Gov. Code s12955.8 NOT READ.

title: Damage, Destruction and Failure to Deliver
bodyText: Tenant may terminate this Lease before the end of the Term if Landlord does not, within a reasonable time after Tenant's request, fulfill Landlord's obligations to place and secure Tenant in quiet possession of the property, to put it into good condition, or to repair it. Tenant may also terminate if the greater part of the property, or the part that was the material inducement to Tenant entering this Lease, is destroyed by any cause other than Tenant's want of ordinary care. If the property is destroyed, this Lease terminates.
notes: CA: Civ. Code ss1932 and 1933, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. Answers two canvass rows that had been open - the fire/casualty termination right and the failure-to-deliver-possession remedy - and CORRECTS an earlier entry: I recorded failure-to-deliver-possession as 'not located' after reading s1925, which only defines hiring. The remedy is in s1932(1), one chapter over. s1932(1) is broader than casualty: it covers failure within a reasonable time after REQUEST to secure quiet possession, to put the property into good condition, OR to repair - a general termination right for landlord non-performance sitting in Chapter 1, separate from the s1942 repair-and-deduct remedy in Chapter 2 and cumulative with it. s1932(2)'s 'material inducement' limb is unusual and worth preserving verbatim in substance: partial destruction suffices if the destroyed part was what induced the tenant to rent. s1933(4): destruction of the thing hired terminates the hiring by operation of law - no notice needed, which is why the body text states it rather than conditioning it on Tenant's election. Both sections date from 1872/1905 and neither has been tested here against s1946.2 just cause; a landlord asserting s1933(4) on a covered property should still expect the s1946.2 notice machinery to apply to the possession claim. NOT RESOLVED. | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-casualty-termination-ca). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: When a landlord may not demand or collect rent at all
bodyText: California bars a landlord from demanding rent, collecting rent, issuing a notice of rent increase, or issuing a three-day notice to pay rent or quit where four conditions all exist. The dwelling substantially lacks one of the standard habitability characteristics, violates Health and Safety Code section 17920.10, or is substandard under section 17920.3 to an extent that endangers life, limb, health, property, safety or welfare. A public officer responsible for enforcing housing law has inspected the premises and notified the landlord in writing of the obligation to abate or repair. The conditions have gone unabated for 35 days beyond service of that notice without good cause. And the conditions were not caused by the tenant. A landlord who violates this is liable for actual damages plus special damages of between $100 and $5,000, and the prevailing party recovers attorney's fees and costs. The court may also order the conditions abated and retain jurisdiction until they are.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1942.4, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. SHOULD HAVE SURFACED EARLIER IN THIS PASS - it is the most consequential habitability remedy in the CA set and it was missed until the canvass forced the question. It bars the landlord's core economic act, not merely the eviction. ALL FOUR CONDITIONS MUST COEXIST, and condition (2) is the practical gate: it requires an INSPECTION AND WRITTEN NOTICE BY A PUBLIC OFFICER, so a tenant's own complaint does not trigger the bar. Condition (3) runs 35 DAYS from service, and s1942.4(a)(3) makes service complete ON DEPOSIT IN THE MAIL, not receipt. s1942.4(d): the tenant need NOT exhaust any other remedy first - so this sits alongside s1942 repair-and-deduct rather than after it, and s1942.4(f) makes it cumulative. s1942.4(e): available in small claims. DIRECT PRODUCT CONSEQUENCE: a three-day notice issued while this bar applies is void ab initio, so the legal tracker's notice generator needs a gate here, not just the CCP s1161(2) content checks - cross-refer edu-three-day-notice-ca. Also note s1942.4(a)(1) cites H&S s17920.10, the OTHER incorporation in s1941.1(a) - READ 2026-09-19, see edu-lead-hazards-ca. A unit with lead hazards at or above the s17920.10(c) thresholds satisfies condition (a)(1) of the bar, and repair work disturbing lead paint without containment can itself create one. s1942.4(f) carve-out: the section does not bind a landlord pursuing Ellis Act rights under Gov. Code s7060 et seq. - NOT READ. FEE EXPOSURE, CCP s1174.21 read 2026-09-19: a landlord who brings a NONPAYMENT unlawful detainer while liable for a s1942.4 violation is liable for the TENANT'S attorney's fees and costs. So filing through the bar costs the landlord the tenant's fees as well as losing the case.

title: Attorney-fee clauses are reciprocal by operation of law
bodyText: In California, if a lease provides that attorney's fees incurred to enforce it will be awarded to one party or to the prevailing party, the party who actually prevails is entitled to reasonable fees whether or not the lease names them. A one-sided fee clause therefore operates in both directions, and any provision waiving that rule is void. The fee provision is read as applying to the whole contract unless both parties were represented by counsel in negotiating and executing it and the lease says so. The court decides who prevailed, may find that nobody did, and there is no prevailing party at all where the action was voluntarily dismissed or dismissed under a settlement.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1717, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19.
