title: Sealed Eviction Records
bodyText: An Arizona court must seal all records of an eviction case if it dismisses the case before judgment or enters judgment for the tenant, and must also seal a case when the landlord and tenant file a written stipulation to set aside the eviction order and seal the file. Sealed records are available only to the parties and their attorneys, the court and the clerk, and may not be sold or released in bulk or individual record transfers to third parties. This covers summary eviction, forcible entry and detainer and special detainer records, including pleadings, findings, orders and exhibits. A court may also seal an eviction case when a landlord fails to respond within 15 days to a tenant's motion to compel satisfaction of a paid judgment. Sealed records are left out of the courts' public remote access.

title: Removing a Guest or Unauthorized Occupant
bodyText: In Arizona, a guest of a tenant who is not named on a written lease and who stays without the tenant's or landlord's permission is not a lawful tenant, and a law enforcement officer may remove a person who knowingly remains, at the request of the tenant or the landlord entitled to possession. Separately, an owner of residential property may bring a forcible detainer action against an unauthorized person who entered while the property was not open to the public, is not a current or former tenant, had no agreement to live there with the owner, is not an immediate family member, and has refused the owner's request to leave, when no other litigation is pending between them; the writ issues immediately after judgment. This route does not apply to landlords and tenants.

title: Bounced Checks and Returned Payments
bodyText: In Arizona, the holder of a dishonored check, draft, order or note may charge the maker a service fee of not more than $25 plus any actual charges the holder's financial institution assessed because of the dishonor. Separately, a person who writes a check with intent to defraud, knowing there is no account or insufficient funds, is liable in a civil action for twice the amount of the check or $50, whichever is greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney fees. Failure to pay within 12 days after notice of nonpayment (given in person, or in writing by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the address on the check) is prima facie evidence of intent to defraud.

title: Renting in a Condominium or HOA Community
bodyText: An Arizona condominium or planned-community association may not require a renting owner to disclose anything about a tenant beyond the names and contact information of adult occupants, the lease period with start and end dates, and a description and license plate numbers of the tenants' vehicles (plus photo ID showing age in an age-restricted community). The association or its manager may charge up to $25 per new tenancy (not for renewals) for that information, payable within 15 days, and no more than $15 for incomplete or late information; otherwise it may not treat rental units differently from owner-occupied units in fees, fines or requirements. It may not demand the tenant's application, credit report or lease, or require the tenant to sign a waiver of due process rights. An owner may use a crime-free lease addendum, the association may enforce a restriction on registered level two and three sex offenders, and the owner of rental property must abate criminal activity.

title: Criminal Activity on Rental Property
bodyText: Arizona treats residential property regularly used to commit crimes as a nuisance. The attorney general, county or city attorney, a homeowners' or condominium association, or an affected resident may sue the owner or manager to abate it. An owner or manager who receives a government notice of documented criminal reports is deemed to know of the activity and must begin within five business days to take legally available action to abate it. If the owner fails to act, a government authority may abate the nuisance and the cost becomes a priority lien on the property. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act supports this: a landlord may give notice of immediate termination for a material and irreparable breach such as drug dealing, gang activity, prostitution, threats or assault on the premises. A city may require the owner of slum-designated or seriously substandard property to hire a licensed property manager and join the city's crime-free multihousing program.

title: What a Landlord Need Not Disclose
bodyText: Arizona bars any criminal, civil or administrative action against a lessor for failing to disclose that the property is or was the site of a natural death, suicide, homicide or other felony; was owned or occupied by a person with HIV, AIDS or another disease not known to spread through common occupancy; or is near a sex offender. Failing to disclose these facts is not grounds to terminate or rescind a lease.

title: Landlord's Remedies After a Tenant's Breach
bodyText: An Arizona landlord may recover all reasonable damages from the tenant's breach of the lease or of the tenant's statutory duties, court costs, reasonable attorney fees and all quantifiable damage the tenant caused to the property, and after termination may claim possession, rent and separate actual damages. The landlord must mitigate damages. If a tenant abandons, the landlord must make reasonable efforts to rerent at a fair rental; the lease ends when a new tenancy begins, or, if the landlord does not try to rerent or accepts the abandonment as a surrender, when the landlord learns of the abandonment. For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, the remaining term for this purpose is one month or one week. A tenant who willfully holds over in bad faith owes up to the greater of two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages. A tenant who ends a lease by falsely claiming domestic violence and is convicted owes treble damages, and the person named in the order or report who provoked the termination is liable to the landlord for the resulting economic losses.

title: Foreclosure Notices to Tenants
bodyText: If an Arizona owner receives a notice of trustee's sale or other foreclosure notice after a tenant has signed a lease, the owner must give the tenant written notice of the possible foreclosure, in the statutory form, within five business days. This applies only to the first such notice received after the lease was signed, and does not apply to multifamily units of four or more connected units. If the owner fails to give the notice (or the move-in notice required for a lease signed after foreclosure began), the tenant may give a notice of landlord noncompliance and recover damages and injunctive relief, and the deposit must be returned. If a foreclosure action began before the lease is signed, give the tenant the statutory move-in notice first; the lease's optional Notice of Possible Foreclosure clause carries its text.

title: Rules, Regulations and Lease Amendments
bodyText: An Arizona landlord's rules bind a tenant only if they promote tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protect the property from abuse or fairly distribute services; are reasonably related to that purpose; apply to all tenants fairly; are explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do; do not evade the landlord's obligations; and the tenant had notice of them when signing. A rule adopted later binds the tenant on 30 days' notice if it does not substantially modify the lease. When a government adopts a new law affecting existing leases, the landlord may amend leases immediately to comply, with written notice describing the amendment and its effective date.

title: No Late-Fee or Application-Fee Cap
bodyText: Arizona's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act sets no dollar cap on late fees or rental application fees. A late fee must be reasonable and stated in a written lease: only a reasonable late fee set forth in a written lease can be required to reinstate a lease before an eviction is filed, and the eviction judgment includes late charges stated in the lease.

bodyText: Arizona's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not require a landlord to hold security deposits in a separate or interest-bearing account or to pay interest on them. During the tenancy a landlord may use refundable deposits as any applicable property management agreement allows, but all refundable deposits must be refunded under the deposit statute at the end of the tenancy.

title: Rent Increases
bodyText: Arizona's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has no rent-increase notice statute and no cap on increases, and local rent control is preempted. Rent is set by the lease; during a fixed term it cannot be changed without the tenant's agreement. For a month-to-month tenancy, a landlord generally changes the rent by giving the 30-day written notice that would end the tenancy. title: City Rental Tax Repealed: No Pass-Through
bodyText: Since January 1, 2025, no Arizona city, town or other taxing jurisdiction may levy a transaction privilege or similar tax on renting residential property. The law that repealed the tax also removed the landlord's former statutory right to adjust rent on 30 days' notice when a city changed its rental tax rate, so a lease clause invoking that right no longer has a legal basis. Through December 31, 2026, a landlord may not charge a tenant the amount of the repealed tax, and in any lawsuit the landlord must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that a challenged charge, assessment or other amount does not represent all or part of the repealed tax. Do not add a 'tax', 'fee' or other line item that replaces the old city rental tax.

title: Foreign Adversary Land Ownership and Lease Ban
bodyText: Since September 12, 2026, Arizona bars a foreign adversary nation or its agent from buying, leasing or otherwise obtaining a substantial interest in Arizona real property, directly or through an entity. The law targets foreign governments, state-owned or state-controlled companies, and entities tied to countries identified on federal national-security lists. It is enforced by the Attorney General, not by landlords. Whether it reaches an ordinary residential lease to an individual tenant is unsettled, and no official guidance exists. Do not screen applicants by citizenship or national origin: that exposes a landlord to fair-housing claims, and the statute itself says enforcement may not be based on race or national origin. If an applicant is a foreign government or a company it controls, get legal advice before signing.

title: Crime-Free Lease Addendum
bodyText: [Optional.] Tenant, each occupant, and each guest or other person on the property with Tenant's consent will not engage in criminal activity, including drug-related criminal activity, on or near the property, and will not permit the property to be used to facilitate criminal activity. A violation is a material noncompliance with this Lease. Where Arizona law treats the violation as a material and irreparable breach, Landlord may deliver a notice of immediate termination as that law provides; otherwise Landlord will give the notice Arizona law requires before terminating. Tenant is responsible for a guest's violation to the extent Arizona law makes a tenant responsible for a guest's actions. This Section does not apply to criminal activity of which Tenant or a member of Tenant's household is the victim, including domestic violence or sexual assault, and nothing in this Section penalizes Tenant or any other person for summoning a law enforcement officer or other emergency assistance.
notes: AZ: Read section-open 2026-09-26/27 in the browser from azleg.gov (official legislative compilation, stated as updated through the 57th Legislature, 2nd Regular Session, 2026). azleg ARS pages print no history lines, so currency rests on the compilation date and the session-law check in the AZ log (s1.1). TAYLOR'S DECISION (2026-09-27): widely used in Arizona but not required, so offered as an optional clause. Statutory footing: A.R.S. §§33-1260.01(G) and 33-1806.01(G) ('An owner may use a crime free addendum as part of a lease agreement' - associations may not prohibit it); §33-1906 (a city may require the owner of slum-designated or seriously substandard property to participate in its crime free multihousing program); §§33-1260.01(I), 33-1806.01(I), 12-991 (owners must abate criminal activity). No statute read prescribes the addendum's content. Drafting limits built in: (1) termination runs through A.R.S. §33-1368(A) - immediate termination only for a material and irreparable breach 'that occurs on the premises' (non-exhaustive list: weapons discharge, homicide, prostitution, gang activity, drug activity, threats, assault, nuisance, conduct jeopardizing health, safety and welfare, serious property damage), special detainer under §33-1377(E); otherwise the 10-day notice; the addendum does not create a shortcut around the statutory notices; (2) guest liability tracks §33-1368(F) (tenant responsible if the tenant could reasonably be expected to be aware and did not try to prevent it) rather than strict liability, to avoid an argued waiver under §33-1315(A)(1); (3) victim carve-out consistent with §33-1318(L) (a landlord may still terminate a victim for UNRELATED acts); (4) no penalty for summoning police or emergency help, which §33-1315(A)(4)-(5) bars (and which some crime-free and nuisance programs have been criticised for). 'On or near the property' KEPT (Taylor's decision 2026-09-27): he wants off-property conduct such as an assault on a neighbor on the neighbor's own property to be a lease violation. Mechanics: off-premises conduct cannot support an immediate termination under §33-1368(A) (the material-and-irreparable breach must occur 'on the premises', which by §33-1310(11) includes grounds and facilities held out for tenants generally), so it goes through the 10-day notice; a completed assault cannot be 'remedied', so the lease ends on the notice date. Fair housing: blanket criminal-activity provisions can draw disparate-impact claims (A.R.S. §41-1491.14; federal FHA, not read); federal HUD guidance on criminal-records screening NOT checked for current status. For federally assisted housing, federal VAWA and HUD lease-addendum rules apply (not read). The Mesa origin of the Crime Free Multi-Housing program is background (recall), not relied on.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: A security deposit refund that a tenant never claims or cashes does not become the landlord's money. Under Arizona's unclaimed property law, a security deposit, refund or credit balance is property that is presumed abandoned three years after the owner's right to demand it or the landlord's obligation to pay it arises, and is then handled under the unclaimed property law administered by the Arizona Department of Revenue.

title: Servicemembers: Lease Protections
bodyText: Arizona's landlord-tenant act has no rule letting a servicemember end a lease of an apartment or house early; the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act governs that. Separately, Arizona law gives members of the National Guard and the armed forces reserves who are ordered to active duty or training by Arizona, another state or the United States the protections that federal servicemember civil-relief law gives people on federal active duty. That can reach Guard members serving on state orders, whom federal law alone may not cover. When a tenant presents military orders with a request to end the lease or pause an eviction, get legal advice before refusing it. Arizona's only military rule inside the landlord-tenant statutes is for mobile home park spaces.

title: Holding Deposits and Earnest Money
bodyText: Arizona statutes have no rule written for holding deposits, earnest money or other money taken from an applicant before a lease is signed. Two rules in the Arizona Residential Landlord and Tenant Act bear on it. First, once the lease is signed, money applied to deposits or prepaid rent counts toward the limit on all security, however named, of one and one-half months' rent (a tenant may still choose to prepay more rent). Second, the landlord must state in writing the purpose of every nonrefundable fee or deposit, and any fee or deposit not designated nonrefundable is refundable. The statutes do not say whether that rule reaches money taken before a lease exists, so a landlord who means to keep a holding deposit if the applicant backs out should say so in writing, with the amount and purpose, before taking it. A real estate broker who takes earnest money on a lease must state in the lease or receipt what form it took (cash, check, promissory note or other item of value) and place it in the designated broker's care.

title: Accuracy of Rental Application
bodyText: Tenant represents that the information Tenant gave Landlord in Tenant's rental application and during screening was true, correct and complete when given, and Tenant acknowledges that Landlord relied on that information in entering into this Lease. If any of that information was materially false or misleading, Tenant is in material breach of this Lease, and Landlord may exercise the remedies this Lease and applicable law provide for a material breach. This Section does not apply to information that Landlord was not permitted by law to request or consider.
notes: NEW SHARED ROW 2026-09-27 (Taylor's decision after the AZ AAR comparison, AZ log §16.4/§17). Uniform text for all 14 states. Classified RECOMMENDED like comparable boilerplate (`no-sublet-assign`, `joint-liability`). title: Towing Vehicles from Rental Property
bodyText: Before a private towing company may remove a vehicle from an Arizona rental property without the vehicle owner's permission, the property owner or the owner's agent must authorize the tow in writing, either by signing each towing order or by a written towing contract that runs for a specific period. The towing company cannot act as the owner's agent, and a tow without that authorization (or a law enforcement request) is a crime for the towing company. Inside a city or town, the owner is treated as allowing unrestricted public parking in any parking area unless signs, clearly visible and readable from anywhere in the parking area and at each entrance, state the parking restrictions, what happens to vehicles that violate them, the maximum cost to the vehicle's owner including storage and other charges, and the phone number and address where the vehicle can be found. Cities and counties may cap private towing rates. Abandoned and junk vehicles follow separate motor-vehicle procedures. Check your city's towing rules before relying on the lease's towing clause.
notes: AZ: Read section-open 2026-09-26/27 in the browser from azleg.gov (official legislative compilation, stated as updated through the 57th Legislature, 2nd Regular Session, 2026). azleg ARS pages print no history lines, so currency rests on the compilation date and the session-law check in the AZ log (s1.1). CONTROLLING TEXT: A.R.S. §9-499.05(A)-(D), (F) (cities and towns: rate regulation; deemed consent to unrestricted public parking unless posted with the four-item signs; tow only on a law enforcement request or the owner's or agent's express written permission after complying with (B), by signing each order or a written contract valid for a specific length of time; carrier may not act as owner's agent; carrier violation class 2 misdemeanor; abandoned/junk vehicles under Title 28, ch. 11 excluded) and §11-251.04 (counties: same written-authorization rule, no sign requirement, city regulation displaces county rates), both read section-open 2026-09-27. §28-4847(A) (release of a towed vehicle on written request and payment) read in part. NOT READ: Title 28, ch. 11 (abandoned vehicles); city towing ordinances (flagged, instruction 20). `parking-vehicle-rules` (tagged) says towing happens 'in accordance with applicable law', so no clause conflict. Found by full-text search: towing (50 hits), towed (28) - landlord-relevant hits read. Source: landlord-experience screen (gap-discovery source 3), AZ log §18.

title: Selling a Rented Property
bodyText: When an Arizona landlord sells a rented dwelling in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser, the seller is released from liability under the lease and the landlord-tenant act only for events after the seller gives the tenant written notice of the sale, unless the parties agreed otherwise. The seller stays liable to the tenant for the security deposit and prepaid rent the tenant is entitled to get back, and whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is also bound by the deposit-return rules. A property manager whose management ends is likewise released only after written notice to the tenant. The owner and manager disclosure given to the tenant must be kept current, and the new owner's information must be on file with the county assessor. Showing the unit to buyers requires at least two days' notice to the tenant unless it is impracticable.
notes: AZ: Read section-open 2026-09-26/27 in the browser from azleg.gov (official legislative compilation, stated as updated through the 57th Legislature, 2nd Regular Session, 2026). azleg ARS pages print no history lines, so currency rests on the compilation date and the session-law check in the AZ log (s1.1). CONTROLLING TEXT: A.R.S. §33-1325(A)-(B) read section-open 2026-09-27 ('He remains liable to the tenant for any property and money to which the tenant is entitled under section 33-1321'); §33-1321 successor clause (see `security-deposit-return-az`); §33-1322(C) disclosure kept current (`landlord-disclosure-az`); §33-1902 (`edu-rental-registration-az`); §33-1343(A), (D) exhibiting to purchasers on two days' notice (`landlords-access-az`). The ch. 10 full read supports the rest. NOT STATED: whether the lease binds the buyer (common law, not researched - the body does not say). title: Water Submeter Billing Disclosure
bodyText: Water Submeter Billing. [Include this section only if Landlord will bill Tenant for water service separately from Rent through a submeter. It must be given in at least 10-point type before this Lease is executed.] Tenant will be billed for water service separately from Rent. Landlord estimates the monthly bill for water service for dwelling units at the property at {{water_bill_estimate}}, based on {{water_bill_estimate_basis}}. Bills are due {{water_bill_due_dates}} and are paid as follows: {{water_bill_payment_procedure}}. Tenant may contact Landlord or Landlord's billing agent with questions about water service billing at {{water_billing_address}}, {{water_billing_email}} and {{water_billing_phone}}. The monthly bill for water service may include only the following charges: the amount due for the usage measured by the submeter, charged at allowable rates; a portion of the fixed fee charged by the water purveyors for water service; a fee for Landlord's or the billing agent's costs; and any late fee, with the amounts and times assessed. Tenant shall notify Landlord of any leaks, drips, water fixtures that do not shut off properly, including a toilet, or other problems with the water system, including problems with water-saving devices, and Landlord is required to investigate and, if necessary, repair these problems within 21 days. Tenant may report any leaks, drips or water fixtures that do not shut off properly to Landlord or Landlord's agent at {{water_repair_address}}, {{water_repair_email}} and {{water_repair_phone}}. Landlord will provide any of the following if Tenant asks: the location of the submeter, the calculations used to determine a monthly bill, and the date the submeter was last certified for use together with the date it is next scheduled for certification. If Tenant believes that the submeter reading is inaccurate or the submeter is malfunctioning, Tenant shall first notify Landlord in writing and request an investigation. This disclosure is only a general overview of the laws regarding submeters, and those laws can be found at Chapter 2.5 (commencing with Section 1954.201) of Title 5 of Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code.
notes: CA: NEW 2026-09-28, gap-discovery source 2 (real-lease comparison). Civ. Code s1954.204, read section-open on leginfo 2026-09-28; the ten subdivisions were also taken verbatim from a FindLaw reproduction before the leginfo read, and the two agree. THE MISS: the whole of Chapter 2.5 (commencing with s1954.201) was flagged as UNREAD in landlord-entry-ca's own notes - s1954(a)(5) names it as an entry ground and the CA pass identified it as the water submetering chapter but never read its substance. A CA landlord who submeters water and bills separately therefore got NO disclosure at all from this library. Surfaced by both professional leases: the CAA form's water-conservation section and the C.A.R. RPOD's water-submeter item. PRESCRIBED FORM, s1954.204: the disclosure must be made BEFORE EXECUTING the rental agreement, IN WRITING, in AT LEAST 10-POINT TYPE, and the statute expressly says it 'may be incorporated into the rental agreement' - which is why this ships as a lease clause rather than education. That is the fifth prescribed type-size floor in the CA set. All ten items are mandatory: (a) separate billing; (b) an estimate computed EITHER from the average or median bill for comparative units at the property over any three of the past six months OR from average indoor use by a family of four of approximately 200 gallons per day plus all other monthly charges - the builder must ask which basis was used and record it; (c) due dates and payment procedures; (d) a mailing address, an email address AND a toll-free or local telephone number for billing questions; (e) the closed list of permitted charges; (f) the tenant's notification duty and the landlord's 21-DAY investigate-and-repair duty; (g) a second set of contact details, for leaks - the statute requires contact details TWICE, for billing and for leaks, and they may differ; (h) three items supplied on request, including the submeter's last and next certification dates; (i) the write-first-and-request-an-investigation route; (j) the pointer to the chapter, which the statute effectively dictates. CLASSIFIED CONDITIONAL, not REQUIRED: the duty is unconditional once the landlord elects to bill separately through a submeter, but that election is the landlord's, so the clause is included only when it applies - the same shape as ordnance-demolition-meter-disclosures-ca and unbundled-parking-ca. SCOPE, s1954.202: 'submeter' is a device measuring an individual rental unit's consumption in a multiunit residential or mixed-use structure, owned and operated by the landlord or the landlord's agent; 'property' is real property of two or more dwelling units served by a single master meter; 'landlord' excludes a tenant subletting to subtenants and excludes a common interest development. OPERATIVE 2018-01-01 by s1954.218. Distinct from Civ. Code s1940.9, the SHARED-METER disclosure in ordnance-demolition-meter-disclosures-ca: s1940.9 is about the tenant's meter serving areas outside the unit; this is about the landlord submetering and reselling. NOT READ: ss1954.207 to 1954.212, 1954.215 to 1954.217 and 1954.219, and the Water Code s537 et seq. multiunit-structure install mandate found by the same search. See edu-water-submeter-billing-ca for the billing, late-fee and termination rules. | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): optional (Taylor's pattern 3): the disclosure is owed before signing; the clause records it. Companion: edu-water-submeter-billing-ca.

title: Billing tenants for water through a submeter
bodyText: If you submeter water and bill tenants separately from rent, California regulates the bill itself, not just the disclosure. You may bill only for the volume measured by the submeter at allowable rates, a share of the fixed charge the water purveyor bills the property, a fee for your own or your billing agent's costs, and a late fee. Submeters must be read within three days of the same point in each billing cycle, payments must be due at the same point in each cycle, and the bill must separately set out the beginning and ending readings and dates, the consumption in gallons, the rates, any amounts carried over, any late fee, the total, the due date and how to reach you with questions. A tenant cannot be required to pay electronically. A late fee may not be imposed until 25 days after the bill is sent, and is capped at seven dollars on the first bill and ten dollars on each later bill, with all late fees in any twelve-month period limited to ten percent of the unpaid amount; partial payments go against the oldest outstanding bill. Two rules matter most. Water service charges are not rent, so unpaid water is never a pay-or-quit matter: once a bill is 180 days overdue or the unpaid amount reaches two hundred dollars, the route is a three-day notice to perform conditions or covenants or quit. And you may not shut off or interfere with water service for any reason, including nonpayment. The submeter disclosure must be given, in at least 10-point type, before the lease is signed; the lease's optional clause carries it.
notes: CA: NEW 2026-09-28, gap-discovery source 2. Civ. Code ss1954.205, 1954.206, 1954.213 and 1954.214 read section-open on leginfo 2026-09-28. Companion to water-submeter-disclosure-ca. s1954.205(a) is a CLOSED LIST of billable items, with three alternative volumetric calculations - (A) the tenant's submeter share of the purveyor's usage dollars, (B) for a tiered rate schedule, either method (A) or dividing each tier's volume evenly among the dwelling units and applying each block's rate, (C) the purveyor's exact per-unit rates where it charges per dwelling unit - plus a share of recurring fixed charges computed either proportionally to volumetric use or by dividing them equally among all residential and nonresidential units, plus an administrative fee under (a)(3). s1954.206: three-day read window, same-point due dates, written consent for electronic bills which the tenant may rescind at any time with 30 days for the landlord to comply, NO requirement to pay electronically, and an eleven-item bill-content list. s1954.213 is the one that will surprise landlords: (a) no late fee until 25 days after mailing or other transmittal, with a business-day rollover; (b)(1) $7 first, $10 each subsequent; (b)(2) all late fees in any 12-month period capped at 10 PERCENT of the unpaid amount, excluding the s1954.205(a)(3) administrative fee; (b)(3) partial payments credited to the OLDEST outstanding bill; (c) at 180 days overdue OR $200 unpaid the landlord may terminate under CCP s1161 with a THREE-DAY NOTICE TO PERFORM CONDITIONS OR COVENANTS OR QUIT; (d) water service charges DO NOT CONSTITUTE RENT; (e) the landlord may not shut off or otherwise interfere with water service FOR ANY REASON, INCLUDING NONPAYMENT. Three consequences for existing rows. (1) late-fee-safe-harbor-ca: this is the only residential late-fee CAP in California, and it applies to water bills, not rent - see that row's revised notes. (2) The s1954.213(c) route is NOT a pay-or-quit, because (d) takes water out of rent; edu-three-day-notice-ca's s1161(3) limb is the applicable one. (3) s1954.213(e) is ABSOLUTE and carries NO intent element, unlike Civ. Code s789.3 in edu-self-help-eviction-ban-ca, which requires intent to terminate the occupancy - so a submetered-water shutoff is unlawful even where s789.3 would not reach it. s1954.214 preserves local ordinances adopted before 2013-01-01 on submeter approval, installation, maintenance, reading, billing and testing, so the municipal layer is live here too (edu-municipal-layer-ca). ALSO FOUND, NOT READ: PUC s739.5 (master-meter rate treatment) and Water Code ss537-537.5 (multiunit-structure submeter install mandate). The application-of-payments shared row is NOT in conflict: it orders payments of rent and lease charges, while s1954.213(b)(3) orders water bills among themselves, and water is not rent. | CA: Pattern-3 sentence added by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29) for water-submeter-disclosure-ca.

title: Mold Booklet Delivery
bodyText: Dampness and Mold. Before signing this Lease, Landlord gave Tenant the consumer-oriented booklet on dampness and mold for renters published by the California Department of Public Health, which describes the potential health risks and the health impact that may result from exposure to mold, and Tenant acknowledges receiving it. Landlord is not required to conduct air or surface testing of the unit or the building for mold. Tenant will promptly notify Landlord of any dampness, water intrusion, leak or visible mold in the unit.
notes: CA: NEW 2026-09-28, gap-discovery source 2 (real-lease comparison). H&S s26148 read section-open on leginfo 2026-09-28. THIS ROW EXISTS BECAUSE edu-mold-disclosure-contingency-ca WAS WRONG - see that row's correction. s26148(a): 'Residential landlords SHALL provide written disclosure to prospective tenants of the potential health risks and the health impact that may result from exposure to mold by distributing a consumer-oriented booklet developed and disseminated by the department.' (b) before entering the rental or lease agreement. (c) the requirements do not apply until the first January 1 or July 1 at least six months after the department APPROVES THE BOOKLET. TWO DIFFERENT CONTINGENCIES IN ONE ARTICLE, and that is the whole point: s26147(e) is contingent on CDPH adopting s26103/s26105 permissible exposure limits and s26130 remediation guidelines, which it has NEVER done; s26148(c) is contingent only on CDPH APPROVING A BOOKLET, which it HAS done. So s26147 is still suspended and s26148 is live. OPERATIVE DATE: CDPH's own Indoor Air Quality mold page states 'As of Jan. 1, 2022, California rental housing providers are required to provide this mold booklet to prospective tenants.' The booklet is 'Information on Dampness and Mold for Renters in California' (CDPH, dated 2021-05-12), which is consistent with a 2022-01-01 operative date under (c). EVIDENTIARY LIMIT, stated rather than glossed: the statute is read from the official revisor site, but the operative date rests on CDPH'S OWN STATEMENT of the requirement, not on a located approval instrument; the formal approval date was not found, and the CDPH page does not cite s26148. If the approval date were shown to be different the operative date could shift, but not the existence of the duty. This is the same class of administrative fact the sibling row already relies on for the s26103 non-adoption. THE DUTY IS DELIVERY, NOT DRAFTING: s26148 requires distributing the booklet, so this clause is the acknowledgment, and the app must actually deliver the current CDPH booklet - a lease recital with no booklet is not compliance. Both professional leases screened do exactly this (C.A.R. RLMM 12/24 paragraph 38A; CAA CA-041 12/24 section 33). The no-testing sentence restates s26147(b), which binds regardless of the (e) suspension. BUILDER: the booklet is a CDPH-hosted PDF that is revised - treat its URL and edition as a maintained app-config value on the legal watch, like the MyHazards address in flood-disclosure-ca. NOT DONE: no check of whether CDPH has issued a later edition than 2021-05-12. | CA: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): optional (Taylor's pattern 3): the disclosure is owed before signing; the clause records it. title: Towing a vehicle from the property
bodyText: A lease clause saying you may tow is not enough in California. Unless the parcel is improved with a single-family dwelling, you may only have a vehicle removed without the vehicle owner's consent if a sign at least 17 by 22 inches, with lettering at least one inch high, is displayed in plain view at ALL entrances to the property, prohibiting public parking, stating that vehicles will be removed at the owner's expense, and giving the telephone number of the local traffic law enforcement agency together with the name and telephone number of every towing company you have a written general towing authorization agreement with. Two other routes exist: 96 hours after a parking-violation notice has been issued, or, for a vehicle missing a major part needed to operate safely, 24 hours after you notify local traffic law enforcement. If you have a vehicle removed without meeting one of those conditions, you are liable for DOUBLE the towing or storage charges. Separately, the towing company may not start a tow without your written authorization, and whoever authorizes it must normally be present and verify the violation. There is one exception built for small landlords: if the property has 15 or fewer units with no onsite owner, agent or employee, the tenant may verify the violation and request the tow from that tenant's own assigned space, giving you a signed request or email either up front or within 24 hours of calling, which you pass to the towing company within 48 hours.
notes: CA: NEW 2026-09-28, gap-discovery sources 2 and 3. Veh. title: Selling the property with a tenant in place
bodyText: Selling a tenanted California property triggers four separate duties. First, showings: entry to exhibit the unit to prospective or actual purchasers needs the ordinary written notice, but if you have given the tenant written notice within the previous 120 days that the property is for sale and that you or your agent may contact the tenant to arrange showings, you may then give ORAL notice a reasonable period before entry, and you must leave written evidence of the entry inside the unit. Second, the deposit: on transferring your interest you must either hand the remaining deposit to the buyer and then notify the tenant in writing of the transfer, the claims made against the deposit, the amount held and the successor's name, address and telephone number, or return it to the tenant with a full accounting. Before a voluntary transfer you must also give the buyer a written statement of the deposit remaining, an itemisation of lawful deductions and which of the two routes you chose. Get this wrong and you and the buyer are jointly and severally liable. Third, the identity disclosure must be kept current and runs against the new owner or manager, who has 15 days to comply and may not serve a nonpayment notice for rent that accrued while out of compliance. Fourth, nothing in California law obliges a tenant to sign an estoppel certificate or a certification of lease terms for your lender or buyer; that is a matter of contract only.

title: Holding deposits and money taken before the lease
bodyText: California has no holding-deposit statute, which is exactly why this is a trap. If you take money from an applicant to hold a unit, it is almost certainly security: the deposit statute defines security as any payment, fee, deposit or charge imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to reimburse you for processing a new tenant or as an advance payment of rent, used for any purpose, however denominated. Security counts toward the one-month cap and is refundable, so calling money a non-refundable holding fee does not make it one. The single exception is the application screening fee, which the statute expressly says is not security and not an advance fee, and which has its own cap, receipt and refund rules. Practical consequence: keep the screening fee separate and documented, and treat anything else you collect before move-in as refundable deposit money, or as first month's rent if that is what it is. Whether a true pre-tenancy holding deposit can be forfeited when an applicant backs out is unsettled in the statutes; the safest course is a short written agreement signed before the money changes hands that says what happens if either side walks away.

title: No Liens for Tenant Improvements
bodyText: The interest of Landlord in the property will not be subject to liens for improvements made by Tenant, whether or not Landlord has consented to the improvements. Before any work begins, Tenant will notify every contractor, subcontractor and supplier that makes or furnishes any improvement to the property for Tenant of this provision.
notes: FL: Lead from the Florida Realtors Residential Lease for Single Family Home or Duplex (RLHD-3x Rev 7/16, (c)2022 Florida Realtors; approved by the Supreme Court of Florida 2010-04-15), gap-discovery source 2 (FL log, gap-discovery backfill). Primary text read section-open 2026-09-27 from the official 2026 Florida Statutes (flsenate.gov), with history line. Opt-in landlord right (instruction 30). Controlling text: Fla. Stat. §713.10 (s. 5, ch. 2023-226 latest). Why it matters: under §713.10(1), when a lessee makes an improvement 'in accordance with an agreement between such lessee and her or his lessor, the lien shall extend also to the interest of such lessor'. no-alterations (tagged FL) has the landlord consenting to alterations, which can create that agreement. §713.10(2)(a): when the lease 'expressly provides that the interest of the lessor shall not be subject to liens for improvements made by the lessee', the lessee must notify the contractor, and a knowing or willful failure makes the contract voidable at the contractor's option. FULL PROTECTION NEEDS RECORDING (§713.10(2)(b)): the lessor's interest is not subject to such liens when the lease terms expressly prohibit it AND either (1) the lease or a short form or memorandum containing the specific prohibiting language is recorded in the county before a notice of commencement, or (2) a parcel-wide notice (lessor's name, legal description, the specific lease language, and a statement that all or a majority of leases on the parcel prohibit such liability) is recorded before a notice of commencement. Contractor demand: a lessor who does not serve a verified copy of the lease provision within 30 days after a contractor's written demand, or serves a false copy, is subject to the lien (§713.10(3)). Landlord steps are in edu-construction-liens-fl. Builder: include by default in FL leases; prompt the landlord about recording. title: Tenant Improvements and Construction Liens
bodyText: In Florida, when a tenant makes improvements under an agreement with the landlord, a contractor's lien can reach the landlord's interest in the property. A lease can prevent this, but only if the lease expressly says the landlord's interest is not subject to liens for the tenant's improvements and the landlord also records, in the county's official records before the contractor records a notice of commencement, either the lease (or a short form or memorandum containing that language) or a notice covering the parcel that states the lease language and that all or most leases on the parcel contain it. The tenant must tell its contractors about the provision. If a contractor sends the landlord a written demand for a copy of the lease provision, the landlord must serve a verified copy within 30 days; failing to respond, or sending a false copy, exposes the property to the contractor's lien.

bodyText: [Use only if the property is in a condominium, cooperative or homeowners' association whose governing documents require the association to approve a lease or a tenant.] This Lease is contingent on the association's approval. Tenant will apply promptly, give the association the information it reasonably requires, and cooperate in the approval process. The association's application fee will be paid by {{association_fee_payer}}. If approval has not been given by {{association_approval_deadline}}, either party may end this Lease by written notice to the other before approval is given, and Landlord will then return all amounts Tenant has paid under this Lease. Tenant will not owe Rent for any period before approval during which Tenant is not permitted to take possession. Any security deposit the association requires of Tenant is separate from the Security Deposit under this Lease.

title: Condominium and HOA Rules for Renting
bodyText: Florida condominium and homeowners' associations can affect a rental in three ways. First, approval: if the association's documents require it to approve leases, a condominium association may charge an approval fee only if its documents provide for one, capped at $150 per applicant (adjusted for inflation every 5 years) and not charged for a renewal with the same tenant; it may also require the tenant to put up a deposit of up to one month's rent to protect the common areas, handled like a landlord's deposit. Second, rental restrictions: a homeowners' association rule adopted after July 1, 2021 that prohibits or regulates rentals binds only owners who buy after it is adopted or who consent to it, except that any association may regulate leases shorter than 6 months and limit rentals to three times a year. Third, rent demands: if the owner of a condominium unit or of a home in a homeowners' association falls behind on association charges, the association can demand in writing, using a notice form set by statute, that the tenant pay the rent to the association until the owner's debt is paid. The tenant must then pay the association and is immune from the landlord's claim for the rent paid to it. For a condominium, the tenant also gets credit against the rent owed to the landlord, and the association can serve Chapter 83 notices and evict the tenant for not paying it. A landlord may not retaliate against a tenant for paying rent to an association on its demand.

title: Removing Squatters (Unauthorized Occupants)
bodyText: A Florida property owner can ask the sheriff to remove squatters from a residential property without going to court if all of these are true: the owner or the owner's agent makes the request; the property includes a dwelling; the people entered unlawfully and are still there; the property was not open to the public when they entered; the owner told them to leave; they are not current or former tenants under a written or oral rental agreement the owner authorized; they are not the owner's immediate family; and there is no pending lawsuit about the property between the owner and them. The owner files a sworn complaint with the sheriff, who then serves a notice to vacate immediately and puts the owner back in possession; the sheriff may charge for standing by while locks are changed and belongings removed. A person wrongly removed can be restored to possession and recover actual damages, statutory damages of three times the fair market rent, costs and attorney's fees. This procedure cannot be used against a tenant or a former tenant, including one who stays after the lease ends; that requires an eviction.

title: Sales Tax on Short Rentals
bodyText: Florida charges a 6 percent state tax on rent for living quarters in a hotel, apartment house, rooming house, tourist or trailer camp, mobile home park, recreational vehicle park, condominium or timeshare resort. The tax does not apply to a tenant with a bona fide written lease longer than 6 months for continuous residence, to a tenant who has lived continuously in the same place for more than 6 months and has already paid the tax for the first 6 months, or to rentals in buildings intended primarily as people's permanent residence. Full-time postsecondary students and active-duty military are also exempt. A lease of 6 months or less can therefore carry sales tax, and county tourist taxes may apply as well. Whether the tax reaches a single-family house is not settled by this statute's list of facility types.

title: Uncashed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: If a tenant never cashes a Florida landlord's deposit refund, the money does not become the landlord's. Under Florida's unclaimed property law, intangible property a business holds or owes is presumed abandoned after a dormancy period, generally 5 years from when it became payable unless another period is specified by law, and must then be reported and delivered to the state. A landlord should keep records of the refund and the tenant's last known address.

title: Towing Tenants' and Guests' Vehicles
bodyText: A Florida property owner, a tenant of the property, or someone either authorizes (including a condominium association's representative) may have a vehicle parked without permission towed by a regular towing business, without paying for the tow. Except for property that is part of a single-family residence, or when the vehicle's owner is told in person that the space is reserved, the owner must first post permanent signs at each driveway entrance: within 10 feet of the road, with light-reflective letters at least 2 inches high stating that unauthorized vehicles will be towed at the owner's expense, the words "tow-away zone" in letters at least 4 inches high, the tower's name and phone number, mounted 3 to 6 feet above the ground, and in place at least 24 hours before any tow. The tower must store the vehicle nearby, notify the police within 30 minutes, release it within 1 hour of request, and stop and release it for half the posted rate if the owner arrives during the tow. A person who improperly causes a tow is liable for the removal and storage costs, damages, attorney's fees and court costs. Counties and cities may add rules and set maximum towing rates.

title: Removing a Squatter Without an Eviction Action (2026 Act)
bodyText: Kansas enacted a removal of squatters act in 2026 (L. 2026, ch. 56; H.B. 2378). It lets the owner of a dwelling unit, or the owner's agent, have a squatter removed by law enforcement instead of filing an eviction case. A squatter is a person occupying a dwelling who is not entitled to occupy it under a lease or rental agreement and is not authorized to occupy it by a tenant. The owner submits a notarized affidavit to local law enforcement stating six things: that the affiant is the owner or the owner's agent; that the person entered and remains unlawfully; that the person was not authorized to enter; that the person is not a tenant or a holdover tenant; that the affiant asked the person to leave and the person refused; and that the person is not an immediate family member. Law enforcement verifies the affiant's ownership and apparent entitlement to relief, and no sooner than 24 hours after receiving the affidavit an officer serves a notice to vacate immediately, either by hand or by posting it on the front door or entrance. Occupancy by a squatter is excluded from the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and removing a squatter does not require an eviction action under that Act. Three limits make this a poor tool to reach for casually. A current or former tenant is not a squatter, and a holdover tenant is expressly excluded, so a tenant who overstays still goes through the Chapter 61 eviction process. An immediate family member cannot be removed this way; the act's list runs to spouse, child, grandchild of any degree, parent, mother-in-law, father-in-law and grandparent, among others. And the downside is severe: a false affidavit is a class A nonperson misdemeanor, and a person wrongly removed may recover possession, actual costs and damages, treble the fair market rent as punitive damages, court costs and attorney fees. Use this only where you are certain there is no tenancy and no family relationship. Anything short of that belongs in an eviction action.

title: Abandonment Ends the Lease Unless You Try to Re-Rent
bodyText: If a Kansas tenant abandons the dwelling unit, you must make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental (K.S.A. 58-2565(c)). This is not only a duty to mitigate damages — the statute attaches a consequence that ends the lease. If you re-rent for a term beginning before the original rental agreement would have expired, the agreement is deemed terminated as of the date the new tenancy begins. And if you fail to use reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the rental agreement is deemed terminated by you as of the date you had notice of the abandonment. Either way rent stops accruing from that date, so a landlord who leaves an abandoned unit sitting and later sues for the balance of the term will find the claim cut off at the notice date rather than running to the end of the lease. Two practical consequences. Document the re-letting effort — when it was listed, at what rent, showings, applications, why any applicant was turned down — because that record is what preserves a rent claim past the abandonment date. And note that the statute deems the termination to be by the landlord, which matters anywhere your rights or a tenant's turn on which party ended the tenancy.

title: What You Can Sue For When the Lease Ends
bodyText: On termination of the rental agreement, K.S.A. 58-2568 gives you a claim and lets you file an action for possession, for rent, or for both. It also gives you a separate claim for actual damages for breach of the rental agreement, and that damages action may be filed before the rental agreement's termination date — you do not have to wait for the term to run out to sue on a breach. Two things follow. Possession and money are not alternatives in Kansas: suing for possession does not make you give up the rent claim, and you can combine them. And because the damages claim is for actual damages, it is bounded by the other Kansas limits already in this library — the re-letting duty on abandonment, which cuts rent off at the notice date (K.S.A. 58-2565(c)), and the holdover cap of one and one-half times periodic rent or actual damages (K.S.A. 58-2570(c)). Kansas gives you no statutory right to accelerate the remaining rent, and no right to recover attorney fees, because K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(3) voids a lease fee-shifting provision outright.

title: Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In a Kansas action for possession based on nonpayment of rent, or an action for rent where the tenant still occupies the premises, the tenant must raise any counterclaim for amounts recoverable under the rental agreement or the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act in that action or forfeit the right to bring it (K.S.A. 58-2561(a)). The court may order the tenant to pay accrued and future rent into court and then determine each party's net obligation; the party owed money is paid first out of the funds on deposit, with any remainder paid by the other party. Where no rent remains due after that netting, the tenant may prevail in the possession action. If the tenant has already vacated and you are suing only for rent, the tenant may still counterclaim but is not required to deposit rent into court (58-2561(b)). What this means in practice is that a habitability counterclaim normally lands inside your own eviction case rather than arriving as a separate suit later. A security-deposit claim is different: the Kansas Court of Appeals held that a claim for the deposit plus damages is not a compulsory counterclaim under this section (Asbury v. Mauk, 9 Kan. App. 2d 699 (1984)), so a tenant can bring it separately. Either way, the rent on deposit is the fund your judgment gets paid from — so expect the case to turn on the net number, not on possession alone.

title: Remedies When Entry Is Refused — and When You Enter Wrongly
bodyText: Kansas attaches remedies to entry in both directions (K.S.A. 58-2571). If the tenant refuses to allow lawful access to the dwelling unit, you may obtain injunctive relief to compel access or terminate the rental agreement, and in either case recover actual damages. If you make an unlawful entry, or a lawful entry in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated demands for entry that are otherwise lawful but have the effect of unreasonably harassing the tenant, the tenant may obtain injunctive relief or terminate the rental agreement, and recover actual damages. Read this with the entry standard itself: Kansas requires only reasonable notice at reasonable hours, with no fixed number of hours, so what counts as a lawful entry is judged against that standard rather than against a statutory clock. The practical point for a landlord is that refusal of access is a remedy you have to go get — Kansas gives you an injunction or termination, not a right to let yourself in — and that a pattern of entry demands can itself be the violation even when each individual entry would have been lawful.

title: The Kansas Eviction Process, Step by Step
bodyText: A Kansas eviction runs as a limited-actions case under Chapter 61, Article 38, and it is separate from the notice the lease and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act require. Before filing, you must give a notice to leave the premises at least three days before starting the lawsuit (K.S.A. 61-3803). That three-day period is counted as three consecutive 24-hour periods, intermediate weekends, legal holidays and days the clerk's office is closed are included in the count, and if you mail the notice you add two days. It may be delivered to the other party, left with a person over 12 years of age at the premises, posted in a conspicuous place, or mailed to the premises. The statute allows this notice to be combined with a notice under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so one properly drafted notice can serve both purposes rather than requiring two. You then file a petition, and the court sets the appearance date in the summons: not less than three nor more than 14 days after the summons issues (K.S.A. 61-3805). After a judgment for possession the court issues a writ of restitution at your request, and the writ must be executed within 14 days after the person named in it receives it (K.S.A. 61-3808). If an appeal stay is entered, execution stops immediately, and if possession has already been restored to you it goes back to the tenant. Nothing in this process lets you shortcut the Act's own notice-and-cure periods, which run first.

title: When a Tenant's Unpaid City Utility Bill Can Become a Lien on Your Property
bodyText: In Kansas, unpaid fees for utility service supplied by a municipally owned utility can become a lien on the property served, certified to the county clerk and collected on the tax roll with the usual tax penalties (K.S.A. 12-808c). One subsection decides who carries that risk in a rental: "A lien shall not attach to property for unpaid utility fees or charges, when the utility service has been contracted for by a tenant and not by the landlord or owner of the property to which such service is provided." So whose name is on the utility account is not an administrative detail — it determines whether the city can put the tenant's unpaid water, sewer, trash, gas or electric bill on your tax bill. If the tenant contracts for the service, no lien attaches to your property. If you keep the account in your own name for convenience, for a master-metered building, or because the tenant could not get service, the exception does not apply and the lien can attach. The practical rule is to require tenant-name accounts wherever the service is separately metered, and to treat any account you hold yourself as your own credit exposure rather than the tenant's. Note the limit: this concerns municipally owned utilities. Investor-owned utilities and rural water districts are outside it, and a rural water district's own collection remedies are a separate question.

title: A Deposit Refund the Tenant Never Cashes Is Not Yours
bodyText: When you mail a security deposit refund and the tenant never cashes it, the money does not revert to you. Under the Kansas Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act it becomes presumed abandoned and has to be reported and delivered to the state. A refund owed to a former tenant falls in the Act's catch-all category, "all other property, five years after the owner's right to demand the property or after the obligation to pay or distribute the property arises, whichever first occurs" (K.S.A. 58-3935(a)(16)). A holder of property presumed abandoned reports it to the state administrator before November 1 each year, covering the 12 months ending the preceding July 1 (K.S.A. 58-3950). There is a small-holder exemption: no report is required if you have no individual item over $100 and your aggregated total is under $250, unless the administrator requires otherwise — which will not cover most deposit refunds, since a typical Kansas deposit is capped at a month's rent and exceeds $100. Two practical points. Keep the unclaimed refund in a form you can still deliver five years later rather than writing it back into income. And this is separate from the deposit return rules themselves: complying with K.S.A. 58-2550's 14-day and 30-day deadlines is what avoids the 1.5-times penalty, while this Act governs what happens to the money afterwards.

title: Holding Deposits Sit Outside the Deposit Cap — Until the Lease Names Them
bodyText: Kansas defines a security deposit as "any sum of money specified in a rental agreement, however denominated, to be deposited with a landlord by a tenant as a condition precedent to the occupancy of a dwelling unit" (K.S.A. 58-2543(m)). Two limits in that sentence matter. It is denomination-blind, so calling money a fee, a reservation charge or a last-month payment does not keep it out — if the lease specifies it and occupancy depends on it, it is a security deposit and the K.S.A. 58-2550 cap, retention rules and return deadlines apply. But it is also agreement-scoped: money taken at application, before any rental agreement exists, is not specified in a rental agreement. A true pre-lease holding deposit therefore sits outside the deposit statute — which also means the tenant does not get 58-2550's remedies for it, and Kansas does not otherwise regulate the rental application process. The trap is the handoff. The moment the signed lease recites the holding money, or credits it toward the deposit or first month's rent, it becomes money specified in a rental agreement, counts against the cap, and starts the return clock. Decide up front which of the two you are taking, say so in writing to the applicant, and if you intend it to become part of the deposit, count it against the cap from the start.

title: Nobody Can Collect the Rent Free of the Habitability Duties
bodyText: Kansas law provides that "A rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with subsection (a) of K.S.A. 58-2553" (K.S.A. 58-2549). Subsection (a) of 58-2553 is the landlord's habitability duty — codes materially affecting health and safety, common areas, the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems, trash removal, running water and reasonable hot water and heat. What the section does is close the gap between who takes the rent and who owes the duties. An assignment of rents to a lender, a deed, a trust deed or a security instrument cannot be drafted so that the party receiving rent escapes the habitability obligation, and neither can the lease itself. This matters in three ordinary situations: financing that assigns rents as collateral, a receiver or lender collecting rents during a default, and a sale where rent is directed to a new party. In each case the duty travels with the rent. Check any rent-assignment language in your loan documents against this section rather than assuming the lease is the only place the problem could arise.

title: No Kansas Foreclosure Notice or Lease-Survival Statute for Tenants
bodyText: Kansas has no state statute requiring a landlord to disclose a pending foreclosure to a tenant or applicant, and no state statute governing whether a lease survives a foreclosure sale. Several states in this library do have one; Kansas does not. What governs instead is Kansas's judicial foreclosure process, including the redemption period in K.S.A. 60-2414, and the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, which requires a successor in interest to honor an existing bona fide lease and to give a bona fide tenant at least 90 days' notice to vacate. Two practical consequences. If you are selling or losing a tenanted property, Kansas law gives you no disclosure obligation to the tenant, but the tenancy is not yours to terminate merely because the property is in foreclosure. And if you are buying at a Kansas foreclosure sale, expect to inherit the tenancy rather than an empty unit, and expect the federal 90-day floor to apply before you can require the tenant to leave.

title: No Foreign-Adversary Property Ownership Restriction in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas has no statute restricting the ownership of real property by foreign adversaries or by entities tied to designated countries. The legislature passed one in 2024 — House Substitute for Senate Bill 172 — and the Governor vetoed it on May 10, 2024. The veto was not overridden: the bill appears in the 2024 session laws only as a governor's veto message, with no session-law chapter number, and no Kansas enactment on the subject followed in 2025 or 2026. So a Kansas landlord selling to, buying from, or leasing to an entity with foreign ownership faces no state-law ownership restriction or registration duty of this kind. Federal rules still apply on their own terms, including CFIUS review of certain real estate transactions near sensitive sites and the federal agricultural foreign-investment reporting requirement, neither of which this Kansas absence affects.

title: No State Towing Rules for Your Parking Lot
bodyText: Kansas does not regulate towing from private rental property the way some states do. There is no state statute requiring signs at the entrances to your lot, no requirement that you sign a written authorization for each tow, and no state cap on what a towing carrier may charge the vehicle's owner. What Kansas does have is an abandoned-vehicle route and a tower's lien. Under K.S.A. 8-1102, where a vehicle is abandoned on private property the public agency for that jurisdiction may remove and dispose of it "upon request of the owner or occupant of such real property" — a request, not a written authorization — and whoever removes the vehicle at that agency's request has a possessory lien on it for the costs of removing, towing and storing it. K.S.A. 8-1103 carries the related lien provisions. The practical upshot is that the lease clause and your own arrangement with the towing company are doing most of the work here, because no state signage or authorization statute backs them up. Two cautions: Kansas cities have home-rule authority and many do regulate towing by ordinance, and the Kansas Corporation Commission regulates motor carriers — neither was researched, so check the ordinance for each property's city before relying on this.

title: No State Pool Barrier Requirement for Rental Property
bodyText: Kansas has no state statute imposing a pool fence, barrier, gate or safety-notice requirement on a residential landlord. The Kansas pool rules that do exist sit in the Department of Health and Environment's child care regulations — K.A.R. 28-4-129 for child care centers and K.A.R. 28-4-594 for family child care homes — and they apply because of the licensed child care activity, not because the property is rented. Pool barrier requirements in Kansas therefore come from whichever building or pool code the city or county has adopted, which varies from place to place. Two things follow for a landlord. Check the local adopted code for each property with a pool rather than assuming a statewide rule exists, since the absence of a state statute is not the absence of a requirement. And note the overlap with the residential-use clause: if a tenant runs a licensed child care operation out of the home, the K.A.R. 28-4 pool and fencing rules start applying to your property through the tenant's license, which is one more reason the residential-use-only restriction is worth enforcing.

title: Taking Money to Hold a Unit: Minnesota's Prelease Deposit Rules
bodyText: If you take money from a prospective tenant before a lease is signed, Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.175) lets you accept it only under a conspicuous WRITTEN agreement that states the circumstances in which you will return it, and states that you must return it within seven days of one of those circumstances occurring. 'Return' means postmarked within seven days, though the applicant may instead ask you to destroy the payment or hold it for pickup. If the applicant does sign a lease, you must apply the money to their security deposit or rent -- you cannot keep it as a fee. Get the return conditions in writing before you take the money: the penalty is the full amount of the deposit plus another one-half of it, and there is no cure once you have taken money with no written agreement. A reasonable applicant screening fee is NOT a prelease deposit and is governed separately.
notes: MN added (gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27, checklist instruction 36 -- sources 2, 3 and 4 only; not a re-audit). Subd. 2(b) defines 'return' as postmarked within seven days, with an applicant-requested alternative of destruction or retrieval. Subd. 4: liability is the deposit plus one-half as a penalty, 'in addition to any other remedies'. History: 1999 c 97 s 1; 1999 c 199 art 1 s 174 -- no recent amendment (Recent History block empty). title: Submetering and Separate Utility Billing: The Rules Outside Chapter 504B
bodyText: If you submeter electricity or natural gas, or apportion gas, in a shared-metered residential building, Minn. Stat. Sec. Sec. 216B.022 to 216B.024 impose a compliance regime separate from Sec. 504B.216, and it puts you under the Public Utilities Commission's authority. The main duties: submeters installed on or after January 1, 2025 must meet ANSI standards, and every submeter, whenever installed, must measure accurately. You may not apportion electricity at all -- electricity may only be submetered. Charge only for what the tenant's own unit used, never for common areas or space you use yourself; divide fixed and non-usage charges equally among the units; and pass through each unit's equal share of any bill credit. Every submetered bill must show the present and previous readings, the reading date, your rate and the utility's rate to you, the tenant's share of taxes and surcharges, any credit, any administrative billing charge, the total, and the due date and late-fee date and amount. If you overcharge, refund promptly; if you undercharge, you may bill back only six months, and you must offer a no-interest, no-fee payment plan where the tenant was not at fault. You must offer a payment plan for any overdue utility bill, and if you cannot agree, tell the tenant they can go to the Commission's consumer affairs office and give them its current phone number and email. When a tenant moves out before the real bill arrives, you may issue an ESTIMATED final bill based on the previous billing period, prorated to the move-out date, with no extra charges beyond the administrative billing charge and a late fee limited to the prior period.
notes: MN added (gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27, checklist instruction 36 -- sources 2, 3 and 4 only; not a re-audit). Official Minnesota Revisor full-text search of the 2025 Minnesota Statutes (api.revisor.mn.gov search service, exact-phrase with word variants), every landlord-relevant hit read section-open on revisor.mn.gov. Sec. 216B.023: subd. 1(b) lease/at-outset notice of billing timing (see utility-billing-schedule-mn) and the no-less-frequent rule; subd. 1(c) the eight mandatory bill-content items; subd. 2(a)(1) electricity may NOT be apportioned; subd. 2(b) the charging methodology (no common areas, equal division of non-usage charges, pro-rata credits); subd. 4 administrative billing charge per Sec. 504B.216 subd. 8 and no other fees; subd. 5 overcharge refund and six-month undercharge limit; subd. 6 late charge per Sec. 504B.216 subd. 9; subd. 7 payment plans plus the consumer-affairs referral; subd. 8 undercharge payment plans with no interest or delinquency fee. title: You Must Hand Over Outstanding Inspection and Condemnation Orders
bodyText: Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.195) makes you give out copies of certain code-enforcement paperwork, and the duty runs to APPLICANTS as well as tenants. If a citation has been issued on an inspection order that the housing inspector marks as threatening a tenant's health or safety, or if there is an outstanding condemnation order or declaration that the premises are unfit for human habitation, you must deliver or mail a copy: to an existing tenant within 72 hours of the citation; to any person BEFORE they sign a lease or pay rent or a security deposit for a new tenancy; and to anyone before they take over ownership. If the order does not involve a health-or-safety violation, you instead post a summary in a conspicuous place in each affected building, together with notice that you will make the order available for review on request by a tenant or prospective tenant, and you must actually provide it when asked. You are not in violation if you have only an initial repair order, if the repair deadline and any extension have not expired, if fewer than 60 days have passed since the deadline expired with no citation issued, or if you finish the repairs in time. Proving you disclosed is an affirmative defense. The tenant's remedy runs through the private attorney general statute, so damages, costs and attorney fees are available, and the duty cannot be waived by the lease.

Subd. 1(a) the three recipients and the 72-hour clock; note (2) is triggered by signing OR paying rent OR paying a security deposit, whichever comes first. Subd. 1(b) the conspicuous-posting alternative for non-health/safety orders plus the on-request production duty. Subd. 2 remedies via Sec. 8.31 subd. 3a plus equitable relief. Subd. 3 the four exceptions. Subd. 4 affirmative defense. Subd. 5 remedies are additional and any lease waiver is 'contrary to public policy and void'. Sec. 504B.195 and 504B.204 both sit in that gap and both are non-waivable landlord duties. title: Never Accept Rent or a Deposit After a Condemnation or Vacate Order
bodyText: Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.204) flatly bars you from accepting rent or a security deposit once the premises have been condemned or declared unfit for human habitation, ordered vacated for violating a housing, health or fire code or a rental licensing ordinance, or ordered vacated under a government taking. If you take money anyway you owe the tenant actual damages PLUS three times everything you collected after the date of the order, plus costs and attorney fees -- and the violation also breaches the statutory habitability covenant, which opens up the tenant-remedies machinery on top. The statute says it must be construed liberally in the tenant's favour, and no lease term can waive it. Practically: the moment a vacate or condemnation order lands, stop collecting, and do not accept a payment a tenant offers voluntarily.

Sec. 504B.385 and 504B.395. Paragraph (b): remedies are additional and any lease waiver is void. title: Cold Weather Notice Before Vacating
bodyText: Between November 15 and April 15, if Tenant removes from, abandons, or vacates the property or any part of it while the Term is still running, Tenant will first give Landlord at least three days' written notice of Tenant's intention to do so. This Section does not apply where the tenancy is ending. Tenant understands that the property contains plumbing and other pipes that can be damaged by freezing, and that Minnesota law makes failure to give this notice a criminal offense.
notes: MN added (gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27, checklist instruction 36 -- sources 2, 3 and 4 only; not a re-audit). Official Minnesota Revisor full-text search of the 2025 Minnesota Statutes (api.revisor.mn.gov search service, exact-phrase with word variants), every landlord-relevant hit read section-open on revisor.mn.gov. Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.155 (TENANT MUST GIVE COLD WEATHER NOTICE BEFORE VACATION OF BUILDING), read section-open in full -- it is a single sentence: 'Except upon the termination of the tenancy, a tenant who, between November 15 and April 15, removes from, abandons, or vacates a building or any part thereof that contains plumbing, water, steam, or other pipes liable to injury from freezing, without first giving to the landlord three days' notice of intention so to remove is guilty of a misdemeanor.' PROOF-OF-ABSENCE VIOLATION, AND THE THIRD OF THIS EXACT SHAPE FOR MINNESOTA. Sec. 504B.155 appeared in the library in exactly one place before this pass: the notes of the shared tenant-maintenance row, which asserted that the 'cold-weather-notice-before-vacating duty (Sec. 504B.155)' was 'already reflected elsewhere in the library.' It was not -- no row existed. That is precisely instruction 19's scenario ('asserted covered, no row ever built'), and precisely what happened to MN with Sec. 504B.206 (domestic violence) and Sec. 504B.212 subd. 2 (retaliation). A false 'already covered' note is worse than an honest absence because no later canvass re-flags it. Found here by the source-3 scenario screen (tenant leaves mid-winter and the pipes freeze), not by any keyword probe. DRAFTING NOTES: the statute says 'notice', not 'written notice' -- the clause requires writing as a contract term, which is permissible and evidentially sensible, and the clause does not purport to create the criminal liability, only to state that the law does. The statute's own carve-out ('Except upon the termination of the tenancy') is carried across, so the clause does not collide with surrender-end-of-term-mn-nd or with a lawful Sec. 504B.147 termination notice. Currency: no amendment since 1999 c 199 art 1 s 12. CROSS-STATE: no other state in the library has a cold-weather vacate-notice row; ND, SD and WY share Minnesota's climate and should be asked. Recommended as a new named-topic checklist row.

title: The Unlawful-Activities Covenant Is in Every Minnesota Lease Whether You Write It or Not
bodyText: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.171 writes a covenant into every Minnesota residential lease, oral or written, so you do not need a crime-free clause to have one. Both you AND the tenant covenant not to allow controlled substances in violation of the criminal drug chapter, prostitution or prostitution-related activity, unlawful use or possession of a firearm, or stolen or robbery-obtained property -- and the covenant reaches the common area and curtilage, not just the unit. The covenant is not broken by a third party's conduct unless you or the tenant knew or had reason to know of it, so what matters in practice is what you did once you found out. The tenant separately covenants not to commit domestic-abuse-type acts against another tenant or authorized occupant. A breach voids the tenant's right to possession. Two limits worth knowing: you cannot prohibit a tenant from legally possessing cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles or hemp-derived consumer products, and the tenant cannot waive that right -- but smoking or vaping them is outside the protection, so a smoke-free policy is still enforceable. And because the covenant binds you too, allowing the conduct is your own breach, not merely a ground against the tenant.
