title: A Nuisance Notice Can Close Your Building for a Year, and Evicting the Tenant Is the Way Out
bodyText: This is the largest landlord-side risk in Minnesota law that has nothing to do with Chapter 504B. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. Sec. 617.80 to 617.87, a prosecuting attorney who believes a nuisance is being maintained in your building must first serve written notice on ALL owners, by personal service or certified mail. A nuisance can be established by a single incident of prostitution-related activity, or by two or more incidents of certain other offences within the previous 12 months, anywhere within the building. The notice tells you what kind of nuisance is alleged, summarises the evidence and dates, and warns that if you do not abate it or otherwise resolve matters with the prosecutor within 30 DAYS, a district court complaint may follow that can enjoin the use of your building FOR ANY PURPOSE FOR ONE YEAR. Your way out is Sec. 617.85: as the owner you may file a motion in that same abatement proceeding to cancel the offending tenant's lease and recover the premises, and maintaining a nuisance is an additional ground for eviction beyond the ordinary grounds. Two features make this genuinely protective. It is no defence that your lease does not list this ground, so a thin lease does not cost you the remedy. And the court must not order abatement of the premises where it cancels that tenant's lease and grants you restitution AND finds both that the acts were committed by that tenant and that the tenant was NOT acting in conjunction with you or under your control. Read that second condition carefully: evicting the tenant protects the building only if you were not party to the conduct, so a landlord who knew and did nothing cannot evict his way out of an abatement order. Do not let the 30 days run.
notes: MN added (gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27, checklist instruction 36 -- sources 2, 3 and 4 only; not a re-audit). Official Minnesota Revisor full-text search of the 2025 Minnesota Statutes (api.revisor.mn.gov search service, exact-phrase with word variants), every landlord-relevant hit read section-open on revisor.mn.gov. Minn. Stat. Sec. 617.81 and Sec. 617.85, both read section-open. Sec. 617.81 subd. 2(a): a public nuisance exists on proof of one incident of the items at (i), (v), (viii) or (ix), or two or more of (ii), (iii), (iv), (vi), (vii) or (x), committed within the previous 12 months within the building. Subd. 4(a): the prosecuting attorney SHALL serve written notice on all owners and interested parties by personal service or certified mail, return receipt requested. Subd. 4(b)(3): failure to abate or resolve within 30 days of service may lead to a complaint that 'could, among other remedies, result in enjoining the use of the building for any purpose for one year or, in the case of a tenant, lessee, or occupant, could result in cancellation of the lease'. Subd. 4(b)(4): the notice must inform the owner of the Sec. 617.85 options. Sec. 617.85: the owner may move to cancel the lease in the abatement proceeding and may assign that right to the prosecuting attorney; nuisance under Sec. 617.81 subd. 2 is 'an additional ground authorized by law' beyond Sec. Sec. 504B.281 to 504B.371; 'It is no defense ... that the lease or other agreement controlling the tenancy or leasehold does not provide for eviction or cancellation of the lease upon the ground provided in this section'; on a finding the court SHALL cancel and grant restitution; and the court 'must not order abatement of the premises' where it cancels the lease, grants restitution of that portion, and finds the acts were committed by that tenant. title: Minnesota's Expedited Eviction Track Changed on August 1, 2026
bodyText: Minnesota has a fast eviction track, and Laws 2026, ch. 81 widened it as of August 1, 2026. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.321 subd. 2 you may seek an expedited hearing where the case is brought on the unlawful-activities covenant, or where the tenant seriously endangers other residents' safety, intentionally and seriously damages property -- and now also where the tenant ASSAULTS you, your employees or your contractors, using the criminal code's definition of assault. You must file an affidavit stating specific facts and instances explaining why expedition is required; a referee or judge screens it, and the hearing is set no less than five and no more than seven days from issuance of the summons, which must be served within 24 hours unless the court orders otherwise. Two cautions. The penalty for seeking expedition without sufficient basis rose from $500 to $750 in the same 2026 act. And -- this part is not new, it has been in the statute since 2023 -- the court may consider ONLY the expedited allegations and may NOT consolidate them with anything else, including breach of lease, holdover, or nonpayment of rent. So if you want unpaid rent as well, that is a separate action; do not bundle it in and expect the court to hear it.

The court may not consolidate claims heard under the expedited procedure with any additional claims, including but not limited to breach of lease, holding over under section 504B.285, or nonpayment of rent under section 504B.291.' EFFECTIVE DATE read from the session law (instruction 34): 'This section is effective August 1, 2026, and applies to eviction actions filed on or after that date.' The assault ground is landlord-FAVOURABLE and the no-consolidation rule is landlord-adverse; both post-date MN's last pass. Ties to edu-unlawful-activities-covenant-mn (Sec. 504B.171 is the first named expedited ground) and to edu-nuisance-abatement-exposure-mn (Sec. 617.85 supplies a separate, additional ground outside Sec. Sec. 504B.281-.371).| *** CORRECTED BEFORE SHIPPING, AND THE ERROR IS WORTH RECORDING. *** My first draft of this row stated that paragraph (e) -- the no-consolidation rule -- was NEW in Laws 2026, ch. 81. THAT WAS WRONG. The codified pre-2026 text of Sec. 504B.321 subd. 2 was read directly and already contains paragraph (e) verbatim: 'The court may only consider allegations under paragraph (a) during an expedited hearing. The court may not consolidate claims heard under the expedited procedure with any additional claims, including but not limited to breach of lease, holding over under section 504B.285, or nonpayment of rent under section 504B.291.' Its history is Laws 2023 c 52 art 19 s 105. What ch. 81 s 5 ACTUALLY changed is exactly two things: paragraph (a) gains 'assaults the landlord or the landlord's employees or contractors' with the Sec. 609.02 subd. 10 assault definition, and paragraph (d)'s civil penalty goes from $500 to $750. Never strip the amendment markers from a session law; they are the only thing distinguishing new language from restated existing language. This is the project's recurring failure shape in a new costume: a correct citation described wrongly. The substantive rule is unchanged and still landlord-relevant -- only its provenance was wrong.

title: If Your Online Rent Portal Goes Down, Minnesota Law Is Now Against You
bodyText: Laws 2026, ch. 81 rewrote Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.118 -- now titled PAYMENT OF RENT -- and added digital-payment rules effective August 1, 2026. A 'digital payment platform' is any electronic application or system under your direct control, or run by a vendor under contract with you, that lets a user conduct financial transactions. If you require or permit tenants to pay through one, then whenever it is not functioning you must offer an alternative way to pay, and you may NOT charge any fee for using that alternative. If you know the platform is down you must either restore access or offer an alternative as soon as practicable. And if a tenant fails to pay because BOTH the platform and the alternative you provided are not working for them, you may not take any adverse action -- the statute names filing an eviction and assessing late fees specifically. The teeth are in the next subdivision: the tenant has an affirmative defence to a nonpayment eviction if you violated the section, and on a showing that you did, the eviction action MUST BE DISMISSED and the tenant gets reasonable attorney fees plus any other equitable relief. Keep dated records of outages and of the alternative you offered. The cash-receipt duty is unchanged and is now subdivision 2.

The section is RETITLED from 'RECEIPT FOR RENT PAID IN CASH' to 'PAYMENT OF RENT' and restructured into four subdivisions: subd. 1 defines 'digital payment platform'; subd. 2 carries the cash-receipt duty forward verbatim; subd. 3(a)-(c) the alternative-payment duty, the no-fee rule, the restore-or-offer duty and the adverse-action bar; subd. 4 the affirmative defence, mandatory dismissal, attorney fees and equitable relief. title: Never Name a Tenant's Child as a Defendant in an Eviction
bodyText: New Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.2136, effective August 1, 2026, says a residential landlord shall not list the minor child of a residential tenant as a defendant in an eviction action complaint against that tenant. The only exception is where a minor is the only person renting the unit from you -- then you may name the minor. The rule cannot be waived or modified by the parties, and any lease provision purporting to waive it is contrary to public policy and void. The tenant recovers actual damages or $300, whichever is greater, for a violation. This is easy to breach by accident: if your process is to name every occupant on the complaint, change it now. It applies to eviction actions filed on or after August 1, 2026.
notes: MN added (gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27, checklist instruction 36 -- sources 2, 3 and 4 only; not a re-audit). Official Minnesota Revisor full-text search of the 2025 Minnesota Statutes (api.revisor.mn.gov search service, exact-phrase with word variants), every landlord-relevant hit read section-open on revisor.mn.gov. Laws 2026, ch. 81 (S.F. 4171), s 3, read from the session-law text: 'proposing coding for new law in Minnesota Statutes, chapter 504B' at [504B.2136] MINORS AS DEFENDANTS PROHIBITED. Paragraph (a) the prohibition and the sole-minor-tenant exception; paragraph (b) non-waivable, any waiver 'contrary to public policy and void'; paragraph (c) 'actual damages or $300, whichever is greater'. EFFECTIVE DATE clause read in full: 'This section is effective August 1, 2026, and applies to eviction actions filed on or after that date.' Signed 2026-05-12; in force as of this pass. NOT A NEW TOPIC LIBRARY-WIDE -- CORRECTED BEFORE SHIPPING. My first draft of this row asserted that no state had a row on who may be named as an eviction defendant. That was wrong, and the topic_key alignment check caught it: Ohio already carries edu-minor-tenant-filing-oh on topic_key 'minor-tenant-filing'. Ohio's rule is stronger in remedy and narrower in target -- naming a minor TENANT alongside a parent or adult guardian means the court SHALL dismiss without prejudice AND SHALL order the landlord to pay the minor tenant's reasonable attorney fees, and Ohio defines 'minor tenant' as an unemancipated tenant under 18. Minnesota's Sec. 504B.2136 instead bars naming the minor CHILD of a tenant (whether or not the child is a tenant), is expressly non-waivable, and fixes damages at actual or $300, whichever is greater. So the two are genuinely different rules on the same topic and both belong. This row shares Ohio's topic_key. The topic IS still missing from the named-topic checklist, which is a real gap -- two of fourteen states now have a rule and no canvass row asks about it. Because the section is brand new it will not appear in the 2025 compilation's chapter index at all, which is instruction 35's trap running in the opposite direction (a section IN FORCE but MISSING from the compilation). Recommended as a new named-topic checklist row: every future state should be asked whether it restricts who may be named as a defendant. Practically this is a process/UI matter rather than lease text -- flagged for the eviction-filing side of the product if it ever generates complaints, alongside MN's other product-level items (Sec. 504B.120 page-1 placement, the Sec. 504B.216 subd. 10 attachment).

title: Towing From Your Lot: Posting Is What Makes It Lawful
bodyText: Minnesota's towing rules live in Minn. Stat. ch. 168B, not in the landlord-tenant chapter, and the timeframes turn on what kind of property you have. A vehicle left unattended may be impounded from private property IMMEDIATELY where the property is single-family or duplex residential, and immediately from ANY residential property that is properly posted. Non-residential private property gets immediate removal if properly posted and 24 hours if not. Read that list carefully: the 24-hour fallback is non-residential ONLY, so a multi-unit residential lot that is NOT posted has no timeframe available to it under that provision. If you manage anything larger than a duplex, post the lot. Two further points. Sec. 168B.035 is about towing by government towing authorities from public property, and it expressly preserves a private property owner's authority to authorize a tow under ch. 168B -- so that section's rules are not your rules. And the statutory lien that a tow operator gets for towing and storage arises on a tow requested by a LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICER, so a tow you order yourself does not create it; settle who pays with your towing company in your contract. Chapter 168B does not define 'properly posted', so follow your city's sign requirements.
notes: MN added (gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27, checklist instruction 36 -- sources 2, 3 and 4 only; not a re-audit). Official Minnesota Revisor full-text search of the 2025 Minnesota Statutes (api.revisor.mn.gov search service, exact-phrase with word variants), every landlord-relevant hit read section-open on revisor.mn.gov. Minn. Stat. Sec. Sec. 168B.04, 168B.011, 168B.035 and 168B.045, all read section-open. Sec. 168B.04 subd. 2(b)(2) is the operative list for private property: '(i) that is single-family or duplex residential property, immediately; (ii) that is private, nonresidential property, properly posted, immediately; (iii) that is private, nonresidential property, not posted, 24 hours; (iv) [vehicle service establishments, five business days after certified-mail notice]; or (v) that is any residential property, properly posted, immediately.' The asymmetry is in the statute, not a paraphrase: clause (iii)'s 24-hour rule is expressly limited to nonresidential property, and there is no unposted-multifamily-residential clause. Sec. 168B.011 subd. 4 defines 'unauthorized vehicle' as one subject to removal under Sec. 168B.035 or Sec. 168B.04 subd. 2 that is not a junk or abandoned vehicle -- so an operable but wrongly parked tenant or guest car is an 'unauthorized vehicle', while the 'abandoned vehicle' definition at subd. 2 additionally requires that the vehicle lack vital component parts or be inoperable. Sec. 168B.035 subd. 5: 'This section does not restrict the authority of the owner of private property to authorize under chapter 168B the towing of a motor vehicle unlawfully parked on the private property.' Sec. 168B.045: the towing and storage lien attaches to a person 'who tows and stores a motor vehicle at the request of a law enforcement officer'. Sec. 168B.011 and 168B.04 but has no definition in Sec. 168B.011 -- checked by reading the definitions section; the row says to follow local sign rules rather than inventing a standard. title: Methamphetamine Contamination: No Disclosure Duty, but an Occupancy Ban and a Recorded Affidavit
bodyText: Minnesota has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose that a property was once a clandestine drug lab. What it has instead is Minn. Stat. Sec. 152.0275 subd. 2, and the practical consequences are bigger than a disclosure duty. A county or local health department or sheriff SHALL order that any property found to be a clandestine lab site and contaminated be prohibited from being occupied or used until it has been assessed and remediated under the Department of Health's cleanup guidelines, and the remediation must be done by a contractor who then verifies the work to you and to the authority within five days; the authority vacates its order after that. If a contractor certifies work that did not meet the guidelines, the contractor is liable to you for the extra remediation cost and your attorney fees, with a six-year limit. Public-health nuisance abatement procedures apply on top. The disclosure happens without you: the authority records an affidavit with the county recorder or registrar of titles naming the owner, describing the property and mapping the contaminated area, expressly to disclose the history 'to any potential transferee', and the recorder must record it so it turns up in an ordinary title search. Affidavits can be filed to show remediation and to vacate the order, after which they stop being notice. Local community health services administrators also keep records of affected properties. So: check the title and the local administrator before you buy, and expect an occupancy prohibition rather than a disclosure form if it happens to you.

title: A Deposit Refund the Tenant Never Cashed Is Not Yours to Keep
bodyText: When you send a security-deposit refund and the former tenant never cashes it, the money does not become yours after a while. Under Minnesota's unclaimed property act (Minn. Stat. Sec. 345.39 subd. 1) intangible personal property held in the ordinary course of your business that stays unclaimed by the owner for more than THREE YEARS after it became payable is presumed abandoned, and the listed examples include customer overpayments, credit balances and miscellaneous outstanding checks. A stale refund check or an uncollected credit balance sits squarely in that category. Do not write it back to income: track it, and when the dormancy period runs, report and remit it to the state. Charges you may lawfully withhold are excluded from the calculation, so what is at issue is the net amount you actually owed the tenant.

Official Minnesota Revisor full-text search of the 2025 Minnesota Statutes (api.revisor.mn.gov search service, exact-phrase with word variants), every landlord-relevant hit read section-open on revisor.mn.gov. Minn. Stat. Sec. 345.39 subd. 1, read section-open: 'All intangible personal property, not otherwise covered by sections 345.31 to 345.60, including any income or increment thereon, but excluding any charges that may lawfully be withheld, that is held or owing in this state in the ordinary course of the holder's business and has remained unclaimed by the owner for more than three years after it became payable or distributable is presumed abandoned', with the enumerated examples at (b) 'deposits or payments for repair or purchase of goods or services', (c) 'customer overpayments', and (g) 'credit balances, accounts receivable and miscellaneous outstanding checks'. The three-year residual period is therefore the applicable one by category, not by a section naming deposits. NOT READ: the holder reporting and remittance mechanics at Sec. Sec. 345.41 to 345.43, and the penalties at Sec. 345.55 -- the row states dormancy and the duty to report, not the filing procedure; flagged if Taylor wants the mechanics. title: Renting Storage Lockers Separately Can Pull You Into the Self-Service Storage Act
bodyText: If you rent storage space to tenants, check whether Minnesota's self-service storage facility act (Minn. Stat. Sec. Sec. 514.970 to 514.979) applies before you rely on your storage clause. A 'self-service storage facility' is real property designed and used for renting or leasing individual storage space to occupants who have access to store and remove personal property; the only exclusions are financial-institution vaults, warehouses that issue documents of title, and commercial short-term parking. There is NO exclusion for storage lockers in an apartment building. If the act applies, Sec. 514.975 imposes real requirements on the rental agreement: it must disclose your lien rights including the right to deny access, and the extent and limits of your insurance on the occupant's property; it must let the occupant name an optional alternate contact person, with a space they initial if they decline; any cap on the value of stored property is effective ONLY if printed in bold type or underlined, and may not be set below $1,000; and there is a uniformed-services disclosure. Most importantly, a rental agreement 'may not exempt an owner from liability for damages to an occupant's personal property caused by the owner's negligence' -- so a negligence disclaimer is void where the act applies. The safer reading is that a locker thrown in with a dwelling at no separate charge is not a self-service storage facility, because the property is not designed and used for renting storage space. But if you rent lockers for a separate fee, to your tenants or to the public, assume the act applies and drop the disclaimer.

Subd. 3 'owner' includes a lessor; subd. 5 'rental agreement' is a written agreement for use of storage space at such a facility. Subd. 2: a value limit binds only if 'printed in bold type or underlined' and may not be less than $1,000. Subd. 3: uniformed-services disclosure. title: No Rekeying or Lock-Hardware Duty in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota imposes no statutory duty to rekey or change locks between tenancies, and no deadbolt or lock-hardware requirement for rental housing. Locks are a matter for your lease and any local housing code. The one statutory lock rule runs the other way and is already covered in the library: a tenant who is a victim of violence has a right to have the locks changed. Rekeying at turnover is good practice, not a legal obligation, so if you want it as an obligation on the tenant's side, put it in the lease.

title: No Fire-Sprinkler Duty for Private Rental Housing
bodyText: Minnesota's only retrofit sprinkler mandate does not reach private landlords. Minn. Stat. Sec. 299F.48 requires automatic sprinkler systems in existing PUBLIC HOUSING buildings, and the section defines that term narrowly: housing for low-income persons and households financed by the federal government and owned and operated by the public housing authorities and agencies formed by cities and counties, in which at least one story used for human occupancy is 75 feet or more above the lowest level of fire department vehicle access. Compliance is due by August 1, 2033. If you are a private owner, none of that applies to you. New construction and remodelling are still governed by the State Building Code and State Fire Code, which Sec. 299F.48 expressly does not supersede.

title: Selling With a Tenant in Place: No Minnesota Statute Beyond the Deposit Handover
bodyText: Minnesota has no general statute governing what you owe a tenant when you sell a tenanted property, and no release-on-sale provision of the kind some states have. What Minnesota does regulate is the money: the security-deposit transfer and successor-liability rules, which are covered separately in the library. Beyond that, selling with a tenant in place is governed by your lease, by common-law rules about whether the buyer takes subject to the tenancy, and by the ordinary entry-notice rules when you show the unit. There is also no statutory requirement to notify tenants that you have sold, and no statutory right of first refusal for residential tenants. So put what you need into the lease and the purchase agreement, because the statute will not supply it.

Official Minnesota Revisor full-text search of the 2025 Minnesota Statutes (api.revisor.mn.gov search service, exact-phrase with word variants), every landlord-relevant hit read section-open on revisor.mn.gov. title: What North Dakota Law Will Not Let the Lease Do
bodyText: North Dakota has no list of prohibited residential lease terms inside its landlord-tenant chapter, and it is easy to conclude from that the lease can say whatever you want. That is wrong. Five sections of Chapter 9-08 void whole categories of contract term, and a lease is a contract like any other. A provision is unlawful if it is contrary to an express provision of law, contrary to the policy of express law though not expressly prohibited, or otherwise contrary to good morals (§ 9-08-01). A provision whose object is, directly or indirectly, to exempt anyone from responsibility for their own fraud, for willful injury to another person or their property, or for violation of law -- whether the violation is willful or negligent -- is against the policy of the law (§ 9-08-02). Penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void outright (§ 9-08-03). A clause fixing damages in advance is void to that extent, unless it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage (§ 9-08-04). And a clause that restricts a party from enforcing its rights by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, or that shortens the time in which it may enforce them, is void unless a North Dakota statute specifically permits it (§ 9-08-05). What this means in practice: a flat "Landlord is not liable" sentence will not protect you where the loss came from your own violation of a statute or building code; a flat early-termination, short-notice, or administrative fee is exposed as a contractual penalty rather than a damages estimate; and Chapter 47-16's own unconscionability section (§ 47-16-13.3) sits on top of all of it as a case-by-case backstop.
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 9-08-01, 9-08-02, 9-08-03, 9-08-04, 9-08-05. All five read verbatim from the official compilation (ndlegis.gov/cencode/t09c08.pdf) on 2026-09-27. | CORRECTS A SHIPPED CONFIRMED-ABSENT FINDING. The exculpation exposure that forced fixes to this clause family in KS and NE therefore does not arise for ND'. § 9-08-02 IS an enumerated statutory ban; it is simply in Title 9 (Contracts) rather than Title 47. The checklist's own topic row L642 'Lease-content restrictions (state-wide, not just the LT chapter)' recorded ND as 'Outside the chapter: NOT CANVASSED' -- this row is that canvass. Found via the gap-discovery source 3 scenario screen, prompted by flat non-liability and indemnification clauses in a real North Dakota lease (source 2). | SCOPE DISCIPLINE -- what § 9-08-02 does NOT say: it does not void an exemption from ordinary negligence as such. Its three targets are fraud, WILLFUL injury, and violation of law (willful or negligent). A disclaimer is therefore exposed where the loss traces to the landlord's breach of a statute or code (§§ 47-16-13.1, 23-13-15, fair housing), not merely to carelessness. Stated at that level deliberately rather than broadened. | NOT READ: North Dakota case law construing § 9-08-02 or § 9-08-04, including any Tunkl-style public-interest test and any decision on whether a residential lease is a contract of adhesion for this purpose. § 9-08-02 is the Field Code provision that Cal. title: The Tenant Can Repair and Deduct, or Just Leave
bodyText: North Dakota gives a tenant three routes when you do not repair, and none of them requires going to court first. If, within a reasonable time after the tenant's notice of dilapidations that you ought to repair, you neglect to do so, the tenant may repair the premises and deduct the expense of the repair from rent; recover that expense from you in any other lawful manner; or vacate the premises -- and a tenant who vacates on that ground is discharged from further payment of rent and from performing the lease's other conditions (§ 47-16-13). There is no escrow mechanism, no statutory dollar cap on the deduction, no requirement that the tenant get your approval of the repair or the contractor, and no notice period fixed in days. Two consequences to plan around. First, a deduction properly made under this section is not unpaid rent, so treating it as a nonpayment default and filing on it is a real risk. Second, on any claim under §§ 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 the court may award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party (§ 47-16-13.6), so a small repair dispute can carry your opponent's fees. Answering a written repair request promptly, in writing, with a date, is the only reliable way to keep this section from being used against you.
notes: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13, with § 47-16-13.6 on fees. Full primary text (complete Chapter 47-16, official compilation ndlegis.gov/cencode/t47c16.pdf, re-verified 2026-09-27). | ADDENDUM L.1 FAILURE FIXED. The consolidated checklist's ND cell at row L635 'Tenant remedy for failure to repair' already recorded this finding in full -- 'Three options, no escrow -- § 47-16-13 ... Plus § 47-16-13.6' -- and no CSV row existed for it. This is exactly the shape instruction 19 and Addendum L.1 were written for: the checklist asserts coverage, the library has none, and the assertion stops any later canvass from re-flagging it. Found by the gap-discovery source 3 scenario screen ('tenant withholds rent or repairs and deducts'). | NO CONFLICT WITH rent-payment: that shared clause says rent is due 'without demand, deduction, or setoff, except as permitted by applicable law', which yields to § 47-16-13 by its own terms. No edit to the shared row is needed, and an ND landlord reading it would nonetheless not know this right exists -- which is why this row is education rather than a clause change. | landlord-maintenance-nd carries § 47-16-13.1 (the duties) but not § 47-16-13 (the tenant's remedies for breach of them); the two were never connected in the library. | NOT DETERMINED: what counts as a 'reasonable time' (no ND case law read), and whether a deduction exceeding one month's rent may be carried forward.

title: Selling a Property With a Tenant in It
bodyText: North Dakota imposes no duty to tell your tenant you are selling, and no statutory notice period before a sale -- but four other things bind you. The security deposit and accrued interest must be transferred to the buyer; you are not released from liability until that transfer actually happens, and the buyer is bound by North Dakota's deposit rules even though the buyer never received the deposit (§ 47-16-07.1(5)). The buyer steps into your rent remedies (§ 47-16-28), your tenant's remedies under the lease run against the buyer (§ 47-16-29), and your remedies run against anyone the tenant assigned to, for claims accruing while they held the assignment -- except where the assignment was security for a loan and was not accompanied by possession (§ 47-16-30). Separately, selling triggers seller-disclosure duties in Chapter 47-10 that have nothing to do with the lease. For a residential dwelling of four or fewer units you must give the buyer a written disclosure of all material facts you are aware could adversely and significantly affect an ordinary buyer's use and enjoyment, before final acceptance of the purchase agreement -- and that applies whether or not a real estate licensee is involved, subject to nine exemptions including foreclosure, fiduciary and immediate-family transfers (§ 47-10-02.1). Since 2025 you must also disclose in writing any knowledge you have of radon concentrations, give the buyer the prescribed radon warning to acknowledge by signature, and hand over any prior test results and evidence of mitigation reasonably available to you; comply and you are immune from radon-based claims (§ 47-10-02.2). And if the property sits in a homeowners' association or condominium project, you have ten days from executing the agreement to deliver the association's governing documents, budgets, assessments, litigation and violation history -- and if you do not, the buyer may void the purchase contract until they are delivered and for five days afterwards (§ 47-10-02.3).
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 47-16-07.1(5), 47-16-28, 47-16-29, 47-16-30 (complete Chapter 47-16 primary text); §§ 47-10-02.1, 47-10-02.2, 47-10-02.3 read from the official compilation ndlegis.gov/cencode/t47c10.pdf on 2026-09-27. | NEW STATUTE CONFIRMED ENACTED, not assumed: § 47-10-02.2 was created by 2025 SB 2204 (69th LA), enrolled 25.0456.03000, Senate 45-0 / House 87-3. Enactment was verified the only way that settles it -- the section is present in the current official compilation of ch. 47-10 with its own number and heading. The enrolled PDF's governor and Secretary of State date lines are blank, so the enrolled document alone would not have supported a VERIFIED. Instruction 17. | §§ 47-16-28, 47-16-29 and 47-16-30 had ZERO rows anywhere in the library before this one, and § 47-16-07.1(5) was covered only by edu-security-deposit-successor-owner-nd, which is the deposit leg alone. | CONSISTENT WITH a prior confirmed absence, not a correction to it: the checklist's ND cell for 'Broader landlord-identity-change notice (proactive tenant notification on sale/management change)' reads 'Confirmed absent', and that stands -- ND has no AZ § 33-1325 analog running to the tenant. The duties this row adds all run to the BUYER. | Found by the gap-discovery source 3 scenario screen ('owner sells the property with a tenant in place'); modelled on edu-selling-rented-property-az § 18.2. | NOT READ: § 47-10-28 (mobile home park transfer of ownership, tenant rights and penalty) beyond its heading -- mobile home parks are a deliberately deprioritized layer, and § 47-32-01.1 already gives the park-eviction defence a row. Whether the lease itself binds the buyer is common law and was not researched. N.D. Real Estate Commission form requirements under § 47-10-02.1 and § 43-23-11.1 not read.

title: No Radon Disclosure Duty When You Rent -- But There Is One When You Sell
bodyText: North Dakota requires no radon disclosure, testing, or warning from a landlord to a tenant, even though the EPA places the whole state in its highest-risk zone. The one mandatory disclosure at the start of a North Dakota tenancy is the signed condition statement (§ 47-16-07.2), and it says nothing about radon. The picture changes the moment you sell rather than rent: since 2025 a seller of residential real property must disclose any knowledge of radon concentrations in writing, give the buyer a prescribed radon warning to acknowledge by signature, and provide any prior test results and evidence of mitigation (§ 47-10-02.2). Testing and disclosing voluntarily to a tenant is still worth considering, since a habitability claim under § 47-16-13.1 does not require a disclosure statute to exist.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT for leases; PRESENT for sellers. Recorded as a row per the standing rule that log-only absences are invisible to future canvasses. | EVIDENTIARY BASIS UPGRADED. The checklist's ND cell previously read 'Confirmed absent -- Nolo: "North Dakota law requires only one disclosure" (§ 47-16-07.2)' -- a secondary source, and the cited section is the condition statement, not a radon rule. Replaced with: (a) the complete Chapter 47-16 primary text, which contains no radon provision; and (b) an official full-text search of ndlegis.gov for "radon" on 2026-09-27, which returned no Century Code hit at all in its top results -- every hit was a bill, committee minute or testimony. | LEGISLATIVE HISTORY worth knowing, because it shows the rental question was actually put and not answered: 2017 HB 1186 (65th LA) proposed a new chapter of title 47 for seller radon disclosure AND to 'amend and reenact section 47-16-07.2' -- that is, to put radon into the landlord-tenant condition statement. § 47-16-07.2 as it now reads contains no radon language. 2017 HB 1188 covered the same ground. Only the seller half ever became law, via 2025 SB 2204 (§ 47-10-02.2, enactment verified against the current compilation of ch. 47-10). | See edu-selling-rented-property-nd for the seller duty.

title: No Mold Disclosure Duty
bodyText: North Dakota has no mold disclosure requirement, no statutory mold standard, and no remediation timeline. Mold is not therefore risk-free: visible mold or the water intrusion behind it can put you in breach of the duty to keep the premises fit and habitable and to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (§ 47-16-13.1(1)(a)-(b)), and a tenant who gives you notice and gets no repair in a reasonable time can repair and deduct, or vacate and stop paying rent (§ 47-16-13). Treat a moisture complaint as a habitability matter on a clock rather than a disclosure question.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT, recorded as a row per the standing rule on log-only absences. | EVIDENTIARY BASIS UPGRADED. The checklist's ND cell read 'Confirmed absent -- corroborated by a dedicated mold-law reference site', which is secondary-source-only. Now resting on the complete Chapter 47-16 primary text (no mold provision) plus an official ndlegis.gov full-text search on 2026-09-27. | SEARCH CAVEAT stated honestly: "mold" is a poor search term in this corpus -- 471 hits, dominated by manufacturing molds, the verb, and unrelated testimony -- so absence here is established primarily by the full-chapter read rather than by the search. A targeted 'landlord mold' search surfaced no Century Code section. | NEAR MISS, not law: 2023 SB 2303 amendments would have required a DEVELOPER to disclose toxic black mold risk in a basement built below the ordinary high water mark, to a PURCHASER. That is a sale-side developer duty in a proposed amendment, not a landlord duty, and it is not in the current code. Recorded because a later canvass searching 'mold' will hit it and could mistake it for an enacted rental rule (K.4 pending-bill trap). | Prompted by gap-discovery source 2: the real lease used carries a tenant duty to prevent and report moisture accumulation, with no statute behind it.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure or Treatment Rule
bodyText: North Dakota imposes no bed bug disclosure duty, no treatment timeline, and no allocation of treatment cost between landlord and tenant. An infestation is handled under the general duties instead: your obligation to keep the premises fit and habitable and to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (§ 47-16-13.1(1)(a)-(b)), against the tenant's obligation to keep the occupied part of the premises as clean and safe as its condition permits (§ 47-16-13.2(2)). Because nothing divides the cost by statute, whatever your lease says about pest treatment is what will govern -- so say it.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT, recorded as a row per the standing rule on log-only absences. | EVIDENTIARY BASIS UPGRADED FROM AN ADMITTED INFERENCE. The checklist's ND cell read 'Confirmed absent (inferred from the same "only one disclosure" statement; not a dedicated search)'. The dedicated search has now been run: official ndlegis.gov full-text search for "bed bugs" and "bed bug" on 2026-09-27 returned 2 hits each, and NO Century Code hit. | THE ONE HIT IS A TRAP THIS PROJECT HAS ALREADY HIT ONCE IN ND. Both searches return N.D. Admin. Code Title 33, Article 39, Chapter 01, which defines 'Infestation' to include bed bugs. That is a Department of Health rule for LODGING ESTABLISHMENTS -- hotels and motels -- and not a residential-tenancy rule. The ND re-audit misattributed N.D. Admin. Code ch. 33-33-05 on exactly this lodgings/lodging-establishment confusion; naming the trap did not confer immunity then and does not now, so it is recorded here against the next reader. Note also that 'lodgings' is its own statutory category inside ch. 47-16 (§§ 47-16-05, 47-16-19, 47-16-20) meaning something different again. | The second hit is unrelated 2013 guardianship testimony. | ADMINISTRATIVE-CODE FLAG (instruction 16): the only ND bed bug rule anywhere is an agency rule, invisible to legislative bill tracking.

title: No Duty to Change the Locks for a Domestic Violence Victim
bodyText: North Dakota's domestic violence tenancy statute gives a victim one thing: the right to terminate the lease early on written notice, without penalty, paying the month of termination plus one additional month's rent subject to your duty to mitigate (§ 47-16-17.1). It does not give the tenant a right to require you to change the locks, and it does not give you a deadline, a cost allocation, or any immunity for doing so. If a tenant asks, you are deciding under the lease and under your own judgment, not under a statute -- and you still owe every remaining tenant on that lease quiet possession (§ 47-16-08) and the confidentiality duty in § 47-16-17.1(4), which bars you from disclosing the documentation the tenant gave you and carries statutory damages of $1,000 plus actual damages, fees and costs.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT, recorded as a row per the standing rule on log-only absences. | Basis: complete Chapter 47-16 primary text (§ 47-16-17.1 read in full, all eleven subsections -- no lock provision) plus an official ndlegis.gov full-text search for "change the locks" on 2026-09-27: 21 hits, NO Century Code hit. | LEGISLATIVE HISTORY: 2013 SB 2194 (63rd LA) would have given a tenant who fears imminent domestic violence the right to 'require a landlord to change the outside locks to residential property leased by the tenant ... without penalty or liability', on the same advance-written-notice structure § 47-16-17.1 now uses for termination. Committee minutes record senators questioning the 48-hour turnaround and the cost. The enacted § 47-16-17.1 has the notice structure and no lock provision. | CROSS-STATE CONTRAST that produced the search: NE has dv-lockchange-ne as a REQUIRED lease clause. ND has no counterpart, so the NE row must not be extended to ND. Found by the gap-discovery source 3 scenario screen. | Other hits reviewed: 2019 SB 2205 (enrolled) concerns affidavits about locks changed on foreclosed mortgaged premises, not tenancies. | POINTER CORRECTED 2026-10-02 (retro, SOP rule 78, found by the full ND pointer sweep). The cross-state contrast read 'NE has dv-lockchange-ne as a REQUIRED lease clause'; that row was switched off by the 2026-09-29 scrub, so the sentence is now stale as written. The substance holds and is the reason the search was run: Nebraska gives a protected tenant a lock-change right and North Dakota does not, so no Nebraska row may be extended to ND on this topic. Treat the reference as historical. Notes only.

title: No Late Fee Cap -- But Do Not Read That as No Limit
bodyText: North Dakota sets no dollar or percentage cap on late fees, and no statutory grace period. It has also declined to set one three times: bills to cap late rent fees were introduced in 2021 (HB 1440, HB 1442) and again in 2025 (SB 2236, which would have amended § 47-16-20 to cap a late fee at eight percent of the overdue rent). None became law. The absence of a cap is not the absence of a limit. Two general contract sections reach a late fee directly: penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void outright (§ 9-08-03), and a clause fixing damages in advance is void unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix (§ 9-08-04). A late fee set at a level that looks punitive rather than like a genuine estimate of what a late payment actually costs you is therefore attackable in North Dakota on grounds that have nothing to do with a cap -- and § 47-16-13.3 unconscionability sits behind that. Keep the figure defensible and keep a reason for it. Separately, North Dakota has no statute setting the order in which you must apply a tenant's payment, so whether a payment goes to rent first or to fees first is a contract question here, not a statutory one.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT as to a cap; the operative limits are elsewhere. | Basis: complete Chapter 47-16 read from the official compilation (ndlegis.gov/cencode/t47c16.pdf) on 2026-09-27 -- confirmed directly that no section in the chapter mentions a late fee, a late charge, a cap, or an order of applying payments; plus an official ndlegis.gov full-text search for "late fee" on 2026-09-27 (792 hits, NO Century Code hit). This closes a gap in how the absence had been supported: late-fee's ND note said 'confirmed: full read of ch. 47-16 contains no late-fee provision', which does not exclude a cap living outside the chapter (instruction 7's failure mode). It has now been excluded statewide. | TWO FAILED 2025 BILLS, both confirmed not enacted against the current compilation rather than by reading the bill history: SB 2236 would have amended § 47-16-20 to add an eight percent cap -- § 47-16-20 as it now reads is the unchanged 'Rents - When payable' section. SB 2235 (69th LA) would have addressed 'rents and the priority of payments under a rental agreement' -- no payment-priority rule exists in the chapter. K.4 pending-bill trap: a later session searching 'late fee' will surface SB 2236's 8% figure in engrossed bill text and could take it for law. | SUPPORTING SECONDARY EVIDENCE, cited as corroboration not authority: 2021 HB 1442 testimony from a renters' legal-aid witness states 'Current ND law does not have a limit on the amount of a late rent fee that can be imposed upon a renter', and High Plains Fair Housing Center testimony on SB 2236 describes leases in its database charging $10 up to '$100 + $100 per week thereafter'. | Prompted by gap-discovery source 2: the real lease used charges a flat $35 after the tenth of the month. See edu-prohibited-lease-terms-nd.

title: Stating the Purpose of the Lease Gives You Two Extra Remedies
bodyText: North Dakota attaches a specific consequence to a lease that states what the property is leased for. When real property is leased for a particular purpose the tenant must not use it for any other purpose, and if the tenant does, you may either hold the tenant responsible for the safety of the property during that use in all events, or treat the contract as rescinded (§ 47-16-11). The first of those is unusual and worth understanding: it is not a negligence standard. During a use outside the stated purpose the tenant answers for the property's safety whatever the cause, which shifts a category of loss you would otherwise carry. The second lets you treat the lease as at an end without waiting on the eviction chapter's grounds. Both depend on the lease actually stating a purpose -- which the residential-use clause does -- so this is a right you either capture in the drafting or forfeit silently.
notes: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-11, complete Chapter 47-16 primary text. | ZERO rows in the library cited § 47-16-11 before this one. Found by the gap-discovery source 3 scenario screen ('tenant runs a business from the unit', 'tenant lists the unit on Airbnb'), which reached it by walking the core chapter section by section against the ND-active rows -- the section is not something a keyword probe for short-term rentals or business use would return. | OPT-IN LANDLORD RIGHT (instruction 30): the remedy is conditioned on the lease stating a particular purpose. residential-use-only (tagged ND) supplies that condition, so ND leases built from this library do capture it; the point of the row is that a landlord who deletes or waters down that clause loses § 47-16-11 as well, which is not obvious from the clause text. | RELATIONSHIP TO THE EVICTION CHAPTER: § 47-32-01(8) makes violating a material term of a written lease an eviction ground on three days' notice of intention to evict. § 47-16-11's rescission route is a separate, direct contractual remedy under ch. 47-16 -- the same distinction edu-early-termination-grounds-nd draws for §§ 47-16-16 and 47-16-17, and this row belongs with those two. | NOT DETERMINED: whether 'treat the contract as rescinded' permits retaking possession without an eviction action. It almost certainly does not -- § 32-03-29's treble damages for forcible exclusion apply regardless of who is right about the lease (see edu-self-help-eviction-ban-nd) -- and the body deliberately does not suggest otherwise. No ND case law read.

title: Notice of Claims Against the Property
bodyText: If Tenant receives notice of any proceeding to recover the property or its possession -- including a foreclosure action, a tax proceeding, or a claim by any person other than Landlord -- Tenant will inform Landlord immediately and deliver the notice to Landlord. Tenant is responsible to Landlord for all damages Landlord sustains because Tenant failed to inform Landlord of a written notice or failed to deliver it. Tenant will not recognize or attorn to any person other than Landlord as the owner or landlord of the property without Landlord's consent or a judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction.
notes: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-25, complete Chapter 47-16 primary text: 'Every tenant who receives notice of any proceeding to recover the real property occupied by the tenant, or the possession thereof, must: 1. Inform the tenant's landlord immediately of the notice; and 2. Deliver the notice to the landlord. The tenant shall be responsible to the landlord for all damages which the landlord may sustain by reason of any omission by the tenant to inform the landlord of the notice or to deliver it to the landlord, if such notice is in writing. The attornment to a stranger is void unless made with the consent of the landlord or in consequence of a judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction.' | ZERO rows in the library cited § 47-16-25 before this one. Found by the gap-discovery source 3 scenario screen ('lender forecloses', 'a third party claims the property'). | WHY A LEASE CLAUSE AND NOT ONLY EDUCATION: the duty and the damages consequence exist by statute whatever the lease says, but they are worthless in practice if the tenant does not know them -- and the statute conditions the damages liability on the notice being 'in writing', which the clause does not restate because a landlord is better served by the broader contractual duty. RECOMMENDED rather than REQUIRED: North Dakota does not require the lease to contain this. | THE ATTORNMENT SENTENCE is the operative protection in a foreclosure or a disputed sale -- it stops a purported new owner from establishing a tenancy relationship directly with your tenant. Tied to edu-selling-rented-property-nd (§§ 47-16-28, 47-16-29, 47-16-30). | NOT PROPAGATED to any other state: § 47-16-25 is ND law. SD's Field Code ancestry makes an analog likely there but that is a candidate for SD's own session, never an inheritance. | No display collision: new topic_key, no supersedes relationship, and no existing ND-tagged row covers this subject.

title: When a Tenant Leaves Early: What You Can Collect and What You Must Do
bodyText: North Dakota's rules here are narrower than they look, and they differ depending on how the tenancy ended. If you evict, the tenant stays liable for rent for the remainder of the term, and that section expressly does not relieve you of the duty to mitigate damages (§ 47-16-13.7). If the lease is terminated, you have a claim for possession and for rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach (§ 47-16-13.4). If a lease ends before the time originally agreed, the tenant must pay the due proportion for the use actually made, unless that use was merely nominal and of no benefit to the tenant (§ 47-16-21). What North Dakota does not have is a general statutory duty to mitigate covering every tenant who simply leaves: the mitigation section is written into the habitability group, applying to a party aggrieved under §§ 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 (§ 47-16-13.5), and the duty otherwise appears only in § 47-16-13.7 for an evicted tenant and § 47-16-17.1(5) for a domestic violence termination. Do not treat that as licence to sit on an empty unit and bill the departed tenant: your own lease promises reasonable mitigation efforts, common law may supply the rest, and a flat early-termination or lease-break fee is separately exposed as a contractual penalty under § 9-08-03 or as liquidated damages under § 9-08-04. Re-rent, document the effort, and charge actual loss.
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 47-16-13.4, 47-16-13.5, 47-16-13.7, 47-16-21, with §§ 9-08-03 and 9-08-04. title: Fire or Casualty Damage
bodyText: If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty to an extent that enjoyment of the property is substantially impaired, Tenant may either (a) immediately vacate the property and notify Landlord in writing within fourteen days afterward of Tenant's intention to terminate this Lease, in which case this Lease terminates as of the date Tenant vacated, or (b) if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate only the part of the property made unusable by the casualty, in which case Tenant's Rent obligation is reduced in proportion to the loss in fair rental value of the property. If this Lease terminates under this Section, Landlord will return all prepaid Rent and the Security Deposit that Tenant is entitled to recover, accounting for Rent as of the date of the casualty. Tenant remains responsible for damage caused by Tenant's own negligence. Nothing in this Section limits any right Tenant has under applicable law.

title: Fire or Casualty - What You Owe Back, and When the Clock Starts
bodyText: If fire or casualty damages the property enough to substantially impair the tenant's enjoyment of it, the tenant may move out immediately and notify you in writing within 14 days that they are ending the lease, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate only the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the loss in fair rental value (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1429). Three details of Nebraska's fire-and-casualty rule catch landlords out. FIRST, the termination date is the date the tenant VACATED, not the date you received their notice: the tenant vacates first and then has fourteen days to notify you in writing, so a notice that arrives two weeks later still ends the tenancy as of the earlier move-out date, and rent is accounted for as of the date of the casualty itself (§76-1429). SECOND, you owe back all prepaid rent plus the security deposit the tenant can recover under §76-1416 - the casualty does not convert the deposit into damages, and the §76-1416 return deadline and penalty still apply. THIRD, a tenant who stays but loses part of the unit owes proportionally less rent, measured by the drop in FAIR RENTAL VALUE, not by floor area. The one thing that stays with the tenant is damage caused by their own negligence. You cannot contract around any of this: §76-1415(1)(a) voids a lease term waiving the tenant's rights under the Act. And if the tenancy ends, §76-1405 puts a duty to mitigate damages on the aggrieved party, so re-letting effort is expected rather than optional.

title: Meth Labs: You Must Report, You Must Not Re-Rent, and You Can Terminate in Three Days
bodyText: Nebraska has a four-section scheme for methamphetamine-contaminated rentals that sits outside the landlord-tenant act entirely, and it imposes real duties on you. YOU MUST REPORT: a property owner with knowledge of a clandestine drug lab on their property must report it as soon as practicable to local law enforcement or the Nebraska State Patrol (§71-2433). YOU MUST NOT RE-RENT: you may not permit human habitation or use of contaminated property until rehabilitation is complete and the local public health department has released the property, and knowingly violating that carries a civil penalty of up to $1,000 enforced by the Department of Health and Human Services (§71-2434(3)). YOU PAY FOR THE OVERSIGHT: the local public health department may charge you for the costs of monitoring the rehabilitation (§71-2434(2)). YOU CAN GET THE TENANT OUT FAST: notwithstanding any other provision of law, if leased property contains a clandestine drug lab you may terminate the lease on THREE DAYS' written notice for the purpose of rehabilitating it (§71-2435) - no cure period, and it overrides the usual 14-day and 7-day notice mechanics. 'Contaminated property' reaches any enclosed area intended for human habitation that has been contaminated by methamphetamine, its residue, or other substances from such a lab (§71-2432(2)).

title: Selling the Property, or Changing Managers - How You Actually Get Off the Hook
bodyText: Nebraska releases a selling landlord from future liability, but only if you do two specific things. FIRST, give the tenant WRITTEN NOTICE of the conveyance: a landlord who conveys the premises in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability under the lease and the Act only as to events occurring AFTER that written notice (§76-1420(1)). Events before it stay yours. SECOND, deal with the deposit separately: the release does NOT cover money and property the tenant is entitled to under §76-1416, so you remain personally liable for the security deposit and prepaid rent unless you ASSIGN them to the purchaser and give the tenant written notice of the assignment - which then does release you. Selling without assigning the deposit leaves you exposed for it after you no longer hold it. The same structure covers a manager: a manager is relieved of liability as to events after written notice to the tenant that their management has ended (§76-1420(2)). Two cautions. The section opens 'Unless otherwise agreed', so a lease or purchase agreement can change this allocation - check what yours says. And a change of owner or manager also restarts your §76-1417 disclosure duty, since the tenant is entitled to the current owner's and manager's name and address.

title: Your House Rules Are Enforceable Only If They Clear Six Tests
bodyText: Nebraska lets you adopt rules about the tenant's use and occupancy of the premises, but a rule is enforceable against the tenant only if ALL SIX of these hold (§76-1422): its purpose is to promote the appearance, convenience, safety or welfare of the tenants, to preserve your property from abusive use, or to distribute services and facilities fairly; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner; it is explicit enough to fairly inform the tenant what they must or must not do; it is not a device for evading your own obligations; and the tenant had notice of it when they entered into the lease. ADDING A RULE MID-TENANCY is allowed on different terms: a rule adopted after the lease is signed binds the tenant if you give reasonable notice of its adoption AND it 'does not work a substantial modification of his bargain'. So a new quiet-hours rule will usually stick; a new rule that effectively re-prices the tenancy or strips away something they bargained for will not. Enforcement runs through the ordinary noncompliance route at §76-1431, which means a rule violation is handled as a lease breach with the notice and cure mechanics that go with it - not as an independent ground for immediate termination.

Closing paragraph quotes the statute's final sentence: 'A rule or regulation adopted after the tenant enters into the rental agreement is enforceable against the tenant if reasonable notice of its adoption is given to the tenant and it does not work a substantial modification of his bargain.' The §76-1431 enforcement hook is express in the statute's opening ('It is enforceable as provided in section 76-1431'). title: Towing From Your Lot - No Signs, No Lawful Tow, and No Kickbacks
bodyText: Nebraska conditions a private tow on posted signs, and the rule splits by city size. OUTSIDE Omaha and Lincoln, parking in a PROPERLY POSTED restricted lot without the consent of the owner or tenant authorized to give permission is an infraction, and the vehicle may be towed at the lot owner's or tenant's request (§60-2401.01). IN Omaha (metropolitan class) and Lincoln (primary class), unless the city has adopted a conforming ordinance, vehicles parked without consent are subject to towing 'if the lot is properly posted' (§60-2401). Either way the signs carry the whole thing, and §60-2402 sets what they must say: they must be readily visible and must state the purpose or purposes for parking on the lot, the hours of restricted parking, and WHO TO CONTACT for information about a towed vehicle. A lot with no signs, or signs missing any of those three items, gives you no lawful tow. DO NOT TAKE A KICKBACK: an owner or tenant causing a vehicle to be towed 'shall not solicit or accept therefor a commission, gift, gratuity, or any form of compensation or wealth' from the towing business (§60-2411). Free towing arrangements and per-tow payments from the operator are exactly what this prohibits. The rest is on the tower, not you, but it affects your tenants: the tower must verify that whoever ordered the tow is really the lot's owner or tenant (§60-2409), notify law enforcement of the plate within 24 hours (§60-2403), and send the vehicle's owner and any lienholder a certified-mail notice within 15 business days (§60-2410(2)). Towing and storage become a lien on the vehicle but never on its contents, and the vehicle can be disposed of after 90 days (§60-2410(1)).

CLASS-OF-CITY SCOPE IS REAL, NOT DECORATIVE: §60-2401 applies to 'cities of the metropolitan or primary class' and §60-2401.01 applies 'Except in cities of the metropolitan or primary class' -- Nebraska's metropolitan class is Omaha and its primary class is Lincoln. The city identifications are from general knowledge of Nebraska's statutory city classes and were NOT read from the classification statute today; the statutory text supports the metropolitan/primary split itself, which is what the row turns on. §60-2401 also carries an 'ordinance conforming to section 60-2401.01' escape that a city may have used, so an Omaha or Lincoln landlord should check the local ordinance -- flagged per instruction 20, not resolved. *** WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: the whole Chapter 60 scheme was cited NOWHERE in the Nebraska library. title: Nebraska Does Regulate Radon - In New Construction, Not in Disclosure
bodyText: Nebraska requires no radon disclosure to tenants, but it does regulate radon in new buildings, and that reaches you if you build or bought new. New construction built after September 1, 2019 that is intended to be regularly occupied by people must be built using radon resistant new construction (§76-3504). The required minimum standards are specific: sealed or gasketed sump lids; a passive subslab depressurization system with a vent pipe of at least three inches running up through the building and terminating at least twelve inches above the roof and at least ten feet from any window or opening; separate vent pipes where interior footings divide the subslab material; visible interior vent pipes labelled 'Radon Reduction System' on each floor and in accessible attics; and an electrical circuit terminated in an approved box near the anticipated fan location so an active system can be added later. THERE ARE ONLY TWO EXEMPTIONS THAT APPLY TO A DWELLING (§76-3505): the project used the design of a licensed architect or professional engineer, or the county's average radon concentration is below 2.7 picocuries per liter as determined by the state. The third exemption - a local building official deciding it is unnecessary - is expressly unavailable 'other than for any residential dwelling unit', so it does not help a rental. Converting the passive system to an active one later is expressly permitted (§76-3506). Nebraska is among the highest-radon states in the country, so a passive system that was never activated is a live habitability and marketing question even though no statute makes you test or disclose.

title: Medical Cannabis Is Now Legal in Nebraska - Your Smoking Ban Still Works, Your Crime Clause Does Not
bodyText: Nebraska voters legalized medical cannabis in 2024, and the practical effect on a lease is narrower than most landlords expect. What changed: it is no longer an offense under state OR local law for a qualified patient to use, possess and acquire an allowable amount of cannabis for a medical condition, or for a caregiver to obtain and deliver it for them, and that conduct is removed from the Uniform Controlled Substances Act (§71-24,105). What did NOT change: nothing in the act requires you to permit cannabis on your property, so a contractual no-smoking clause remains enforceable against a qualified patient as an ordinary lease term. What you should stop relying on: any lease or statutory hook keyed to ILLEGAL or CRIMINAL drug activity. A registered patient's medical use is no longer illegal under state law, so it cannot support Nebraska's fast-track eviction for drug-related criminal activity under §76-1431, and treating it as criminal conduct is a real risk. Enforce it as a breach of your smoking or house-rules term instead, on the ordinary notice-and-cure track. Two further cautions: cannabis remains illegal under federal law, which still matters for federally assisted housing; and a request to use a non-smoked form as a disability accommodation is a fair-housing question under §20-319(2)(b), not a cannabis question.

But §71-24,104's definitions and the Patient Protection Act's remaining sections were not read, so this is recorded as strong-but-not-exhaustive rather than closed. title: No Duty to Pay Interest on a Security Deposit
bodyText: Nebraska imposes no duty to hold a security deposit in an interest-bearing account, to pay the tenant interest on it, or to keep it in a separate or escrow account. You may hold it with your own funds and keep any interest it earns. What Nebraska does regulate is the amount (one month's rent, plus up to one quarter of a month's rent as a pet deposit) and the return: a written itemized accounting and refund within fourteen days of demand after the tenancy ends, with a penalty for wrongful retention (§76-1416). If you operate in other states, do not carry this one across - deposit-interest duties are one of the most common state divergences in this area, and several states in this library do impose them.
