title: How a Nebraska Eviction Runs - and the Second Statute Nobody Reads
bodyText: Nebraska has TWO possession procedures, and which one you are in matters. The landlord-tenant act's own route is an action for possession: you file a complaint for restitution of the premises (§§76-1440, 76-1441), the case is tried on a short statutory timetable, and on a judgment for you the court issues a writ of restitution (§76-1446), with appeal governed by §76-1447. Separately, Nebraska's older forcible entry and detainer statutes, §§25-21,219 to 25-21,235, supply a parallel route with their own jurisdiction, notice-to-leave, trial, restitution and appeal-bond mechanics, and §25-21,220 says expressly that those provisions are not exclusive. Three things to keep straight. First, you cannot take possession yourself: self-help lockouts, removals and service shutoffs give the tenant remedies under §76-1430, and §76-1436 limits recovery of possession to the statutory process. Second, the tenant can turn the nonpayment case into a money fight - in an action for possession based on nonpayment, or an action for rent where the tenant is still in possession, the tenant may counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or the Act, and the court may order rent paid into court and net the two sides off (§76-1428). If no rent remains due after that netting, judgment on possession goes to the TENANT. Third, that cuts your way too: if the tenant's defense or counterclaim is without merit and not raised in good faith, you may recover reasonable attorney's fees (§76-1428(1)).
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-27 from nebraskalegislature.gov (official legislative compilation) in the built-in browser, via the official keyword search at /laws/search_keyword.php. Gap-discovery backfill, instruction 36 sources 3 and 4. CONTROLLING TEXT: Neb. Rev. Stat. §76-1428 read verbatim section-open, both subsections -- the counterclaim, pay-into-court and netting mechanics and the bad-faith attorney-fee award are all quoted from it. The Chapter 25 forcible entry and detainer sections are identified by section number and title from the official search (§§25-21,219 jurisdiction, 25-21,220 against whom / not exclusive, 25-21,221 notice to leave, 25-21,226 trial and judgment, 25-21,230 writ of execution form, 25-21,234 and 25-21,235 appeal and supersedeas) and were NOT read in full today. The 'not exclusive' statement rests on §25-21,220's title, which is a title-level claim and is flagged as such -- the row says the route exists and is parallel, and deliberately states no Chapter 25 notice period or bond figure, because those were not read. §§76-1440, 76-1441, 76-1446, 76-1430 and 76-1436 are carried from the original NE pass. *** WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: Nebraska had no eviction-procedure row at all, while SD, TX, FL and AZ each have one, and §76-1428 was cited NOWHERE in the library -- it is one of the two sections (with §76-1429) that the NE citation inventory skipped between 76-1427 and 76-1430. *** THE §76-1428 FEE AWARD IS A LANDLORD-FAVOURABLE OMISSION, not just a gap: edu-statutory-attorney-fee-actions-ne told Nebraska landlords which statutory fee awards exist and did not list this one. That row is amended today to add it. NOT RESEARCHED: the actual Chapter 25 timetables and bond amounts, when a landlord would choose the FED route over the Act's route, and whether the two can be pleaded in the alternative. This row is a map, not a procedure manual, and says so by omission.

title: Things Nebraska Has No Statute For - Checked Across the Whole Code
bodyText: Seven things landlords ask about that Nebraska has no statute on anywhere in its code, not merely nothing in the landlord-tenant act. (1) NO TENANT PROTECTION ON FORECLOSURE: Nebraska has no statute requiring notice to tenants of a pending foreclosure and none giving a tenant the right to stay after a foreclosure sale. The federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act is what governs, and it is federal law that does not depend on Nebraska adopting anything. (2) NO CASH-RENT RECEIPT DUTY: nothing requires you to give a written receipt for rent paid in cash. Give one anyway - it is your proof of payment as much as theirs. (3) NO HOLDING-DEPOSIT RULES: nothing regulates a pre-lease holding or reservation deposit, what it may be used for, or whether it is refundable if the applicant backs out. Your written agreement is the only thing governing it, so put the terms in writing. (4) NO STATE RENTAL REGISTRATION OR LICENCE: there is no statewide rental registry or landlord licence. Omaha and Lincoln run their own programmes and are not resolved here. (5) NO SQUATTER-SPECIFIC REMEDY: Nebraska has no separate unauthorized-occupant or squatter-removal statute; an occupant with no right to be there is removed through the ordinary possession and forcible-entry routes. (6) NO MOLD RULES: no mold disclosure duty, no remediation standard, no mold-specific habitability provision. (7) NO TYPOGRAPHY REQUIREMENTS: no Nebraska statute makes any residential lease term depend on being bold, underlined, capitalised, in a minimum type size, or in a separate document. Nothing in your lease is void for how it is formatted.
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-27 from nebraskalegislature.gov (official legislative compilation) in the built-in browser, via the official keyword search at /laws/search_keyword.php. Gap-discovery backfill, instruction 36 sources 3 and 4. SEARCH-ENGINE CHARACTERISTICS (material to every absence below): the Nebraska keyword search is NOT an exact-phrase engine, unlike Arizona's azleg.gov search. Quoting does not force a phrase ('"convenience fee"' returned MORE results than the bare terms), and multi-word input is matched loosely across the words, so 'holding deposit' returned 58 banking-deposit sections and 'application fee' 648. A nonsense control term ('zzzqqqxyzzy') returned 0, so a 0-hit result IS meaningful. Method therefore used the most DISTINCTIVE SINGLE WORD per topic and reviewed every hit across all result pages (pagination is the 'start' POST parameter; 25 per page). Absences below are statutes-only: the Nebraska Administrative Code, municipal codes and case law were not searched. CONFIRMED ABSENT x7, STATUTE-WIDE, each with the terms run. (1) FORECLOSURE: 'foreclosure tenant' (11 results, all reviewed: §§25-202, 25-1104, 25-328, 76-238, 76-301, 77-203, 40-101, 71-15,113, 25-1533, 36-105 -- none a tenant protection). The statute-wide 'landlord' sweep returned no foreclosure section. Several other states in this library DO have one (NV, CA, MN, NJ, FL, AZ), so this is a real divergence, not an untested guess. The PTFA reference is general knowledge, NOT read from primary source -- flagged per instruction 16 as federal and outside any state bill-tracking watch. (2) CASH RECEIPT: 'written receipt' (508 results -- heavy false-positive load from the loose word matching, top pages reviewed and all insurance, tax, lien and licensing provisions; no landlord-tenant hit). Corroborated by the 'landlord' sweep returning no receipt section. WEAKEST of the seven because the result set was too large to review exhaustively -- recorded honestly as such rather than as a clean absence. (3) HOLDING DEPOSIT: 'holding deposit' (58 results, all banking), 'holding fee' (101, all licensing and permit fees); no hit regulates a pre-lease deposit. (4) RENTAL REGISTRATION: 'rental registration' (17 results, all tax, vehicle and gaming). Omaha and Lincoln programmes flagged, not resolved, per instruction 20. (5) SQUATTER: 'unauthorized occupant' (1 result, §25-21,277, diversion of utility services -- not a removal remedy). (6) MOLD: 'mold' (6 results: §§79-10,110, 79-10,110.02, 77-2701.47, 44-5004, 2-3991, 2-2624 -- school health-and-safety levies, manufacturing equipment, health insurance and dairy packaging), 'mildew' (1, §2-2624), 'fungus' (6, all pesticide, nail-technology and plant-pest definitions). This is the cleanest absence in the set. (7) TYPOGRAPHY (instruction 28): 'underlined' (3 results: §§21-214, 25-2602.02, 45-808 -- co-operative definitions, an arbitration-contract statement and a consumer contract; none landlord-tenant), 'boldface' (25 results, all reviewed -- the Chapter 76 hits are §76-2110 condominium and time-share disclosure, §§76-2719, 76-2720, 76-2722 equity-purchase contracts, §76-2713 foreclosure consulting and §76-3112 private transfer fees, none of which reaches a residential lease), 'conspicuous' and 'separate writing' (143 and 123 results; no §76-14xx hit on the pages reviewed). CONCLUSION: NO bold, underline, capitalisation, type-size or separate-document rule conditions any Nebraska residential lease term -- the sharpest contrast in the library with Texas, where 17 terms are void or ineffective without specific formatting. *** BOUNDARY, stated plainly: statutes only. The Nebraska Administrative Code, municipal codes and case law were NOT searched, so each item above is 'no Nebraska STATUTE', which is what the row claims and no more.

title: Steam Radiator Cover Notice
bodyText: [BUILDER: attach as a rider to the lease wherever the unit has steam radiators; Landlord must also give this notice in writing at least once a year and post it in the common area where tenant notices are posted.] Steam Radiator Covers. Tenant may ask Landlord in writing to cover each steam radiator in Tenant's unit with an insulating material or cover that protects tenants, occupants and others from burns caused by contact with the radiator. Landlord will install the covers within 90 days after receiving Tenant's written request.
notes: NJ: Gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36). Source 2 (real-lease comparison) lead: NJ Realtors Form 125-10/2022 carries a steam-radiator rider. Verified against the chapter law on the Legislature's site: P.L.2021, c.259 (approved 2021-11-08; effective the first day of the third month after enactment), codified N.J.S.A. 52:27D-198.20. 1.a: within 90 days of a tenant's written request, 'an owner of a residential rental property shall cover each steam radiator in the tenant's unit' with insulating material or a cover protecting against burns. 1.b: owner must notify tenants of the right to request covers 'as a rider to any written residential lease agreement and in writing at least annually', and post in common areas where tenant notices are displayed. 1.c: fine up to $500 by the enforcing agency; 1.d: injured tenant, occupant or other person has a private action. The act does not define 'residential rental property' (so no unit-count threshold stated) - builder should include this rider for any unit with steam radiators. No prescribed wording; body tracks the statute. Relation to case law: J.H. v. R&M Tagliareni, LLC (N.J. 2019) held no landlord duty where the tenant controlled the radiator heat - the statute now imposes the duty on request. LAYOUT: lease RIDER (instruction 28); annual written notice and common-area posting are outside the lease. CONDITIONAL on steam radiators.

title: Private Well Water Test Results
bodyText: The property's drinking water comes from a private well. Tenant acknowledges receiving a written copy of the most recent water test results for the property under the New Jersey Private Well Testing Act.
notes: NJ: Gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36). Source 2 lead: NJ Realtors Form 125-10/2022 §42 (Private Well Testing). Controlling text read on the FindLaw host copy (current as of 2024-01-01; not compared with the official site): N.J.S.A. 58:12A-32 (Private Well Testing Act, N.J.S.A. 58:12A-26 to -37): a lessor of property whose potable water supply is a private well must test within 18 months after 2002-09-14 and at least once every five years thereafter; give a written copy of results to each rental unit within 30 days after receipt; give a new lessee a written copy of the most recent results; seasonal rentals may instead post the results inside the unit. Test parameters, certified-lab requirement and penalties are elsewhere in the Act (not read). CONDITIONAL on a private-well water supply. Lease text is an acknowledgment plus the ongoing duty; the duty exists regardless of the lease. | NJ: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): kept the tenant's acknowledgment of receipt; the testing and delivery duty moved to edu-private-well-testing-nj.

title: Fire and Other Casualty
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire without the fault of Tenant, Landlord will repair it as quickly as possible, and Rent will stop until the property has been fully repaired. If the building is totally destroyed by fire or otherwise without the fault of Tenant, Rent will be paid up to the date of destruction, and this Lease will then end.
notes: NJ: Gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36). Source 2 lead: NJ Realtors Form 125-10/2022 §21 (Fire and Other Casualty). NJ had no casualty row. Controlling text read section-open 2026-09-26 (official N.J.S.A. text pasted by Taylor): N.J.S.A. 46:8-6 (fire injury without lessee's fault: landlord repairs 'as speedily as possible'; in default of repair 'the rent shall cease' until complete repair) and 46:8-7 (total destruction 'by fire or otherwise' without lessee's fault: rent paid to the time of destruction, then the lease ends). Both apply only where the lease does not 'otherwise stipulate', so this clause restates the statutory defaults rather than varying them - a deliberate choice (tenant-neutral; no waiver risk under N.J.S.A. 46:8-48). Form 125 departs from the defaults (90-day repair window / cancellation); not adopted. Partial-destruction-by-other-casualty (non-fire) is not addressed by either section; the clause is silent on it. Checklist row 63 already cited these sections without a row. | NJ: SCRUB 2026-09-29 (checklist instruction 66, three-bucket test): switched off, not deleted. It restates a tenant right or landlord duty that applies whatever the lease says, so the content moved to education (edu-casualty-nj). Kept for a possible comprehensive-lease option.

title: Owners Must Carry Liability Insurance
bodyText: New Jersey requires the owner of a rental unit to carry liability insurance of at least $500,000 for combined property damage and bodily injury, or at least $300,000 for an owner-occupied multifamily home of four or fewer units. Owners must register the certificate of insurance with the municipality each year. A municipality can fine a noncompliant owner $500 to $5,000.
notes: NJ: Gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36). Source 2 lead: NJ Realtors Form 125-10/2022 §22 cites the insurance minimums. Verified against the chapter law on the Legislature's site: P.L.2022, c.92 (signed 2022-08-05), codified N.J.S.A. 40A:10A-1 (coverage: $500,000; $300,000 for owner-occupied multifamily of four or fewer units) and 40A:10A-2 (annual registration of the certificate with the municipality; fine $500-$5,000 by summary proceeding). Effective: 90 days (new policies) / 180 days (renewals and the multifamily provision) after enactment; DCA Local Finance Notice 2022-23 gives 2022-11-03 and 2023-02-01. The chapter law states no definition of 'rental unit' (per the fetched text). Not lease content; no clause. Outside the landlord-tenant title (gap-discovery source 4 shape).

title: Towing From Rental Property
bodyText: A New Jersey landlord cannot simply have a tenant's or visitor's car towed because the lease allows it. A tow without the vehicle owner's consent is lawful only if the landlord has a private-property towing contract with the tow company, has authorized removal of that particular vehicle, and the car goes to secure storage within a reasonable distance. Most properties must also post a sign at least 36 by 36 inches at every vehicle entrance stating when parking is allowed, that violators will be towed at the owner's expense, and the tow company's name, contact details, charges and storage address.
notes: NJ: Gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36). Source 3 (scenario screen) gap: 'car towed from the lot' - parking-vehicle-rules defers to law (NJ note added 2026-09-26); an education row makes the preconditions visible, as AZ did (edu-towing-az). (L.2007, c.193); 56:13-13 (amended 2017, c.321): contract, 36x36-inch sign content at all vehicular entrances, per-vehicle owner authorization, secure storage within a reasonable distance; the host summary reports the signage requirement does not apply to single-family units or owner-occupied structures of six or fewer units (not read verbatim - body says 'most properties'); 56:13-16 (amended 2023, c.132): no patrol/surveillance towing without the owner's specific request; release of a hooked-but-unmoved vehicle; notice to owner, lessor and lienholder within 30 days.

title: Occupancy by Children
bodyText: Children who are members of Tenant's household may live at the property. Each child who will live at the property is to be listed with the other occupants under this Lease's occupancy terms. Landlord places no restriction on occupancy by children other than those occupancy terms, which apply to every occupant regardless of age. [If the property is housing for older persons that qualifies for the fair-housing exemption for such housing, replace this Section with a statement of the property's age requirements for occupancy.]

Surfaced by gap-discovery source 2 (NV log backfill section, Part 1): the GLVAR lease's occupant clause is silent on children too, and mapping it against the (3) list exposed the gap. 118A.200(5)(a) presumes no restriction on children absent a written agreement. Familial status is a protected class (NRS 118.100, edu-fair-housing-nv), so the clause states no child-specific limit; neutral occupancy limits stay in permitted-occupants. title: Required Fees
bodyText: In addition to the Monthly Rent and any deposit stated in this Lease, Tenant is required to pay the following fees, for the purposes stated: [list each required fee - its amount, when it is due and the purpose for which it is required, e.g. "a nonrefundable cleaning charge of $___, due at signing, to pay for cleaning the premises after Tenant vacates" - or state "None"]. Any required fee that is payable every rental period is included in the Monthly Rent and is not charged in addition to it, except a utility fee that this Lease identifies with the Monthly Rent as the law allows. No charge applies to a late or partial payment of Rent, or to a dishonored check or other returned payment, except a late fee or returned-payment charge stated in this Lease.
notes: NV: NRS 118A.200(3)(e) and (3)(g), Section-open read of revisor text on leg.state.nv.us in Taylor's browser 2026-09-27 (compilation Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated; section history line checked): the lease must contain provisions relating to "fees which are required and the purposes for which they are required" and "charges which may be required for late or partial payment of rent or for return of any dishonored check". Before this row no NV clause listed required fees with their purposes, and late-fee-nv and returned-payments-nv are optional rows, so a lease without them said nothing on (3)(g). The last sentence closes (3)(g) whether or not those rows are used, and covers partial payments, which no NV row mentioned (118A.200(5)(c)'s no-charge presumption applies only where there is no written agreement). Periodic fees: 118A.200(6)-(8) (rent-single-figure-nv). BUILDER: a payment whose purpose is to remedy a rent default, repair damage or clean is a security deposit whatever it is called (118A.240). It counts toward the three-month cap (security-deposit-cap-nv) and must be refundable, except a reasonable nonrefundable cleaning charge (118A.242(8)). Don't let a user list a "nonrefundable pet fee" or "damage fee" here. This row gives security-deposit-return-nv's "nonrefundable cleaning charge ... stated in this Lease" a place in the lease. Surfaced by gap-discovery source 2: the GLVAR lease's summary-of-monies section lists each fee by name, the library had no counterpart. title: Tenant-Performed Repairs and Maintenance
bodyText: [Optional. Include only if Landlord and Tenant agree that Tenant will perform specified tasks.] Tenant agrees to perform the following specified repairs, maintenance tasks or minor remodeling: [list each task specifically, e.g. replace heating and air-conditioning filters every [number] months with filters Landlord provides; replace light bulbs; keep the pool clean and its water balanced]. Landlord and Tenant make this agreement in good faith. Tenant is not entering into it because Landlord or Landlord's agent refused to perform any repair, maintenance task or remodeling that Landlord is required by law to perform, and it does not reduce Landlord's obligations to any other tenant. Landlord remains responsible for keeping the property habitable as applicable law requires, and nothing in this Section requires Tenant to pay any fee or charge for work that is Landlord's duty, except work needed because of a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, a member of Tenant's household, or another person on the premises with Tenant's consent.
notes: NV: NRS 118A.290(2)-(5), Section-open read of revisor text on leg.state.nv.us in Taylor's browser 2026-09-27 (compilation Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated; section history line checked) (A. 1999, 2007, 2023). (2): landlord and tenant "may agree that the tenant is to perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks and minor remodeling only if" the agreement is in good faith and does not diminish the landlord's obligations to other tenants. (3): not in good faith if the landlord owes the work under (1) and the tenant agrees because the landlord refused it. (4): no fee or charge for work that is the landlord's (1) duty (the 2023 home-warranty deductible ban, edu-habitability-duty-nv). (5): charges allowed for tenant-caused conditions. OPT-IN LANDLORD RIGHT (instruction 30): without a written list the tasks stay with the landlord. The recital cannot make the agreement good faith; it records the facts the statute tests. Drafted conservatively: tasks are listed specifically, habitability stays with Landlord, and there is no charge for landlord-duty work. Whether (2) lets a (1) repair itself be shifted is not settled by the text and is not relied on. Include only if Landlord wants to designate who performs this work.] If applicable law permits Tenant to have work done at Landlord's expense because Landlord failed to make a repair or to supply an essential service after notice, that work must be performed by [name the person or firm, or describe a class of persons or firms qualified to do the work, e.g. "a contractor holding a Nevada license for that type of work"], and Tenant will comply with this specification. This Section does not otherwise limit any remedy applicable law gives Tenant.

Built now because instruction 30 asks for a CONDITIONAL row or a recorded reason. "Or otherwise" means a separate written designation also works; the lease is the natural place. The class must be "qualified to do the work"; a designation that makes the remedy unusable in practice invites a challenge (not researched). The remedies themselves are in edu-tenant-repair-remedies-nv. Surfaced by gap-discovery source 3 (scenario: tenant repairs and deducts).

title: Political Signs in HOA and Condo Communities
bodyText: If the rental is in a common-interest community (a homeowners' or condominium association), the association may not prohibit a unit's owner or an occupant - which includes your tenant - from displaying political signs in the part of the property the owner or occupant has the right to use exclusively. Protected signs are those supporting or opposing a candidate, political party or ballot question in a federal, state, local or association election. Each may be no larger than 24 by 36 inches, only one sign per candidate, party or ballot question is protected, and signs must follow any law on posting political signs. While a tenant occupies the unit, you as the owner may not display a political sign there unless the tenant consents in writing. The rule binds the association and its governing documents; it does not address what your lease may say about signs.
notes: NV: NRS 116.325, Section-open read of revisor text on leg.state.nv.us in Taylor's browser 2026-09-27 (compilation Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated; section history line checked) (added 2005, A. 2009, no later amendment). (1): "The executive board shall not and the governing documents must not prohibit a unit's owner or an occupant of a unit from exhibiting one or more political signs" in the exclusive-use area, subject to (a) 24x36 inches, (b) owner may not exhibit any political sign in a tenant-occupied unit without the tenant's written consent, (c) posting laws, (d) one per candidate, party or ballot question. (2): minimum rights. (3): definition. Found by gap-discovery source 2 (the GLVAR lease cites NRS 116 for political signs). Source 4's full-text search ("political sign(s)") hit 116.325, 116B.715 (condominium hotels), 118B.145 (mobile-home parks), 405.030 and 405.110 (highways), 410.400 and 704.638. None is a landlord-tenant rule for dwellings, so common-area-use's sign-consent sentence applies in NV as written. topic_key political-signs matches political-signs-ca, a CA-only lease clause; no NV collision.

title: Removing a Squatter or Unauthorized Occupant
bodyText: A person who enters your property without the authority of you, your representative or your tenant and does not leave after a written notice to surrender is guilty of forcible detainer, as is anyone who holds possession by force or threats. For a squatter there is a fast court process. Serve a written notice to surrender the way eviction notices are served. It must name the court and tell the occupant: that they may contest by filing an affidavit before the court closes on the fourth judicial day after service; that the court may order the sheriff or constable to remove them within 24 hours; and that property left behind will be stored safely and may be disposed of after 14 calendar days, with inventory, moving and storage costs payable before release. When the notice expires, file an affidavit of complaint with a copy of the notice and proof of service. If the occupant did not contest, or the contest raises no legal defense, the court must order removal within 24 hours; if it raises a defense, a hearing is held within 7 judicial days. An occupant who entered peaceably under an invalid lease or someone else's fraud may be given up to 20 days to leave. Keep property left behind in safe storage for 21 days after the removal or surrender before disposing of it: the notice says 14 days, but the removal section separately requires 21 days' storage. Vehicles go through the abandoned-vehicle law. If every unauthorized adult occupant has been arrested for housebreaking or unlawful occupancy, you may instead retake possession and change the locks, posting a notice with the court and contest details for at least 21 days and filing a copy with the court within 1 day. You may recover three times your actual damage to real and personal property from a person guilty of forcible entry or forcible detainer. Your tenant, as an occupant you authorized, may use the same process. For a tenant or former tenant, use the eviction procedures for tenants instead.

title: Lease Translation When You Advertise in Another Language
bodyText: If, in your business, you advertise a rental in a language other than English and negotiate the lease in that language - orally or in writing, yourself or through an employee or agent - you must give a translation of the lease in that language to the tenant, and to anyone else who may sign it, before it is signed. This applies to a lease or rental agreement of at least one month for a dwelling used as a residence. The translation must include every term and condition; names, addresses, numbers, dollar amounts, dates and words with no accepted translation may stay in English. A later document that substantially changes the parties' rights needs a translation too; routine house rules and furniture inventories do not. If you don't comply, the tenant may cancel (rescind) the lease, and a knowing violation is a deceptive trade practice.

(3)(b): "a lease, sublease, rental contract or agreement or other contract or agreement containing a term of tenancy" of at least 1 month for a dwelling, apartment, mobile home or other dwelling unit used as a residence. title: Repair Orders and Receivership for Multifamily Rentals
bodyText: If you rent out two or more units on one parcel, your county (outside cities) or city must act when it finds that the property violates a habitability standard, a housing or building code, or a habitability, building-safety or fire-safety law badly enough to substantially endanger the health and safety of residents or the public. It must order you to repair, rehabilitate or abate the condition by a deadline. The notice and order is posted on the property and sent by certified mail to you and each affected resident, and it states that you may not retaliate against any tenant. If you don't comply, the county or city can sue to have the property declared substandard and obtain a repair order and civil penalties, and the local government or a nonprofit representing tenants can ask the court to appoint a receiver after 30 days' posted and mailed notice. Once a receiver is appointed you may not collect rent, interfere with the receiver, or encumber or transfer the property; the receiver collects the rents, makes the repairs and may borrow against the property. The court will order you to pay the local government's costs and attorney's fees. If tenants cannot safely stay, it will also order moving costs and up to 120 days of rent differential as relocation benefits, plus a first right to return; a tenant who caused the conditions gets no relocation benefits.

title: Health District Rules for Rental Units
bodyText: In a county served by a district board of health, the board may adopt and enforce regulations on health hazards in rental dwelling units - any biological, physical or chemical exposure, condition or public nuisance that may harm health - and recover its enforcement costs. If it has adopted regulations on the condition of rental units, you must give a copy to a tenant who asks for one. A tenant who gave you written notice of a habitability failure that you did not fix, or reasonably try to fix, within the statutory time may send a copy of that notice to the district board of health. If an inspection finds that you or the tenant failed to keep the unit habitable, the board may take enforcement action or refer the matter to its administrative hearing process.

title: Former Drug-Lab Properties
bodyText: A building that was used to manufacture a controlled substance illegally, such as methamphetamine, is a public nuisance if it has not been deemed safe for habitation by the board of health and the owner either lets it be used for any purpose before a certified or licensed entity has removed or remediated the contamination, or fails to have that done within 180 days after the manufacturing stops. Maintaining a public nuisance is a misdemeanor, so do not rent such a property until it has been remediated and deemed safe. The statutes set no separate duty to disclose a former drug lab to a tenant. The statute that makes certain facts immaterial in a sale deliberately leaves methamphetamine manufacture off that list, so disclosure is the safer course.

bodyText: Nevada statutes do not require a residential landlord to disclose mold, and they set no separate mold-remediation duty. Mold is handled through your general duty to keep the unit habitable and to comply with housing and health codes. In a county with a district board of health, the board can also regulate health hazards in rental units.

title: Rent-Reporting Programs Are Voluntary
bodyText: The state Housing Division may run a free, voluntary program for reporting tenants' rent payments to a credit reporting agency. You may not require a tenant to take part in that program, and you may not impose any penalty or other consequence on a tenant for not taking part.

title: Ohio Private Tow-Away Zones Have Hard Sign Rules
bodyText: Before a towing service may remove a vehicle from your rental property without the vehicle owner's permission, the property must be a valid private tow-away zone. Ohio sets the signs by statute: at least eighteen inches by twenty-four inches, visible from every entrance to the property, and stating that it is a tow-away zone, who may park there (for residential property, tenants and their guests), the property address or business name, the hours of enforcement if it is not around the clock, a telephone number and the address where a towed vehicle can be recovered, and a warning that an unclaimed vehicle may lose its title. You may modify existing signs with stickers or addenda rather than replacing them. Only the property owner or an authorized agent may order a tow, and the towing service must hold a written contract with you. If the vehicle owner arrives before the vehicle is actually removed, they may reclaim it for no more than half the removal fee. Get the signs wrong and the tow is unlawful: the vehicle owner may sue under R.C. 4513.611.
notes: OH: R.C. 4513.601, private tow-away zones, read section-open 2026-09-27; effective 2023-04-07, H.B. 507 (134th G.A.). FOUND BY THE OUTSIDE-TITLE SEARCH (source 4) and the landlord-scenario screen (source 3) - Title 45 Motor Vehicles, invisible to a ch. 5321 read. Division (K) defines 'owner of private property' to include title holders, LESSEES, SUBLESSEES, MANAGERS and their agents, so a property manager is directly covered. Other duties fall on the towing service, not the landlord: notice to the sheriff or municipal police within two hours (division E); certified or express mail notice to the vehicle owner and lienholder within five business days, with a second notice if the vehicle is unclaimed 30 days later (division F); storage within 25 linear miles where practicable, well-lit and near public transit. Violation of division (H) is a minor misdemeanor for the carrier. PUCO sets the fee schedule. NOT READ: R.C. 4513.60, 4513.602, 4513.611 in full, and municipal towing licensing. Same gap shape as Arizona's edu-towing-az (AZ log 18.2).

title: If Utilities Are In Your Name, A Tenant Can Redirect Your Rent
bodyText: Where you are the utility customer of record - master-metered buildings, or any unit where you include utilities in the rent - an unpaid bill is not just your problem with the utility. Before disconnecting, the utility gives you fourteen days' notice and then attempts a separate ten-day notice to each tenant unit and posts notice conspicuously on the building. That ten-day notice tells your tenants their options, and two of them cost you money. A tenant may stop the disconnection by paying an amount equal to the current month's bill, which the utility credits to your account. Or a tenant may use the rent-deposit remedy under R.C. 5321.07 to deposit rent with the court and ask the court to spend it on the utility bill - so the rent you were owed pays the utility instead. If you are the one asking for disconnection, you get ten days' notice and you are liable for everything consumed in that period. Separately, between November 15 and April 15 the utility must give your occupants five days' notice before shutting off, and must tell them about state and federal bill-payment aid.
notes: OH: R.C. 4933.121 (effective 2005-05-18, H.B. 426, 125th G.A.) and OAC 4901:1-18-08 'Landlord-tenant provisions' (effective 2015-04-15), both read section-open 2026-09-27. FOUND BY THE OUTSIDE-TITLE SEARCH (source 4): Title 49 Public Utilities plus the PUCO administrative code - neither reachable from a ch. 5321 read. INSTRUCTION 16 FLAG: OAC 4901:1-18-08 is ADMINISTRATIVE CODE, changed by PUCO rulemaking with no bill and no legislative-tracking signal, the same monitoring problem as Ohio's assistance-animal rule (OAC 4112-5-07). The rule carries a model tenant ten-day notice as its appendix A, supplied by the utility, not drafted by the landlord. The rule read is the ELECTRIC chapter (4901:1-18); parallel gas and water rules were NOT read and may differ - flagged. The R.C. 5321.07 link matters: this is the same escrow mechanism as repair-escrow-exemption-notice-oh, and the 4901:1-18-08 route is NOT subject to 5321.07(C)'s three-or-fewer-units exemption on its face - not determined, flagged.

title: A No-Firearms Clause Does Not Bind a Licensed Ohio Tenant
bodyText: Do not put a handgun ban in an Ohio residential lease expecting it to work. R.C. 2923.126(C)(3)(b) provides that a landlord may not prohibit or restrict a tenant who holds a concealed handgun license, or the tenant's guest while the tenant is present, from lawfully carrying or possessing a handgun on the residential premises, for any rental agreement entered into on or after September 9, 2008. The restriction runs against you, not the tenant, so a lease term to the contrary is simply unenforceable against a licensee. It is narrower than it first looks: the protection is written for a licensee and for that licensee's guest while the licensee is present, and it covers lawful carrying and possession of a handgun.
notes: OH: R.C. 2923.126(C)(3)(b), read section-open 2026-09-27; section effective 2025-04-09, amended by H.B. 452, S.B. 98 and H.B. 33 (135th G.A.). FOUND BY THE OUTSIDE-TITLE SEARCH (source 4) - Title 29 Crimes, concealed-carry article; no ch. 5321 read reaches it. This is an OHIO LEASE-CONTENT RESTRICTION sitting entirely outside 5321.13, so Ohio's prohibited-terms coverage (edu-bilateral-fee-ban-oh for 5321.13(C), edu-one-way-delegation-oh for 5321.13(A),(E),(F)) did not include it. Also not researched: long guns, and whether a landlord may restrict discharge or storage as distinct from carrying or possession.

title: A Tenant Or Neighbor Can Put Your Building Into Receivership
bodyText: Ohio's habitability remedies are not the only exposure for a building in poor condition. Under R.C. 3767.41 a municipal corporation, a township, a neighbor, a tenant, or a nonprofit housing organization may bring a civil action alleging that the building is a public nuisance on grounds of structural safety, habitability, fire hazard or inadequate maintenance. If you have refused or failed to abate, the court may appoint a receiver who takes possession and control of the building, collects the rents and income, pays operating expenses and liens, hires managing agents and carries out rehabilitation work. Approved receiver expenditures and fees become a first lien on the building, superior to all prior and subsequent liens including tax liens, and the property can be sold to satisfy them. Owner-occupied buildings with three or fewer units are excluded.
notes: OH: R.C. 3767.41, read section-open 2026-09-27; effective 2023-10-03. FOUND BY THE OUTSIDE-TITLE SEARCH (source 4) - Title 37 Health-Safety-Morals, nuisance chapter. Surfaced as a landlord-relevant hit in the official code search for 'landlord' (54 results). Distinct from the R.C. 5321.07 escrow route in kind, not just degree: escrow redirects rent temporarily; a 3767.41 receiver takes possession and its lien outranks the mortgage. FIFTH OHIO PORTFOLIO THRESHOLD: owner-occupied with three or fewer units - see edu-portfolio-thresholds-oh, updated in the same delta. NOT READ: the procedural detail of 3767.41 (notice, hearing, who may be appointed, how the receivership ends) and the related nuisance sections in ch. 3767. Arizona's nearest analogue is edu-crime-nuisance-abatement-az, which is a criminal-activity statute, not a condition-based receivership - do not treat them as the same topic.

title: Ohio Requires No Radon Disclosure To A Tenant
bodyText: Ohio imposes no radon testing, mitigation or disclosure duty on a residential landlord toward a tenant. Ohio does regulate radon, but only the professionals: R.C. Chapter 3723 licenses radon testers, mitigation specialists, mitigation contractors and laboratories. Nothing in it reaches the landlord-tenant relationship. Do not be misled by R.C. 5302.30: that is the residential property disclosure form for SALES, and it does not apply to a lease.

title: Ohio Has No Residential Bed Bug Statute
bodyText: Ohio imposes no bed bug disclosure duty and sets no treatment timeline for residential rental property. Bed bugs in an Ohio rental are handled through the general habitability duty in R.C. 5321.04(A)(1)-(2) and the tenant's own duties in R.C. 5321.05, not through a dedicated statute. Ohio's bed bug provisions sit in the hotel chapter and do not reach a residential tenancy.

title: Ohio Has No Mold Disclosure Or Remediation Statute

title: Ohio Gives A Tenant No Right To Install EV Charging
bodyText: Ohio has no right-to-charge law. A residential tenant has no statutory right to install an electric vehicle charging station, and a landlord has no statutory duty to permit or accommodate one. Whether a tenant may install or use charging equipment is a matter for the lease and for R.C. 5321.06, which lets the parties agree to any term not inconsistent with Chapter 5321 or other law. Local zoning and building codes may still govern the installation itself.

title: Ohio Gives A Domestic Violence Victim No Statutory Way Out
bodyText: Ohio has no statewide domestic violence lease-termination right, no DV anti-termination protection, and no DV lock-change duty. A survivor who leaves early remains liable on the lease under ordinary contract principles, and a landlord may pursue the remaining rent, subject only to the common-law duty to mitigate. Seven other states in this library give the survivor a statutory release; Ohio does not. Tenants in federally subsidised housing are covered by the federal Violence Against Women Act instead, which is a separate regime.

title: Ohio Has No Right-To-Call-Emergency-Services Statute
bodyText: Ohio gives a tenant no statutory, non-waivable right to summon police or emergency services. R.C. 5321.02's retaliation protection is close but narrower, and its trigger list is closed: complaining to a governmental agency about a code violation materially affecting health and safety, complaining to the landlord about a R.C. 5321.04 violation, or joining with other tenants to bargain collectively. Calling 911 is on none of those. So a landlord who penalises a tenant for repeated emergency calls faces no specific statutory bar in Ohio - and because Ohio also has no domestic violence tenancy protection, a survivor making repeated calls has no state-law shield either.

title: No Ohio Source-Of-Income Rule, With One Disability Exception
bodyText: Ohio's fair housing statute, R.C. 4112.02(H), does not list source of income or receipt of housing assistance as a protected class, and Ohio has no statewide voucher-acceptance mandate. There is one exception worth knowing, and it is easy to trip over. OAC 4112-5-07(A)(1)(c) makes it unlawful disability discrimination to refuse to consider the sources of a DISABLED applicant's income, or to subject that applicant's source of income or ability to generate income to automatic discounting in whole or in part, because of the disability. So a blanket 'no vouchers' or 'wages only' screening rule applied to an applicant whose income is disability-related benefits can become a disability claim even though Ohio has no general source-of-income protection. Several Ohio cities do protect source of income by ordinance.

title: Ohio Has No Servicemember Residential Lease Termination
bodyText: Ohio gives a servicemember no state-law right to terminate a residential lease on military orders. Two Ohio provisions come close and neither does it. R.C. 1349.02 lets a deployed servicemember or spouse terminate a lease, but it is confined to MOTOR VEHICLE leases - read the definition before relying on it. R.C. 1923.062 gives a deployed tenant a stay or adjustment of an eviction action, not a termination, it runs 90 days unless justice requires otherwise, it reaches only rental agreements entered on or after May 18 2005, and it does not apply to a landlord operating fewer than four residential premises. A servicemember's actual termination right in Ohio is the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which R.C. 5321.04(A)(10) separately requires you to comply with.

title: Ohio Does Not Regulate Immigration-Status Inquiries By Landlords
bodyText: Ohio has no statute prohibiting a landlord from asking about immigration or citizenship status, and no immigrant tenant protection act. R.C. 4112.02(H) protects national origin and ancestry, and R.C. 4112.02(H)(8) bars making inquiries, eliciting information, keeping records or using application forms concerning national origin or ancestry in connection with a lease - so an inquiry framed around national origin is already unlawful. But Ohio has nothing like the immigration-status-specific prohibitions some states have enacted, and nothing barring disclosure of status to third parties.

title: Ohio Requires No Meth-Contamination Disclosure - But Permitting Drug Abuse Is A Crime
bodyText: Ohio imposes no duty to disclose to a prospective tenant that a property was used to manufacture methamphetamine or was otherwise drug-contaminated, and sets no decontamination standard for residential rental property. Four states in this library have such a disclosure; Ohio does not. What Ohio has instead runs the other way, against you: under R.C. 2925.13 an owner, lessee, occupant or person having custody, control or supervision of premises or real estate, including vacant land, who KNOWINGLY PERMITS it to be used for the commission of a felony drug abuse offence commits permitting drug abuse, a first-degree misdemeanour, rising to a fifth-degree felony where the underlying offence is manufacturing or trafficking or involves Schedule I or II manufacturing chemicals with actual knowledge.

title: Two Ohio Lease Terms That Are Never Recognised
bodyText: Two clauses that appear in ordinary lease forms have no effect at all in Ohio, and no amount of careful drafting saves them. R.C. 5321.13(D): no agreement by a tenant to the exculpation or limitation of ANY liability of the landlord arising under law, or to indemnify the landlord, shall be recognised in any rental agreement or other agreement. That reaches the whole familiar family - 'Landlord shall not be liable for', 'Tenant releases Landlord from', 'Tenant agrees to indemnify, defend and hold Landlord harmless', and a hold-harmless buried in a pet, parking, storage or utilities clause. Making it mutual does not help. Narrowing it to a specific risk does not help. Hedging it with 'to the extent permitted by law' does not help either, because the statute does not limit such a clause, it declines to recognise it. R.C. 5321.13(B): no warrant of attorney to confess judgment is recognised in any rental agreement, or in any other landlord-tenant agreement for the recovery of rent or damages. A cognovit provision in an Ohio residential lease is dead on arrival. What you use instead is insurance, not drafting: require the tenant's renter's insurance, carry your own liability cover, and rely on the statutory allocation of duties in R.C. 5321.04 and 5321.05 rather than trying to contract out of it.

The OHFA lease's section 15 is a sweeping exculpation-plus-indemnity clause of exactly the kind (D) refuses to recognise, and its sections 9 and 17 add 'no liability' and 'relieved of all liability' language. A document published by an Ohio state agency carries it, which is the proof that a landlord will write one unless told not to. That was right for (A), (C), (E) and (F) and WRONG for (B) and (D): nothing in the Ohio set mentioned confession of judgment, and nothing told a landlord that exculpation and indemnity clauses are void. 5321.13(D) was already applied as a SCREEN across the Ohio lease clauses - four rows cite it (services-utilities-provided-ks-oh, parking-ks-oh-ca, storage-space-ks-oh-ca, tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca, plus pet-policy) - but a screen on the library's own text is not the same as telling the landlord the rule. topic_key reuses prohibited-lease-terms, which KS, NE, NV and TX already carry; Ohio had no row in the family. Ohio's (D) is BROADER than Kansas's K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(4), which carves out a landlord's liability for fire, theft or breakage in common areas - Ohio has NO such carve-out. Do not import the Kansas clause. title: Ohio Has Two Cure Tracks, and Picking the Wrong One Loses the Case
bodyText: Before you terminate for a tenant breach, work out which track the breach is on, because Ohio has two and they carry different notice periods. TRACK ONE - the tenant broke a duty R.C. 5321.05 imposes, and the breach materially affects health and safety. R.C. 5321.11 requires written notice specifying the act or omission and stating a termination date NOT LESS THAN THIRTY DAYS after the tenant receives it, and the tenant may cure within that window. This is not advisory: R.C. 1923.02(A)(8) says that before commencing an action on that ground, notice shall be given and compliance secured with 5321.11. It is a condition precedent to filing, so a shorter notice does not merely weaken your case, it defeats it. TRACK TWO - the tenant broke an obligation your written lease imposes, with no health-and-safety dimension. R.C. 1923.02(A)(9) carries no 5321.11 requirement, so whatever period your lease sets is the period that governs. Then, on either track, the separate three-day notice to leave the premises under R.C. 1923.04(B) still has to be served before you file, in the words the statute prescribes. Two exceptions run on their own clocks: nonpayment of rent needs no cure period, and drug activity under 5321.05(A)(9) is carved out of 5321.11 entirely and goes to the mandatory three-day notice under 5321.17(C). The practical trap: many breaches sit in both buckets at once, and if a court reads yours as Track One after you noticed it as Track Two, you filed on a defective notice. When it is genuinely arguable, give thirty days.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.11 and 1923.02(A)(8),(A)(9), BOTH READ SECTION-OPEN 2026-09-27. 5321.11 effective 1990-08-22; 1923.02 effective 2023-10-03, H.B. 33 (135th G.A.) - the same budget bill already on Ohio's legal watch. FOUND BY THE REAL-LEASE COMPARISON (source 2). The OHFA lease's section 16 gives SEVEN days for material noncompliance. That is operative under 1923.02(A)(9) for a written-lease breach and UNENFORCEABLE under (A)(8) for a 5321.05 health-and-safety breach, where 5321.11's thirty days is a condition precedent to filing. A landlord relying on the form would file on a bad notice. WHY IT WAS MISSING: default-by-tenant-ks-ne (Ohio's default clause) defers to 'the time period specified by applicable law' and points to edu-tenant-noncompliance-notice-ks for the figures - a KANSAS row, not tagged OH - so an Ohio landlord got no number from anywhere in the library. The checklist recorded the R.C. 5321.11 30-day cure and the R.C. 1923.02(A)(8) condition precedent on 2026-09-18 and no row was ever written: the same Present-in-the-checklist-absent-from-the-CSV failure as landlord-maintenance and retaliation. topic_key reuses notice-and-cure, previously SD-only. 5321.11's carve-out of 5321.05(A)(9) matches 5321.13(F)'s - the drug duty is the one obligation a landlord may neither assume nor give extra time on; see edu-mandatory-drug-termination-oh. title: Towing From Private Property
bodyText:
South Dakota regulates towing from private property through its abandoned-vehicle chapter, and the duties fall on the tow company rather than on you. A vehicle counts as an abandoned motor vehicle on private property only if it was left there without the permission of the landowner or tenant (SDCL 32-36-2(1)). No removal agency may remove an abandoned motor vehicle from private property without the written permission of the landowner or tenant, and a violation is a Class 2 misdemeanor (SDCL 32-36-4.1); once it has that authorization the agency may enter the land to make the removal (SDCL 32-36-4). Removal agency includes an ordinary tow business, and motor vehicle reaches boats, house trailers, trailers, campers, snowmobiles and off-road vehicles as well as cars (SDCL 32-36-2(4), (5)). After a removal the agency must mail certified notice to the registered owner and to all readily identifiable lienholders within forty-five days on a form provided by the Department of Revenue, and if it does not mail that notice within ten days of the removal it may charge no storage beyond the ten-day period until the notice goes out (SDCL 32-36-8). The agency holds a possessory lien for the reasonable costs of taking custody and storage, but no more than five hundred dollars against the contents of the vehicle, and no lien at all against the tools a person keeps for their trade or business, or against clothing or food (SDCL 32-30-18).

Two consequences matter in practice. First, a tenant's own vehicle parked with your permission is not an abandoned motor vehicle, so this chapter gives you no authority to tow it for breaking a parking rule - that is a lease-compliance matter to take up with the tenant, not a towing matter. Second, South Dakota imposes no signage requirement for towing from private property; your written authorization is what makes the tow lawful. The statute does not say whether that authorization must be a per-tow order or may be a standing written contract, so it does not settle which form to use.

title: Removing Someone Who Is Not a Tenant
bodyText:
When someone who is not your tenant will not leave, South Dakota's criminal trespass statute is the usual tool and it moves faster than an eviction. Under SDCL 22-35-6 a person who enters or remains anywhere knowing they are not privileged to do so, where notice against trespass has been given by actual communication to that person, by posting in a manner reasonably likely to come to a trespasser's attention, or by a fence or other enclosure a reasonable person would recognise as designed to exclude trespassers, is guilty of a Class 2 misdemeanor. If that person then defies an order to leave communicated personally by the owner of the premises or by any other authorized person, the offence becomes criminal trespass, a Class 1 misdemeanor.

Two limits decide whether this is actually available to you. A tenant is privileged to be on the property under the lease, so trespass is never the route against a tenant - use the forcible entry and detainer process instead. And SDCL 22-35-7 makes it an affirmative defence that the person reasonably believed the owner, or another person permitted to license access, would have permitted them to enter or remain. Your tenant is such a person, so a guest your tenant still welcomes has that defence available. A guest who overstays with the tenant's blessing is therefore a lease-violation problem to take up with the tenant under the guest and default provisions, not a trespass problem. Where someone took possession by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth against your prior actual possession, or holds possession by force, threats or menacing conduct, forcible entry and detainer is independently available under SDCL 21-16-1(1) to (3) without regard to trespass.

title: Medical Cannabis Cardholders
bodyText:
South Dakota's medical cannabis law limits how you may treat a registered cardholder. Under SDCL 34-20G-19 a cardholder may not be refused a lease by a landlord, or otherwise be penalized by a landlord, solely for the person's status as a cardholder - unless failing to do so would violate federal law or regulations, or would cause you to lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law or regulation. That carve-out is what matters for federally subsidized housing. The same section then provides that it does not prevent a landlord from imposing reasonable restrictions on the medical use of cannabis by a cardholder who resides at the landlord's property.

Two things you may clearly do. SDCL 34-20G-27(3) provides that nothing in the chapter requires a landlord to allow the cultivation of cannabis on the rental property, so a cultivation ban is squarely permitted. SDCL 34-20G-27(2) provides that nothing requires a person in lawful possession of property to allow a guest, client, customer or other visitor to smoke or vape cannabis there. Read that second one carefully: it is written about visitors, not about your resident tenants, so it is not the authority for restricting a tenant's own use. The reasonable-restrictions sentence in 34-20G-19 is.

Steinoak's Smoking Policy clause prohibits smoking and vaping of any kind, including of marijuana, rather than prohibiting possession or non-combusted use, and it applies to every tenant rather than to cardholders as such. That is the shape most likely to qualify as a reasonable restriction: it leaves other methods of medical use available and it is not a penalty imposed for cardholder status. But reasonable is not defined anywhere in the chapter and no South Dakota decision applying it was located, so treat the margin as argued rather than settled. Do not screen out an applicant, raise their rent, refuse a renewal or threaten them because they hold a card, and note that the clause as written says nothing about cultivation even though South Dakota would let you prohibit it.

title: Selling the Property With a Tenant in Place
bodyText:
South Dakota has no statute moving security deposit liability to a buyer when a rented property is sold, and none releasing the selling landlord. Several states do: Kansas, Nebraska, North Dakota, Minnesota, California, Nevada, Texas, New Jersey, Florida and Arizona all have an express successor-liability or transfer-or-return provision. South Dakota does not, and nothing in chapter 43-32 - read in full - requires you to notify a tenant that the property is for sale or has been sold, or imposes a landlord-identity or identity-change disclosure duty.

So in South Dakota the question is answered by your purchase agreement and by ordinary property and contract law rather than by statute. A buyer takes the property subject to an existing lease as a general matter, but no South Dakota statute makes the buyer answerable for a deposit the seller is holding, and none discharges the seller's own obligation under SDCL 43-32-24 to account for that deposit. The practical consequence is that the deposit obligation stays with whoever took the money unless your sale documents move it. Transfer the deposit at closing against a written acknowledgment that the buyer has assumed the accounting duty, keep a copy of the accounting you would have owed, and tell the tenant in writing who now holds the deposit and where to send the mailing address or delivery instructions that start the twenty-one-day clock. If you sell without doing any of that, you remain the person the tenant can pursue.

title: An Uncashed Deposit Refund Is Unclaimed Property
bodyText:
A deposit refund your former tenant never cashes does not become yours. South Dakota's Uniform Unclaimed Property Act presumes all intangible property abandoned when it has remained unclaimed by the owner for more than three years after it became payable or distributable, less any lawful charges, and the owner's failure to make demand or to present the instrument does not stop that clock (SDCL 43-41B-2(a), (b)). Expiry of any limitation period does not prevent the property from being presumed abandoned or affect your duty to report it (SDCL 43-41B-18).

Before you file, you must communicate with the owner and exercise due diligence to find them, and for property worth fifty dollars or more you must mail notice to each person entitled to it - unless your records indicate the address is inaccurate - stating that you hold property that appears to be theirs and that it will escheat to the state (SDCL 43-41B-18). The report goes to the administrator, must be verified, and is due before November 1 each year as of the preceding June 30. It must give the owner's name and last known address for property worth ten dollars or more, the nature and amount of the property, the date it became payable, and the date of your last transaction with the apparent owner; items worth under ten dollars each may be reported in the aggregate. If you took over the property from a previous holder, or your own name has changed while you held it, the report must list every previous holder's name and address.

One practical point: reissuing a stale cheque does not restart the three years, because the period runs from when the refund first became payable rather than from the date of any replacement instrument. For a South Dakota deposit that is when your accounting was due under SDCL 43-32-24 - though the Act does not say so in those terms, so treat it as the better reading rather than a stated rule.

title: Winter Utility Disconnection
bodyText:
South Dakota does not impose a winter moratorium on utility disconnection, but it does lengthen the notice. Under ARSD 20:10:20:10, from November 1 through March 31 a utility may not disconnect residential service without adding thirty days to the time periods in ARSD 20:10:20:03(2), and it must notify the customer before the normal disconnection date that the customer has that additional thirty days. The underlying periods are a payment period of not less than twenty days from the billing transmittal date to the due date, plus a further notice period of not less than ten days during which the bill has been owing. So the runway before a nonpayment disconnection is roughly thirty days outside the winter window and roughly sixty days inside it.

Scope matters more than the numbers here. These are Public Utilities Commission rules made under SDCL 49-34A, and they reach the gas and electric utilities subject to that chapter. Whether a municipal utility or a rural electric cooperative is bound by them was not determined, and water and sewer service is not covered by this rule at all. Two consequences for you. If the tenant is the customer of record, a winter shutoff takes considerably longer than you might assume, which changes how quickly an unpaid utility becomes a habitability or lease-compliance problem rather than a private matter between the tenant and the utility. If you are the customer of record - a master-metered building, or a lease where you pay a utility - the extension and the notice are yours, and the notice will come to you rather than to the tenant.

None of this touches SDCL 43-32-6, which separately prohibits you from willfully diminishing services by interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service in order to force a tenant out, and gives the tenant damages of two months' rent plus return of advance rent and deposit.

title: Service-Animal Misrepresentation Reaches Public Accommodations, Not Housing
bodyText:
South Dakota now has a criminal penalty for misrepresenting a service animal, and it does not reach housing. SDCL 22-35-9, added in 2026, makes it a Class 2 misdemeanor for an individual to misrepresent an animal in that individual's possession as a service animal, directly or indirectly through statements or conduct, intentionally and in any place of public accommodation, in order to obtain rights or privileges available to someone who qualifies for a service animal under state or federal law, knowing they are not entitled to them. For that section service animal means a dog trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability as set out in 28 C.F.R. 36.104 (January 1, 2026), and the section states expressly that a dog's crime-deterrent effect and the provision of emotional support, well-being, comfort or companionship do not constitute work or tasks.

A leased dwelling is not a place of public accommodation, so do not expect this offence to cover a tenant or applicant who misrepresents a pet as a service or support animal, and do not threaten anyone with it. Your remedy in housing remains civil: SDCL 43-32-36 permits eviction and a damage fee of up to one thousand dollars where a tenant knowingly makes a false claim of disability requiring a service or assistance animal or knowingly supplies fraudulent documentation, which is what the Assistance Animal clause states.

One trap follows from this. South Dakota now carries three different service-animal standards in three places: the civil housing framework in SDCL 43-32-33 to 43-32-36; the criminal prohibition in SDCL 20-13-23.4 on a landlord barring a service animal, which covers only tenants who are totally or partially physically disabled, blind or deaf; and this public-accommodations definition, limited to dogs performing trained tasks and expressly excluding emotional support. Do not carry one section's definition into another, and in particular do not use this section's exclusion of emotional-support animals to deny an assistance-animal accommodation in housing, where federal fair housing law and the chapter 43-32 framework govern and both reach support animals.

The correct reading in both directions is that SD legislates housing and public accommodations separately and their definitions do not travel. title: Residential Rent Is Exempt From Sales Tax
bodyText:
Residential rent is not subject to South Dakota sales tax. The Department of Revenue's Lease and Rental guidance states that the lease or rental of real property is exempt from sales tax, and lists the lease or rental of real property among the transactions exempt from sales and use tax. So you do not collect or remit state sales tax on rent under an ordinary residential lease, and you should not add a tax line to the rent or describe part of the rent as tax.

Two boundaries were not resolved and they matter if you operate outside ordinary residential leasing. Short-term lodging is taxed under a different regime, alongside South Dakota's tourism tax and municipal gross receipts tax, and the point at which a stay stops being an exempt rental of real property and becomes taxable lodging was not researched here - so do not read this as covering a short-term or vacation rental. It is also unresolved whether separately stated charges for furnishings, equipment or services supplied with the dwelling fall outside the real-property exemption, since the exemption is written about real property. If you charge separately for anything other than the dwelling itself, get that specific question answered before deciding not to collect tax on it.

title: When a Tenant Abandons the Unit
bodyText: Texas has no statute that defines when a residential tenant has abandoned a unit, and no notice-and-storage procedure for belongings a living tenant leaves behind. The Property Code lets you exclude a tenant in order to remove the contents of premises the tenant has abandoned, and lets you remove the contents of an abandoned residence. If the tenant had not in fact abandoned, the exclusion is an unlawful lockout: the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover one month's rent plus $1,000, actual damages, court costs and attorney's fees (less any rent owed), and can get an ex parte writ of reentry. Because 'abandoned' is undefined, a lease definition is your main protection; the optional abandonment Section of this lease supplies one, and Texas's standard apartment-association lease also defines it. Before you treat a unit as abandoned, document the signs and give written notice with time to respond. Different rules apply when a sole tenant dies (the certified-mail and 30-day procedure unless the lease sets another) and after an eviction (the officer places belongings outside under the writ). Once the tenant has surrendered, the 30-day deposit refund clock runs, and you must try to re-let to limit your damages.

title: Abandonment and Property Left Behind
bodyText:
[Optional. Texas law does not define when a residential tenant has abandoned the dwelling; this Section supplies the definition. Tex. Prop. Code §§92.0081(b)(2), 54.044(d).]
ABANDONMENT. The dwelling is abandoned only when all of the following have occurred: (a) Landlord reasonably believes that all occupants have moved out, based on facts such as the removal of substantially all of Tenant's belongings or the disconnection of utility service in Tenant's name; (b) Rent is delinquent; and (c) Landlord has posted a written notice on the inside of the main entry door, and mailed a copy to Tenant at the dwelling and to any other address Tenant has given Landlord (and e-mailed a copy if Tenant has given Landlord an e-mail address), stating that Landlord considers the dwelling abandoned, and Tenant has not responded in writing or in person within 5 days after the notice was posted. Once the dwelling is abandoned, Landlord may enter, take possession, change the locks, and remove any personal property left in the dwelling. Landlord will store that property for at least 30 days after the dwelling is abandoned and will release it to Tenant, or to a person Tenant designates in writing, on request during that period. Landlord may charge Tenant the reasonable cost of removing and storing the property but will not refuse to release the property because that cost is unpaid. After the 30-day period, Landlord may donate the property to a charitable organization or discard it. Landlord may discard trash, perishable food, and items that pose a health or safety hazard at any time. Nothing in this Section allows Landlord to exclude Tenant from the dwelling except as Section 92.0081 of the Texas Property Code permits. If Tenant is the sole occupant and dies, Section 92.014 of the Texas Property Code and the provisions of this Lease on the death of Tenant apply instead of this Section.

title: Pools at Multiunit Rentals
bodyText: If you own a multiunit rental complex (two or more units under common ownership and management on the same or adjacent lots, including a condominium project, but not a stand-alone single-family home) with a pool, or a rental unit in a condominium, cooperative or town-home project with a pool, Health and Safety Code chapter 757 applies. A pool includes a permanent swimming pool, wading pool, hot tub or spa more than 18 inches deep. The pool yard must be fully enclosed at least 48 inches high, with limits on openings (no chain link on enclosures built after January 1, 1994); gates must self-close and self-latch, open outward, be lockable, and generally have the latch at least 60 inches high. Unit doors may not open directly into the pool yard where the building or pool first got electrical service on or after January 1, 1994; older doors and windows that do must have specified latches and bolts. You must use reasonable care to inspect, maintain and repair the enclosure, gates and self-closing latches, and inspect them at least once every 31 days, and repair pool-yard window and sliding-door latches, pins and bars after a tenant reports a problem. These duties cannot be waived. A tenant may report those problems orally unless the lease requires written notice in a provision printed in capital letters and underlined, or in 10-point bold type. A tenant or anyone else can sue for a compliance order, actual damages, punitive damages for intentional, malicious or grossly negligent failures, and a civil penalty of up to $5,000 if you do not comply within a reasonable time after a tenant's written notice; the attorney general, a city, a county or a local health department can also enforce. Cities generally may not require a different enclosure than the chapter allows. Your security-device duties under the Property Code still apply.

title: Removing a Squatter Without an Eviction
bodyText: Since September 1, 2025, the owner of residential property, or the owner's agent, can ask the sheriff or a constable to remove immediately a person who unlawfully entered and is living in a dwelling without the owner's consent, without filing an eviction suit. It is available only if the property was not open to the public when the person entered, there is no pending lawsuit between you and the person, you have told the person to leave and they have not, and the person is not your current or former tenant under any oral or written lease and not an immediate family member. You submit a sworn complaint in the statutory form, with a copy of your government-issued ID (and, for an agent, proof of authority). The officer verifies that you are the record owner or agent, then without delay serves a notice to vacate immediately (by hand or by posting on the front door) and puts you in possession; the officer may arrest occupants for trespass or other offenses. You pay the same fee as for executing a writ of possession, plus an hourly rate if you ask the officer to stay while you change the locks and move the occupants' belongings to your property line. You are not liable for damage to belongings removed under this procedure, but a person wrongfully removed can sue to recover possession plus actual damages, three times the fair market rent, court costs and attorney's fees, and a false complaint is perjury. Anyone who was ever your tenant, including a holdover or a tenant whose lease has ended, must be removed through an eviction suit.
