title: Holdover Charge
bodyText: If Tenant remains in possession after the end of the Term, and Landlord has not agreed in writing to a continued tenancy or accepted Rent for one under the Holdover section of this Lease, then, in place of the actual damages and reasonable rental value described in that section, Tenant will pay Landlord a holdover charge of {{holdover_daily_rate}} for each day Tenant remains in possession. Landlord and Tenant agree that Landlord's loss from a holdover, including delay in making the property available to a new tenant, is difficult to estimate accurately in advance, that this charge is a reasonable estimate of that loss, and that it is not a penalty. Landlord's acceptance of a holdover charge is not acceptance of Rent for a continued tenancy. This Section does not limit Landlord's right to recover possession, unpaid Rent and other amounts due for the period before the Term ended, or damages for harm to the property.

title: Fire or Other Casualty
bodyText: If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty not caused by Tenant, members of Tenant's household, or Tenant's guests, and the damage makes the property unfit to live in or substantially impairs Tenant's use of it, either Landlord or Tenant may end this Lease by written notice to the other, effective on the date Tenant moves out. Rent will be prorated to that date, any prepaid Rent refunded, and the Security Deposit returned as this Lease and Pennsylvania law provide. If the casualty makes only part of the property unusable and Tenant stays in possession, Rent will be reduced in proportion to the part of the property Tenant cannot use until Landlord completes repairs. This Section does not limit any other right Tenant has under Pennsylvania law.

title: Pennsylvania Landlord and Tenant Law: What Applies
bodyText: Pennsylvania's main landlord-tenant statute is The Landlord and Tenant Act of 1951, an unconsolidated act cited as 68 P.S. § 250.101 (Act § 101) and following. It is short: it covers written and oral leases, notices to quit, eviction before a magisterial district judge, security deposits, property left behind, death of a tenant, drug-related removal, and rights of tenants in buildings with three or more households. It does not set entry notice, late-fee limits, a landlord repair code or a general retaliation rule; much of Pennsylvania landlord-tenant law, including the implied warranty of habitability, comes from court decisions. A 'tenant' includes anyone occupying with the owner's express or implied consent, by oral or written lease or by the owner's acceptance of rent; the Act does not apply to a person who is not and never has been a tenant. A lease of more than three years must be in writing and signed; if it is not, it has the effect of a tenancy at will only, unless the tenancy has lasted more than one year and both sides have treated it as valid by claiming and paying the rent, in which case it becomes a year-to-year tenancy. A buyer of rented property takes on the seller's rights and duties, and a subtenant is bound by the lease. Local ordinances, especially in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, add rules this library does not cover.

title: Pennsylvania Security Deposit Rules
bodyText: A residential security deposit may not exceed two months' rent in the first year of a lease and one month's rent in the second and later years or on renewal; after five years' possession a rent increase cannot require a larger deposit. Deposits over $100 must be held in an escrow account at a regulated institution, and the landlord must tell the tenant in writing the institution's name and address and the amount; a guarantee bond may be used instead. After the second anniversary of the deposit, the account must earn interest: the landlord keeps 1% a year as its only administrative charge and pays the rest to the tenant every year on the lease anniversary. Within 30 days after the lease ends or the landlord accepts surrender, the landlord must give a written list of damage and refund the balance with unpaid interest. Missing the 30-day list forfeits all rights to withhold any part of the deposit and to sue for damage to the property; a late or short refund can cost double the amount wrongly kept. Otherwise the landlord may keep the deposit for unpaid rent or another breach; whether that survives a missed list is not settled by the statute's text. A tenant who does not give a new address in writing relieves the landlord of liability under the return section. None of these rules can be waived. Whether last month's rent paid in advance counts toward the cap is not settled by the statute. An uncashed refund may become unclaimed property reportable to the State Treasurer after three years.

title: Notice to Quit (Notice to Move Out)
bodyText: Before filing to recover possession, a Pennsylvania landlord gives the tenant a written notice to quit unless the lease waives it or shortens it. The periods are: 10 days for failure to pay rent after demand; 15 days at the end of a lease of one year or less, a lease with no fixed end, or a forfeiture for breach of such a lease; 30 days at the end of, or on forfeiture of, a lease of more than one year; and 10 days where the lease ends for illegal drug activity. Which period applies depends on the kind of tenancy, not on what the lease calls itself. By the statute's wording, a week-to-week, month-to-month or year-to-year tenancy (each term is one year or less) and a tenancy at will (no fixed end) all get 15 days; only a fixed term longer than one year gets 30 days. The 10-day notice for unpaid rent is the same for every kind of tenancy. The notice may be handed to the tenant, left at the main building on the premises, or posted conspicuously on the premises. A lease may provide a shorter notice or a waiver. Mobile-home park spaces follow different, longer rules. The notice rules do not apply to someone who is not and never was a tenant. Federal law may require a 30-day notice for properties with federally backed mortgages or federal assistance, whatever the lease says.

title: Eviction in Pennsylvania
bodyText: Eviction starts with a complaint before the magisterial district judge where the property is (in Philadelphia, the Philadelphia Municipal Court). The complaint states that notice to quit was given or that the lease required none, and for each tenant the landlord attaches an affidavit about military service. The hearing is set 7 to 15 days after filing, and the landlord must appear and prove the case even if the tenant does not come; there is no default judgment. Some counties offer or require mediation by local rule. If the landlord wins, the judgment covers possession, unpaid rent, damages for unjust detention, physical damage and costs. For a residential lease the landlord may request an order for possession after the 10th day and within 120 days after judgment; the officer serves it, and may remove the tenant on or after the 11th day after service. In a case for unpaid rent only, the tenant can stop the removal by paying the rent in arrears and costs before possession is delivered. A tenant may appeal to the court of common pleas within 10 days (30 days for a victim of domestic violence, who may also file an affidavit that holds off removal for up to 30 days after judgment). An appeal stops the eviction only if the tenant deposits the lesser of three months' rent or the rent in arrears and then pays each month's rent into court, or files a low-income affidavit. Where the appeal goes to compulsory arbitration and the arbitrators rule for the tenant, the court rules' official commentary says the landlord may not obtain an order for possession between the entry of that award and the landlord's own appeal, even if the tenant stops paying into court. A judgment for possession by confession is not available on a residential lease signed by an individual. Wages may be attached for up to 10% of net pay on a final residential-lease judgment, but not against a protected abuse victim for physical damage the abuser caused. Only a court officer may remove a tenant.

title: No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: Pennsylvania's eviction procedure is the only lawful way to remove a tenant: only a constable or sheriff executing an order for possession may enter by force and put a tenant out. The 1951 Act describes itself as a complete and exclusive system. No Pennsylvania statute sets a specific money penalty for a lockout, but courts treat self-help as unlawful, and a landlord who disposes of or takes control of property in an occupied unit without the tenant's express permission owes treble damages, attorney fees and costs. A landlord who holds the utility account may not have service shut off at its request unless the tenants agree, and may not retaliate against tenants who pay the utility to keep service on.

title: Retaliation Protections
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no general anti-retaliation statute for residential tenants, but several statutes protect specific acts. A landlord may not end or refuse to renew a lease because a tenant or family member takes part in a tenants' organization. A landlord who threatens or takes reprisals against a tenant for paying a landlord's unpaid utility bill to keep service on, or for deducting that payment from rent, owes the greater of two months' rent or actual damages, plus costs and attorney fees, and a notice to end the tenancy, a rent increase or a substantial change in terms within six months is presumed retaliatory. In cities covered by the Rent Withholding Act, a tenant may not be evicted for any reason while rent is paid into escrow for a unit certified unfit. A municipality may not penalize a tenant or landlord for calls for police or emergency help by or for a victim of abuse or crime.

title: Rent Withholding for Units Certified Unfit
bodyText: In a city of the first, second, second class A or third class, if the city's code or health agency, or the county health department, certifies a dwelling unfit for human habitation, the tenant's duty to pay rent and the landlord's right to collect it are suspended until the unit is certified fit or the tenancy ends for a reason other than nonpayment. A tenant who stays pays the rent into an approved escrow account. The escrow goes to the landlord if the unit is certified fit within six months of the unfit certification; otherwise it goes back to the tenant, except that it may be used to make repairs and to pay utilities the landlord is obliged to pay. No tenant may be evicted for any reason while rent is in escrow. The certifying agency must send the landlord a monthly statement of the escrowed funds.

title: Habitability and Repairs
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute lists a residential landlord's repair duties. Pennsylvania courts recognize an implied warranty of habitability in residential leases, which a lease cannot waive, and local housing and property-maintenance codes set the working standards. By statute, a landlord of a building or complex with three or more households must use reasonable care to keep stairways, passages, roadways and other common facilities safe for tenants and their guests, and tenants must obey applicable codes and must not damage the property or disturb other tenants. In certain cities a unit certified unfit triggers rent withholding. Courts may set up housing courts for code and landlord-tenant cases. Under the state blight law, an owner who takes no substantial step within six months of an order to correct a serious code violation can be sued personally by the municipality, have other assets liened and be denied municipal permits for other properties; repeat convictions for the same serious violation are a crime; and an out-of-state owner charged with a code crime may be extradited.

title: When the Landlord Holds the Utility Account
bodyText: If a landlord is the utility's customer for gas, electric, steam, water or sewer serving tenants, the utility must give the landlord 37 days' written notice before shutting service off for nonpayment and must notify the tenants at least 30 days ahead. The landlord must give the utility the tenants' names and addresses within 7 days of a request unless it pays or arranges to pay; failing to do so costs $500 to $1,000 a day in liquidated damages. Tenants may pay the bill for the last month to keep service on, then deduct what they paid from rent or recover it from the landlord. A landlord may not retaliate against them. A landlord who asks the utility to end service must certify that the units are vacant or the tenants consent, have the tenants tell the utility they consent, or give the utility the tenants' names so it can notify them. Owners of rental buildings with units that are not individually metered must tell each utility that the property is rented, and they remain responsible for the bills. A utility two or more months unpaid may ask the court to appoint a receiver to collect rents. Tenants cannot waive these rights. Separately, where a municipal authority or a third class city supplies water or sewer service through a tenant's own account at a unit the owner does not live in, the owner can be made to pay the tenant's unpaid bill if the authority or city notifies both the owner and the tenant within 30 days after the bill first becomes overdue; for water, the owner is not liable for service more than 90 days after it became overdue unless a court order stopped the shutoff.

title: Plain Language Rules for Pennsylvania Leases
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Plain Language Consumer Contract Act applies to residential leases (not commercial leases or contracts over $50,000). A lease must be written, organized and designed to be easy to read. Courts consider whether it uses short words, sentences and paragraphs; active verbs; few legal terms; no Latin; personal pronouns or the parties' names; one condition per sentence; clear cross references; no double negatives; readable type size, line length, margins and spacing; boldface section captions; and sharply contrasting ink. It must also carry a statement describing what the tenant could lose on default and listing the tenant's waivers of rights. A landlord that fails the test owes the tenant actual loss, $100, costs and attorney fees, unless it made a good-faith and reasonable effort to comply; the lease stays valid and class actions are barred. The Attorney General will preapprove a lease on request; its guideline is an average of 25 words or fewer per sentence and 60 per paragraph. The Act excludes consumer contracts involving more than $50,000, and the text does not say how that amount is measured for a lease (for example, total rent over the term), so a high-rent or long lease may fall outside it.

title: Confession of Judgment
bodyText: Many older Pennsylvania leases let the landlord 'confess judgment' against the tenant without a hearing. A confessed judgment for possession is abolished for a residential lease signed by an individual, so a landlord must use the ordinary eviction process. Confession of judgment for money is abolished for consumer credit transactions; whether that reaches a residential lease is not settled by the rule's text, and courts view these clauses with suspicion. The library includes no confession-of-judgment clause for Pennsylvania.

title: Electronic Signatures and Notices
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Electronic Transactions Act gives electronic records and signatures legal effect when the parties agree to act electronically. But a paper consumer contract, such as a lease signed on paper, may authorize doing business electronically only if the tenant agrees in a separate and express acknowledgment that says which parts of the transaction will be electronic and how. Using e-payment alone does not show agreement. Federal law separately says electronic delivery cannot replace paper for notices of default or eviction on a primary residence. Pennsylvania's notice-to-quit statute lists its own delivery methods: personal delivery, leaving it at the main building, or conspicuous posting.

title: Pennsylvania Fair Housing Law
bodyText: The Pennsylvania Human Relations Act bars housing discrimination because of race (including hair texture and protective hairstyles), color, familial status, age (40 and over), religious creed, ancestry, sex, national origin, handicap or disability, a known relationship with a person with a disability, or use of a guide or support animal. It adds age to the federal classes. A landlord may not evict before the end of the lease because of pregnancy or the birth of a child, and may not ask questions, keep records or use application forms about protected characteristics. Landlords must allow reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense (with restoration where reasonable) and make reasonable accommodations. Every covered landlord must post the Human Relations Commission's fair practices notice in its place of business. The Act does not cover renting part of an owner-occupied building of no more than two units, a room in a landlord-occupied rooming house with a common entrance, or qualifying housing for older persons. Occupancy limits based on bedrooms and unit size are allowed. Pennsylvania has no statewide source-of-income protection.

title: Pennsylvania Service and Assistance Animal Law
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Assistance and Service Animal Integrity Act lets a landlord ask for documentation of a disability and the need for an assistance or service animal only when the disability or need is not readily apparent or known to the landlord. The documentation must be written, reliable, based on direct knowledge of the person's disability and need, and must describe the need. An 'assistance animal' includes an emotional support animal that qualifies as a reasonable accommodation. A landlord is not liable for injuries caused by an assistance or service animal it permits as a reasonable accommodation. Lying about a disability or need, or making materially false statements to obtain documentation, to get an animal accepted in housing is a third-degree misdemeanor; creating false papers or putting a service vest on an animal that is not one is a summary offense with a fine up to $1,000. The Human Relations Act separately bars refusing to rent because a person uses a guide or support animal. Pennsylvania's criminal service-dog discrimination statute covers places of public accommodation, not rental housing.

title: Servicemember Rights in Pennsylvania
bodyText: Besides the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, Pennsylvania lets a member of the U.S. armed forces, or of the Pennsylvania National Guard on full-time duty or serving as a civil service technician, end a housing lease on at least 30 days' written notice after receiving permanent change of station orders, temporary duty orders of more than three months, an honorable discharge or release, or orders to government quarters that forfeit the housing allowance. The tenant must give the landlord a copy of the orders, or a commanding officer's letter, before the termination date. Final rent is prorated; rent paid in advance for after the termination must be refunded within 30 days; a court may modify the relief if the landlord applies before the termination date. Holding a servicemember's deposit or belongings to force payment of rent after a lawful termination is a summary offense. For Guard and reserve members called to active duty, no eviction may be made without leave of court, and the court may stay the case for six months.

title: When a Sole Tenant Dies
bodyText: If the only tenant on a residential lease dies during the term, the executor or administrator of the estate may end the lease by giving the landlord 14 days' written notice, effective on the later of the last day of the second calendar month after the month of death or the date the unit is surrendered and all the tenant's property removed. The estate still owes rent and other debts up to the termination, including damage to the premises and costs the landlord incurs because of the death, but owes no penalty or damages for ending early. The rule applies to leases entered into or extended after it took effect in 2016. Property a deceased tenant leaves behind is handled under Pennsylvania estate law, not the abandoned-property rules.

title: Drug and Other Criminal Activity at the Property
bodyText: By statute, a first conviction for selling, making or distributing illegal drugs on the rented dwelling or any part of a multiple dwelling, a second violation of the drug laws there, or a police seizure of illegal drugs on the leased premises, is a breach of the lease and grounds to remove the tenant, on a 10-day notice to quit. Not acting on one violation does not waive the landlord's rights for later ones. Separately, the Expedited Eviction of Drug Traffickers Act lets a landlord, a tenant organization, a district attorney or, at a district attorney's request, the Attorney General bring an expedited civil action in the court of common pleas to evict tenants or remove other people involved in drug-related criminal activity on or near leased residential premises. Neighbors, tenants and others may also sue under the Drug Nuisance Law, where a court can order repairs, security measures, rent escrow for up to 90 days, a rent trustee or suspension of subsidies until the nuisance ends.

title: Calls for Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: A Pennsylvania municipality may not penalize a tenant, resident or landlord because police or emergency help was called by or for a victim of abuse or crime, or a person in an emergency, when the caller reasonably believed help was needed or it actually was. 'Penalize' includes revoking, suspending or refusing to renew a rental license, fines, and evicting or causing an eviction. A tenant or landlord may sue the municipality for an order to stop, damages, attorney fees, costs and reinstatement of a rental license. Local nuisance or disorderly-property ordinances that conflict are preempted. The rule does not limit the Expedited Eviction of Drug Traffickers Act or alarm-device ordinances.

title: Tenant Rights in Buildings with Three or More Households
bodyText: In a building or complex with three or more households, a tenant may invite employees, business visitors, tradespeople, delivery people and suppliers of goods and services, and may have social guests, family and visitors for a reasonable time, as long as the tenant meets the tenant's obligations. A lease cannot waive these rights, and the landlord may not charge a fee or extra rent for them or restrict where the tenant buys goods and services. The landlord owes reasonable care for the safety of common areas it controls. Tenants may also order cable television from a franchised operator; the landlord may not charge different rent to cable subscribers and non-subscribers, and it deals with the operator over installation terms and compensation.

title: Condominium and Cooperative Conversion
bodyText: When a rented building is converted to a condominium, cooperative or planned community, the developer must give each residential tenant a conversion notice at least one year before requiring the tenant to move, by hand delivery or certified or registered mail, with a public offering statement. For six months the tenant has the right to buy the unit, and for six months after that the unit may not be offered to others on better terms. During the notice year the tenant cannot be required to move out, even if the lease ends sooner, except for nonpayment of rent, waste, or conduct that disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment. The lease terms cannot be changed during that year but can be enforced, and failing to give notice is a defense to eviction. After receiving the notice the tenant may end the lease on 90 days' written notice without liability. Coercion, harassment and withholding services are banned. A tenant who is 62 or older or disabled, lives in the unit as a principal residence (in a condominium or planned community, for at least two years) and proves eligibility within 60 days of the notice may stay for two years after the notice on the same limited grounds, with any rent increase in that extension capped at the lesser of 5% or the rise in the cost of living.

title: Towing from Rental Property
bodyText: Nobody may park or leave a vehicle on private property without the consent of the owner or the person in possession, except in an emergency or breakdown. The rule reaches private parking lots only if they are posted with the parking restrictions. The owner or person in possession may have a violating vehicle removed at the vehicle owner's reasonable expense and has a lien for the removal and storage costs; unless the municipality sets rates, storage is limited to $25 a day. Municipalities may regulate towing rates and towers, and Philadelphia has its own removal rules. A 2026 law adds penalties for improper towing at accident scenes and for towing storage facilities, effective December 2026; it does not govern private-lot towing.

title: Distress for Rent
bodyText: The 1951 Act still prints an old remedy called distress: seizing and selling a tenant's belongings from the premises for unpaid rent, with appraisal, notice and sale by a constable, and exemptions for $300 of property, clothing, Bibles, school books and some other items. The Rules of Civil Procedure for district judges do not cover it, its use against residential tenants has been challenged in the courts as unconstitutional, and a landlord who distrains wrongly faces damages up to double or treble. The library does not use or offer distress, and Pennsylvania landlords should not rely on it without a lawyer.

title: Selling or Losing a Rented Property
bodyText: A buyer of rented property takes on the seller's rights and duties toward the tenant. After a sheriff's or other judicial sale, the purchaser may collect rent as landlord from the date of its deed; a tenant whose lease is older than the judgment or mortgage behind the sale keeps a right to possession that outranks the purchaser, and rent paid in advance is protected unless paid with notice of the proceedings or to defeat the purchaser. A tenant for years has no priority over a tax-sale purchaser. After a foreclosure, federal law generally requires 90 days' notice to bona fide tenants. Utilities may ask a court to appoint a receiver to collect rents when a landlord falls two months behind on master-metered service.

bodyText: Federal law requires the lead warning statement, disclosure of known lead hazards, available records and the EPA pamphlet before renting pre-1978 housing. title: Carbon Monoxide and Smoke Alarms
bodyText: Owners of rental apartment buildings with three or more households must install an approved carbon monoxide alarm in each apartment that has a fossil fuel-burning heater or appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage, replace missing alarms before a new tenant moves in and make sure the batteries work at move-in; tenants maintain, test and replace batteries during the tenancy and report problems in writing. Willful failure is a summary offense with a fine up to $50. One- and two-family homes have only a disclosure duty when sold. Pennsylvania has no statute requiring landlords to provide smoke alarms in rentals; building codes and local ordinances may, and municipalities may set stricter carbon monoxide rules.

bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute on how much notice a landlord must give before raising rent or how much it may raise it; there is no statewide rent control. title: No Domestic Violence Lease Termination Right
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute letting a domestic violence victim end a private residential lease early, change the locks or remove an abuser from the lease. Protections that do exist: a victim of domestic violence gets 30 days, instead of 10, to appeal an eviction judgment; a landlord who knows of a protection-from-abuse order must hold the tenant's belongings 30 days after an eviction; wages cannot be attached against a protected victim for physical damage the abuser caused; municipalities may not penalize calls for help; public housing authority tenants may request emergency relocation; and a protection-from-abuse order can give the victim possession of a home the parties lease together and exclude the abuser (the statute does not address the lease itself).

title: Security Deposit Limit
bodyText: Pennsylvania caps residential security deposits by statute. The cap applies whether or not the lease mentions it, and a tenant cannot waive it. During the first year of a lease, a landlord may not require more than two months' rent as a deposit. In the second and later years, and on any renewal, the amount required may not exceed one month's rent. Once a tenant has been in possession for five years, a rent increase cannot require a larger deposit. Money held against damage or unpaid rent counts toward the cap, including a pet deposit. The statute does not say what happens to a first-year deposit of more than one month's rent when the second year begins; the cautious course is to return the excess then and to require no more than one month's rent on renewal. Whether last month's rent paid in advance counts toward the cap is not settled by the statute. The statute counts by years of a lease and by renewals and does not say how that works for a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, where each new period could be read as a renewal of the original lease. A landlord who wants to avoid the question can hold no more than one month's rent for a periodic tenancy, or have a Pennsylvania lawyer confirm that the two-month first-year limit applies.

title: Setting Your Own Lease Terms for Property Left Behind
bodyText: Pennsylvania's abandoned-property statute sets a default procedure: a written notice by first class mail, 10 days from the postmark for the tenant to collect the property or ask for storage, and storage for up to 30 days, at the tenant's cost, if asked. The statute also says that where a written lease conflicts with it, the lease controls. So a landlord may write its own terms for property left behind into the lease, for example a shorter collection period or no storage. The limits: (1) The protection-from-abuse hold cannot be changed: after an order for possession is carried out, a landlord who knows of a protection-from-abuse order protecting the tenant or a member of the tenant's immediate family may not dispose of or take control of the property for 30 days from the notice, and must store it for up to 30 days if asked. (2) The statute says that under no circumstances may a landlord dispose of or take control of property in a unit someone still lives in without the tenant's express permission; whether a lease term could change that is not settled, so a lease term should not try. (3) Only a written lease can change the procedure. (4) A term that takes away the tenant's statutory rights is a waiver the lease's statement of consumer restrictions must list, and it must be written in plain language. (5) The statute does not reach a deceased tenant's property, which goes through estate law, and manufactured-home communities have their own rules. (6) A landlord that violates the statute owes triple damages, attorney fees and court costs, so have a Pennsylvania lawyer review any custom term. This library's lease clause follows the statute.

title: Late Fee Limits
bodyText: Colorado limits residential late fees (C.R.S. 38-12-105) and backs the limits with real money. You can't charge a late fee until rent is at least 7 days late, and it can't exceed the greater of $50 or 5% of the past-due rent. The fee has to be disclosed in the rental agreement, which your lease's Late Fee clause does by stating your amount. You must give the tenant written notice of a late fee within 180 days after the rent it relates to was due, or you cannot charge it. You may not charge a late fee more than once for the same late payment unless the total still fits under the cap, may not charge interest on a late fee, and may not recoup a late fee out of a rent payment - which is why the lease applies payments to rent first. A late fee is not rent, so an unpaid late fee on its own can neither support an eviction nor terminate the tenancy. And none of the subsidy-paid portion of rent can carry a late fee at all. The consequences of getting it wrong: a non-complying lease provision is void and unenforceable, you owe the tenant a $50 penalty for each violation, you have 7 days from written notice to cure, and if you don't the tenant can sue for damages plus a penalty of $150 to $1,000 per violation plus attorney fees - and can raise the violation as a defense in your eviction. Treat these as hard guardrails when you enter the amount for a Colorado lease.

title: Returned Payment Fees
bodyText: Colorado sets no dollar cap on a landlord's returned-payment fee, but the charge should be reasonable under the dishonored-instrument statute (C.R.S. 13-21-109), and you may add the actual bank charges you incur. Don't call it rent or treat it as rent: it isn't subject to a rent late fee and can't be the basis of a remedy for nonpayment of rent. Your lease's Returned Payments clause states your fee.

title: Domestic Violence and Stalking: Tenant's Right to End the Lease
bodyText: A Colorado tenant who is a victim of unlawful sexual behavior, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse may end the lease and move out without further obligation by giving you written notice with one of these: a police report written within the preceding 60 days, a valid protective or restraining order, or a qualifying advocate's written statement (C.R.S. 38-12-402(2)(a.5)). Your compensation for actual damages from that termination is limited to one month's rent, whatever the lease's early termination terms say, and you must give the tenant a written statement of those damages within 30 days of the termination date. You also owe the tenant confidentiality (see the separate confidentiality note).
notes: CO: Moved from dv-stalking-termination-co by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content unchanged: C.R.S. § 38-12-402(2)(a.5) (police-report window 60 days, corrected from 120 on 2026-08-27).

title: Tenants' Right to Install EV Charging
bodyText: Colorado gives tenants the right to install a Level 1 or Level 2 electric vehicle charging system at their own expense for their own use (C.R.S. 38-12-601). You can't charge a fee for placing or using it, other than reimbursement for the electricity actually used or a reasonable access fee in place of metering (plus a reasonable fee to reserve a space in a shared parking area). You also can't restrict a tenant's parking because the vehicle is a plug-in hybrid or electric vehicle. What you may require (registration within 30 days, safety and appearance requirements, insurance naming you, reimbursement if you install it) is in the lease's EV charging clauses.
notes: CO: Moved from ev-charging-rights-co by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content unchanged: C.R.S. § 38-12-601 (subsections not isolated). The landlord-side EV clauses (ev-charging-requirements-co, -shared-area-co, -end-of-tenancy-co) stay in the lease.

title: No Late Fee on the Subsidy Portion of Rent
bodyText: If a housing subsidy pays part of the rent, you can't charge the tenant a late fee for late payment or nonpayment of any portion the subsidy provider is responsible for paying (C.R.S. 38-12-105(1)(f)). A late fee can apply only to the tenant's own share.
notes: CO: Moved from subsidy-late-fee-co by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content unchanged: C.R.S. § 38-12-105(1)(f) (a total ban, not a $20 cap; corrected 2026-09-13).

title: Subsidized Tenancies: Rent Proration When Part of the Unit Is Uninhabitable
bodyText: If a housing subsidy pays part of the rent and the property becomes partly uninhabitable, rent is reduced in proportion to the part affected, calculated on the total rent including the subsidy-paid portion. Rent already paid for that period is refunded pro rata (C.R.S. 38-12-507, as amended by HB25-1240). Whether the proration covers the subsidy-paid portion rests on the Division of Real Estate's summary of the bill, not the enrolled text.
notes: CO: Moved from subsidy-habitability-proration-co by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and caveat unchanged: C.R.S. § 38-12-507; HB25-1240.

title: Bed Bugs: Disclosure on Request and Entry Notice
bodyText: Two Colorado bed-bug rules. Disclosure (C.R.S. 38-12-1005): when a prospective tenant asks, you must disclose whether the unit has had a known bed-bug infestation in the previous eight months and the date of the most recent bed-bug inspection, if any. The duty is owed on request and before the lease is signed, so putting it only in the lease can come too late; the lease's optional Bed Bug Disclosure clause records what you disclosed. Entry (38-12-1004(1)(a)): before you, an inspector or a pest-control agent enters for a bed-bug inspection or treatment, give the tenant at least 48 hours' written or electronic notice, unless the rental agreement sets a different minimum; your lease's Access clause states your period.

title: Termination Notice Periods and Contents
bodyText: Colorado sets minimum notice to end a periodic tenancy, or to decline to renew a fixed term, scaled to how long the tenancy has run (C.R.S. 13-40-107): at least 91 days for a tenancy of one year or longer; 28 days for six months to a year; 21 days for one to six months; 3 days for one week to one month, or a tenancy at will; and 1 day for less than a week. These are minimums, so a lease period can be longer but never shorter. The notice must be in writing, expire at the end of the period or term, describe the property and the date the tenancy ends, and be signed by the party giving it or their agent or attorney. Once a tenancy has run 12 months, a covered landlord also needs a legal reason to end it (see the for-cause eviction note). Your lease states your chosen notice period; use these minimums as the guardrail.

title: Safe Homes Act: A Tenant Who Leaves Because of Abuse Owes No Later Rent
bodyText: Under Wyoming's Safe Homes Act (Wyo. Stat. 1-21-1303), a tenant who moves out because of a credible imminent threat of domestic abuse or sexual violence at the property, or because the tenant or a household member was a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence at the property within the preceding 60 days, is not liable for rent accruing after moving out. The tenant must give you written notice at least 7 days before moving out, stating the reason and, where applicable, the date of the incident with supporting medical, court or police evidence. If hospitalization, or seeking shelter or counseling, prevented notice within the 60 days, notice given as soon as practicable afterward still counts. Rent owed for the period before the tenant moved out and gave the notice is still owed, and your remedies for it are unaffected. These rights can't be waived (see the Safe Homes nonwaiver note).
notes: WY: Moved from dv-safe-homes-wy by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and citation unchanged: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1303(a), (b), (d).

title: Your Basic Habitability Duties
bodyText: Wyoming puts two different duties on you in one subsection, and they are not equally firm. The first is absolute: you must maintain the unit in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation (W.S. 1-21-1202(a), first sentence). Nothing in the statute lets a lease undo that one. The second is the utilities list -- operational electrical, heating and plumbing, with hot and cold running water -- and that sentence, and only that sentence, ends 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties'. See the separate note on what that escape hatch actually does before you consider using it. Separately, the section does not prevent renting seasonal units such as summer cabins that were never intended to have those amenities, so a genuinely seasonal property is outside the utilities requirement without any agreement at all. The tenant must cooperate in maintaining the property (W.S. 1-21-1202(b)). See also the notes on responding to a habitability notice, on trivial conditions, and on reassigning a specific duty by written agreement.
notes: WY: Moved from habitability-baseline-wy by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and citation unchanged: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a), (b). | WY: RETRO 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.15 follow-up). ACCURACY FIX, found by reading W.S. 1-21-1202(a) section-open. The shipped text read 'Wyoming requires you to keep the property safe and sanitary and fit for human habitation, including operational electrical, heating and plumbing systems with hot and cold running water, UNLESS YOU AND THE TENANT AGREE OTHERWISE IN WRITING' -- which attaches the waiver to the whole duty, habitability included. The statute does not. Subsection (a) is three sentences: the safe-and-sanitary / fit-for-human-habitation duty stands alone with no qualifier; 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties' attaches only to the second sentence, the electrical/heating/plumbing/hot-and-cold-water list; and the third is a seasonal-rental proviso. The old wording would have told a Wyoming landlord that habitability itself is waivable by agreement, which is wrong and is the more dangerous direction to be wrong in. ALSO ADDED: the seasonal-rental proviso, previously recorded in this row's own notes as 'not drafted (N/A for typical use case)' -- it is now drafted, because it is the legitimate use case for the waiver and a landlord who knows about it often does not need the waiver at all. Pointer added to the new row edu-habitability-waiver-wy (rule 63). title: Returning a Separate Utility Deposit
bodyText: If you hold a deposit identified separately as a utility deposit, refund it within 10 days after the tenant shows that all utility charges they incurred are paid. If the tenant hasn't shown that within 45 days after the lease ends, apply the deposit to the tenant's outstanding utility debt within 15 days after that period ends, then refund any remaining balance within 7 days after applying it, or within 15 days after receiving the tenant's forwarding address, whichever is later (Wyo. Stat. 1-21-1208(b)).
notes: WY: Moved from utility-deposit-return-wy by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and citation unchanged: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(b).

title: Deposit Return Deadline and Itemization
bodyText: Within 30 days after the lease ends, or within 15 days after receiving the tenant's forwarding address, whichever is later, deliver or mail the balance of the deposit and any prepaid rent with a written itemization of any deductions and the reasons for them. If the property is damaged, the period is extended by another 30 days (Wyo. Stat. 1-21-1208(a)). See the penalty note for what happens if you miss it. Two things Wyoming allows that the library's deposit clause deliberately does not use, both in the tenant's favour: Wyo. Stat. 1-21-1208(a) lets you deduct the cost of cleaning the unit back to its condition at the start of the tenancy, where the library's clause allows cleaning costs only if the unit is substantially less clean; and it lets you apply the deposit to any other costs the lease provides for, which the library's clause doesn't list. Both are lawful, so a landlord who wants them can add a custom clause.

Stat. § 1-21-1208(a). | WY: Added the two 2026-08-28 deliberate giveaways (WY log §6.1), lawful and not used. (2026-10-01, Claude Code, rule 54 backfill after the WY retro: a lawful option the library declines gets an education row. The log recorded this decline; the row did not say it.)

title: Deposit Return Deadline and Itemization
bodyText: If you keep any part of the deposit for damages or other allowable charges besides rent, return the balance within 14 days after determining the amount kept, and no later than 30 days after the lease ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands the deposit. If the tenant doesn't demand it within 30 days after the lease ends, mail the balance to the tenant's last known address. Itemize anything you keep in a written notice to the tenant (K.S.A. 58-2550(b)). See the penalty note for what happens if you don't.
notes: KS: Moved from security-deposit-return-ks by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and citation unchanged: K.S.A. 58-2550(b).

title: Your Basic Habitability Duties
bodyText: Except when prevented by an act of God, a failure of public utility services or other conditions beyond your control, Kansas requires you to: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety; take reasonable care of common areas; keep the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems you supply in good and safe working order; provide trash receptacles and arrange removal, unless a government entity does; and supply running water and reasonable hot water and heat, unless the building isn't required by law to have them or the unit's heat or hot water comes from a tenant-controlled installation on a direct utility connection. You also can't interfere with or refuse a tenant access to a municipally franchised cable or communication service (K.S.A. 58-2553(a)). See the note on when you can shift some of these duties to the tenant.

title: Domestic Violence, Sexual Assault, Trafficking and Stalking: Housing Protections
bodyText: Kansas protects a tenant or applicant who has been, is, or is in imminent danger of becoming a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, human trafficking or stalking within the preceding 12 months (K.S.A. 58-25,137). You can't deny tenancy to, evict, or find a lease violation against that person based on that status if they otherwise qualify. A tenant who asks to end the lease early under this protection owes no rent after moving out, though you may charge a reasonable early-termination fee of up to one month's rent, and you may ask for supporting documentation as the law allows. The lease continues for any remaining co-tenants. Neither side can waive these rights. See the note on the consequences of violating this protection.

title: If You Can't Deliver Possession on Time
bodyText: If you fail to deliver possession as the lease requires, rent abates until you do, and the tenant may either end the lease on at least 5 days' written notice, in which case you return the full deposit, or demand that you perform, sue for possession against you or anyone wrongfully in possession, and recover damages. If your failure is willful and not in good faith, the tenant can recover up to 1.5 times the periodic rent or 1.5 times actual damages, whichever is greater (K.S.A. 58-2560).
notes: KS: Moved from possession-delay-ks by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and citation unchanged: K.S.A. 58-2560.

title: Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options
bodyText: If fire or casualty damages the property enough to substantially impair its use and habitability, the tenant may move out immediately and notify you in writing within 5 days that they are ending the lease, which then ends on the date they moved out; or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate only the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the drop in the property's fair rental value (K.S.A. 58-2562). If the lease ends this way, return the part of the deposit the tenant is entitled to and account for rent as of the date they moved out.
notes: KS: Moved from fire-casualty-termination-ks by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and citation unchanged: K.S.A. 58-2562.

title: Deposit Return Deadline, Itemization and Unclaimed Deposits
bodyText: If you keep any part of the deposit, deliver or mail the balance and a written itemization of what you kept within 14 days after the lease ends (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1416(2)). If the tenant gave no forwarding address or delivery instructions, mail it by first-class mail to the tenant's last known address. If that mailing comes back undeliverable, or the balance stays unclaimed for a year, report and send it to the State Treasurer as unclaimed property (69-1329). See the penalty note for what happens if you miss the deadline.
notes: NE: Moved from security-deposit-return-ne by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and citation unchanged: Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1416(2); § 69-1329.

title: Domestic Violence: Lease Release, Removing the Abuser, and Lock Changes
bodyText: Nebraska gives a tenant who, or whose household member, is a victim of domestic violence three rights, each triggered by a qualifying protective order or third-party domestic-violence certification plus written notice (see the documentation note). Lease release (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1431.01): the tenant names a release date at least 14 and no more than 30 days after the notice and any household members also released; they owe rent for the month the lease ends but nothing after the release date, and no fee solely because of the release. The release doesn't extend to another tenant on the lease who isn't a household member. Removing the abuser (76-1431.02): if the abuser is a co-tenant or other occupant of the unit, the victim can have them removed from the lease and excluded, and you then proceed against the abuser only under Nebraska's expedited removal procedure; you aren't liable for actions taken in good faith. Lock change (76-1431.03, 76-1431.04): if the abuser isn't a co-tenant or occupant, change the locks within 24 hours of a written request; if you don't, the tenant may change them in a workmanlike manner with locks of similar or better quality, must tell you promptly, and must give you a new key or code. On the lock change, one point runs your way: you may require the tenant to pay the actual and reasonable cost you incur in changing the locks (§76-1431.04(4)).

Stat. §§ 76-1431.01, 76-1431.02, 76-1431.03, 76-1431.04. | NE: Read section-open 2026-09-30 from nebraskalegislature.gov in the built-in browser. The whole URLTA (§§76-1401 to 76-1449, 54 sections, 78,605 chars, SHA-256 73533d60a357f1a7f89f4dd8da75b8f2) was loaded via display_html.php and pattern-screened in page; named sections were then read individually. Retro checks, SOP 1.10. RULE 54 (SOP 1.10, optional clauses) — LANDLORD RIGHT ADDED. §§76-1431.03 and 76-1431.04 read section-open. The row set out the lock-change duty and the tenant's self-help remedy but omitted §76-1431.04(4): 'The landlord may require the tenant to pay for the actual and reasonable cost incurred by the landlord in changing the locks under this section.' That is a cost-recovery right running to the landlord inside a tenant-protection scheme, which is exactly the kind of provision rule 54 exists to surface, and it was missing from the row that is now the only place Nebraska's DV rules are recorded (the three DV lease clauses were switched off by the 2026-09-29 scrub and folded into this row). Recorded as education rather than a clause: the right is statutory and does not depend on lease language, so no clause is owed. CURRENCY NOTE (rule 16): both sections carry 'Laws 2025, LB80, § 50' in their source lines, i.e. they were amended after Nebraska's original pass; the text read today is the current compilation. Whether LB80 changed the substance of these subsections was NOT traced to the session law — flagged, not resolved, and outside a scalpel retro.

title: Your Basic Habitability Duties
bodyText: Except when prevented by an act of God, a failure of public utility services or other conditions beyond your control, Nebraska requires you to: substantially comply, after written or actual notice, with minimum housing codes materially affecting health and safety; make all repairs and do whatever is necessary, after written or actual notice, to keep the property fit and habitable; keep common areas clean and safe; maintain the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems and appliances you supply in good and safe working order; provide waste receptacles and arrange removal; and supply running water and reasonable hot water and heat, unless the building isn't required by law to have them or the unit's heat or hot water comes from a tenant-controlled installation on a direct utility connection (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1419(1)). See the note on delegating some duties to the tenant.
notes: NE: Moved from habitability-baseline-ne by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and citation unchanged: Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1419(1).

title: If You Can't Deliver Possession on Time
bodyText: If you fail to deliver possession as the lease requires, rent abates until you do, and the tenant may either end the lease on at least 5 days' written notice, in which case you return all prepaid rent and the full deposit, or demand that you perform, sue for possession against you or anyone wrongfully in possession, and recover damages. If your failure is willful and not in good faith, the tenant can recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1426).
notes: NE: Moved from possession-delay-ne by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and citation unchanged: Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1426.

title: Deposit Return Deadline, Interest and Withholding
bodyText: Within three weeks after the lease ends, and after receiving the tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions, return the deposit with the simple interest Minnesota law requires, or give the tenant a written statement of the specific reasons for withholding any of it. You may withhold only what is reasonably necessary to remedy a default in paying rent or other money due under the lease, or to restore the property to its condition at the start of the tenancy, ordinary wear and tear excepted (Minn. Stat. 504B.178). If the tenant leaves because the building is legally condemned for reasons the tenant didn't cause, the return window is five days. See the inspection-notice penalty note.
notes: MN: Moved from security-deposit-return-mn by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and citation unchanged: Minn. Stat. § 504B.178.

title: New Construction Not Ready by the Start Date
bodyText: If the property is new construction (a new building, rehabilitation, reconstruction or addition) and you know it won't be ready by the start date, notify the tenant in writing at least seven days before the start date and offer a choice of: alternative housing you provide, reasonably equivalent in size, amenities and location, until the property is ready; a payment equal to the rent to help cover alternative housing the tenant arranges; or ending the lease. If the tenant takes one of the first two options and the property still isn't ready within 90 days of the original start date, the tenant may then end the lease (Minn. Stat. 504B.153).
notes: MN: Moved from possession-delay-mn-new-construction by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and citation unchanged: Minn. Stat. § 504B.153.

title: Victims of Violence: Tenant's Right to End the Lease
bodyText: A Minnesota tenant may end the lease without penalty or liability if the tenant or another authorized occupant fears imminent violence after being subjected to domestic abuse, criminal sexual conduct, sexual extortion or harassment (Minn. Stat. 504B.206). The tenant must give you signed and dated advance written notice, before the tenancy ends, by mail, in person or by a form of written communication the tenant regularly uses with you, stating that they fear imminent violence from a person named in a qualifying document, that they need to end the tenancy, the termination date, and instructions for any remaining belongings; a qualifying document must come with it. Moving out before that date doesn't by itself end the tenancy. You may ask for the perpetrator's name to protect other residents, but the tenant may decline for safety reasons. A sole tenant owes rent for the full month in which the tenancy ends, gives up the claim to the deposit, and owes nothing for the rest of the term; if there are several tenants, the lease ends for all of them (see the qualifying-documents note). Debts owed before termination are unaffected, and the tenant's notice, documents, new address and status are confidential.
notes: MN: Moved from dv-lease-termination-mn by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and citation unchanged: Minn. Stat. § 504B.206.

title: Fire or Casualty: The Tenant May Leave
bodyText: If the property is destroyed, or becomes uninhabitable or unfit for occupancy, through no fault or neglect of the tenant or any occupant, the tenant may move out and surrender it; rent is prorated to the date they leave and they owe no rent after that (Minn. Stat. 504B.131). The fault condition is doing real work: a tenant who caused the damage has no statutory right to walk away, so the lease continues and rent keeps running -- see tenant-caused-damage-mn for what you can recover. Your duty to keep the property fit and in reasonable repair continues and can't be waived. The statute lets a tenant or occupant expressly agree otherwise, except where Minn. Stat. 504B.161 (the fitness and repair covenant) prohibits it, so a lease could limit this move-out right. The library does not offer that clause: it trades away a tenant protection the statute gives by default, and the line between what can be waived and what 504B.161 protects has not been reviewed. A landlord who wants it can add a custom clause, after taking advice.

title: Receipts for Cash Rent
bodyText: If a tenant pays rent or any other payment in cash, give a written receipt immediately if they pay in person, or within three business days if they don't (Minn. Stat. 504B.118).
notes: MN: Moved from cash-rent-receipt-mn by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and citation unchanged: Minn. Stat. § 504B.118.

title: Limits on Apportioning Shared-Meter Utilities
bodyText: If you apportion utilities in a shared-metered building, Minnesota requires that you stay the bill payer and customer of record for the building; you may not apportion or bill tenants for electricity (it may only be submetered as the law allows); any administrative billing charge may not exceed $8 per billing period; a late charge on utilities billed separately from rent may not exceed $5 a month and may not compound; you must give tenants copies of the underlying bills on request; and you may not disconnect or cause disconnection of a tenant's service for nonpayment of utility charges (Minn. Stat. 504B.216). The required disclosure attachment is covered in its own note.
notes: MN: Created by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29) from utility-apportionment-mn; content and citations unchanged: Minn. Stat. § 504B.216; § 216B.023.

title: Your Basic Habitability Duties
bodyText: Minnesota requires you to keep the property and common areas fit for the use the parties intended and in reasonable repair, including heat of at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit in all places meant for habitation, kitchens and bathrooms included, from October 1 through April 30 (unless a utility company requires it lowered), and extermination of insects, rodents, vermin and other pests (Minn. Stat. 504B.161). These duties don't apply to disrepair caused by the tenant's own willful, malicious or irresponsible conduct, or that of someone under the tenant's direction. You must also keep the property in compliance with health and safety laws, including any local rental-licensing ordinance, and make it reasonably energy efficient where that is cost-effective.
notes: MN: Created by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29) from habitability-baseline-mn, which keeps only the tenant's repair-notice duty; content and citations unchanged: Minn. Stat. § 504B.161.

title: Tell Prospective Tenants About a Pending Foreclosure
bodyText: If you've received notice of a contract-for-deed cancellation or a mortgage foreclosure sale affecting the property, you must tell a prospective tenant in writing, before signing the lease and before accepting rent or a deposit, including the date the cancellation period or redemption period ends (Minn. Stat. 504B.151). The lease's optional clause records that you did; the duty itself is owed before signing.
notes: MN: Created by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29) as the pattern-3 companion to foreclosure-disclosure-mn; content from that row: Minn. Stat. § 504B.151.

title: Deposit Return Deadline and Unclaimed Deposits
bodyText: Within 30 days after the lease ends and the tenant delivers possession, or after a different starting point North Dakota law sets (such as a domestic-violence termination), return the deposit with any interest the law requires, less lawful deductions, and a written itemization of anything you kept (N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.1). If the deposit goes unclaimed for a year after the lease ends, report and remit it under North Dakota's unclaimed property law (47-30.2-04). See the notes on interest, penalties and domestic-violence timing.

title: If a Tenant Dies
bodyText: If a tenant dies, a surviving co-tenant or the tenant's estate may choose to end the lease. It then ends on the last day of the month after the month of death, unless the term would have ended sooner, and the estate owes rent through that date (N.D.C.C. 47-16-18).

title: Fire or Casualty: When the Lease Ends
bodyText: If the greater part of the property, or the part that was the tenant's material reason for leasing it, is destroyed or damaged through no fault of the tenant, the tenant may end the lease (N.D.C.C. 47-16-17(2)). If the property is destroyed, the leasing terminates automatically (N.D.C.C. 47-16-14(4)) — and that provision has no fault exception, so a total loss the tenant caused still ends the lease and leaves you a damages claim rather than a continuing tenancy. North Dakota has no statutory rent abatement during repairs and no proportional reduction: the tenant's casualty right is all or nothing.

(a) RULE 54t: each exit provision was checked separately for its own tenant-fault exception, as the rule directs. § 47-16-17(2) HAS one — the tenant may terminate where the property perishes 'from any cause other than the ordinary negligence of the lessee' — and the row already carried it as 'through no fault of the tenant'. § 47-16-14(4) HAS NONE: 'The leasing of real property terminates: ... 4. By the destruction of the property leased.' The row stated the automatic termination without that point, which is the one a landlord facing a tenant-caused fire needs. Two sentences added: the missing fault asymmetry, and the confirmed absence of any statutory abatement or proportional-reduction mechanism in ND (checked because rule 54t asks whether a no-abatement lease term would waive a statutory right — here there is no such right to waive). The landlord-side gap this leaves is filled by the new optional clause tenant-caused-damage-nd. (b) RULE 79 / RULE 78 BASIS: created by the 2026-09-29 scrub with provenance only and no basis. title: Domestic Violence: Tenant's Right to End the Lease
bodyText: A North Dakota tenant who is a victim of domestic violence by a family or household member, or who fears imminent domestic violence against themselves or their minor children by such a person if they stay, may end the lease without penalty or liability (N.D.C.C. 47-16-17.1). The tenant must give you advance written notice, by mail, fax or in person before the tenancy ends, stating that they fear imminent domestic violence from a person named in a court order, an order prohibiting contact, a civil protection order or another record filed with a court; that they need to end the tenancy; and the date it will end. The tenant owes rent for the full month in which the tenancy ends plus one more month's rent, subject to your duty to mitigate, and must pay that on or before termination to be released from the rest of the term; rent and other amounts already owed remain due. The tenancy, including the right of possession, ends on the date in the notice, and it continues for any other tenants. See the notes on confidentiality and deposit timing.

title: Termination Notice Periods
bodyText: In North Dakota, either party may end a month-to-month tenancy by giving at least one calendar month's written notice, unless the parties agreed in writing to a longer period or a different notice time; rent is due through the termination date. If a lease doesn't specify its term, notice must be at least as long as the term itself, up to one calendar month. A lease that converts to month-to-month ends on the last day of a month with at least one calendar month's notice (N.D.C.C. 47-16-15). A lease notice requirement longer than one month only binds the tenant if they initial it (see the initialing clause). One asymmetry to plan around: the agreed period binds either party, so if you write a longer period into the lease you are bound to give it too — but the initialling rule that lets a tenant escape a longer period has no equivalent for you.

title: Domestic Abuse or Stalking: Tenant's Right to End the Lease
bodyText: If a South Dakota tenant or a household member is the victim of alleged domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking, the tenant may end the lease without an early-termination penalty, effective on a specified date, by giving you written notice that the termination is due to fear of imminent danger or injury, with one of these dated within the 30 days before the notice: a signed police report on the incident, a protection order issued in response to it, or documentation from a licensed health care provider who examined the person and has reasonable cause to believe they were a victim (SDCL 43-32-19(3), 43-32-19.1). The tenant owes no otherwise-applicable early-termination fee and no rent for the month after the month they move out.
notes: SD: Moved from dv-lease-release-sd by the three-bucket scrub (2026-09-29); content and citation unchanged: SDCL 43-32-19(3); SDCL 43-32-19.1.

title: Disclose Known Prior Meth Manufacturing
bodyText: If you actually know methamphetamine was previously manufactured on the property, you must tell the tenant before they become obligated under the lease. For a building of two or more units, the duty covers only the unit you know about (SDCL 43-32-30). The lease's optional clause records the disclosure.
