title: Notice to End a Tenancy
bodyText: How much notice Missouri requires depends on the kind of tenancy. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date with no notice to quit. A month-to-month tenancy ends by written notice from either party ending it on a rent-paying date at least one month after the other party receives it. A tenancy at will, by sufferance or for less than a year (such as week-to-week) may be ended by the landlord on one month's written notice. A year-to-year tenancy needs written notice at least 60 days before the end of the year. A lease that is not in writing and signed is treated as month-to-month. These notices are not needed before a rent-and-possession case for unpaid rent. A mobile-home lot tenancy has a longer 60-day rule. Missouri also lets the parties dispense with the notice to quit by special agreement (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.070). The library does not offer a clause that does this: it would remove the one-month notice from a month-to-month tenancy, how far a court lets such an agreement reach has not been reviewed, and a term like this is read strictly against the landlord who drafted it. It is lawful, so a landlord who still wants it can add a custom clause, after taking advice.

title: Demand for Rent Before Filing
bodyText: Missouri has no pay-or-quit notice period for unpaid rent. Before filing a rent-and-possession case, you must demand the rent that is due from the tenant or the person occupying the property; the demand is valid any time after the rent is due, and in a suit for possession when one month's rent or more is in arrears and you have a right by law to re-enter for the nonpayment, serving the complaint and summons counts as the demand. If your written lease declares the lease forfeited for nonpayment 'for a specified time', you cannot start the case until that time has passed, so avoid building a grace period into a forfeiture clause unless you mean it.

title: Missouri Eviction Process
bodyText: Missouri has two main eviction tracks. A rent-and-possession case (for unpaid rent) is filed with an associate circuit judge after a demand for rent; the court date must be within 21 business days of the summons unless you agree to later, the tenant may stop the case by paying all rent and costs on the judgment date, and the officer must deliver possession within 5 days of receiving the execution. An unlawful detainer case covers a tenant who holds over after the lease ends and refuses to leave after a written demand for possession; execution for possession may issue no sooner than 10 days after judgment, and the judgment awards double damages and double monthly rent until possession is restored. In a rent-and-possession case the tenant has 10 days from the judgment to move to set it aside or apply for a trial de novo, and in either track an appeal stays execution only with a sufficient bond (in rent cases, one covering rent). If service is only by posting and mailing and the tenant defaults, no money judgment is entered. Self-help eviction is prohibited, and local governments may not impose eviction moratoriums.

title: Lease Violations and Illegal Use
bodyText: Missouri gives no cure period for lease violations. If a tenant violates a condition of a written lease, assigns or sublets without your written consent (for terms of two years or less, at will or by sufferance), or commits waste, you may give 10 days' notice to vacate (in writing, to be safe) and then recover possession through the courts. If a tenant allows illegal gaming, a bawdyhouse or the illegal possession, sale or distribution of controlled substances on the premises, the lease becomes void and you have the same remedies as against a tenant holding over. You are not liable for relying on a written notice from law enforcement that the premises are being used for illegal drug activity.

title: Expedited Eviction for Drug Activity and Emergencies
bodyText: A landlord or prosecutor may bring an expedited eviction in the associate circuit court, heard within 15 days of service, where drug-related criminal activity occurred on or near the property or the tenant's household or guests engaged in it, or where an emergency makes ordinary eviction too slow to prevent physical injury or major property damage (only after first trying to abate it through police or mental health services). No notice to vacate is needed first, except that if someone other than the tenant committed the activity, you must give the tenant 5 days' written notice and a chance to seek a protective order or report it to police. An innocent tenant who did not know of the activity can defend, and the court may then remove only the person responsible. On eviction the tenant has 24 hours to vacate. Rent continues to accrue during the case.

title: Property Left After an Eviction
bodyText: When a judgment for possession is carried out, you are not liable for loss of or damage to the tenant's belongings you remove or dispose of under the court-ordered execution, except for willful, wanton or malicious acts. But if property left behind is conspicuously and permanently labelled as belonging to a third party, you must notify that person by certified mail, return receipt requested, and give them five business days after receiving the notice to recover it. If the officer has not delivered possession within seven days after receiving the writ, you may, within 60 days of the judgment and with a local law enforcement officer present, remove the locks, take possession and remove belongings, after showing the officer the judgment and execution and filing the officer's written acknowledgment with the court within five days.
notes: MO: Mo. Rev. Stat. § 535.040(2)-(3) (2009 S.B. 231); Mo. Rev. title: Removing Squatters
bodyText: Since August 28, 2024, a property owner may file a verified petition to remove people unlawfully occupying a residential property who were never tenants. The court issues an ex parte removal order immediately on good cause, with a hearing within 48 hours, and the sheriff enforces it. This fast track is available only if, among other things, the property had not been leased to anyone for three consecutive months, the occupants are not current or former tenants or immediate family, and there is no pending litigation with them. A person wrongly removed may recover $1,000 in statutory damages plus actual damages. For current or former tenants, use the ordinary eviction process.

title: Holdover Damages
bodyText: Missouri sets several double measures for tenants who stay too long. A tenant for life or years who willfully holds over after the term ends, and after you make a demand and give written notice requiring possession, owes double the yearly value of the property for the time you are kept out. A tenant who gives written notice of intent to leave on a date and does not leave owes double the rent for as long as the tenant stays. In an unlawful detainer judgment, the court awards double the damages found and double the monthly rent found until possession is restored. After a written lease ends, oral evidence that it was renewed or extended is not admissible in a possession suit.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Missouri does not require a reason to end a tenancy at the end of a fixed term or on proper notice for a periodic tenancy. title: Domestic Violence, Sexual Assault and Stalking Protections
bodyText: You may not deny tenancy to, evict, or find a lease violation against an applicant or tenant because the person is, has been, or is in imminent danger of becoming a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, if the person otherwise qualifies. The protection does not apply if the person let the named abuser into the premises, or if you reasonably believe the named abuser threatens other occupants or the property. A tenant who vacates has a defense to rent for the period after leaving if a court finds the tenant was a victim or in imminent danger and the tenant notified you and gave any documentation you asked for (a signed statement from a victim-service provider or health professional, or a police, court or agency record). You may charge a reasonable termination fee when a tenant ends a lease early under this law. False information may be grounds to deny or evict. Missouri has no domestic-violence lock-change statute.

title: Military Lease Termination
bodyText: A member of the U.S. Armed Forces on active duty, or a Missouri Army or Air National Guard member on full-time duty or serving as a civil service technician, may end a residential lease after receiving permanent change of station orders, temporary duty orders of more than 90 days at least 25 miles away, discharge or release from that duty, or orders to live in government quarters. The member gives written notice of termination effective on a stated date at least 15 days after service, and gives you a copy of the orders or a signed letter from the commanding officer before that date. The final payment is due by the termination date, and the member is entitled to the full return of the security deposit and any pet deposit if the lease and the deposit law were otherwise followed. The federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act gives additional rights.

title: When the Tenant Causes Damage
bodyText: If a tenant causes damage, Missouri law gives you these points. The rule that a tenant owes no rent after a disaster destroys the residence does not apply if the tenant caused the disaster. A tenant who commits waste owes treble damages, and waste is a ground for 10 days' notice to vacate. But no action may be brought against a tenant in whose home a fire accidentally begins, and a repair promise in a lease does not require a tenant to rebuild after a fire the tenant did not cause through procurement, connivance or neglect unless the tenant specially agreed to rebuild. Whether a careless fire counts as 'accidental' under that rule is unsettled.

title: Missouri Fair Housing Law
bodyText: The Missouri Human Rights Act bars refusing to rent, setting different terms, misrepresenting availability, or advertising a preference because of race, color, religion, national origin, ancestry, sex, disability or familial status. You must allow reasonable disability modifications at the tenant's expense (and may, where reasonable, require restoration of the interior) and make reasonable accommodations in rules and policies. Exempt, except from the advertising ban: a private owner renting a single-family house without a broker or advertising who owns no more than three such houses, and rooms or units in an owner-occupied building for four or fewer families. Missouri does not protect source of income or age in housing; federal law adds its own rules and exemptions.

title: Delivering Notices
bodyText: Missouri sets delivery rules for particular notices rather than one general method. Notices ending a tenancy must be in writing. title: Towing From Rental Property
bodyText: To have a vehicle towed from your property without a police officer's authorization, you (or a full-time property or security manager) must be present, and either post a sign in plain view at every entrance at least 17 by 22 inches with letters at least 1 inch high that prohibits public parking, states that unauthorized vehicles will be removed at the owner's expense, discloses the maximum towing and storage fee, and gives the phone number of the local traffic law enforcement agency or a 24-hour staffed emergency information line, or notify police and wait 10 hours (owner-occupied property of four units or fewer) or 96 hours (other private property). title: When the Tenant Causes the Damage - You Can Charge Them, But You Cannot Stop Them Leaving
bodyText: If a tenant, occupant or guest causes damage that makes the home uninhabitable, Nebraska splits the answer in a way that catches landlords out. WHAT YOU CAN RECOVER: the tenant is liable for the damage. §76-1429(2) says that notwithstanding the rest of the casualty rule 'the tenant is responsible for damage caused by his negligence', and the Nebraska Supreme Court has gone further - because a specific statute holds a tenant responsible for negligent fire damage, a lease provision doing the same cannot be struck down as void against public policy or unconscionable (SFI Ltd. Partnership 8 v. Carroll). Your Tenant Maintenance clause already carries that liability. If the tenancy ends you may also pursue possession, a claim for rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach (§76-1435), which can include rent lost while the property is repaired - subject to §76-1405's duty to mitigate, so re-letting effort is expected. WHAT YOU CANNOT DO: stop the tenant leaving, or switch off the rent reduction. Nebraska's landlord-noncompliance and essential-services remedies each carry an express tenant-fault exception - the tenant may not terminate or claim for a condition caused by their own or their household's deliberate or negligent act (§§76-1425, 76-1427). The casualty section has NO such exception. §76-1429 makes the tenant pay for the damage but still lets them vacate and end the lease on 14 days' written notice, or stay and pay proportionally reduced rent, even where they caused the fire. A lease term saying rent will not abate or that a tenant at fault cannot terminate would take away a right the Act gives them, which §76-1415(1)(a) voids - and if you used it knowing it was prohibited, §76-1415(2) adds the tenant's actual damages and attorney's fees. Charge for the damage; do not try to trap the tenant in the lease.

title: Converting to Condominiums: 60 Days, a For-Cause-Only Window, and a Right of First Refusal
bodyText: If you are converting a building to condominiums, Nebraska gives the sitting residential tenants and subtenants a set of rights that override your ordinary notice position (§76-886). NOTICE: you must give each residential tenant and any subtenant in possession notice of the conversion, with the public-offering statement if there is one, no later than 60 days before they are required to vacate, hand delivered to the unit or sent by prepaid US mail, and the notice must set out generally the rights this section gives them. FOR THOSE 60 DAYS YOU ARE IN A FOR-CAUSE-ONLY WINDOW: no tenant or subtenant may be required to vacate on less than 60 days' notice except for nonpayment of rent, waste, or conduct that disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment - and you may not alter the terms of the tenancy during that period. If you skip the notice, that failure is a defense to your action for possession. RIGHT OF FIRST REFUSAL: for 60 days after the notice you may offer to sell each unit occupied for residential use to the tenant who leases it; if you make the offer and they do not buy within those 60 days, you may not offer that unit to anyone else on better price or terms for the next 30 days. That does not apply to a unit that will be restricted to non-residential use, or where the converted unit's boundaries do not substantially match the residential unit. TWO MORE POINTS: a conversion notice that specifies a date by which the unit must be vacated counts as a notice to vacate, and nothing in the section lets you terminate a lease in breach of its own terms. A tenant can waive these protections, but only by a written instrument signed AFTER the date of the notice - so your lease cannot do it in advance.

title: In Nebraska Every Payment Under the Lease Is "Rent" - Which Cuts Both Ways
bodyText: Nebraska defines rent broadly by statute: 'Rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement' (§76-1410(13)). You do not need a lease sentence designating fees as additional rent - the definition already does it. The consequence runs both ways. In your favour, an unpaid fee that the lease requires the tenant to pay to you is on its face 'rent', which matters because §76-1431(2) lets you terminate when rent is unpaid and the tenant does not pay within seven calendar days of your written notice. Against you, anything the lease makes payable to you is swept into every other rule that turns on 'rent' - including the deposit cap, which is measured in rent, and the holdover and damages measures. Note that the standard Tenant Default clause says that failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying rent, will not by itself support termination or eviction. That is a choice to ask for less than Nebraska law allows, not a legal requirement.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix the Tenant's Breach and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Nebraska did not adopt the URLTA provision that lets a landlord remedy a tenant's breach and charge the cost as rent. If the tenant fails to do something the lease or §76-1421 requires, your statutory routes are the notice-and-cure termination at §76-1431(1), damages and injunctive relief under §76-1431(3) - with attorney's fees if the noncompliance was willful - and, for a tenant who breaches the duty to maintain, the ordinary measures. There is no statutory self-help-and-bill mechanism, so doing the work yourself and adding it to the next rent demand is a contract claim, not a statutory one, and treating it as rent risks a defective nonpayment notice.

title: No Rule Against Blank Spaces, and No Duty to Give the Tenant a Copy
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute requiring a written lease to have every blank space completed, and no statute making an incomplete lease a material noncompliance. It also imposes no duty to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and no consequence for failing to - unlike states where that failure is a defense to enforcement. Fill in the blanks and hand over a copy anyway: both are ordinary evidence of what was agreed, and Nebraska's broad deceptive-practices standard is a live backstop even without a specific rule.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession in a Lease
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute writing a covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession into a residential lease. The one statutory provision on quiet enjoyment, §76-207, is about covenants in CONVEYANCES of real property - deed warranties broken by actual or constructive eviction by someone with paramount title - and does not reach a landlord and tenant. What Nebraska does give the tenant instead is specific and narrower: the habitability duties at §76-1419, the remedies for an unlawful ouster or a cut-off of services at §76-1430, and the bar on recovering possession except through the Act at §76-1436. A common-law implied covenant may still exist; that is case law, not statute.
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-30 from nebraskalegislature.gov in the built-in browser. The whole URLTA (§§76-1401 to 76-1449, 54 sections, 78,605 chars, SHA-256 73533d60a357f1a7f89f4dd8da75b8f2) was loaded via display_html.php and pattern-screened in page; named sections were then read individually. Retro checks, SOP 1.10. RULE 27 (SOP 1.10) — CONFIRMED ABSENT as a landlord-tenant covenant. Pattern 'quiet (enjoyment|possession)' against the full URLTA text: NO HIT. Statute-wide search 'quiet enjoyment' returned 7 results, the only relevant being §76-207 (Covenants; breach; constructive eviction; acts constituting), read section-open: it governs 'Covenants of quiet enjoyment and covenants of warranty in conveyances of real property' breached 'by reason of the hostile assertion of a paramount title holder', and lists three constructive-eviction situations all framed around a paramount title holder. That is a conveyancing provision, not a lease term, and must not be cited as a tenant's quiet-enjoyment right. EXPRESSLY LEFT OPEN and labelled as such in the row: whether Nebraska recognises a common-law implied covenant of quiet enjoyment in a lease. That is doctrine I have NOT read (rule 76), so the row says a covenant 'may still exist' rather than denying one. Note `no-disturbance` already obliges the tenant not to disturb other tenants, and §76-1419(1)(c) and §76-1421 carry the statutory analogues.

title: Nebraska Prescribes No Lease or Notice Forms
bodyText: Nebraska supplies no statutory form for a residential lease, a disclosure, or any notice a landlord gives a tenant. There is no prescribed wording you must copy and no official template, so your notices need only contain what the relevant section requires - for example a termination notice specifying the acts constituting the breach and the termination date under §76-1431(1), or 30 days to the periodic rental date under §76-1437(2). The two places Nebraska does prescribe contents are court documents, not lease documents: the complaint for restitution (§76-1441) and the summons (§76-1442).

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras or Video Doorbells
bodyText: Nebraska has no statute giving a tenant the right to install a security camera or video doorbell, and none restricting one. So it is governed by your lease: the No Alterations clause already requires your written consent before the tenant attaches anything to the property, and the Use of Property & Common Areas clause covers fixing things to exterior surfaces. Two cautions that are not lease questions. A camera that records audio can raise wiretapping issues, and one that overlooks another tenant's unit can raise privacy ones; neither is answered by the landlord-tenant act. Treat a request from a tenant with a disability as a reasonable-accommodation question instead.

title: Good-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: New Jersey is a good-cause state. In most residential rentals a landlord may remove a tenant, or refuse to renew a lease, only for one of the causes the Anti-Eviction Act lists, proven in court; the end of a lease term is not a cause. The Act does not cover owner-occupied buildings with no more than two rental units or transient and seasonal rentals. The full rules are in the Anti-Eviction Act entry.

title: Eviction Court Rules: Landlord Duties
bodyText: New Jersey court rules add duties to an eviction case. A default judgment for possession needs the landlord's affidavit stating the facts that give good cause and that every charge claimed as rent, other than base rent, is allowed to be charged as rent by the lease and by law; a landlord's attorney must certify the same, and any required notice to quit must be attached with a statement that it was served and is true. A business entity other than a sole proprietor, or a partner in a general partnership, must appear through an attorney. A consent judgment for possession against an unrepresented tenant must be reviewed and signed by a judge that day. When the landlord believes service at the rental may fail, the landlord must also ask for service by mail at another address. A warrant of removal cannot issue until three business days after judgment (two days for a seasonal tenancy) and cannot be executed before the third business day after it is served; if the landlord does not apply for it within 30 days of judgment, or it is not executed within 30 days of issuance, the landlord must apply to the court with seven days' written notice to the tenant. A court may stay a warrant for up to seven days for an orderly move. A levy on belongings inside a home may be made only between 6:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m.

title: Eviction Records Kept From Public Access
bodyText: New Jersey court records of a landlord-tenant case are not public if the case ended without a judgment for possession, or if the judgment for possession was entered seven or more years ago. Eviction records for nonpayment during the COVID-19 emergency period are also shielded and may not be used in screening. No statute gives a landlord a right to object.

title: Electronic Notices
bodyText: New Jersey's electronic-transactions law applies only when both sides have agreed to do business electronically, and either side may later refuse further electronic dealings. It does not cover notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a lease of someone's home, so those must go by the methods the eviction statutes require (personal delivery, leaving a copy at the home with a family member over 14, or certified mail, with regular mail if certified mail is not claimed). An electronic record the sender stops the tenant from printing or saving cannot be enforced against the tenant.

title: Plain Language Rules for New Jersey Leases
bodyText: New Jersey's plain-language law applies to residential leases: a lease must be written in a simple, clear, understandable and easily readable way, judged as a whole. Courts and the Attorney General look at guidelines such as confusing cross-references, needlessly long sentences, double negatives and exceptions to exceptions, and illogical order, and whether sections are logically divided and captioned, a lease over 3,000 words has a table of contents or index, and conditions and exceptions get the same prominence as the main promise in at least 10-point type. Technical terms alone are not a violation, and wording a law or agency requires or approves is protected. A landlord who violates the law owes the tenant actual damages if the tenant was substantially confused, plus up to $50 and attorney's fees up to $2,500, but not if both sides performed, the landlord tried in good faith to comply, the contract follows an Attorney General opinion, or the tenant supplied the wording. The Attorney General will certify a form on request for a fee of up to $50.

title: Consumer Fraud Act and Leases
bodyText: New Jersey's Consumer Fraud Act makes it unlawful to use any unconscionable commercial practice, deception, fraud, misrepresentation, or knowing omission of a material fact in connection with the sale or advertisement of merchandise or real estate, and the Act defines a sale to include a rental. It is also unlawful to ask a consumer to sign a document evidencing a transaction without giving a full and accurate copy at the same time, so give each tenant a complete copy of the signed lease when they sign. A person who loses money or property because of an unlawful practice recovers three times the damages plus attorney's fees and costs. The Act lists no rule about blank spaces in a lease.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: If a New Jersey tenant, occupant or guest causes damage, the statutory protections tied to damage do not help the tenant: rent stops after a fire only if the damage happened without the tenant's fault, the lease ends on total destruction only if it happened without the tenant's fault, and a rent-into-court case fails if the condition was caused maliciously or by abnormal or unusual use by the petitioning tenant or family. Willful or grossly negligent damage is a cause for removal on three days' notice, with no notice to cease first. You may apply the security deposit to damage after the tenancy ends, never while the tenant stays, and you may sue for the cost of repair. Lost rent after the tenancy ends is recoverable as damages, subject to your duty to try to re-rent.

Each provision checked separately for its own fault exception: casualty abatement N.J.S.A. 46:8-6 ("without the fault of the lessee"), total destruction 46:8-7 (same), rent into court 2A:42-91(b) (narrower: "maliciously or by abnormal or unusual use"; mere negligence is not a defense), removal ground 2A:18-61.1(c) with 2A:18-61.2(a) notice. Deposit: 46:8-21.1 (no deduction in possession; edu-security-deposit-rules-nj). Essential-services withholding and constructive eviction rest on case law (Marini v. Ireland), not read; damages and mitigation (Sommer v. Kridel) also case law, not read. Optional clause offered: tenant-caused-damage-nj. title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, and Tenant's tenancy ends because of the damage, then Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term (for a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, up to the earliest date Tenant could have ended the tenancy by notice), less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage, and it does not limit any proceeding New Jersey law allows Tenant to bring to deposit Rent with a court.
notes: NJ: Retro check 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.12), rule 54t. OPTIONAL clause (not a default), state version of tenant-caused-damage-tn (read; TN row not tagged), following tenant-caused-damage-sc: only TN part (2) is used. Part (1) (no abatement while the lease continues) is left out because N.J.S.A. 46:8-6 already denies abatement where the tenant is at fault, and a broad no-abatement promise could be read to waive the rent-into-court remedy, whose tenant-fault defense covers only malicious or abnormal use (2A:42-91(b)); waiver of that remedy is barred (edu-truth-in-renting-lease-provisions-nj). Lawful stipulation: 46:8-6 and 46:8-7 yield to the lease, and the clause only restates damages for the tenant's own fault, with mitigation (Sommer v. Kridel, case law, not read). Periodic-tenancy measure (rule 37). Gap it fills: lost rent after the tenancy ends, which otherwise rests on case law. Rule 47: no clearly established right is limited. title: Fees Treated as Rent
bodyText: In New Jersey, late fees, attorney's fees and other charges count as rent in an eviction for nonpayment only if the lease expressly says so, and never for Section 8 or public-housing tenants. This library's lease does not call any fee rent, so an unpaid fee cannot support an eviction for nonpayment; collect it another way. In a default judgment for possession, the landlord must swear, and a landlord's attorney must certify, that every charge claimed as rent other than base rent may be charged as rent under the lease and the law.

title: Algorithmic Rent-Setting Ban
bodyText: From July 1, 2027, New Jersey's FAIR Act makes it a violation of the state antitrust law for a rental property owner, or its agent, to pay for or use the services of a "coordinator": software or a device that sets or recommends rents, material lease terms or occupancy levels using competitively sensitive, nonpublic information from two or more owners, or that recommends the same pricing to competing owners. Tacit or express price coordination between owners is also barred. Publicly available free rent estimates, research that is not used to set rents, equal-access brokerage listing databases and government affordability controls are excluded, as are spreadsheets without artificial intelligence that need human analysis.

bodyText: New Jersey prescribes the exact wording or form of several lease items: the Department of Community Affairs Flood Risk Notice, the renter's flood-insurance sentence every lease must contain, the window-guard notice for buildings of three or more units, the Truth in Renting statement, the condominium or cooperative conversion statement, the bold tenant attorney-fee sentence, and the foreclosure notice to tenants. title: Cannabis in Rentals
bodyText: Adult cannabis use is legal in New Jersey, but a landlord may still limit it. The owner of a building with three or more units may prohibit or regulate smoking, vaping or aerosolizing cannabis there; the owner of other property may prohibit or regulate eating or otherwise consuming cannabis on the property, but that power is not given for multi-unit buildings. A landlord may not refuse to rent to someone, or penalize a tenant, because cannabis metabolites are found in the person's body from lawful use, unless that would break a federal contract or cost federal funding. The cannabis law does not change landlord-tenant law otherwise.

title: Use of Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant shall pay Landlord a security deposit of {{security_deposit}} (Security Deposit) prior to occupancy. Landlord may use the Security Deposit only to: (1) reimburse Landlord for actual damages to the property or any ancillary facility that are not the result of ordinary wear and tear; (2) pay Rent in arrears under this Lease, and Rent due because Tenant ends this Lease before the end of the Term; (3) reimburse Landlord for utility or sewer charges that are Tenant's obligation under this Lease, that Landlord paid and that Tenant did not pay; and (4) pay the Rent for the last payment period, but only if Landlord and Tenant have agreed in writing that the Security Deposit will serve as the last payment of Rent due. Unless Landlord has so agreed in writing, Tenant may not apply the Security Deposit to Rent. Landlord will not apply the Security Deposit to ordinary wear and tear or to any damage or defective condition that existed before the tenancy. The Security Deposit does not limit Landlord's right to recover other damages to which Landlord is entitled.
notes: IN: Overrides security-deposit-use, whose 'remedy a Tenant default under this Lease' is broader than Indiana's closed list: a security deposit 'may be used only for' (1) actual damages to the rental unit or any ancillary facility not the result of ordinary wear and tear, (2) all rent in arrearage and rent due for premature termination by the tenant, (3) the last payment period if a written agreement stipulates that the deposit will serve as the last payment of rent, and (4) unpaid utility or sewer charges that are the tenant's obligation and that the landlord paid (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-13). 'Unless otherwise agreed, a tenant is not entitled to apply a security deposit to rent' (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-12(a)); rule 50: the default here is no application, and item (4) lets the landlord agree in writing. The base row's cleaning sentence is dropped: whether cleaning cost is 'actual damages' under Ind. Code § 32-31-3-13(1) is case law, not read. 'Security deposit' includes prepaid rent beyond the first full rental period, a sum above the average rent, and any other amount returnable on the unit's return in the required condition (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-9(b)), so a refundable pet deposit is part of it (pet-policy-in). No cap and no interest or holding rule (whole read of Ind. Code ch. 32-31-3; IN batteries 40, 76); local deposit regulation is preempted (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-20(c)(2)). A landlord may accept but not require a lien on the tenant's motor vehicle as security (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-13.5); not offered. Waiver of the chapter is void (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-17). See edu-security-deposit-rules-in. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: Not more than 45 days after Tenant's occupancy of the property ends, Landlord will return the Security Deposit to Tenant, less any amounts applied as this Lease and Indiana law allow, with a written itemized list of the amounts applied. For each item of damage claimed, the list will state the estimated cost of repair. Landlord will mail the list, with a check or money order for the balance, to the mailing address Tenant gives Landlord in writing. Tenant will give Landlord that mailing address in writing when Tenant moves out.
notes: IN: Ind. Code § 32-31-3-12(a): on termination the landlord returns the deposit minus accrued rent, damages from the tenant's noncompliance and unpaid utility or sewer charges, all itemized in a written notice delivered not more than 45 days after termination of the rental agreement and delivery of possession; the landlord is not liable under the chapter until the tenant supplies a mailing address in writing. Ind. Code § 32-31-3-14: not more than 45 days after the termination of occupancy, the landlord mails an itemized list of damages with the estimated cost of repair for each damaged item, with a check or money order for the balance. Failure to give the list is agreement that no damages are due, and the full deposit must be remitted at once (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-15); the landlord is liable for the amount withheld plus reasonable attorney's fees and costs (Ind. Code §§ 32-31-3-12(b), 32-31-3-16). The two sections count the 45 days from different events (Ind. Code § 32-31-3-14: termination of occupancy; Ind. Code § 32-31-3-12(a): termination of the rental agreement and delivery of possession); the clause runs from the end of occupancy, which is never later than either, so a landlord who follows it meets both (IN log §10). A protected individual who ends the lease under Ind. Code § 32-31-9-12 is entitled to deposits as if the tenancy expired (Ind. title: Returned Payments
bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes is returned or fails because of insufficient funds, a closed or nonexistent account, a stop-payment order or any other reason, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of [amount; for a check, draft, order or similar instrument that is dishonored or returned unpaid, Indiana law limits the charge to $20 plus the amount Landlord's bank actually charges for the returned item], and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. If more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term are returned or fail, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent to be made by cashier's check, certified check or money order.
notes: IN: Overrides returned-payments, whose 'not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' states only a ceiling (rule 53). Ind. Code § 26-1-3.1-502.5(a): a person to whom a check, draft, order or like instrument is tendered may, if it is dishonored or returned unpaid for any reason, charge the maker or drawer 'an amount not to exceed twenty dollars ($20) plus an amount equal to the actual charge by the depository institution for each returned or dishonored instrument'; the charge is not interest or a finance charge. Whether a failed electronic (ACH) payment is a 'like instrument' is not settled by the text. Separate statutory remedies are in Ind. Code ch. 26-2-7: 18% interest and collection costs (Ind. Code § 26-2-7-5), and, after certified-mail notice and 30 days, three times the face amount if $250 or less or the face amount plus $500 (Ind. Code § 26-2-7-6(b)) (edu-dishonored-check-remedies-in). title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord: [list approved pets, or state that no pets are permitted]. Tenant will pay a pet deposit of {{pet_deposit}}, if applicable. Under Indiana law a refundable pet deposit is part of the Security Deposit, so Landlord will hold, use and return it under this Lease's Security Deposit terms. Tenant will pay pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month, if applicable. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor and disturbance caused by a pet, and will reimburse Landlord for claims caused by Tenant's pet, except to the extent a claim arises from the negligence of Landlord or Landlord's agents or employees. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern, and Tenant will then remove the pet within [number] days after Landlord's written notice; failure to do so is a default under this Lease. Landlord may enter the property in connection with a pet only as this Lease's Access & Entry terms permit, or without notice in an emergency, and will not seize, remove or dispose of a pet without a court order. This Section does not limit animal control or law enforcement acting under their own authority. This Section does not apply to a service animal or assistance animal.
notes: IN: Overrides pet-policy, whose term letting the landlord 'enter the property and remove a pet, without liability to Tenant to the extent applicable law permits' conflicts with Ind. Code § 32-31-5-5(a): except as provided in Ind. Code § 16-41-27-29 (mobile home community liens), Ind. Code ch. 32-31-3 or Ind. Code § 32-31-5-1(c)). The self-limiting phrase would hide that conflict (rule 53). Pet deposit: 'security deposit' includes 'any other amount of money or property returnable to the tenant on condition of return of the rental unit' in the required condition (Ind. title: Handling of Property Left Behind
bodyText: When this Lease ends or Tenant gives up possession, Tenant will remove all of Tenant's personal property from the property. (1) If Tenant has vacated the property and a reasonable person would conclude that Tenant has surrendered possession of personal property left there, that property is considered abandoned, and Landlord may remove, store or dispose of it and is not liable for its loss or damage. [Optional: Before disposing of abandoned property that appears to have value, Landlord will mail Tenant a notice at Tenant's forwarding address (or, if none, the property address) and hold the property for [number] days.] (2) If a court awards Landlord possession of the property, Landlord may ask the court for an order allowing removal of Tenant's personal property; property Tenant does not remove by the date in the order may be removed and delivered to a warehouse or a storage facility approved by the court, after the order and the warehouse's or facility's name and location are personally served on Tenant. Medically necessary items, items Tenant uses for a trade or business, and a week's supply of seasonal clothing, blankets and items needed for the care and schooling of a minor child will be released to Tenant without payment; other property may be sold if not claimed within 45 days after Tenant receives notice. (3) While Tenant remains in possession, Landlord will not take, remove, deny Tenant access to or dispose of Tenant's personal property to enforce Tenant's obligations, change or add locks to exclude Tenant, or interrupt essential utilities to force Tenant out, except as this Section or a court order permits. This Section does not apply to motor vehicles, which are handled under Indiana vehicle law.
notes: IN: Part (1) follows Ind. Code § 32-31-4-2(a)-(b): a landlord has no liability for loss or damage to a tenant's personal property if it has been abandoned, and property is abandoned 'if a reasonable person would conclude that the tenant has vacated the premises and has surrendered possession of the personal property'; a rental agreement 'may not define abandonment differently' (Ind. Code § 32-31-4-2(c)), so the clause uses the statutory test word for word and adds only an optional courtesy notice. A dwelling unit is abandoned for the lockout rule if the tenants failed to pay or offer rent and a reasonable person would conclude they surrendered possession (Ind. Code § 32-31-5-6(b)). Whether the statute authorizes disposal, as distinct from relieving liability, is not stated; case law not read. Part (2): Ind. Code §§ 32-31-4-2(d)-(e), 32-31-4-3 (personal service of the removal order and the warehouse identity; exempt property released free; waiver void), 32-31-4-1 (exempt property), 32-31-4-4 (warehouse lien), 32-31-4-5 (sale after 45 days, cut from 90 by P.L. 154-2025, effective July 1, 2025; IN log §1.2). Part (3): Ind. Code §§ 32-31-5-5, 32-31-5-6(c). A tenant's representative on death or incapacity has the tenant's Ind. Code ch. 32-31-4 rights (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-23(h)). Vehicles: Ind. Code §§ 9-22-1-15, 9-22-1-16 (edu-towing-in). Real-lease lead: the CRM lease defines abandonment by its own terms and lets the landlord remove property 'left on the street'; Ind. Code § 32-31-4-2(c) bars the first (IN log §15). See edu-post-eviction-property-in. Rule 15: written section-open. bodyText: Management and notices. The person residing in Indiana who is authorized to manage the property is: [name and address]. The duty binds successor landlords, owners and managers (Ind. title: Smoke Detectors
bodyText: [Tenant to complete when Landlord delivers the property:] Tenant acknowledges that the property is equipped with a functional smoke detector. Tenant's initials: ______ Date: ______. During the tenancy, Tenant will ensure that each smoke detector installed in the property remains functional and is not disabled, will test each smoke detector at least once every six months, and will replace the batteries in any battery-operated smoke detector as necessary. Tenant will give Landlord written notice if a smoke detector needs to be repaired or replaced, including a hard-wired smoke detector Tenant believes is not functional (for a hard-wired detector Tenant may send the notice by certified mail, return receipt requested), and Landlord will repair or replace it within seven days after receiving the notice. Tenant will not tamper with or remove a smoke detector except when necessary for maintenance.
notes: IN: Ind. Code § 32-31-5-7(a): 'At the time a landlord delivers a rental unit to a tenant, the landlord shall require the tenant to acknowledge in writing that the rental unit is equipped with a functional smoke detector.' Ind. Code § 32-31-5-7(b): the smoke-detector requirements of Ind. Code § 22-11-18-3.5 cannot be waived in a rental agreement or separate writing. Tenant duties: keep each detector functional and not disabled, replace batteries, and give notice under Ind. Code § 22-11-18-3.5(e)(2) for a hard-wired unit believed not functional (Ind. Code § 32-31-7-5(6)); detectors must be tested by the occupant at least every six months (Ind. Code § 22-11-18-3.5(d)(3)); no tampering or removal except for maintenance (Ind. Code § 22-11-18-3.5(f)). Owner duties: install, and repair or replace within seven working days after written notice (Ind. Code § 22-11-18-3.5(e)). A landlord commits a Class B infraction (Class A for a repeat) for a violation at delivery or for failing to fix a hard-wired detector within seven days after certified-mail notice (Ind. Code § 22-11-18-5.5); others commit a Class D infraction (Ind. Code § 22-11-18-5(c)). The clause promises repair within seven days, the shorter of the seven working days in Ind. Code § 22-11-18-3.5(e)(2) and the seven days that trigger the infraction in Ind. Code § 22-11-18-5.5(2). Ind. Code § 22-11-18-2(b) exempts a totally sprinkled building from Ind. Code ch. 22-11-18, but Ind. Code § 32-31-5-7(a) has no such exception, so the acknowledgment stays REQUIRED. The acknowledgment is owed at delivery, so the bracket tells the builder to collect it then (IN log §4). Restating the tenant's statutory duties serves the landlord; the acknowledgment is the required text (rule 55). Real-lease lead: the CRM lease has the acknowledgment (IN log §15). See edu-alarm-duties-in. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Ending a Month-to-Month Tenancy
bodyText: If this Lease continues as a month-to-month tenancy, either Landlord or Tenant may end it by giving the other written notice at least one month before the end of a monthly rental period, and the tenancy will end at the end of that rental period. Rent remains payable through the date the tenancy ends. This Section does not limit either party's right to end this Lease earlier where this Lease or Indiana law allows it.
notes: IN: Ind. Code § 32-31-1-4: for a tenancy of not more than three months that extends from one period to another by express or implied agreement, 'Notice to the tenant equal to the interval between the periods is sufficient' to end it; a general tenancy by the landlord's express or constructive consent is month to month (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-2). The statute speaks only of notice to the tenant and sets no form; the clause makes the notice written and mutual and ends it at a period boundary, which is at least the statutory interval. Other tenancy types (rule 37): a tenancy at will ends on one month's written notice delivered to the tenant and cannot arise without an express contract (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-1); a week-to-week tenancy ends on a week's notice under Ind. Code § 32-31-1-4; a year-to-year tenancy ends on notice not less than three months before the end of the year (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-3; form in Ind. Code § 32-31-1-5); a fixed term ends without notice (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-8(1)-(2)). Service: Ind. Code § 32-31-1-9. See edu-notice-to-quit-in. Holdover with accepted rent becomes month to month under holdover-ca. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Holdover Charge
bodyText: If Tenant remains in possession after the end of the Term, and Landlord has not agreed in writing to a continued tenancy or accepted Rent for one under the Holdover section of this Lease, then, in place of the actual damages and reasonable rental value described in that section, Tenant will pay Landlord a holdover charge of {{holdover_daily_rate}} for each day Tenant remains in possession. Landlord and Tenant agree that Landlord's loss from a holdover, including delay in making the property available to a new tenant, is difficult to estimate accurately in advance, that this charge is a reasonable estimate of that loss, and that it is not a penalty. Landlord's acceptance of a holdover charge is not acceptance of Rent for a continued tenancy. This Section does not limit Landlord's right to recover possession, unpaid Rent and other amounts due for the period before the Term ended, or damages for harm to the property.
notes: IN: Optional clause (rule 54; standing GA decision: offer an opt-in holdover rate where no statutory measure exists). No Indiana holdover statute or double-rent measure (IN battery 34: 19 sections, none a residential holdover rule; known-positive test passed); a general tenancy by the landlord's consent is month to month (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-2), and notice is not required to terminate the lease of a tenant at sufferance (Ind. Code § 32-31-1-8(4)); whether a tenant holding over without consent is one is case law, not read. Text is holdover-rate-ga's, an add-on to holdover-ca (tagged IN). Whether a given rate is liquidated damages or a penalty is Indiana case law, not read; the agreed-estimate sentence is common drafting, not a safe harbour. Whether accepting money after the Term creates a month-to-month tenancy despite the acceptance sentence is also case law, not read. title: Fire or Casualty
bodyText: If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire, storm or other casualty not caused by Tenant, members of Tenant's household or Tenant's guests, and the damage makes the property unfit to live in or substantially impairs Tenant's use of it, either Landlord or Tenant may end this Lease by written notice to the other, effective on the date Tenant moves out. Rent will be prorated to that date, any prepaid Rent refunded, and the Security Deposit returned as this Lease and Indiana law provide. If the casualty makes only part of the property unusable and Tenant stays in possession, Rent will be reduced in proportion to the part of the property Tenant cannot use until Landlord completes repairs. This Section does not limit any other right Tenant has under Indiana law.
notes: IN: Optional clause (rule 54; standing GA decision: offer landlord casualty termination where no statute controls it). No Indiana statute addresses fire or casualty damage to leased residential premises, rent abatement or termination (IN battery 121: 41 sections, none a residential casualty rule; known-positive passed; whole read of Ind. Code art. 32-31). The landlord's duties to deliver and keep the premises habitable and to maintain systems cannot be waived (Ind. Code §§ 32-31-8-4, 32-31-8-5), and the clause does not waive them. Common-law rules on casualty are case law, not read. Same structure as casualty-termination-mo without a statutory release sentence (edu-casualty-in). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage.
notes: IN: Optional clause (rule 54, tenant-caused damage). Model: tenant-caused-damage-tn. title: No Criminal Activity
bodyText: Tenant, members of Tenant's household and Tenant's guests will not commit a crime on or near the property that affects the health or safety of another tenant, Landlord or Landlord's agents, and will not allow the illegal possession, manufacture, sale or distribution of a controlled substance on the property. A breach of this Section is a material breach of this Lease, for which Landlord may end this Lease and seek possession, including by a petition for an emergency possessory order where Indiana law allows, without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure. This Section controls over any other provision of this Lease that would require notice and an opportunity to cure. This Section does not apply to criminal activity of which Tenant or a member of Tenant's household is the victim.

title: Tenant's Representative on Death or Incapacity
bodyText: If Tenant is the sole occupant of the property and dies, or Landlord believes that Tenant is incapacitated and absent from the property, Landlord will notify Tenant's representative, give the representative access to the property at a reasonable time to remove Tenant's personal property, may require the representative to prepare and sign an inventory of the property removed, and will pay the representative the Security Deposit and unearned Rent to which Tenant would otherwise be entitled. Tenant designates the following person as Tenant's representative: [name, address and telephone number]. The representative accepts the appointment by giving Landlord written notice. A person Tenant later designates in a separate written document delivered to Landlord takes priority over this designation. Tenant will tell Landlord in writing if this information changes.
notes: IN: Optional clause (rule 54). Ind. Code § 32-31-1-23 (P.L. 184-2021): if the landlord knows of the death of a tenant who was the sole occupant under a lease, or believes a sole-occupant tenant is incapacitated and absent, the landlord shall notify a tenant's representative, give access at a reasonable time to remove personal property, may require a signed inventory, and shall pay the security deposit and unearned rent due under Ind. Code § 32-31-3-12 ((a), (b)). Representatives in decreasing priority: (1) a person designated by the tenant in a written document delivered to the landlord; (2) 'A person designated, in writing, by the tenant in a written lease between the tenant and the landlord'; then an attorney in fact, guardian, heir, or a probate-court appointee ((c)); the representative accepts by written notice to the landlord ((d)). A complying landlord is not liable to the tenant, the estate or other claimants; a willful violation makes it liable for actual damages ((f), (g)). The representative also has the tenant's Ind. Code ch. 32-31-4 rights ((h)). A named representative is what lets the landlord comply quickly and earn the immunity, so the clause serves the landlord; it states that a separate later designation outranks it, matching (c)(1)-(2). The statute does not end the lease on death; whether it ends is case law, not read (edu-tenant-death-in). Same topic as emergency-contact-va and deceased-tenant-contact-tx. title: Mid-Term Rent Increase
bodyText: During the Term, Landlord may increase Monthly Rent to the rent charged for comparable market rentals by giving Tenant at least 30 days' written notice stating the new Monthly Rent and the date it takes effect. bodyText: Indiana limits local rental programs. A penalty for a code violation requires notice and a stated reasonable time to cure first. title: Rent Increases
bodyText: Indiana has no statute aimed specifically at rent increases. In a fixed-term lease the rent is set for the term unless the lease provides for a change (see the optional Mid-Term Rent Increase clause). A change to a rental agreement needs at least 30 days' written notice unless the written lease sets a different procedure. In a month-to-month tenancy, a landlord who wants more rent can also end the tenancy on notice equal to the rental period and offer a new one. Raising rent in response to a tenant's protected activity is retaliation, except an increase to comparable market rent at the end of the term, or during it if the lease provides for that.

title: Mid-Term Rent Increases
bodyText: An Indiana fixed-term lease can allow rent increases during the term, but only if the lease says so. Without the optional Mid-Term Rent Increase clause, the rent stays fixed until the term ends. If you include it: (1) Retaliation: you may not raise rent because a tenant did something the statute protects, such as complaining to a code-enforcement agency, complaining to you in writing about repairs, a lockout or entry, or joining a tenant organization; but raising rent to what comparable market rentals charge is not retaliation, and an increase during the term is covered only when the lease provides for it. An increase above comparable market rent loses that protection, which is why the clause ties the new rent to market rent instead of a number. (2) Notice: Indiana requires at least 30 days' written notice before changing a rental agreement, unless the written agreement sets something different; the clause uses 30 days. (3) Tenant's choice: the tenant may end the lease instead of paying the increase. That exit keeps the clause from locking the tenant into the term at a price you set alone. (4) Leasing impact: tenants usually expect a fixed rent for a fixed term, so a mid-term increase clause may affect how readily applicants sign.

Indiana case law on clauses that let one side change the rent was not read; neither was case law applying the consumer-protection unconscionability standard (Ind. Code § 24-5-0.5-10(b)) to leases. title: Retaliation
bodyText: Indiana bars a landlord from retaliating because a tenant complained to a code-enforcement agency about a violation materially affecting health or safety, complained to the landlord in writing about a lockout, utility shutoff or improper entry or about the landlord's repair duties, sued under the emergency-possession or landlord-duty laws, organized or joined a tenant organization, or testified against the landlord. Retaliation means raising rent, cutting or interfering with services, or bringing or threatening a possession, eviction or early-termination action. You may still decline to renew at the end of the term, raise rent to comparable market rent at the end of the term (or during it if the lease provides for it), cut services for all tenants equally, and bring a possession action where the problem was caused by the tenant or the tenant's household or guests, rent is unpaid after the cure time, code compliance requires work that displaces the tenant, the tenant's breach materially affects health or safety, the tenant holds over after a fixed term, the action was begun in good faith before the protected activity, or you in good faith want the unit back at the end of the term to live in, to renovate in a way that displaces the household, or to take off the rental market for at least six months. The rule cannot be waived.

title: Bad Check Remedies
bodyText: For a dishonored check you may charge the writer up to $20 plus your bank's actual charge. Separately, a writer found liable under other law who stops payment without valid legal cause, or lets a check be dishonored for lack of funds, no account or a missing signature, is also liable for interest at 18% a year from the check date, court costs, attorney's fees (at least $100 if an outside attorney sues) and other collection costs. A writer whose check was dishonored (not stopped) escapes this chapter by paying the full amount within 10 days after you give notice of nonpayment. If the writer has not paid within 30 days after you send written notice by certified mail, the court must award three times the check (if $250 or less) or the check plus $500 (if more). You must choose between this remedy and a claim under another statute the chapter names, which was not reviewed here.

title: Indiana Security Deposit Rules
bodyText: An Indiana security deposit includes prepaid rent beyond the first full rental period and any other amount returnable when the unit is returned in the required condition. You may use it only for actual damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, rent owed (including rent due because the tenant ended the lease early), unpaid utility or sewer charges the tenant owed and you paid, and the last period's rent if agreed in writing. Within 45 days after the tenant's occupancy ends you must mail an itemized list of damages, with the estimated repair cost of each item, and a check or money order for the balance; you are not liable under the deposit law until the tenant gives you a mailing address in writing. If you do not send the list, you are treated as agreeing that no damages are due and must return the whole deposit at once, and the tenant can recover the amount withheld plus attorney's fees and court costs. These rules cannot be waived. Deposit cases may be filed in small claims.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: The owner at the end of the tenancy is bound by Indiana's deposit-return rule. title: Smoke Detectors
bodyText: Every Indiana dwelling must have at least one functional smoke detector outside each sleeping area and on each additional story, including basements, installed as the statute describes; a totally sprinkled building that met building code standards when built is exempt from the smoke detector chapter. The owner, or its manager or rental agent, must install the required detectors and repair or replace one within seven working days after written notice. When you deliver the unit you must get the tenant's written acknowledgment that it has a functional smoke detector, and the occupant must test detectors at least every six months. A landlord who violates the rule at delivery, or does not fix a hard-wired detector within seven days after certified-mail notice, commits a Class B infraction (Class A for a repeat). These requirements cannot be waived, and local codes may be stricter. Indiana has no statute requiring carbon monoxide alarms in rentals.

title: Disability Modifications and Accommodations
bodyText: Indiana's fair housing law requires you to allow reasonable modifications of the premises at the tenant's expense when necessary for a person with a disability to fully enjoy them, and to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices and services. title: Emotional Support Animals
bodyText: Under Indiana's emotional support animal law, if a person's disability is not readily apparent you may require written verification from a health service provider who treats the person (not one who only sells verification letters) that the person has a disability, has a disability-related need for the animal, and is helped by it; a person who moves from another state may provide documentation from a physician, psychiatrist, social worker or other mental health professional licensed there with whom the person has an ongoing treatment relationship. You may evaluate the documents, but may not charge any fee to keep an emotional support animal. You may require the tenant to follow the lease and rules like other residents, pay for damage the animal causes as other pet owners would, and sign an addendum setting out the owner's responsibilities. A landlord who allows an emotional support animal as a reasonable accommodation is not liable for injuries it causes to others, subject to any other federal, state or local law. The law does not apply to dwellings exempt from Indiana's fair housing act.

title: Lead-Safe Work in Older Rentals
bodyText: If you renovate, remodel or maintain target housing built before 1960 that is occupied by someone other than you or your immediate family, and the work disturbs more than 20 square feet of exterior paint, more than 2 square feet in any one room, or more than 10% of the painted surface area, Indiana bans open-flame burning, machine sanding, grinding or abrasive blasting without HEPA exhaust control, heat guns above 1,100 degrees or that char paint, and most dry scraping and dry sanding; bars volatile chemical strippers in unventilated spaces; and requires visible exterior paint chips to be cleaned up within 48 hours. title: Notice for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: In Indiana you may end a lease for unpaid rent on at least 10 days' notice, unless the parties agreed otherwise or the tenant pays the rent in full before the notice period expires. The statute supplies a form notice to vacate within 10 days unless the rent is paid. No notice is needed where the lease expressly requires rent in advance and the tenant does not pay it. A notice may be served on the tenant; if the tenant cannot be found, on a person living at the premises (who must have it explained); and if no one is found, by attaching it to a conspicuous part of the premises. Because of the 'unless the parties agreed otherwise' wording, a lease could shorten or waive the 10-day notice, but the library does not offer that clause: how courts read the phrase has not been reviewed, and the library's lease terms keep a written notice and the statutory cure time. It is lawful, so a landlord who still wants it can add a custom clause, after taking advice.

title: Ending a Tenancy
bodyText: Indiana notice rules depend on the tenancy. A fixed-term lease ends at the end of its term without notice. A month-to-month or other periodic tenancy of three months or less ends on notice equal to the rental period (a week for week-to-week, a month for month-to-month); occupancy by the landlord's consent without other terms is month to month. A tenancy at will ends on one month's written notice and cannot exist without an express contract. A year-to-year tenancy ends on notice at least three months before the end of the year. No notice is needed for a tenant at sufferance or a tenant at will who commits waste. Indiana supplies form notices for year-to-year tenancies and unpaid rent.

title: Eviction Court Process
bodyText: Indiana evictions are court cases. A possession case where the rent due when filed is $10,000 or less may be filed on a small claims docket, and filing there waives your right to a jury; the tenant may request a jury within 10 days after receiving the notice of claim. Attach a copy of a written lease to the claim. Small claims venue between landlord and tenant cannot be changed by contract. An order of possession may not be issued more than 30 days after judgment, and it lasts no more than 30 days. Before final judgment, a court may order possession only after you post a court-approved bond, and the officer may not remove occupants until 48 hours after the order is served. If the case settles before final judgment, you must move to dismiss it unless you are still seeking damages, including keeping the deposit; eviction diversion programs must be voluntary.

title: Emergency Possessory Orders
bodyText: Indiana has a fast court track. A landlord may petition the small claims docket for an emergency possessory order if the tenant has committed or threatens waste, if the tenant or a guest committed a crime affecting the health and safety of another tenant, the landlord or the landlord's agent, or if the tenant gave materially false information to get the lease. The court must hold a hearing within three business days, and a continuance is allowed only on clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would otherwise result. On a crime or false-application finding, the tenant must return possession within 7 days of the hearing. Tenants may use the same track against lockouts and utility shutoffs. The track does not override the rights of a tenant who is a crime victim.

title: Eviction Record Sealing
bodyText: Indiana courts must, on their own, seal the records of an eviction case that is dismissed (including when the landlord settles or stops prosecuting), that ends in the tenant's favor, or whose judgment against the tenant is overturned on appeal. If a judgment was entered against the tenant, the tenant may move to seal the records once any money judgment is paid, or after seven years if there was no money judgment. Sealed records are open only under a court order, to law enforcement, or as the law requires. If you file an eviction and then settle, you must dismiss the case unless you still seek damages, and a case you leave idle for 180 days may be dismissed and sealed.

bodyText: After a court awards you possession, you may ask the court for an order allowing removal of the tenant's property. title: Domestic Violence, Sexual Offense and Stalking Protections
bodyText: Indiana protects a tenant or applicant who is a victim (or alleged victim) of domestic or family violence, a sex offense or stalking and who has a civil protection order or criminal no-contact order. You may not terminate, refuse to renew, refuse to enter into a lease, or retaliate solely because the person or a household member is protected, or because the person ended a lease under this law. A protected tenant may end the lease with written notice at least 30 days before the termination date, with a copy of the order and, for domestic violence or sexual assault, a safety plan from an accredited program, dated within 30 days, recommending relocation. The tenant owes rent prorated to the termination date and no early-termination rent or fees, and owes nothing if the notice comes at least 14 days before the right to occupy begins. Other adult tenants stay bound, and you need not account for the deposit until 45 days after all tenancies end. These rights cannot be waived.

title: When a Tenant Dies or Is Incapacitated
bodyText: If you know that a tenant who was the sole occupant has died, or believe a sole-occupant tenant is incapacitated and absent, Indiana law requires you to notify the tenant's representative, give the representative reasonable access to remove the tenant's belongings, and pay the representative the deposit and unearned rent the tenant would have received; you may require a signed inventory. The representative is, in order of priority, a person the tenant named in a separate written document delivered to you, a person named in the lease, an attorney in fact, a guardian, an heir, or a person the probate court appoints, and accepts by written notice to you. If you comply you are not liable to the tenant, the estate or others; a willful violation makes you liable for actual damages. The statute does not say whether the lease ends.

bodyText: Indiana has no state statute letting a servicemember end a residential lease; the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act governs, and Indiana treats a violation of it as a violation of state law. bodyText: Using a leased house, apartment or building to commit a controlled-substance offense is a nuisance under Indiana law. The prosecutor, a city or county attorney, the Attorney General or the property owner may sue to abate it; anyone other than the owner must give each tenant and the owner 45 days' notice first. title: Indiana Fair Housing Law

The act does not bar discrimination based on a conviction for illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance. Indiana's civil rights law also names ancestry and status as a veteran among protected traits.

title: Eviction Court Rules: Landlord Duties
bodyText: Arizona's Rules of Procedure for Eviction Actions put several duties on a landlord who files an eviction. The complaint must state the specific reason for the eviction and when and how the notice was served, attach the notice, and be verified. A money claim must state the rent, the due dates, how late fees are calculated, the amounts due and any rent concession claimed. A nonpayment complaint must tell the tenant how to reinstate before judgment, and the landlord must serve the lease provisions the eviction relies on and, in a nonpayment case, the last six months of the tenant's charges and payments. A landlord who accepted a partial payment must show the court the partial-payment agreement the tenant signed, or the case is dismissed. The court awards late fees and other periodic fees only if a written lease specifies them, and attorney fees only where a statute or written contract provides for them, never more than the landlord paid or agreed to pay. A property manager may not represent the owner in court unless the manager is a lawyer. After a default judgment the landlord must mail or deliver a copy to the tenant. The landlord has 45 days after a judgment for possession to apply for a writ without explaining the delay. If the landlord later concludes the eviction was not valid, it must promptly move to set the judgment aside. Once a judgment is paid in full, the landlord must file a satisfaction of judgment within 30 days under the court rule (the statutes say 40 days) and serve a copy on the tenant; a landlord who does not answer a tenant's motion to compel satisfaction within 15 days risks having the case sealed.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Arizona has no just-cause eviction rule for houses and apartments. Either party may end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date (10 days' notice for a week-to-week tenancy), with no reason required, and a fixed-term lease ends on its expiration date; no length of tenancy changes this. The limits are situational: a landlord may not raise rent, cut services, or bring or threaten an eviction in retaliation for a tenant's code complaint, repair complaint, or joining or organizing a tenants' union or similar organization (a complaint within the prior six months creates a presumption of retaliation); fair housing law applies; and the domestic-violence statute preserves eviction of a victim for actions unrelated to the violence. Arizona has no condominium-conversion notice for apartments and no rule barring eviction while rent is paid into court. Mobile home parks have their own termination rules.

title: Electronic Notices and Signatures
bodyText: Arizona's Electronic Transactions Act lets an electronic record or signature satisfy a law that requires a writing or a signature, but only between parties who have agreed to do business electronically, and either party may refuse to do a later transaction electronically. A notice the law requires in writing can be sent electronically only in a form the recipient can print and store; a record the sender keeps the recipient from printing or storing cannot be enforced against the recipient. Where a law sets a delivery method, the electronic record must still go by that method: an abandonment notice, for example, must be sent by certified mail and posted. Arizona's landlord-tenant act treats a notice as received when it comes to the tenant's attention or is delivered in hand or mailed by registered or certified mail; email is not one of the listed methods, so an emailed notice rests on proof that it reached the tenant. A lease signed on paper may authorize doing business electronically only through the tenant's separate and express agreement that says which parts will be electronic and how, gives an email address, and promises to report a change. The Act has no special exclusion for eviction, default or cure notices.

title: Tenant-Caused Damage
bodyText: If a tenant, a family member or a guest damages the property, Arizona law makes the tenant responsible. The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or knowingly let anyone else do so, and the landlord may recover all reasonable damages from the breach and all quantifiable damage the tenant caused to the premises, plus court costs and reasonable attorney fees. Where the damage materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning, the landlord may give 14 days' written notice, then do the work and bill it as rent on the next rent due date, or for immediate payment if the lease has ended. The tenant's own repair remedies do not apply to a condition the tenant, a family member or a guest caused: no termination for the landlord's breach, no repair-and-deduct, and no essential-services remedies. The fire and casualty section is different. It lets a tenant leave, or pay reduced rent for the part that can't be used, after damage that substantially impairs enjoyment, and it states no exception for damage the tenant caused; a lease cannot take that right away. Whether rent lost after a tenant leaves under that section counts as damages the landlord can recover is not settled by statute.

title: Fees and Rent
bodyText: Arizona's landlord-tenant act defines rent as the payments made to the landlord in full consideration for the rented premises, so late fees and other charges are not rent unless a statute treats them that way. One does: if a tenant doesn't fix a maintenance problem after the landlord's 14-day notice, the landlord's repair cost can be billed as rent on the next rent due date. The 5-day nonpayment notice covers rent only, but to reinstate before an eviction is filed the tenant must also pay a reasonable late fee set out in a written lease. In an eviction, the court awards late charges only if a written lease specifies them, and other periodic charges (such as extra-person, pet, storage, signage or common-area fees) only if a written lease specifies them and they are collected periodically with rent; anything else must be sued for separately. A partial payment of rent or other charges keeps the landlord's eviction rights only with the tenant's contemporaneous signed agreement.

title: Landlord's Right to Fix a Tenant's Neglect
bodyText: If a tenant's failure to keep up the unit materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacing a damaged item or cleaning, an Arizona landlord may give written notice that describes the problem and asks the tenant to fix it within 14 days, or as promptly as an emergency requires. If the tenant does not, the landlord may enter, have the work done in a workmanlike manner, and bill the actual and reasonable cost, or the fair and reasonable value, as rent on the next rent due date, or for immediate payment if the lease has ended. This is one of the few entries the access statute allows without the tenant's consent. No lease clause is needed for this right.

title: No Statutory Quiet-Enjoyment Covenant
bodyText: Arizona's landlord-tenant act has no express covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession. It protects possession in other ways: a landlord may not lock out a tenant, remove belongings or cut essential services, and owes the greater of two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages for an unlawful ouster; an unlawful or harassing entry costs actual damages of at least one month's rent. Whether a covenant of quiet enjoyment is implied in an Arizona lease is a question of case law, which was not reviewed.
