title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Arizona prescribes few forms for residential landlords. The one lease form is the foreclosure notice: a lease signed after a foreclosure action has started must include a notice substantially in the statute's words, and the same notice goes to existing tenants within five business days after the owner receives a first notice of trustee's sale (not for buildings of four or more connected units). The pool safety notice is a Department of Health Services document, not statutory text. No form is required for eviction notices: courts and agencies may not require a mandatory or technical form, and a notice that meets the statute's content requirements is enough. In court, the eviction summons must include the Arizona Supreme Court's Residential Eviction Information Sheet on a separate page.

bodyText: Arizona statutes do not address tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells. The lease's alteration and installation terms govern. Laws on recording and surveillance were not reviewed.

title: Consumer Fraud Act and Leases
bodyText: Arizona's Consumer Fraud Act makes deception, false promises, misrepresentation and concealment of material facts in the sale or advertisement of merchandise unlawful. Merchandise includes real estate, and a sale expressly includes leases and rentals of real estate subject to a deed restriction imposed in an earlier sale; whether the Act reaches other residential leases depends on case law, which was not reviewed. The Act has no list of specific lease practices such as blanks filled in after signing. Arizona's landlord-tenant act covers those directly by requiring a completed lease and a signed copy. Arizona has no plain-language statute for leases.
notes: AZ: NEW 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.13 retro, rule 51). Controlling text: A.R.S. §44-1521(5), (7); §44-1522(A)-(C); §33-1322(E). title: Holdover Charge
bodyText: [Optional.] If Tenant remains in possession after this Lease ends and Landlord has not consented in writing to a continued tenancy, Tenant will pay Landlord a holdover charge of {{holdover_daily_rate}} for each day Tenant remains in possession, in place of Rent and actual damages for the use of the property during that time. Landlord and Tenant agree that Landlord's loss from a holdover, including delay in making the property available to a new tenant, is difficult to estimate accurately in advance, that this charge is a reasonable estimate of that loss, and that it is not a penalty. Landlord's acceptance of a holdover charge is not consent to a continued tenancy and is not acceptance of Rent. This Section does not limit Landlord's right to recover possession, unpaid Rent and other amounts due for the period before this Lease ended, damages for harm to the property, or any amount Arizona law allows for a holdover that is willful and not in good faith.
notes: AZ: NEW 2026-09-30 (SOP 1.13 retro, rule 54 holdover shape, NE 5; Taylor confirmed the rule-54 approach 2026-09-30). A.R.S. §33-1375(C) sets a measure only for a holdover that is 'willful and not in good faith'; an ordinary holdover leaves the landlord actual damages, so the lease may set a measure for the cases the statute leaves out (§33-1314(A)). Model holdover-rate-ga; variable {{holdover_daily_rate}} reused. Companion holdover-az. title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term, less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 54t / rule 54). Modelled on tenant-caused-damage-tn, which was read, not tagged. OFFERED BECAUSE THE LAW LEAVES THE GAP OPEN: Wyoming has no casualty or untenantability statute at all (Article 12 read in full 2026-09-30; Title 34 ch. 2 index read 2026-09-27 -- no destruction, untenantability or rent-abatement section), so there is no statutory tenant exit or abatement right for this clause to waive, which is what bars the equivalent clause in several other states. Each Wyoming abatement or exit route was checked separately for its own tenant-fault exception and all three already carry one: W.S. 1-21-1203(c) (owner need not correct a condition caused by the renter, the renter's family or guests by inappropriate use or misuse), W.S. 1-21-1206(a) (the renter's repair remedies are available only to a renter in compliance with 1-21-1204 and 1-21-1205), and the library's own casualty-termination-wy, which is a contract term and is already limited to casualty 'through no fault of Tenant'. There is no rent-into-court or repair-escrow statute in Wyoming, so that limb does not arise. CONDITIONAL, offered not defaulted, per rule 54. Companion education row: edu-tenant-caused-damage-wy. title: When Your Tenant Causes the Damage
bodyText: Wyoming law is unusually good to the landlord here, and it works without any lease clause. A renter must not intentionally or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the unit, or knowingly let anyone else do so (W.S. 1-21-1205(a)(i)). If the renter damages the property you may apply the deposit to the damage, and the renter stays liable for whatever the deposit does not cover, plus interest at ten percent a year on the unpaid balance, and you may take any legal action available to recover it (W.S. 1-21-1211(b)). Two defences the tenant would otherwise have are switched off. You are not required to correct any condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, guests or invitees through inappropriate use or misuse (W.S. 1-21-1203(c)). And the renter's repair remedies -- the notice-to-repair ladder, the civil action, the court-ordered termination -- are available only to a renter who is in compliance with the renter-duty and prohibited-act sections (W.S. 1-21-1206(a)), so a renter who caused the damage is generally outside them. What Wyoming does not give you is a rule about rent. There is no casualty or untenantability statute in Wyoming at all, so nothing in the statutes says whether rent keeps running while a unit the tenant wrecked is repaired, or whether you can recover the rent you lose if the lease ends. That is left entirely to the lease, which is why the optional Damage Caused by Tenant clause exists. Without it you are arguing common-law damages and mitigation from scratch.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 54t). Every cited section read section-open 2026-09-30. Companion to the optional clause tenant-caused-damage-wy. The 10% figure in W.S. 1-21-1211(b) is the statute's, already carried as a CONSTRAINED term by unpaid-damages-interest-wy; repeated here as context, not as a second source of truth. title: Utility Deposit Identified Separately
bodyText: Of the amounts Tenant pays Landlord before occupancy, {{utility_deposit}} is held separately as a utility deposit, identified apart from the Security Deposit, and is held to cover utility charges Tenant incurs during this Lease. Landlord will refund it as Wyoming law provides once Tenant shows that all utility charges Tenant incurred have been paid.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, targeted fix 18 with rules 50 and 54). The 2026-09-29 scrub switched off utility-deposit-return-wy and moved its content to edu-utility-deposit-return-wy. Fix 18's question -- did that clause carry a written notice or disclosure a statute requires? -- answers NO: W.S. 1-21-1208(b), read section-open 2026-09-30, imposes refund duties on the owner and requires nothing to appear in the lease, so the switched-off clause only restated a duty the law imposes anyway and is correctly left off. But reading 1-21-1208(b) for that question surfaced a separate point the scrub did not touch: the subsection applies only to 'property or money held and SEPARATELY IDENTIFIED as a utilities deposit'. The separate identification is the trigger for the whole regime, including the landlord-favourable limb that lets the owner apply the deposit to the tenant's outstanding utility debt after 45 days. Nothing in the library identified one, so a Wyoming landlord taking a utility deposit fell outside 1-21-1208(b) and the money was treated as ordinary deposit under 1-21-1208(a). This clause supplies the identification. CONDITIONAL: include only where a utility deposit is actually taken. Note W.S. 1-21-1207 separately requires the rental agreement to state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable, which reaches a utility deposit too -- carried by nonrefundable-deposit-notice-wy. New {{variable}} for the builder backlog: {{utility_deposit}}. title: What You List, You Must Maintain
bodyText: Wyoming turns part of your own lease into a statutory duty. W.S. 1-21-1203(a)(iv) requires an owner to 'maintain other appliances and facilities as specifically contracted in the rental agreement' -- so whatever you list in the lease stops being a courtesy and becomes an obligation under the Residential Rental Property Act, enforceable through the renter's remedy ladder in W.S. 1-21-1206: written notice, then a formal notice to repair, then a civil action in circuit court that can award the renter costs, damages, rent improperly retained, an order to repair, or termination of the lease. List the window air conditioner and you have to keep it running. Two related levers run the other way. The baseline in W.S. 1-21-1202(a) -- operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water -- applies 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties'. And W.S. 1-21-1202(d) lets any duty or obligation in the article be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties. Wyoming is unusually permissive on this; most states make habitability non-waivable. Both are real, and both are blunt instruments: a lease that contracts away heat or hot water is a lease you will have to defend. The practical rule is to list appliances deliberately rather than generously, and to treat any shifting of a core duty as a decision to take advice on, not a form field.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 44 -- terms the statute turns into landlord duties). W.S. 1-21-1202 and 1-21-1203 read section-open 2026-09-30. The rule-44 wording screen found five 'as agreed in the rental agreement' hooks in Article 12: 1-21-1201(a)(i) (agent as owner for notice unless the agreement says otherwise -- already carried by agent-capacity-designation-wy), 1-21-1202(a) (habitability baseline 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing'), 1-21-1202(d) (any duty assignable by explicit signed written agreement -- already carried by edu-habitability-modifiable-wy), 1-21-1203(a)(iv) (appliances and facilities 'as specifically contracted') and 1-21-1204(a)(v) (occupancy above the number 'specified in the rental agreement' -- already carried by permitted-occupants). 1-21-1203(a)(iv) was the one with no row: the shared appliances-included clause, tagged WY among 26 states, silently creates a statutory maintenance duty in Wyoming. RULE 78 POINTER NOTED, NOT FIXED HERE: appliances-included tells the tenant Landlord will maintain the listed items 'as described in this Lease's Maintenance & Repairs Section', but the 2026-09-29 scrub switched off habitability-baseline-wy and did not restore the shared landlord-maintenance clause, so a Wyoming lease has no landlord-repair clause and that pointer resolves to a section containing only tenant duties. The legal outcome is unaffected because 1-21-1203(a)(iv) supplies the duty directly, but the lease reads as promising something it does not contain. appliances-included is shared across 26 states, so under rule 62 this is flagged in the log's propagation section rather than edited. title: Which Notices You Cannot Send by Email
bodyText: Wyoming's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (W.S. 40-21-101 through 40-21-119) is broad: it excludes only wills, codicils and testamentary trusts, most of the Uniform Commercial Code, and the Uniform Computer Information Transactions Act (W.S. 40-21-103(b)). Unlike some states, it carves out nothing for eviction, default or cure notices, and nothing for residential leases. That does not make email safe for the notices that matter, because the landlord-tenant statutes prescribe their own service. The three-day notice to quit that must precede any forcible entry and detainer action is served 'by leaving a written copy with the defendant or at his usual place of abode or business' (W.S. 1-21-1003) -- a physical delivery. The habitability notices under W.S. 1-21-1203(b) and the renter's notice to repair under W.S. 1-21-1206(b) must go by certified mail or in the manner W.S. 1-21-1003 specifies. The abandoned-property notice under W.S. 1-21-1210(a)(i) is deemed served only by certified mail to an address the renter furnished in writing for that purpose, by personal service under Rule 4, or by newspaper publication. UETA itself says a transaction it covers is still subject to other applicable substantive law (W.S. 40-21-103(d)), so these methods control. Two further limits. The act applies only between parties who have each agreed to conduct transactions electronically, judged from the context and the parties' conduct (W.S. 40-21-105(b)). And a party who has agreed may still refuse to conduct other transactions electronically -- a right the statute says in terms 'may not be waived by agreement' (W.S. 40-21-105(c)). A blanket lease clause consenting to electronic notice for everything cannot take that away.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 45 -- the electronic-transactions act read itself, not only the landlord-tenant section that refers to it). W.S. 40-21-103 and 40-21-105 read 2026-09-30 on law.justia.com (current edition); W.S. 1-21-1003, 1-21-1203(b), 1-21-1206(b) and 1-21-1210(a)(i) read section-open the same day on the official wyoleg.gov 2026 text. NO CLAUSE DEFECT FOUND: the shared notices clause is self-limiting ('Where applicable law requires a particular method, form, timing, or content for a notice, that requirement will control over this Section, and nothing in this Lease designates an alternative method of delivery for any notice governed by law'), and electronic-signatures reaches execution of the lease, not notices under it -- and UETA does not exclude leases, so that clause is sound. This row exists because the screen produced a real landlord-facing answer, not because a clause failed. CITATION FLAG (rule 21): W.R.C.P. Rule 4, cited through W.S. 1-21-1210(a)(i)(B), is a court rule, not a code section, and needs separate monitoring.

title: Does Consumer Law Reach Your Lease?
bodyText: Wyoming has no plain-language statute for consumer contracts, so there is no readability test to meet and no required statement of the rights a tenant is giving up. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act (W.S. 40-12-101 and following) is the only general consumer statute in play, and whether it reaches a residential lease is genuinely unsettled on the words. It defines 'merchandise' to include 'any service or any property, tangible or intangible, real, personal or mixed' -- real property is expressly in. But it reaches only a 'consumer transaction', defined as the advertising, offering for sale, sale or distribution of merchandise to an individual for primarily personal, family or household purposes. Renting a home is plainly for household purposes; whether letting it is a 'sale or distribution' is the open question, and the statute does not answer it. No Wyoming case law on the point was reviewed. What the Act does not contain is worth knowing, because other states do have these: there is no provision making it unlawful to leave blank spaces in a contract to be filled in after signing, and none requiring that the consumer be given a copy at signing. The unlawful-practice list in W.S. 40-12-105 runs to misrepresentation, false pricing, bait-and-switch and the like, with a catch-all at (a)(xv) for 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices'. If the Act does reach leases, that catch-all is the realistic exposure -- a lease term or a rental advertisement that misleads -- rather than anything about formatting. Practical reading: draft honestly and fill in every blank before signing, but do not expect a Wyoming consumer-law formatting rule, because there is not one.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 51). W.S. 40-12-102 (definitions) and 40-12-105 (unlawful practices) read 2026-09-30 on law.justia.com, current edition; the definitions were read as rule 51 requires, not only the practice list. Checked for and NOT found: a plain-language consumer-contract statute, an express residential-lease exclusion, a blank-spaces-filled-after-signing practice, and a copy-at-signing practice. The reach question is left open rather than resolved because the text does not resolve it and no case law was read -- stated that way in the body. Overlaps but does not duplicate edu-no-rental-fee-transparency-law-wy, which answers the narrower fee-transparency question from the same section; that row keeps topic_key fee-transparency and this one takes consumer-protection-act. Rule 40 note: no type-size, bold, underline, conspicuousness or placement requirement appears in the WCPA either.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule
bodyText: Wyoming statutes do not regulate the use of algorithmic or software pricing tools to set residential rents. Wyoming regulates rent lightly in general: there is no rent control, no rent-increase notice period and no cap. Federal antitrust law and any city ordinance may still apply.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 27). Verdict: CONFIRMED ABSENT. Basis: Title 1 ch. 21 articles 10, 12 and 13 read in full section-open 2026-09-30 -- Wyoming's entire residential landlord-tenant code -- plus the existing primary-verified absence in edu-no-rent-increase-statute-wy. Search boundary stated per rule 19: this is three articles read whole, not a full-text search of the Wyoming code; the shell could not reach any statute host (organization egress policy, 403) and the official site publishes no loadable bulk text, so no code-wide battery with a nonsense control was possible. Municipal ordinances not checked, per the state-law-only scope.

title: Fees Are Not Rent in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming's Residential Rental Property Act never defines 'rent', and no statute converts a fee into rent. That matters most at the eviction door. A forcible entry and detainer action for nonpayment is available only 'after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due' (W.S. 1-21-1002(a)(i)); unpaid late fees, pet fees or utility charges are not rent, and calling them 'additional rent' in the lease does not make them the thing the statute names. Trying to evict on unpaid fees alone is how a Wyoming nonpayment case gets dismissed. The statutes keep the two apart elsewhere too: a deposit may be applied to 'accrued rent' and separately to 'other costs provided by any contract' (W.S. 1-21-1208(a)), and in an FED judgment the court finds 'the amount of rent due and payable' and adds costs and attorney's fees as the lease provides (W.S. 1-21-1008(b)). You can still collect fees -- sue for them, deduct them from the deposit, or treat them as a lease breach. What you cannot do is run them through the three-day nonpayment route.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 27). Verdict: CONFIRMED ABSENT (no statute makes fees rent), with the affirmative consequence stated. W.S. 1-21-1002(a)(i), 1-21-1008(b) and 1-21-1208(a) read section-open 2026-09-30; Article 12's definition section (1-21-1201(a)) read in full and contains no definition of 'rent'. Consistent with the shared default-by-tenant clause, which already says Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent, does not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate or pursue eviction -- that sentence is correct for Wyoming and this row explains why. title: No Right to Fix It and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Some states let a landlord give notice, do work the tenant should have done, and add the cost to the next rent payment. Wyoming does not. Nothing in the Residential Rental Property Act gives an owner a self-cure right, a notice period for one, or a way to bill the cost as rent. What you do have: the renter owes the statutory duties in W.S. 1-21-1204 and must not commit the prohibited acts in W.S. 1-21-1205, and may not unreasonably refuse you entry to make repairs or inspect (W.S. 1-21-1205(a)(iii)). Breach of either section is a ground for a forcible entry and detainer action in its own right (W.S. 1-21-1002(a)(vi)). If the renter damages the property you may apply the deposit and sue for the rest plus ten percent interest (W.S. 1-21-1211(b)). So the Wyoming route is entry, then damages or possession -- not self-help repair billed forward as rent. A lease clause purporting to make repair costs 'additional rent' would also run into the point that Wyoming's three-day nonpayment eviction reaches rent only.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 27). Verdict: CONFIRMED ABSENT. Basis: Article 12 read in full section-open 2026-09-30, all eleven sections -- no analogue to the URLTA 4.105 / A.R.S. 33-1341(8) self-cure right. Article 10 read in full the same day. title: No Blank-Space or Lease-Copy Rule
bodyText: Wyoming imposes no statutory requirement that a written lease have every blank space completed, and none that the landlord give the tenant a signed copy. Neither failure is a statutory breach the way it is in some states. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act does not list either one among its unlawful practices. Two things still bite. Wyoming recognises oral rental agreements -- the Act's definition of 'rental agreement' covers 'any agreement, written or oral' (W.S. 1-21-1201(a)(ii)) -- so an incomplete written lease does not leave you with no lease; it leaves you arguing about terms. And several Wyoming rights turn on something being in the rental agreement in writing: the nonrefundable-deposit statement (W.S. 1-21-1207), the agent notice opt-out (W.S. 1-21-1201(a)(i)), appliances you must maintain (W.S. 1-21-1203(a)(iv)), the occupancy number (W.S. 1-21-1204(a)(v)) and any reassignment of duties (W.S. 1-21-1202(d)). A blank left in one of those is a right left on the table. Fill in every blank, bracket and placeholder before signing, and give the tenant a copy -- not because a statute says so, but because the statutes that matter all point back at the document.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rules 27 and 51). Verdict: CONFIRMED ABSENT. Basis: Article 12 read in full section-open 2026-09-30; W.S. 40-12-105 (WCPA unlawful practices, all seventeen paragraphs) and 40-12-102 (definitions) read 2026-09-30 and checked specifically for a blank-spaces practice and a copy-at-signing practice -- neither is present. The affirmative half of this row (which Wyoming rights depend on written lease text) comes from sections read section-open the same day. title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: Wyoming's Residential Rental Property Act contains no covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession running from the landlord to the tenant. The Act's only 'peaceful enjoyment' language runs the other way: it is a renter's duty not to 'interfere with another person's peaceful enjoyment of the residential property' (W.S. 1-21-1205(a)(ii)), which protects neighbouring tenants from this one, not this tenant from you. Possession is protected instead by the shape of the eviction process: the three-day notice to quit, the court action, and a sheriff acting on a court order (W.S. 1-21-1003, 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017, 1-21-1211(a)). Wyoming attaches no statutory damages to an unlawful ouster, which is the gap covered separately in the self-help row. Whether a covenant of quiet enjoyment is implied in a Wyoming lease as a matter of common law was not researched and is not answered here.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 27). Verdict: CONFIRMED ABSENT as a statute; case law explicitly NOT LOCATED and the boundary stated in the body per rule 19. Basis: Articles 10, 12 and 13 read in full section-open 2026-09-30. The W.S. 1-21-1205(a)(ii) point -- that Wyoming's only peaceful-enjoyment provision is a tenant duty, not a landlord covenant -- was read directly and is the substantive finding here. Cross-reference: edu-no-self-help-eviction-statute-wy. title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Wyoming prescribes no form for a residential lease, no form for an eviction notice and no agency-issued tenant-rights document that has to be attached to anything. There is no 'substantially in the following form' language anywhere in the residential rental statutes. What the statutes prescribe is content, not form, and in two places only. The abandoned-property notice must describe the property claimed to be abandoned and state that it will be disposed of seven days after service unless the renter acts (W.S. 1-21-1210(a)(i)), and it is deemed served only by certified mail to an address the renter furnished in writing for that purpose, by personal service under Rule 4, or by newspaper publication. The renter's own 'notice to repair or correct condition' has five prescribed contents under W.S. 1-21-1206(b) -- that one is the tenant's to draft, but knowing its required elements tells you whether a notice you received is effective. Outside the landlord-tenant title, the bad-check demand under W.S. 1-1-115(a) has prescribed content too: it must state that the drawer has to pay the value of the check and the collection fee, and state the amount of that fee.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rule 27). Verdict: CONFIRMED ABSENT for forms; PRESENT for three content-prescribed notices, each read section-open 2026-09-30. Rule 19 form-search terms applied to the read text: 'following form', 'substantially as follows', 'as follows:' and 'substantially in the form' -- the only 'as follows' hits are W.S. 1-21-1210(a) ('disposed of as follows') and W.S. 1-21-1206(b) ('This notice shall:'), both introducing content requirements rather than a form. title: Specific Maintenance Duties Assigned to Tenant
bodyText: Landlord and Tenant expressly agree, as an explicit written agreement under Wyoming Statutes section 1-21-1202(d), that responsibility for the following specific items is assigned to Tenant rather than Landlord: {{reassigned_duties}}. For each item listed, Tenant will keep it in good working order, arrange and pay for its routine servicing and its repair, and promptly tell Landlord in writing of any condition affecting it that Tenant cannot correct. This assignment is limited to the items listed. It does not reach, and Landlord remains responsible for, the property's electrical, heating and plumbing systems and its hot and cold running water; the safe and sanitary condition of the property as a whole and its fitness for human habitation; and the common areas. Nothing in this Section assigns to Tenant any duty that applicable law does not permit to be assigned. If Tenant does not maintain an item assigned under this Section, Landlord may, after written notice to Tenant and a reasonable opportunity to correct it, have the work done and recover the reasonable cost from Tenant as a debt under this Lease, which is not Rent.
notes: WY added 2026-09-30, RETRO (SOP 1.15, rules 50 and 54). TAYLOR'S DECISION, 2026-09-30: asked in chat whether to offer this and answered yes; scope as recommended -- named non-core items only, core baseline expressly excluded. W.S. 1-21-1202(d), read section-open 2026-09-30: 'Any duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties.' Wyoming is an outlier in permitting this; most states make habitability non-waivable, which is why this clause exists for WY and must not be inherited by any other state. The signed lease is the explicit written agreement the subsection requires, so no separate document is needed (rule 48 checked: 1-21-1202(d) imposes no separate-document requirement, unlike 1-21-1207). DELIBERATE SCOPE LIMIT: the carve-out tracks W.S. 1-21-1202(a) (operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water) and W.S. 1-21-1203(a)(i)-(iii) (not renting unless reasonably safe, sanitary and fit; common areas; electrical, plumbing, heating, hot and cold water). What remains assignable in practice is the 1-21-1203(a)(iv) category -- 'other appliances and facilities as specifically contracted' -- plus discrete site items such as a well pump, a septic system, a propane tank or an outbuilding, which is the real rural-Wyoming use case. A separate decision was made NOT to offer any clause under 1-21-1202(a)'s 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties', which would let a lease contract away heat or hot water: lawful in Wyoming, declined as a product. UNREAD RISK, LABELLED (rule 76): no Wyoming case law construing 1-21-1202(d) was read, so how far a court would enforce a reassignment against the 1-21-1203(a) owner duties -- which the statute states without an express 'unless agreed' qualifier -- is unknown. The narrow scope and the final savings sentence are the response to that uncertainty, not a resolution of it. CONDITIONAL: include only where the landlord is actually assigning a named item. The cost-recovery sentence is contractual and deliberately says the cost is NOT Rent, keeping it consistent with edu-no-landlord-self-cure-wy (Wyoming gives no statutory fix-and-bill-as-rent right) and edu-fees-as-rent-wy (the three-day nonpayment route reaches rent only). Shares topic_key habitability-modifiable with its education companion edu-habitability-modifiable-wy, per rule 58; no display collision, that row is LANDLORD_EDUCATION. New {{variable}} for the builder backlog: {{reassigned_duties}}. title: The Utilities Waiver -- Legal in Wyoming, and Still a Bad Idea
bodyText: Wyoming lets a lease do something almost no other state allows. The sentence in W.S. 1-21-1202(a) requiring operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water ends with 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties'. Read plainly, a signed lease can remove the requirement itself -- not shift who maintains the water heater, but agree there need not be hot water. Keep that separate from the other flexibility in the same section. W.S. 1-21-1202(d) lets you assign a specific duty to the tenant: the unit still has to have a working well pump, the tenant just looks after it. That one is in the lease library as an optional clause. The (a) waiver removes the amenity from the deal altogether, and it is not offered as a clause -- deliberately. Three reasons to leave it alone. The habitability duty in the first sentence of 1-21-1202(a) -- safe, sanitary, fit for human habitation -- carries no such escape, so a unit with no heat in a Wyoming winter may well fail that duty whatever the lease says, and you would be arguing the point in front of a judge. No Wyoming case law on this sentence was reviewed for this library, so how far a court would let it stretch is unknown. And a tenant's agreement to go without heat is exactly the kind of term that invites an unconscionability argument and reads badly to everyone who later looks at it. If what you actually have is a cabin, you may not need the waiver at all: the same subsection says it 'shall not prevent the rental of seasonal rental units such as summer cabins which are not intended to have such amenities'. A genuinely seasonal property sits outside the utilities requirement by statute. If after all that you still want the term, it is lawful and you can add it as your own custom clause. Put the specific amenity and the reason in writing, keep it off anything that touches safety, and get advice first.
notes: WY added 2026-10-01, RETRO follow-up (SOP 1.15, rules 50 and 54). TAYLOR'S DECISION, 2026-10-01: having declined the clause, he asked whether an education row covered the point, reasoning that a landlord who wants the term after reading it can write their own. It did not -- W.S. 1-21-1202(a)'s waiver appeared only as nine unexplained words inside edu-habitability-baseline-wy (and that row attached them to the wrong sentence; fixed in the same delta). This row is the result and is the better design: the library explains the lawful option without shipping it. W.S. 1-21-1202(a) read section-open. Three sentences, and the distinction matters: (1) safe and sanitary, fit for human habitation -- NO waiver language; (2) operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water -- 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties'; (3) 'Provided, however, this section shall not prevent the rental of seasonal rental units such as summer cabins which are not intended to have such amenities'. The waiver reaches sentence (2) only. NEW topic_key habitability-waiver, no other state has one. Rule 58 weighed: this could have shared habitability-modifiable with edu-habitability-modifiable-wy and duty-reassignment-wy, but waiving a requirement and reassigning a duty are different mechanisms with opposite risk profiles, and conflating them is precisely what went wrong in the baseline row. A separate key also makes the cross-state check ask every other state whether its habitability duty is waivable -- in most the answer is 'no, void', which is worth recording per state. Collapse it at sync if Taylor prefers one key. UNREAD RISK, LABELLED (rule 76): no Wyoming case law construes 1-21-1202(a), and the unconscionability point is doctrinal, not read from a Wyoming decision. Stated in the body as untested rather than as a prediction. Overlaps in passing with edu-contracted-appliances-duty-wy, which mentions the same waiver accurately while explaining a different subject (1-21-1203(a)(iv)); that row is left unchanged. W.S. 1-21-1202 read section-open from the official Wyoming Legislature NXT gateway, 2026 Wyoming Statutes; text confirmed identical in the 2024 and 2026 editions.

title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: When this Lease ends, Tenant must ask for the Security Deposit back by written demand to Landlord, and should include in the demand the address to which the refund should be sent. Landlord may apply the Security Deposit to accrued Rent and to damages Landlord has suffered because Tenant did not comply with this Lease or the Oklahoma Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, as itemized in a written statement that Landlord will deliver to Tenant by mail, return receipt requested, or in person. Within 45 days after the tenancy ends, Tenant has delivered possession of the property and Landlord has received Tenant's written demand, Landlord will return the balance of the Security Deposit, without interest. IMPORTANT: If Tenant does not make a written demand for the Security Deposit within six months after the tenancy ends, the Security Deposit becomes Landlord's property and Tenant's interest in it ends.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 115(B): the deposit may be applied to accrued rent and damages from the tenant's noncompliance with the act and the rental agreement, itemized in a written statement delivered by mail, return receipt requested, to be signed for by any person of statutory service age at the address, or in person; the balance is returned without interest within forty-five (45) days after termination of tenancy, delivery of possession and written demand by the tenant; if the tenant makes no written demand within six (6) months after termination, the deposit reverts to the landlord and the tenant's interest terminates. Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 115(E): a landlord who fails to comply lets the tenant recover the deposit and any prepaid rent. The six-month reversion is the landlord-serving reason for the clause (the statute does not require the warning in the lease; it is stated so the tenant cannot say he was unaware). Rule 37: the 45 days run from termination of the tenancy, which for a periodic tenancy is the date set by the termination notice (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 111). bodyText: [Use if the property has been flooded within the past five years and Landlord knows it.] FLOODING DISCLOSURE: The premises have been flooded within the past five years: [describe what Landlord knows, including when and which areas were affected]. For this disclosure, 'flooded' means general and temporary conditions of partial or complete inundation of normally dry land areas and structures on those areas from the overflow of lakes, ponds, streams, rivers, creeks or other inland waters.

title: Handling of Property Left Behind
bodyText: When this Lease ends or Tenant gives up possession, Tenant will remove all of Tenant's personal property from the property. If Tenant abandons or surrenders possession of the property, or is lawfully removed through eviction proceedings, and leaves household goods, furnishings, fixtures or other personal property behind, Landlord may take possession of it. (1) If, in Landlord's judgment, the property has no ascertainable or apparent value, Landlord may dispose of it without any duty of accounting or liability, and may dispose of perishable property in any manner Landlord considers fit. (2) If, in Landlord's judgment, the property has an ascertainable or apparent value, Landlord will send Tenant a written notice by certified mail to Tenant's last known address stating that property not removed within the time specified in the notice will be deemed abandoned. Property left with Landlord for 30 days or longer is conclusively abandoned, and Landlord may then dispose of it in any manner Landlord deems reasonable and proper without liability to Tenant or anyone else. (3) While Landlord holds the property, Landlord will store it in a place of safekeeping and exercise reasonable care, and is responsible only for loss caused by Landlord's deliberate or negligent act. If Landlord stores it in the property, the storage cost will not exceed the fair rental value of the property; if it is moved to a commercial storage company, the storage cost includes the actual charge for storage and moving it there. If Tenant removes the property within the time allowed, Tenant will pay the storage cost for the time Landlord held it plus all other costs that accrued under this Lease.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 130(A)-(E), followed closely: no-value property may be disposed of without accounting or liability; perishables in any manner; valuable property: written notice by certified mail to the last-known address that property not removed within the time specified will be deemed abandoned, and property left thirty (30) days or longer is conclusively determined to be abandoned; storage in a place of safekeeping with reasonable care, liability only for deliberate or negligent loss; storage in the unit capped at fair rental value; commercial storage includes actual charges; a tenant who removes the property within the time pays storage and accrued costs; compliance shields the landlord, but a deliberate or negligent violation makes the landlord liable for actual damages (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 130(E)). The statute sets no minimum time for the notice beyond the 30-day conclusive rule; the clause does not invent one. The procedure is the act's; Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 103(B) makes a conflicting agreement unenforceable, so the clause mirrors the statute rather than shortening it. Separate procedure for a deceased sole tenant: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 130.1 (tenant-death-contact-ok, edu-tenant-death-ok). Pointed to by surrender-end-of-term-ks-ne ('Handling of Property Left Behind Section'). Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 130 read whole. title: Contact Person if Tenant Dies
bodyText: Tenant names the following person to contact if Tenant dies: [name, address and telephone number]. Tenant will tell Landlord in writing if this information changes. If Tenant dies while Tenant is the sole occupant of the property, Tenant authorizes Landlord to: (1) give this person access to the property at a reasonable time and in the presence of Landlord or Landlord's agent; (2) allow this person to remove any of Tenant's property found at the property, after signing an inventory of the property removed; and (3) refund the Security Deposit, less lawful deductions (including the cost of removing and storing Tenant's property), to this person. Landlord may remove and store all property found in the property. If this person does not remove the property by the thirtieth day after the postmark date of Landlord's written request sent by certified mail, return receipt requested, and no one has contacted Landlord claiming the property before Landlord discards it, Landlord may discard it.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 130.1(A): on the landlord's written request the tenant shall provide the name, address and telephone number of a person to contact on the tenant's death and sign a statement authorizing the landlord to grant that person access at a reasonable time in the landlord's presence, allow removal of the tenant's property, and refund the deposit less lawful deductions to that person; (C): on the death of a sole occupant the landlord may remove and store all property, shall turn it over to the designee or anyone lawfully entitled who asks before it is discarded, shall refund the deposit less lawful deductions including removal and storage costs, the remover signs an inventory, and the landlord may discard the property if the certified-mail request (return receipt requested) goes unanswered by the thirtieth day after the postmark and no one has claimed it; (D): a written lease may set a different procedure; (E): a tenant who knowingly fails to provide the information after a notice of request relieves the landlord of responsibility for the property; (F): a landlord who knowingly violates (C) after being furnished the section is liable to the estate for actual damages. The clause is the Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 130.1(A) statement placed in the lease (rule 54: a right the lease can invoke) and follows the (C) procedure rather than using (D) to vary it. title: Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy
bodyText: If this Lease continues as a month-to-month tenancy, either Landlord or Tenant may end it by giving the other written notice at least 30 days before the date the tenancy is to end, counted from the day the notice is served. If the tenancy is shorter than month-to-month, such as week-to-week, either party may end it by written notice served at least seven days before the date the tenancy is to end. Notices will be served in the way Oklahoma law requires. Rent remains payable through the date the tenancy ends. This Section does not limit either party's right to end this Lease earlier where this Lease or Oklahoma law allows it.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 111(A): month-to-month or at will, written notice at least thirty (30) days before the termination date, the period running from service under subsection E; Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 111(B): less than month-to-month, written notice served at least seven (7) days before; Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 111(C): a definite term expires without notice unless otherwise agreed; Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 111(E): personal service, else delivery to a family member over twelve (12) residing with the tenant, else posting plus certified mail (or the Firm Mailing Book); a landlord who cannot be served personally is served by certified mail to the Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 116 person. Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 110: without a written definite term, a weekly-paying roomer or boarder is week-to-week and every other tenancy month-to-month. The older general rules (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, §§ 4, 5, 9: thirty days, three months for year-to-year, a ten-day floor for posted notices) sit outside the act; the act controls residential tenancies (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 103(A)). Tenancy type (rule 37): monthly 30 days, shorter periods 7 days, fixed term none. Okla. Stat. tit. 41, §§ 110, 111 read whole. Rule 15: written section-open. bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes is returned or fails because of insufficient funds, a closed or nonexistent account, a stop-payment order or any other reason, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of [amount], and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord: [list approved pets, or state that no pets are permitted]. Tenant will pay a pet deposit of {{pet_deposit}}, if applicable. Under Oklahoma law a refundable pet deposit is a deposit like the Security Deposit, so Landlord will hold, apply and return it under this Lease's Security Deposit terms. Tenant will pay pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month, if applicable. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor and disturbance caused by a pet. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern, and Tenant will then remove the pet within [number] days after Landlord's written notice; failure to do so is a default under this Lease. Landlord may enter the property in connection with a pet only as this Lease's Access & Entry terms permit, or without notice in an emergency. This Section does not limit animal control or law enforcement acting under their own authority. This Section does not apply to a service animal or assistance animal.
notes: OK: Base pet-policy not tagged: its indemnity sentence ('will indemnify Landlord from claims arising from Tenant's pet(s)') is a term Okla. title: Fire or Casualty
bodyText: If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty not caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, a member of Tenant's family, Tenant's animal or pet, or another person or animal on the premises with Tenant's consent, and the damage substantially impairs Tenant's use and enjoyment of the property, Landlord may end this Lease by written notice to Tenant, effective on the date stated in the notice or, if earlier, the date Tenant vacates. Rent will be accounted for as of the date of the fire or casualty, and Landlord will return all prepaid and unearned Rent and the Security Deposit as this Lease and Oklahoma law provide. This Section does not limit Tenant's own right under Oklahoma law to vacate and end this Lease, or to vacate the unusable part of the property with a proportionate reduction in Rent, after such a casualty.

title: No Criminal Activity
bodyText: Tenant, members of Tenant's household, Tenant's guests and other persons under Tenant's control will not engage in criminal activity that threatens the health, safety or right of peaceful enjoyment of the premises by other tenants or is a danger to the premises, and will not engage in any drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises. This Section controls over any other provision of this Lease that would require notice and an opportunity to cure. This Section does not apply to domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking of which Tenant or a member of Tenant's household is the victim.

title: Rules and Changes to Rules
bodyText: Tenant will comply with the rules and regulations for the property in effect when this Lease is signed: [attach or describe the rules, or state that there are none]. Landlord may adopt new rules or regulations, or amend existing ones, during the Term by giving Tenant written notice. A rule binds Tenant only if its purpose is to promote the convenience, peace, safety or welfare of the tenants, preserve the property from abusive use, or make a fair distribution of services and facilities; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner; it is explicit enough to tell Tenant what to do or not do; and it is not for the purpose of evading Landlord's obligations. A new or amended rule that works a substantial modification of Tenant's bargain under this Lease binds Tenant only if Tenant consents to it in writing.

title: Oklahoma Security Deposit Rules
bodyText: Any damage or security deposit you require must be kept in an escrow account for the tenant at a federally insured financial institution in Oklahoma; misappropriating it is a crime punishable by up to six months in county jail and a fine of up to twice the amount taken. When the tenancy ends you may apply the deposit to accrued rent and to damages caused by the tenant's noncompliance with the lease or the Landlord and Tenant Act, itemized in a written statement delivered by mail, return receipt requested, or in person. You must return the balance, without interest, within 45 days after the tenancy ends, the tenant delivers possession and the tenant makes a written demand. If the tenant makes no written demand within six months after the tenancy ends, the deposit becomes yours. If you do not follow these rules, or do not return prepaid rent the Act requires you to return, the tenant may recover the deposit and the prepaid rent. Unless the lease allows it, the tenant may not use the deposit as the last month's rent. When you sell or otherwise lose your interest in the property, you must within a reasonable time either transfer the deposits to your successor and tell the tenants in writing who holds them, or return them.

title: Deposits When You Sell

title: No General Retaliation Statute
bodyText: Oklahoma's Landlord and Tenant Act has no general anti-retaliation section like the uniform act's. title: Landlord Duties
bodyText: During the tenancy you must: keep common areas clean, safe and sanitary (except in a single-family residence); make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to keep the unit and premises fit and habitable; keep electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning facilities and appliances you supply (or must supply) in good and safe working order; provide trash receptacles and arrange frequent removal (except in one- or two-family residences or where a government provides it); and supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat (except in a single-family residence or where the unit is independently metered). title: Tenant Remedies for Repairs
bodyText: If you materially fail to comply with the lease or with your repair duties in a way that materially affects health or safety, the tenant may give written notice that the lease will end on a date at least 30 days after you receive it unless you fix the problem within 14 days. If the problem materially affects health and can be fixed for no more than one month's rent, the tenant may give written notice and, if you do not fix it within 14 days (or as promptly as an emergency requires), have the work done in a workmanlike manner and deduct the actual, reasonable cost from rent after giving you an itemized statement. If you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant may, after written notice, end the lease immediately, buy the service and deduct the cost, recover damages for the reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing and pay no rent for the period. If the unit becomes uninhabitable or poses an imminent threat to health and safety and you do not fix it promptly, the tenant may end the lease immediately by written notice. None of these rights arises until the tenant gives you written notice, or if the tenant, a family member, a pet or a person or animal there with the tenant's consent caused the problem. A tenant evicted for rent withheld over a good-faith essential-services claim, who gave you written notice within 10 days after the rent was due, may cure within 72 hours of judgment by paying the judgment, costs and fees.

title: Landlord Entry
bodyText: A tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs or improvements, supply services, or show the unit to buyers, lenders, tenants, workers or contractors. title: Nonpayment of Rent
bodyText: If rent is unpaid when due you may sue for it at any time, or wait out the cure period first. To end the lease for nonpayment, give the tenant written notice demanding payment; if the tenant does not pay within five days after the notice, you may terminate. The notice may be given before or after you file suit, and a demand for past-due rent counts as a demand for possession, so no separate notice to quit is needed. The notice must be served as the Landlord and Tenant Act requires: personally; if the tenant cannot be located, by delivery to a family member over 12 living with the tenant; otherwise by posting it conspicuously on the unit and mailing a copy by certified mail.

Stat. tit. 41, §§ 6, 7: ten days for tenancies of three months or longer, five days for shorter, with payment curing) sit outside the act; for dwelling units the act's five-day rule governs (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 103(A)). Time is counted excluding the first day and including the last, skipping a last-day legal holiday (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 61). title: Other Lease Violations
bodyText: For a breach other than nonpayment, your remedy depends on the breach. If it can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning and the tenant does not fix it within 10 days after written notice (or as promptly as an emergency requires), you may enter, have the work done and bill the reasonable cost as rent due on the next rent date (you may not then terminate for that breach). For a material breach, you may serve written notice that the lease will end on a date at least 15 days after the tenant receives it unless the tenant remedies the breach within 10 days; if the tenant remedies it, the lease continues, but any later breach allows immediate termination on written notice. If the breach causes or threatens imminent and irremediable harm to the premises or any person and is not remedied promptly, you may terminate by immediately filing an eviction. Criminal activity that threatens other tenants' health, safety or peaceful enjoyment or endangers the premises, and drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises, by the tenant, a household member, a guest or another person under the tenant's control, are grounds for immediate termination. Notices are served as the Act requires (personally, to a family member over 12, or by posting plus certified mail).

title: The Eviction Case
bodyText: An eviction (forcible entry and detainer) is filed in district court by an affidavit on a form the Oklahoma Bar Association develops, and for cases on the small claims docket the court clerk prepares the affidavit and summons and assists unrepresented plaintiffs. Claims for rent, damage to the premises and Landlord and Tenant Act claims may be joined, but no others. Cases within the small claims limit go on the small claims docket, and a court may assign any eviction there to decide possession. The summons sets trial not less than five nor more than ten days after it issues and must be served at least three days before trial; if the tenant cannot be served personally or through a resident over 15, it may be served by certified mail, or (for possession only) posted and mailed at least five days before trial. Possession is tried without a jury; a jury may be requested only on the money claims, which are then severed. A reasonable attorney fee goes to the prevailing party. After judgment the writ of execution issues; you, your agent or an officer must give notice that you will return in 48 hours to restore possession, and may ask the sheriff or city police for help. A motion for new trial must be filed within three days and does not stay the writ. The tenant may post a supersedeas bond within two days after judgment (a judge may extend this to seven days); while an appeal is pending the tenant must keep paying current rent into the court clerk's office, and failing to pay is treated as abandoning the appeal.

title: Property Left After an Eviction
bodyText: After a tenant is lawfully removed through an eviction, the Landlord and Tenant Act's abandoned-property procedure applies to belongings left in or around the unit: property with no apparent value may be disposed of; property of apparent value requires written notice by certified mail, and property left 30 days or longer is conclusively abandoned. Store it with reasonable care in the meantime. Executing a writ in the lawful manner does not expose you to an unlawful-entry claim. A person who returns to live on the property without authority after being removed by court process commits a misdemeanor, as does anyone who wrongfully refuses to surrender possession when the writ is served.

title: Tenant Who Stays After the Lease Ends
bodyText: If a tenant stays without your consent after the lease ends or is terminated, you may sue at once for possession and damages. If the holdover is willful and not in good faith, you may also recover up to twice the average monthly rent, prorated daily, for each month or part of a month the tenant stays. If you consent to the tenant staying, a month-to-month tenancy is created unless you agree otherwise. Separately, an older statute makes double rent the measure of damages when a tenant who gave notice of intent to leave fails to give up the premises. If you accept rent after the term ends without any agreement, an older presumption of renewal on the same terms (for up to a year) may be argued; say in the lease what happens instead.

title: Domestic Violence, Sexual Violence and Stalking
bodyText: You may not deny, refuse to renew or terminate a tenancy because an applicant, tenant or household member is a victim or alleged victim of domestic violence, sexual violence or stalking, whether or not there is a current protective order, and you may not deny a tenancy to or retaliate against someone because they previously ended a rental agreement as a victim. A victim may end the lease without penalty by giving you written notice and a protective order within 30 days of the incident, unless you waive that time limit. The lease cannot waive a tenant's right to call the police or other emergency help.

title: Removing Unauthorized Occupants and Squatters
bodyText: Someone who never had a rental agreement with you and whom you never accepted as a tenant is not protected by the Landlord and Tenant Act's termination rules: you may demand that the person leave without filing an eviction, and refusing within a reasonable time is a trespass (fine up to $500). An occupant living with a tenant who breaches the lease must leave on your written request (trespass, fine up to $500 or 30 days in jail). For squatters, an owner or authorized agent may file a verified complaint on the statutory form asking the sheriff for immediate removal, if the property was not open to the public, the occupants were told to leave, they are not current or former tenants, cannot show a lease signed by the owner or government mail at the address in the last 12 months, are not the owner's immediate family, and no litigation is pending. The sheriff serves a notice to vacate and puts the owner in possession. A person wrongfully removed this way can recover actual damages, three times the fair market rent, costs and fees. The squatter law does not override the Landlord and Tenant Act.

title: Tenant Who Abandons During the Lease
bodyText: Every party to a lease must mitigate damages. If a tenant wrongfully abandons during the term, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent. If you re-rent for a term starting before the old lease ends, the old lease ends when the new tenancy starts. If you do not make reasonable efforts, or accept the abandonment as a surrender, the lease is treated as ended by you on the date you learned of the abandonment. If you make reasonable efforts but cannot re-rent at a fair rent, the tenant owes the rent (or the shortfall) for the rest of the term; for a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy the 'term' is one month or one week.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, §§ 105(A), 129(B). Belongings left behind: abandoned-property-ok. Rule 37: periodic term measured as one period (Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 129(B)). title: Fire or Casualty
bodyText: If fire or another casualty substantially impairs the tenant's use of the unit, the tenant may move out and notify you in writing within one week of an intent to end the lease (the lease ends on the date of moving out), or, if the unit can still be partly used, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion. These rights do not apply if the tenant, a family member, a pet or a person or animal there with the tenant's consent caused the damage deliberately or negligently. If the lease ends, return the deposit and all prepaid and unearned rent, accounting as of the date of the casualty. The statute gives you no termination right of your own; the lease can add one.

title: Damage the Tenant Causes
bodyText: The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or let anyone, or any animal, do so. Oklahoma's casualty, repair-and-deduct, essential-service and habitability remedies are each unavailable when the tenant, a family member, a pet or a person or animal there with the tenant's consent caused the condition, so a tenant who causes a fire cannot use the casualty statute to walk away rent-free or reduce the rent. You can recover the repair cost and your other damages, subject to your duty to mitigate. The optional Damage Caused by Tenant clause states in the lease that rent does not abate and that the tenant owes lost rent if the lease ends because of the damage.

title: Tenant Duties
bodyText: Oklahoma law requires the tenant to: keep the part of the premises the tenant uses as safe, clean and sanitary as its condition permits; dispose of garbage and waste safely; keep plumbing fixtures as clean as their condition permits; use electrical, plumbing, heating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances safely; not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or let any person or pet do so; not disturb other tenants' quiet enjoyment or let others do so; follow valid rules; and not engage in threatening criminal activity or drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises, personally or through household members or guests. The tenant must also report defects the tenant has reason to believe you do not know about as soon as practicable, and must promptly tell you about any legal proceeding to recover the property.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: You may ask each tenant in writing for the name, address and phone number of a person to contact if the tenant dies, and for a signed statement authorizing you to let that person in (with you present), let them remove the tenant's belongings and refund the deposit to them. If a sole occupant dies, you may remove and store the belongings; you must hand them over to the designated person, or anyone else lawfully entitled, who asks before they are discarded; refund the deposit less lawful deductions (including removal and storage costs); and have anyone who removes property sign an inventory. You may discard the property if you mailed the designee a certified-mail request, return receipt requested, the property was not removed by the 30th day after the postmark, and no one has claimed it. A lease may set a different procedure. A tenant who knowingly refuses to provide the information after your request relieves you of responsibility for the belongings; a landlord who knowingly violates the procedure after receiving a copy of the statute is liable to the estate for actual damages.
notes: OK: Okla. Stat. tit. 41, § 130.1 (2006 Okla. Sess. Laws ch. 23) read whole. The act does not say whether the lease itself ends at the tenant's death (case law and probate law unread). title: Landlord's Lien on Tenant Property
bodyText: Oklahoma gives a residential landlord a lien on the tenant's property in the unit, in an amount reasonably related to the debt, for proper charges owed and the cost of enforcing the lien, with a right to possession until paid. The lien is secondary to a prior chattel mortgage or conditional seller, and does not reach tools, instruments and books used in a trade, family portraits, clothing, medical and health aids and appliances, bedding, washers, refrigerators, food, cooking and eating utensils, baby beds and baby-care items, among others. It is enforced like any other general lien under the lien statutes. A lease may not create any other lien on the tenant's property.

bodyText: The Oklahoma Residential Landlord and Tenant Act governs rental agreements for dwelling units in Oklahoma, including lots leased for manufactured or mobile homes. title: Oklahoma Fair Housing Law
bodyText: Oklahoma's Discrimination in Housing Act makes it unlawful to refuse to rent, to set different terms, to advertise a preference, or to falsely say a unit is unavailable because of race, color, religion, gender, national origin, age, familial status or disability. 'Familial status' covers a person who is pregnant, lives with a child under 18 as parent, legal custodian or with the parent's written permission, or is getting custody of a child; 'age' protects adults 18 and older. You may not refuse to consider a verified source of income such as public assistance, alimony or court-awarded child support where the refusal is because of one of those protected classes. You must allow reasonable modifications for a person with a disability at that person's expense (the person may be required to provide a surety bond guaranteeing restoration), and make reasonable accommodations in rules and policies. The Act does not protect any other class, and it does not prohibit refusing a person convicted of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance. It does not apply to a single-family house rented by an owner of no more than three such houses without a broker or discriminatory advertising (if the owner was not the most recent resident, only one such sale or rental every 24 months), to rooms or units in a building of up to four families where the owner lives in one of them, to certain religious and private-club housing, or (for familial status) to qualifying housing for older persons. A complaint to the Attorney General may be filed within one year; a court may award actual and punitive damages and attorney fees. Federal fair housing law applies separately and its exemptions differ.

title: Assistance Animals and Service Dogs
bodyText: A person with a disability may ask for a reasonable accommodation to keep an assistance animal (a service animal or an emotional support animal). Unless the disability or the need is readily apparent, you may ask for reliable supporting documentation that verifies the disability under the Fair Housing Act, describes the accommodation needed and shows how it relates to the disability, and you may independently verify it. Documentation that was bought is presumed fraudulent. You are not liable for injuries caused by an assistance animal you allowed as an accommodation. If a tenant got the accommodation by knowingly making a false claim or giving fraudulent documentation, you may use the ordinary lease-breach notice procedure, and in an eviction you may be awarded court costs, fees and up to $1,000 in damages. You may not refuse to rent to a blind, deaf or disabled person because of a properly trained guide, signal or service dog, or charge an extra nonrefundable fee or an unreasonable deposit for one, but the tenant may be liable for damage the dog does.

title: Foreign Ownership and Leasing of Land
bodyText: Oklahoma's Constitution and statutes bar an alien who is not a bona fide resident of Oklahoma from acquiring title to or owning land, and require an affidavit with each recorded deed. Starting November 1, 2026, the statute also says that such a person, a designated foreign terrorist organization, a Specially Designated National, or a foreign government adversary may not lease land in Oklahoma. The ban does not apply to an alien who is or becomes a bona fide resident of Oklahoma. Whether an ordinary residential lease of a home is 'leasing land' under this statute has not been decided in anything read here. Starting July 1, 2027, a foreign principal from a foreign adversary country (including an individual domiciled there who is not a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident) may not rent or otherwise control real property within ten miles of a military base or installation, a military operating area or other critical infrastructure, and conflicting rental agreements are invalid; a landlord who is not such a foreign principal is not required to inquire and has no civil or criminal liability under that section. title: Registered Sex Offenders
bodyText: Two or more people required to register as sex offenders may not live together in the same individual dwelling (a house, an apartment, a room in a boarding house, or a unit in a multi-unit building), unless they are married to each other or are blood relatives; separate units in a properly zoned apartment building are allowed. A person or entity that knowingly leases or owns a structure where registrants are allowed to live together in violation of this rule commits a crime (a misdemeanor, rising to a felony on a third conviction). Renting rooms to registrants as a boarding house or group home is unlawful unless treatment services are provided. A registrant also may not live within 2,000 feet of a school, child care facility, qualifying park or playground or the victim's home, and a registrant whose victim was a minor may not live with a minor child except his or her own child, stepchild or grandchild who was not the victim; those duties fall on the registrant. Oklahoma's fair housing law does not protect people because of a criminal record.

title: Medical Marijuana Patients
bodyText: Oklahoma allows medical marijuana for licensed patients; recreational marijuana is not legal. You may not refuse to lease to, or otherwise penalize, a person solely because he or she is a licensed medical marijuana patient, unless leasing to that person would put you at risk of losing a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law. You may prohibit smoking or vaporizing marijuana on the premises, inside its structures and within ten feet of the entry, but a patient may not be denied other lawful, non-smoked products. A patient or caregiver may grow marijuana only on property he or she owns or with the property owner's written permission, and the plants must not be accessible to the public or visible from the street. Extraction using butane, propane, carbon dioxide or another hazardous material is prohibited in a residential property.

title: Penalties and Fixed Damages in a Lease

bodyText: Every tenant is entitled to safe and healthy housing under Colorado's warranty of habitability. Verbatim duty: "On and after January 1, 2025, every rental agreement between a landlord and tenant must include a statement in at least twelve-point, bold-faced type that states that every tenant is entitled to safe and healthy housing under Colorado's warranty of habitability and that a landlord is prohibited by law from retaliating against a tenant in any manner for reporting unsafe conditions in the tenant's residential premises, requesting repairs, or seeking to enjoy the tenant's right to safe and healthy housing." title: Two Habitability Statements Your Colorado Lease Must Carry
bodyText: Since January 1, 2025 every Colorado residential lease must carry two separate statements, both in at least twelve-point bold-faced type (C.R.S. 38-12-505(3)(c) and (3)(d)). The first says the tenant is entitled to safe and healthy housing under the warranty of habitability and that you may not retaliate for reporting unsafe conditions, requesting repairs or asserting that right. The second must appear in both English and Spanish, and must give an address where the tenant can mail or hand-deliver written notice of an uninhabitable condition and an email address or online tenant portal for the same notice - both, not either. Two practical points. If you offer an online tenant portal, the same English-and-Spanish statement must also be posted conspicuously inside the portal (38-12-505(3)(e)). And whatever channels your lease names become channels that count: a tenant notice is sufficient if it uses any method the rental agreement permits (38-12-503(3)(f)(I)), so you have to actually monitor the mailbox, the inbox and the portal. Never name a phone number or any verbal method - a lease that lets the tenant give habitability notice verbally waives your right to written notice entirely (38-12-503(3)(f)(II)).

title: Surrender at End of Term
bodyText: When Tenant's right to possess the property ends - because the Term expires and applicable law does not entitle Tenant to remain, because Landlord lawfully terminates this Lease, because Tenant gives notice and vacates, because Landlord and Tenant agree to end the tenancy, or because a court enters and lawfully executes a judgment for possession - Tenant will surrender possession of the property and return all keys to Landlord immediately. The property will be left in the same condition as at the start of the Term, except for ordinary wear and tear, and free of all personal property of Tenant and any occupants. Personal property left at the property after Tenant vacates may, to the extent permitted by applicable law, be treated as abandoned and disposed of at Tenant's cost.
notes: CO: CITED - C.R.S. § 38-12-1303(1), (2)(c); § 38-12-1305; § 13-40-104(1)(c). NEW row, CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 41. Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. Tenant will surrender possession" is wrong for a covered Colorado tenancy: expiration alone is not cause (§ 38-12-1303(2)(c) limits the holdover ground to nonresidential premises and the § 38-12-1302(1)(a), (b), (d), (e), (f) exemptions), and § 38-12-1305 voids a lease provision that modifies part 13. title: Only the Monthly Occupancy Payment Is Rent
bodyText: For the purpose of any remedy to collect Rent, including eviction, "Rent" under this Lease means only the set monthly payment for occupancy of the property. No other amount or fee set out in this Lease - including any pet fee, pet rent, late fee, returned-payment charge, utility or service charge, or other charge - is Rent for that purpose, and Landlord will not pursue eviction or any other remedy for the collection of Rent on the basis of Tenant's failure to pay such an amount. Landlord may pursue any other remedy applicable law allows for those amounts. This Section controls over any contrary provision of this Lease.

Such amounts and fees include any fees for utilities or services and any other charge that is not rent." § 38-12-801(3)(b): any provision included in violation of subsection (3) "is void and unenforceable". § 38-12-105(7) says the same for late fees specifically and cross-refers § 13-40-104(1)(d). title: In Colorado, Only the Monthly Rent Is Evictable Rent
bodyText: Colorado bars you from writing a lease that treats anything except the set monthly payment for occupancy as "rent" with all the rent-collection remedies, eviction included (C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(V)). Utility and service charges are named in the statute, and so is "any other charge that is not rent". A provision that breaks this rule is void and unenforceable (38-12-801(3)(b)), and a late fee gets the same treatment in its own section (38-12-105(7)). The practical consequence is the part landlords most often get wrong: you can charge pet rent in Colorado, up to the 38-12-106(2) cap, but you cannot evict for it. Online guidance that says unpaid pet rent is grounds for a 10-day demand and an eviction is wrong here. Same for unpaid utility charges, late fees and returned-payment charges: they are real debts you can sue for, but not a basis for a possession action. Two carve-outs: subsection (3)(a)(V) does not apply to a mobile home in a mobile home park (38-12-801(4)) or to a duplex, triplex or accessory dwelling unit where you live in one of the units or on the same lot (38-12-801(8)).
notes: CO: CITED - C.R.S. § 38-12-801(3)(a)(V), (3)(b), (4), (8); § 38-12-105(7); § 38-12-106(2). NEW row, CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 27 (topic fees-as-rent). Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). Resolves an open question carried in this project: the widely-copied claim that Colorado pet rent is rent and supports an eviction is wrong on the enacted text. § 38-12-106(2) permits "additional rent" for a pet up to the greater of $35/month or 1.5% of monthly rent, so the charge is lawful; § 38-12-801(3)(a)(V) separately forbids making it evictable. title: Electronic Notices: What Colorado Will Not Let You Email
bodyText: Colorado's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act carves residential landlords out of exactly the notices that matter most. It does not apply to any notice of default, acceleration, repossession, foreclosure or eviction, or of the right to cure, under a rental agreement for an individual's primary residence (C.R.S. 24-71.3-103(3)(b)(II)), nor to a notice cancelling or terminating utility service including water, heat and power (3)(b)(I). So a 10-day demand for payment or compliance, a notice to terminate and a notice of default get no help from the electronic-records statute: email or portal delivery of one of those rests on ordinary proof that it actually reached the tenant, not on a statutory rule that electronic counts as writing. Three more limits. The Act only applies between parties who have each agreed to transact electronically, and a party who agrees once may refuse the next transaction - a right that cannot be waived by agreement (24-71.3-105(2), (3)). An electronic record satisfies a writing requirement only if the recipient can retain it at the time of receipt, and if your system stops the tenant printing or storing it the record is not enforceable against them (24-71.3-108(1), (3)). And those requirements cannot be varied by agreement (24-71.3-108(4)), so no lease clause fixes any of this. Send default, cure, termination and eviction notices the way article 40 of title 13 requires, and keep habitability notices separate - those the law positively requires you to accept by email or portal.
