Clause screen result: no CO-tagged clause relies on electronic delivery of an excluded notice. The shared notices row is what protects the library - its closing sentence ("nothing in this Lease designates an alternative method of delivery for any notice governed by law") is load-bearing in Colorado and should not be trimmed. landlords-access-co's "written or electronic" bed-bug entry notice is NOT an excluded notice and is expressly authorised by § 38-12-1004(1)(a). Habitability notice runs the other way: § 38-12-505(3)(d) requires an email or portal channel in the lease. Contrast with edu-written-notice-strictly-required-co, which is about the landlord's right to receive written notice.

title: Mandatory Mediation Before Filing, and the Waiver You Cannot Put in the Lease
bodyText: Before filing an eviction against a residential tenant who receives SSI, Social Security disability insurance under Title II, or Colorado Works cash assistance, you must have gone through mandatory mediation and had it fail, and your complaint must carry an affidavit saying so (C.R.S. 13-40-110(1)(a)). You are exempt if you are a 501(c)(3) that offers tenants mediation, or a landlord with five or fewer single-family rental homes and no more than five total rental units including any single-family homes. The tenant can also take you out of it by not disclosing, or declining to disclose in writing, that they receive one of those benefits in response to your written inquiry - which is a good reason to make that written inquiry. Mediation is free to the tenant; you pay only your share; the Office of Dispute Resolution must schedule it within 14 days of your request. Getting this wrong is fatal to the case: non-compliance is an affirmative defense and the court "shall dismiss the case without prejudice" (13-40-110(1)(d)). The part that touches your lease: a tenant may voluntarily waive mandatory mediation, "but a waiver must not be in any lease agreement or other agreement" (13-40-110(1)(b)), and 38-12-801(3)(a)(III)(E) separately voids a lease waiver of it. A lease clause also may not let you recoup mediation costs from the tenant (38-12-801(3)(a)(VII)). So the waiver has to be a separate, later, voluntary document - never a lease term.

NEW row, CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 48 (also rules 47, 50). Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). Flagged for the legal watch; cite by the act where the number matters.

title: When the Tenant Causes the Damage
bodyText: Colorado handles this in one place rather than remedy by remedy, and it handles it in your favour. If a condition is substantially caused by the misconduct of the tenant, a member of the tenant's household, a guest or invitee, or someone under the tenant's direction or control, that condition "does not constitute a basis for a breach of the warranty of habitability" (C.R.S. 38-12-503(9)). Because every tenant remedy in 38-12-507 - the 10-to-60 day termination right, the recurrence termination right, repair-and-deduct, appliance replace-and-deduct, the damages claim including any reduction in fair rental value, and injunctive relief - is predicated on a breach of that warranty, tenant-caused damage switches all of them off at once. You also stop being the one who pays: 38-12-503(7) makes the landlord responsible for remedying at the landlord's own expense "except as described in subsection (9)". There is one exception to the exception: it is not misconduct if the condition resulted from domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking against the tenant and you have notice of it. Colorado has no casualty or untenantability statute in article 12 giving a tenant a separate right to walk away after a fire, so there is no second door for them to leave by; the only casualty termination is yours, under 38-12-503(11), and it needs your lease to permit it. Recovering the money runs through ordinary channels - the tenant's maintenance obligations, the deposit (38-12-103(1)(b) allows retention for repair of damage beyond normal wear and tear) and a contract claim for lost rent. No special Colorado clause is needed or offered, and a clause purporting to strip abatement rights more broadly than 38-12-503(9) does would be void under 38-12-503(10).

Rule 54t asks for each abatement or exit provision to be checked separately for its own tenant-fault exception: in Colorado there is a single gate at § 38-12-503(9) that conditions the whole of part 5, so every § 38-12-507 remedy inherits it and no per-remedy check diverges. title: Colorado Regulates AI That Prices or Screens Housing
bodyText: Colorado has no rent-setting-cartel statute of the kind some states have passed, but it does have something broader that reaches the same software. The Colorado Artificial Intelligence Act (C.R.S. 6-1-1701 et seq.) regulates systems that make, or substantially contribute to, a "consequential decision" - and housing is one of the listed domains (6-1-1701(3)(f)). If you deploy an AI or algorithmic tool to set rents, score applicants or decide renewals, you are a deployer, with duties to avoid algorithmic discrimination, run a risk-management programme, disclose the system to the consumer and report discovered discrimination (6-1-1702 to 6-1-1705). Violating part 17 is itself a deceptive trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act (6-1-105(1)(hhhh)), which carries treble damages, so the exposure is not theoretical. Watch the date: SB 26-189 repealed and reenacted part 17, and the new version applies to consequential decisions made on or after January 1, 2027, with a narrower "covered domain" structure and express carve-outs for low-stakes and routine decisions. Until then the 2024 version governs. Separately, the Colorado Privacy Act gives consumers an opt-out of profiling in decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects, which it defines to include the provision or denial of housing.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix a Tenant's Neglect and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Colorado gives a landlord no statutory self-cure right of the kind several states have - there is no provision letting you notice a tenant's neglect, do the work yourself and add the cost to the next rent payment. Two Colorado rules get in the way of writing one into the lease. Entry for repairs is governed by the habitability sections rather than a general access statute, so a self-cure entry has no statutory authorisation to rest on. And you could not bill the cost "as rent" even if you did the work: 38-12-801(3)(a)(V) reserves rent, and the remedies that go with it, to the set monthly payment for occupancy. The routes that do work are the ordinary ones - a 10-day demand for compliance or possession under 13-40-104(1)(e), the tenant's maintenance obligations, the security deposit for damage beyond normal wear and tear, and a money claim. Nothing stops you contracting for the right to do the work and recover the cost as a debt rather than as rent, but you would be drafting that from scratch and should take advice first.

title: No Blank-Space Rule, But a Real Copy Duty
bodyText: Colorado has no statute of the kind some states have requiring every blank space in a written lease to be completed, and no consumer-protection provision making a blank-filled-after-signing lease an unlawful practice. What Colorado does have is a copy duty with a deadline: you must give the tenant a copy of the written agreement signed by both of you no later than the seventh day after the tenant signs, and it may be electronic unless the tenant asks for paper (C.R.S. 38-12-801(1)). Colorado also prescribes specific content the agreement must contain - the landlord or agent name and address (38-12-801(2)), the source-of-income statement for a non-exempt landlord (38-12-801(2.5)), and the two bold-faced habitability statements (38-12-505(3)(c) and (3)(d)). So the discipline still applies even without a blank-space statute: fill or strike every bracket and placeholder before anyone signs, because an unfilled habitability-notice address or a missing identity statement is a missing required disclosure, not just an untidy lease.

title: Quiet Enjoyment Is Non-Waivable, With One Carve-Out You May Use
bodyText: Colorado does not spell out a covenant of quiet enjoyment, but it does something more useful to know about: it makes a lease waiver of the implied covenant void. A written rental agreement must not include a waiver of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment, or of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and any provision included in breach of that is void and unenforceable (C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(III)(C), (D) and (3)(b)). The same subsection then hands you a narrow permission: "a written rental agreement may provide that the landlord is not responsible for any violation of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment that is committed by a third party acting beyond the reasonable control of the landlord". That is worth using, and it is the only quiet-enjoyment disclaimer Colorado allows - a broader one is void. Two carve-outs from the prohibition itself: it does not reach a mobile home in a mobile home park (38-12-801(4)) or an owner-occupied duplex, triplex or accessory dwelling unit (38-12-801(8)). Quiet enjoyment also shows up as a limit on entry, which is why the Colorado access clause ties the notice period to it.

title: Statutory Forms in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado prescribes no form of lease, but it does prescribe text and forms you have to use. The radon warning statement is given in the statute's own words and must appear in bold-faced type "in substantially the same form" (C.R.S. 38-12-803(2)(a)(I)), inside a separate document the tenant signs. The source-of-income statement is set out in 38-12-801(2.5)(a) and the two habitability statements in 38-12-505(3)(c) and (3)(d) are prescribed by content, language and type size. On the court side, an eviction is commenced "using the standard form of eviction complaint and affidavit for a residential tenancy that is available online through the judicial department's website" (13-40-110(1)(a)), though the court must accept a different form that meets the section's requirements (13-40-110(1)(f)). The Judicial Branch also publishes the JDF demand, notice, summons, answer and writ forms; those are court forms, not statutory text, and are worth using because they are kept current. No form is prescribed for the 10-day demand itself - what matters is that its content matches 13-40-104.

title: No Tenant Security-Camera Rule
bodyText: Colorado statutes do not address tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells. The lease governs, through its alteration and installation terms and its rules on fixing things to the building. If you do allow one, remember that a doorbell camera is an alteration to the property for which the no-alterations clause requires your written consent, and that Colorado's wiretap, eavesdropping and privacy-tort law was not reviewed here and is the place any recording question gets answered.

title: The Radon Disclosure Cannot Live in the Lease
bodyText: Colorado does not let the lease carry this one. Before the lease is signed, you must give the tenant a separate written radon disclosure "in a document that the tenant signs to acknowledge receipt" (C.R.S. 38-12-803(2)(a)), and that document has to contain three things: the radon warning statement in bold-faced type, clearly legible and in substantially the form the statute sets out; everything you know about radon at the property - whether a test has been done, the current records and reports, any concentrations detected, any mitigation or remediation performed, and a description and documentation of any mitigation system; and a copy of the most recent radon brochure the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment publishes. The tenant acknowledges receipt by signing that document, not the lease (38-12-803(2)(b)). Your lease's Radon Disclosure Acknowledgment says the tenant received all of that - so if you never produced the separate document, you have had the tenant sign a statement that is not true, which helps them and not you. Produce the document first, get it signed, then sign the lease. One thing to watch: the statute says "a copy of" the brochure, so emailing a link may not be enough; attach the brochure itself.

title: Jury Waiver for a Possession Hearing
bodyText: Landlord and Tenant each waive the right to a jury trial in any hearing to determine possession of the property, to the extent Colorado law permits that waiver. This waiver applies only to a hearing to determine possession. It does not waive either party's right to a jury trial on any claim for damages or on any other issue, and it does not waive any other right either party has under applicable law. This Section does not apply to a rental agreement concerning the occupancy of a mobile home in a mobile home park.
notes: CO: CITED - C.R.S. § 38-12-801(3)(a)(III)(A). NEW row, CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, rule 54, added on Taylor's decision 2026-10-01. Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). Verbatim basis: a written rental agreement must not include a waiver of "The right to a jury trial; except that the parties may agree to a waiver of a jury trial in a hearing to determine possession of a dwelling unit." The clause is drafted to the carve-out and no further: a waiver reaching damages or any other issue falls back inside the prohibition and is void under § 38-12-801(3)(b). Mutual rather than one-sided, because the statute speaks of "the parties" agreeing and a mutual waiver gives no unconscionability handle. OPTIONAL BY DESIGN - offered per lease, never auto-included: no choice_group and no is_default, so nothing marks it as a library default; the builder's "add my default clauses" feature runs off flags the USER sets at runtime, so no library field change is needed to honour this (Taylor, 2026-10-01). The clause is scoped away from mobile-home-park tenancies because those run under the Mobile Home Park Act (part 2 of this article; § 38-12-801(5) preserves MHPA rights), which was NOT read this pass. title: The Repayment Plan You Must Offer a Victim-Survivor
bodyText: This one is a three-business-day clock that can end your eviction case, and it is easy to miss because it sits in the eviction statute rather than the domestic-violence part. If a tenant tells you they are a victim-survivor of domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking and backs it with any one of the accepted documents - a police report, a valid protection or restraining order, a self-attestation affidavit, or a letter from a qualified third party such as a victim-service worker, attorney, social worker, medical professional, faith leader or mental health provider - then you shall offer a repayment plan no later than three business days after you serve a demand for unpaid rent, or three business days after you receive the documentation, whichever is later (C.R.S. 13-40-104(4)(e)(I)(A)). Not offering one is an affirmative defense to your unlawful-detainer action. The plan is structured at the tenant's discretion, must require full repayment of all lawfully owed rent in monthly payments of at least $25, and cannot run more than nine months. You may not charge any fees, interest or penalties connected to it (4)(e)(I)(C). The protections cannot be waived in the lease or any other agreement (4)(c). Two things that run in your favour: the tenant waives the affirmative defense if they neither accept your plan nor propose a conforming alternative within seven days of receiving yours; and if they miss a payment or make three or more late ones, you can serve a notice of default demanding all remaining rent and then move for judgment. None of this stops you seeking possession against a different tenant who is the one responsible for the abuse (4)(d).

title: The Terms Colorado Will Not Let Your Lease Contain
bodyText: Colorado gives you a closed list of terms a written rental agreement "must not include", and anything on it that ends up in your lease is void and unenforceable (C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a) and (3)(b)). The list, in the statute's order: a penalty on either party stemming from an eviction notice or an eviction action that results from a lease violation; a one-way fee-shifting clause - any fee-shifting provision must award attorney fees to the prevailing party once the court finds they prevailed and the fee is reasonable; a waiver of the right to a jury trial, except that the parties may agree to waive a jury in a hearing to determine possession; a waiver of the ability to pursue, bring, join, litigate or support any joint, class or collective claim arising from the tenancy; a waiver of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; a waiver of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment, except that the lease may say you are not responsible for a third party's violation of it beyond your reasonable control; a waiver of the mandatory mediation required by 13-40-110(1); a fee, damages or penalty for a tenant failing to give notice of nonrenewal before the end of the agreement, except your actual losses from the missing notice; characterising any amount other than the set monthly payment for occupancy as "rent" with rent remedies including eviction; requiring the tenant to pay a markup or fee on a service a third party bills you, beyond either 2% of what you were billed or $10 a month, but not both; letting a voucher or subsidy provider pursue possession based solely on unpaid utilities; and recouping the cost of mandatory mediation from the tenant. Two practical warnings. The class-action waiver is the one most often imported by accident - it is boilerplate in form leases from other states, and in Colorado it is simply void, so do not paste a lease in from elsewhere without checking. And the nonrenewal item is narrow rather than absent: you cannot charge a fee or a set amount for a missing nonrenewal notice, but your actual losses are still recoverable, so there is nothing to gain from a fee clause and something to lose. Who is exempt: 38-12-801(4) switches off the jury, good-faith, quiet-enjoyment, nonrenewal, fees-as-rent, markup and voucher items for a mobile home in a mobile home park, and 38-12-801(8) switches off the whole waiver group and those same items for a duplex, triplex or accessory dwelling unit where you live in one of the units or on the same lot. The eviction-penalty and fee-shifting items have no exemption and apply to everyone.
notes: CO: CITED - C.R.S. § 38-12-801(3)(a)(I), (3)(a)(II), (3)(a)(III)(A)-(E), (3)(a)(IV), (3)(a)(V), (3)(a)(VI), both subsections numbered (3)(a)(VII), (3)(b), (4), (8); § 13-40-110(1). NEW row, CO retro (SOP 1.16) 2026-10-01, resolving Q4 on Taylor's decision 2026-10-01 ("One edu-prohibited-lease-terms-co row"). Statute read section-open in the official 2026 C.R.S. (Colorado OLLS whole-title HTM, olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-38.htm / -13 / -24 / -06 / -00). WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: Colorado had NO row on the prohibited-lease-terms topic although 20 of the other 25 states do, and Colorado has one of the longest such statutes - the list was covered piecemeal across edu-eviction-penalty-clause-ban-co, edu-fee-shifting-co, edu-quiet-possession-co, edu-fees-not-rent-co, edu-rubs-uncertainty-co, edu-mandatory-mediation-co and jury-waiver-possession-co, with no row stating the list as a list. Two subsections had no CO row at all and are now covered: (3)(a)(III)(B) the joint/class/collective-action waiver, and (3)(a)(IV) the nonrenewal-notice fee. ON (3)(a)(IV) - THE Q4 QUESTION: Taylor's call was that the content is education, not a lease clause, and he was right on the rule 55 three-bucket test. It is not a required disclosure (the statute requires no lease text), not a constrained term (no landlord figure to state), and it does not serve the landlord: "responsible only for actual losses" plus a list of charges that do not apply is a restatement of a statutory CEILING in the tenant's favour, which the restatement check and this project's own statutory-ceiling rule both send to education. My earlier argument for a clause rested on creating the carve-out's "notice required pursuant to the rental agreement" hook, but that hook already exists in month-to-month-notice-co-exempt and month-to-month-notice-co-covered, and a sentence capping the tenant's exposure deters nothing. No lease clause offered. RULE 21 FLAG: § 38-12-801(3)(a) contains TWO subsections numbered (VII) in the official 2026 compilation, a single-session double-amendment artifact - shown here rather than silently renumbered; cite by the act where the number matters. Rule 47: the sanction is voidness under (3)(b), not conditioned on knowing use. Detail rows as listed above; fee-shifting also interacts with § 13-40-123 (no fees for a prevailing residential party unless the lease provides for them) - see edu-fee-shifting-co.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Georgia has no just-cause eviction rule for houses and apartments. A fixed-term lease ends on its last day, and a tenancy with no end date (a tenancy at will, including month-to-month) ends on 60 days' notice from the landlord or 30 days' notice from the tenant, with no reason required; no length of tenancy changes this. The limits are situational. Within three months after a tenant in good faith exercises a legal or lease right, gives a notice to repair, complains to a code-enforcement agency or utility, or forms or joins a tenant organization about habitability, a landlord who files a dispossessory action, ends the lease or raises the rent faces a retaliation claim, unless the action rests on unpaid rent, intentional damage or threats, a breach of written lease rules against serious misconduct or criminal acts, or a holdover after notice ending the lease at the end of its term as the written lease provides. When an apartment building is converted to condominiums, the developer must give each qualifying tenant at least 120 days' notice and may not require the tenant to leave during that time except for nonpayment of rent, waste, or conduct that disturbs other tenants. Georgia has no repair rent-escrow procedure that bars eviction; the only rent paid into court is rent the tenant pays into the court registry while a dispossessory case is pending. Fair housing law applies.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 41b; rule 41). CONFIRMED ABSENT (statutes) of a just-cause rule for dwellings, with situational limits, so rules 27 and 41 give the same answer. Controlling text: O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-6, 44-7-7 (tenancy at will; notice); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-24(b)(1)-(4), (c), (d)(2)(A)-(E) (retaliation, three months, tenant organization; holdover after the landlord's end-of-term notice 'as agreed upon in the written lease' is a safe harbour, offered as `end-of-term-notice-ga`); O.C.G.A. § 44-3-87(a), (d), (g), (j) (conversion condominiums created after 1980-07-01: 120-day notice; tenants not in default and in residential occupancy; a notice naming a vacate date is also a demand for possession); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-54 (registry payments during a dispossessory only). Official O.C.G.A. full-text search 2026-10-01 (nonsense control 0 hits; GA retro battery B1-B4): 'good cause' near eviction or termination words, 30 hits, none for dwellings; 'just cause' or 'for cause' near tenant or eviction words, 3 hits (innkeepers, O.C.G.A. §§ 43-21-1, 43-21-3.1; estates, O.C.G.A. § 53-2-7); conversion near tenant near condominium or apartment, 3 hits (O.C.G.A. § 44-3-87); tenant-organization and rent-escrow patterns, 6 hits, known positives O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-24 and 44-7-54 returned, no repair rent-escrow statute. Rule 41 wording screen: no just-cause rule, so no wording that converts the end of the term into a for-cause event. Model: `edu-no-for-cause-eviction-az` (read, not tagged). title: Notice That This Lease Ends at the End of the Term (Optional)
bodyText: This Lease ends at the end of the Term whether or not Landlord gives notice. Landlord may also give Tenant written notice, at least {{end_of_term_notice_days}} days before the last day of the Term, that this Lease will end at the end of the Term and will not be renewed or extended. If Landlord gives that notice, Tenant will vacate the property by the end of the Term.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rules 50 and 54). OPTIONAL clause (CONDITIONAL, not a default). The lease choice it makes: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-24(d)(2)(E) says a landlord is not liable for retaliation for a dispossessory action or termination when 'The tenant holds over after the landlord gives notice of termination at the end of the rental term as agreed upon in the written lease'. Without an agreed end-of-term notice in the written lease, that safe harbour has nothing to point to, and a landlord who declines to renew within three months of a tenant's repair notice, code complaint or tenant-organization activity relies on the other exceptions only (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-24(c)(4) lists terminating the lease). The first sentence keeps the notice optional, so the Term still ends on its own (a fixed term needs no notice; only a tenancy at will does, O.C.G.A. § 44-7-7). It does not replace the demand for possession a dispossessory needs (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50(a), (d)), and it sits beside `holdover-ca`, whose continued-tenancy limb still applies if Landlord later accepts Rent. Same family as the GA pass's other safe-harbour clauses, `rent-escalation-ga` ((d)(1)(A)) and `serious-misconduct-prohibition-ga` ((d)(2)(C)). Whether a court requires more than the statute's words for the safe harbour is case law, not read. BUILDER: show only when the lease has a fixed Term and the landlord opts in; require {{end_of_term_notice_days}} (same placeholder as `end-of-term-notice-fl`); no statute sets the number; a landlord who wants the tenant to have time to move might use 30 to 60 days (judgment, not statute). Basis: SERVES_LANDLORD (the landlord's own notice right). title: Waiver of Exemptions (Optional)
bodyText: Tenant waives and renounces Tenant's right to the benefit of the exemption from levy and sale provided by Article 1 of Chapter 13 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, as to any amount Tenant owes under this Lease. This waiver does not apply to wearing apparel or to $300.00 worth of household and kitchen furniture and provisions, which Georgia law protects despite any waiver.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 54: a waiver the statute lets a tenant give in the contract). OPTIONAL clause (CONDITIONAL, off by default), same treatment as `exemption-waiver-al` (Taylor's AL decision 4: offer it for consistency, never default). Controlling text: O.C.G.A. § 44-13-40 ('Any debtor may, except as to wearing apparel and $300.00 worth of household and kitchen furniture and provisions, waive or renounce his right to the benefit of the exemption provided for by this article by a waiver, either general or specific, in writing simply stating that he does so waive or renounce such right, which waiver may be stated in the contract of indebtedness'); 'this article' is Article 1 ('Constitutional Exemptions') of Title 44 ch. 13, whose O.C.G.A. § 44-13-1 exempts $5,000.00, or $21,500.00 for property that is the debtor's primary residence. After a levy the debtor sets apart the $300 by schedule and affidavit (O.C.G.A. §§ 44-13-41, 44-13-42); a levy made to harass can cost the creditor up to 25% of the value levied (O.C.G.A. § 44-13-41). The clause uses the statute's own words ('waives and renounces', the two excepted items) per rule 59. Not barred by O.C.G.A. § 44-7-2(b) (its list does not include exemptions). UNREAD: whether a residential lease is a 'contract of indebtedness' and how courts treat such waivers (case law); the bankruptcy exemptions (O.C.G.A. § 44-13-100) are a separate article and not addressed. Education: `edu-exemption-waiver-ga`. Basis: SERVES_LANDLORD. title: Waiver of Collection Exemptions
bodyText: Georgia exempts from levy and sale a debtor's property worth up to $5,000, or up to $21,500 for property that is the debtor's primary residence. A debtor may waive that exemption in writing, including in the contract that creates the debt, except as to wearing apparel and $300 worth of household and kitchen furniture and provisions; after a levy the debtor can claim that $300 of property back by filing a schedule. The library offers an optional waiver clause (`exemption-waiver-ga`), off by default. Whether a residential lease counts as a 'contract of indebtedness' for this purpose, and how courts treat such waivers, is case law this library has not reviewed. It is a collection term aimed at the tenant that many residential leases leave out, so use it only as a deliberate choice.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 54). Controlling text: O.C.G.A. §§ 44-13-1, 44-13-40, 44-13-41, 44-13-42 (see `exemption-waiver-ga` notes). title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term (for a tenancy with no fixed Term, up to the earliest date Tenant could have ended the tenancy by notice), less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will make repairs as Georgia law requires and will use reasonable efforts to re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 54t). OPTIONAL clause (CONDITIONAL, not a default), state version of `tenant-caused-damage-tn` (read; TN row not tagged). Each abatement or exit route checked for a tenant-fault exception: (i) casualty: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-15 ('The destruction of a tenement by fire or the loss of possession by any casualty not caused by the landlord or from a defect of his title shall not abate the rent contracted to be paid') gives no abatement and no exit, so part (1) waives no statutory right; the opt-in `casualty-termination-ga` already excludes damage caused by Tenant, household members, guests or invitees; (ii) essential services and landlord-breach termination: no Georgia statute (ch. 7 read whole); (iii) rent into court: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-54 is registry rent during a dispossessory only. Repair duty: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-13(a) has no tenant-fault carve-out in its text and cannot be waived or avoided (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-2(b)(1)); whether courts relieve a landlord for tenant-caused damage is case law, not read. So TN's 'Landlord will use reasonable efforts to repair' became 'Landlord will make repairs as Georgia law requires', which cannot be read as softening that duty. Part (2) fills a gap: no Georgia statute measures lost rent when the lease ends because of tenant-caused damage. Tenancy-type limb (rule 37) from `tenant-caused-damage-al`: a tenancy at will ends on the tenant's 30 days' notice (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-7). Deposit: damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, including from negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, household members, invitees or guests, may be kept from the deposit (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-34(a)). Education: `edu-tenant-caused-damage-ga`. Basis: SERVES_LANDLORD. title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: Georgia law leaves much of the cost of tenant-caused damage with the tenant. Destruction by fire, or loss of possession through a casualty the landlord did not cause, does not reduce the rent unless the lease says otherwise, and the library's optional casualty clause (`casualty-termination-ga`) gives no termination or rent reduction for damage caused by the tenant, household members, guests or invitees. The landlord may keep from the security deposit the cost of damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, including damage from negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, household members, invitees or guests, and may sue for the rest. The landlord's statutory duty to keep the premises in repair has no stated exception for damage the tenant caused and cannot be waived; whether courts relieve a landlord of it in that case is case law, not reviewed here. No Georgia statute measures the landlord's lost rent if the lease ends because of tenant-caused damage; the library offers an optional clause that does (`tenant-caused-damage-ga`).
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 54t). Controlling text: O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-15, 44-7-34(a), 44-7-13(a), 44-7-2(b)(1); see `tenant-caused-damage-ga` notes. title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: Georgia law makes rent bear interest from the time it is due. Where the lease states no rate, the legal rate is 7% a year simple interest. Parties may set a different rate by written contract, but where the principal amount involved is $3,000 or less, the rate on a forbearance to enforce the collection of a sum of money may not exceed 16% a year simple interest, and Georgia defines interest broadly, as a charge for the use of money computed in any way or form. How those limits apply to unpaid rent, and whether a late fee counts toward them, were not reviewed, so the library offers no interest clause. A landlord who wants a contract rate can add one, and should take advice first.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 54: a measure the lease can set). DECLINED OPTION, education row per rule 54 (lawful, not offered, why). Controlling text: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-16 ('All contracts for rent shall bear interest from the time the rent is due'); O.C.G.A. § 7-4-2(a)(1)(A) (7 percent simple 'where the rate percent is not established by written contract'; written contract may set any rate where the principal is more than $3,000.00 and less than $250,000.00), (a)(2) ('Where the principal amount involved is $3,000.00 or less, such rate shall not exceed 16 percent per annum simple interest on any loan, advance, or forbearance to enforce the collection of any sum of money'), (a)(3) (interest 'computed in any other way or any other form'). Why not offered: one month's rent is usually under $3,000, so a contract rate meets the 16% ceiling, and whether a late fee is 'interest' under (a)(3), and whether a lease arrearage is a 'forbearance', are usury questions not reviewed (case law and O.C.G.A. § 7-4-18 not read); MO took the same course (`edu-legal-interest-mo`). `edu-landlord-remedies-ga` keeps the one-line interest statement. title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule
bodyText: Georgia statutes do not regulate the use of algorithmic or software pricing tools to set residential rents. Georgia also has no rent control and bars cities and counties from regulating the amount of rent on private rental property (`edu-local-preemption-ga`). Federal antitrust law may still apply.

title: Fees and the Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: Georgia's eviction statute names fees alongside rent rather than treating them as rent. For leases entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2024, when a tenant fails to pay the rent, late fees, utilities or other charges owed to the landlord, the landlord may give a notice to vacate or pay all of them within three business days and then file a dispossessory action. Other steps still turn on rent: a tenant can stop a nonpayment case by tendering all rents claimed plus the cost of the dispossessory warrant within seven days of service (the landlord must accept that only once in any 12 months), and while a case is pending the tenant pays into the court registry the rent and utility payments the lease makes the tenant's responsibility. The library's shared Default clause gives up one part of this on purpose: except where the law requires otherwise, an unpaid late fee alone, apart from the Rent itself, does not let the landlord end the lease or evict. Other unpaid charges are not covered by that sentence.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 27). Verdict: PRESENT (by statute; no statute converts fees into rent, the eviction statute names them directly). Controlling text: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50(c) ('fails to pay the rent, late fees, utilities, or other charges owed to the landlord'; three business days; HB 404 § 6, leases entered into or renewed on or after 2024-07-01; older tenancies at will: `edu-eviction-process-ga`); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-52(a) ('all rents allegedly owed plus the cost of the dispossessory warrant'; 'only once in any 12 month period'); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-54(a) ('All rent and utility payments which are the responsibility of the tenant payable to the landlord under terms of the lease'). Library choice: `default-by-tenant` ('Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate this Lease or pursue eviction'), kept as the library default. title: No Statutory Right to Fix It and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Some states let a landlord give notice, do work the tenant failed to do, and add the cost to the rent. No provision of Georgia's landlord-tenant chapter gives a landlord that right, sets a notice period for it, or makes the cost rent. What Georgia law does give: the landlord may keep from the security deposit the cost of damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, may sue for the rest, and for unpaid charges owed to the landlord may use the three-business-day notice to vacate or pay. Whether a repair cost the lease makes the tenant's responsibility is such a charge is not settled by the statute's text.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 27). Verdict: NOT LOCATED. Boundary: O.C.G.A. Title 44 ch. 7 arts. 1-4 read whole (the GA pass, and arts. 3-4 again this retro on the official code): no analogue to a URLTA-style self-cure right (compare A.R.S. § 33-1341(8)); no code-wide full-text pattern was run, because no known positive exists in Georgia to test one against (rule 19), so this is not a confirmed absence. Controlling text for the routes named: O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-34(a), 44-7-50(c). Model: `edu-no-landlord-self-cure-wy` (read, not tagged). title: No Blank-Space or Lease-Copy Rule
bodyText: Georgia imposes no statutory requirement that a written residential lease have every blank completed, and none that the landlord give the tenant a signed copy. Georgia's Fair Business Practices Act reaches residential leases, but its list of unlawful practices has no blank-space or copy-at-signing item for an ordinary lease. Several Georgia rules still turn on what the lease says: the owner and agent disclosure, the statement of where the deposit is held, and any delivery methods for the three-day notice and demand for possession that the lease adds to posting on the door. A blank left in one of those is a right or a duty left unclear. Fill in every blank before signing and give the tenant a copy, as good practice rather than a statutory duty.

Fair Business Practices Act: 'consumer transactions' include the lease or rental of property (O.C.G.A. § 10-1-392(a)(10)); the O.C.G.A. § 10-1-393(b) list has no blank-space or copy-at-signing practice, and its (b)(20) lease statements apply only to foreclosure-rescue sale-leasebacks (read in the browser, browser hash only, a weaker method; case law on the Act's reach to leases not read). title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: Georgia's statutes contain no covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession running from the landlord to the tenant. Possession is protected instead by the dispossessory process: a landlord recovers possession through a court action and a writ executed by an officer, not by self-help (`edu-prohibited-practices-ga`). Whether Georgia implies a covenant of quiet enjoyment in a lease is case law; case notes in the official code refer to one, but the cases were not read and this row does not rely on them.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 27). Verdict: CONFIRMED ABSENT as a statute; case law NOT LOCATED (boundary stated in the body, rule 19). title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Georgia prescribes no form for a residential lease, and none for the three-day notice to vacate or pay or the demand for possession; the statute prescribes how those notices are delivered (posted in a sealed envelope on the door, plus any method the lease adds), not their wording. Two prescribed forms can reach a landlord: the written demand sent before suing on a dishonored check, which must be in substantially the statutory form (`edu-dishonored-payment-remedies-ga`), and, for a property covered by the federal CARES Act, the CARES Act affidavit form in the Uniform Magistrate Court Rules (`edu-eviction-process-ga`). Magistrate courts' own dispossessory filing forms were not reviewed.
notes: GA: NEW 2026-10-01 (SOP 1.18 retro, rule 27). Verdict: PRESENT (two forms; no lease or eviction-notice form). Controlling text: O.C.G.A. § 13-6-15(c) (demand 'in substantially the form which follows'); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50(d) (delivery, not wording); Uniform Magistrate Court Rule 46 (CARES affidavit; gasupreme.us PDF read in the browser). title: No Tenant Security-Camera Rule
bodyText: Georgia statutes do not address tenant-installed security cameras, video doorbells or similar devices. The lease's alteration terms govern; in this library that is the Alterations section, which requires the landlord's written consent before a tenant adds or changes a fixture. Georgia's eavesdropping and surveillance laws, and any homeowners' association rules, were not reviewed and may limit what a camera records rather than its installation.

title: Truth in Renting Act Notice
bodyText: "NOTICE: Michigan law establishes rights and obligations for parties to rental agreements. This agreement is required to comply with the Truth in Renting Act. If you have a question about the interpretation or legality of a provision of this agreement, you may want to seek assistance from a lawyer or other qualified person."
notes: MI: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.634(2): a rental agreement 'shall state in a prominent place in type not smaller than the size of 12-point type, or in legible print with letters not smaller than 1/8 inch, a notice in substantially the following form'; the notice is quoted verbatim, quotation marks included as the statute prints them (rule 59). Builder: prominent place (near the top), 12-point type or larger (MI log §4, §10). A lessor may cure an omission by written notice to current tenants (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.635(2)); an uncured omission after the tenant's written notice exposes the lessor to $500 or actual damages and voiding of the agreement (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.636(2)), and without prior notice where the lessor actually knew (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.636(3)(c)). A commercial seller may not sell a printed form that omits it (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.638). The Truth in Renting Act, Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 554.631-554.641, read whole. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Security Deposit Notice
bodyText: SECURITY DEPOSIT NOTICE. Landlord's name and address for receipt of communications about the Security Deposit: {{landlord_name}}, {{landlord_notice_address}}. The Security Deposit will be held at: [name and address of the regulated financial institution where the Security Deposit is deposited, or, if Landlord has deposited a bond with the Michigan Secretary of State, the name and address of the surety company or a statement that a cash bond is on deposit with the Secretary of State]. Tenant must provide Landlord, in writing and within 4 days after Tenant's occupancy ends, a forwarding mailing address. You must notify your landlord in writing within 4 days after you move of a forwarding address where you can be reached and where you will receive mail; otherwise your landlord shall be relieved of sending you an itemized list of damages and the penalties adherent to that failure.
notes: MI: Required whenever a security deposit is taken. Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.603: a landlord 'shall not require a security deposit unless he notifies the tenant no later than 14 days from the date a tenant assumes possession in a written instrument' of the landlord's name and address for communications under the act, the name and address of the financial institution or surety required by Mich. title: Early Termination: Senior Housing or Inability to Live Independently
bodyText: If Tenant has occupied the property for more than 13 months, Tenant may terminate this Lease by giving Landlord 60 days' written notice if, during the Term, either of the following occurs: (a) Tenant becomes eligible to take possession of a subsidized rental unit in senior citizen housing and gives Landlord written proof of that eligibility; or (b) Tenant becomes incapable of living independently, as certified by a physician in a notarized statement.
notes: MI: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.601a(1): 'A rental agreement shall provide that a tenant who has occupied a rental unit for more than 13 months may terminate a lease by a 60-day written notice to the landlord if' (a) the tenant becomes eligible during the lease term to take possession of a subsidized rental unit in senior citizen housing and provides written proof, or (b) becomes incapable during the lease term of living independently, as certified by a physician in a notarized statement. 'Senior citizen housing' means subsidized housing for individuals 62 or older (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.601(e)). Applies to leases entered into, renewed or renegotiated after June 15, 1995 (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.601a(2)). The parties may not waive it (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.606). Tracks the statute sentence by sentence (rule 59). The RPOA 2024 lease carries the same paragraph (MI log §15). title: Domestic Violence, Sexual Assault or Stalking: Notice of Rights
bodyText: A tenant who has a reasonable apprehension of present danger to him or her or his or her child from domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking may have special statutory rights to seek a release of rental obligation under MCL 554.601b.

The content of the written notice shall be identical to the provision in this section.' title: Condominium or Homeowner Association Compliance
bodyText: If the property is a condominium unit, Tenant and every other occupant will comply with all of the conditions of the condominium documents of the condominium project, including the master deed, bylaws, and rules and regulations. title: Use of Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant shall pay Landlord a security deposit of {{security_deposit}} (Security Deposit) prior to occupancy. Landlord may use the Security Deposit only to: (1) reimburse Landlord for actual damages to the rental unit or any ancillary facility that are the direct result of conduct not reasonably expected in the normal course of habitation of a dwelling; and (2) pay Landlord for Rent in arrears under this Lease, Rent due because Tenant ended this Lease early, and utility bills Tenant did not pay. Landlord will not apply the Security Deposit to ordinary wear and tear or to any damage or condition that existed before the tenancy. Tenant may not apply the Security Deposit to Rent, including the last month's Rent, without Landlord's written consent. The Security Deposit does not limit Tenant's liability for amounts greater than the Security Deposit.
notes: MI: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.607: a security deposit 'may be used only for' (a) actual damages to the rental unit or any ancillary facility that are the direct result of conduct not reasonably expected in the normal course of habitation, and (b) all rent in arrearage, rent due for premature termination by the tenant, and utility bills not paid by the tenant; items (1)-(2) track it (rule 59). The base's 'remedy a Tenant default' and cleaning sentence are broader, and the act may not be waived (Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 554.606, 554.633(1)(b)); this row supersedes security-deposit-use for MI. The deposit amount is the landlord's figure; the 1 1/2-month cap (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.602) is enforced in the builder and explained in edu-security-deposit-cap-mi (rule 55). The deposit is the tenant's property until the landlord establishes a right to it (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.605). Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 554.601-554.616 read whole. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: Within 4 days after Tenant's occupancy ends, Tenant will give Landlord a forwarding address in writing, at the address in the Security Deposit Notice, where Tenant can receive mail. Within 30 days after Tenant's occupancy ends, Landlord will either return the full Security Deposit or mail Tenant a notice of damages that itemizes each charge against the Security Deposit, with the estimated cost of repair of each damaged item, and returns the balance by check or money order with the notice or by electronic transfer to Tenant's account within 10 days after mailing the notice. Tenant must respond to a notice of damages by ordinary mail, at the address in the Security Deposit Notice, within 7 days after receiving it, stating in detail whether Tenant agrees or disagrees with each charge. If Tenant does not respond in time, Tenant forfeits the amount claimed. If Tenant disputes a charge in time, Landlord will, within 45 days after Tenant's occupancy ends, either return the disputed amount, agree with Tenant in writing on how it will be handled, or start a court action for it.
notes: MI: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.611 (tenant's written forwarding address within 4 days; failure relieves the landlord of the notice of damages but does not prejudice the tenant's later claim); Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.609(1)-(4) (notice of damages mailed within 30 days after termination of occupancy, itemized with estimated cost of repair of each item and the amounts and bases of assessment; balance by check or money order with the notice, or, from Sept. 21, 2026, by direct deposit or electronic transfer within 10 days after mailing the notice, 2026 Mich. Pub. Acts 102; the notice carries a prescribed 12-point boldface statement, edu-security-deposit-penalty-mi); Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.612 (tenant's detailed response by ordinary mail within 7 days; the mailing date is the response date); Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.613(1) (within 45 days after termination of occupancy the landlord must sue for a money judgment for claimed damages or return the balance or an amount agreed in writing; retention without a judgment only where the tenant gave no forwarding address, did not respond, agreed in writing, or the claim is entirely accrued unpaid rent). The 7-day forfeiture follows the statutory notice text (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.609(4)) and Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.613(1)(b). Rule 37: every window runs from 'termination of occupancy', the same for fixed and periodic tenancies. The tenant duty is the landlord-serving reason for the clause. title: Tenant Default
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due or fails to comply with any other obligation under this Lease. If Tenant fails to pay Rent, Landlord may serve Tenant a written demand for possession for nonpayment, and Tenant may cure by paying the Rent due within 7 days after the demand is served, or as Michigan law otherwise allows. For any other breach that can be corrected, Landlord will give Tenant written notice describing the breach, and Landlord may end this Lease if Tenant does not correct the breach within [number] days after the notice. No opportunity to cure applies to a breach of this Lease's criminal activity terms, or where Michigan law lets Landlord end the tenancy without one, including when Tenant, a member of Tenant's household or a person under Tenant's control causes or threatens physical injury to an individual, other than Tenant or a member of Tenant's household, on real property Landlord owns or operates and the police have been notified. Except as required by applicable law, Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to end this Lease or pursue eviction. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may exercise all remedies available under Michigan law, including ending this Lease, recovering possession through the courts, and recovering unpaid Rent, late fees, and court costs as allowed by statute, less amounts properly applied from the Security Deposit. Landlord will mitigate its damages as Michigan law requires.
notes: MI: Supersedes default-by-tenant for MI (default-by-tenant-ks-ne is not tagged either). (1) Fees: a rental agreement may not make a party liable for 'legal costs or attorney fees incurred by another party, in connection with a dispute arising under the rental agreement, in excess of costs or fees specifically permitted by statute' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(g)); the base's prevailing-party sentence and the ks-ne variant's 'reasonable costs and expenses' are replaced by 'court costs as allowed by statute' (summary-proceeding costs, Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5759; MCR 4.201(L)(4)) (rules 49, 53). (2) Rent limb: Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(a) (holding over 7 days after service of a written demand for possession for nonpayment; rent due excludes accelerated amounts), demand form and service Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 600.5716, 600.5718; the 7 days is the statute's period, not an added notice (rule 43). Payment of the judgment amount and costs also prevents the writ (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5744(7)). (3) Other breaches: possession after termination 'pursuant to a power to terminate provided in the lease' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(c)(i)); the cure period is the landlord's figure (hand-filled bracket). Case law: the notice and demand of possession operates as the landlord's assertion of its intention to forfeit (Gurunian v Grossman, 331 Mich 412, 418 (1951)); accepting rent for a period after the date in the notice, when the tenant has not received notice that summary proceedings have begun, waives the notice, and a landlord who has habitually accepted late payments must give notice that strict compliance will be required before forfeiting for lateness (Park Forest of Blackman v Smith, 112 Mich App 421, 425-428 (1982); edu-acceptance-of-payment-mi); case law on a minimum cure period was not searched (MI log §1.4). No agreement can take away the tenant's statutory right to cure by paying the judgment amount (Birznieks v Cooper, 405 Mich 319 (1979)); the clause does not try to. (4) No-cure carve-out in its own sentence reaching both limbs (rule 43): the drug ground runs on 24 hours' notice under a lease clause (Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 554.134(4), 600.5714(1)(b); criminal-activity-mi), and the threatened-injury ground on a 7-day notice to quit with no cure, only if the police department with jurisdiction has been notified, and not where the person injured or threatened is the tenant or a household member or where it would violate federal housing regulations (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(e)); the clause states the police and household conditions and relies on 'where Michigan law lets Landlord' for the federal-regulation exception. (5) Mitigation may not be released (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(k)); summary-proceeding rights may not be waived (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(j)). Chapter 57 of the Revised Judicature Act, Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 600.5701-600.5759, read whole. Court rule: MCR 4.201 read whole from the Michigan Court Rules PDF updated Sept. 2, 2026 (courts.michigan.gov) (MI log §1). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Landlord's Entry
bodyText: Landlord, its agents and contractors may enter the property at reasonable times to inspect it, make repairs or perform maintenance, and show it to prospective tenants, purchasers or lenders. Except in an emergency, Landlord will give Tenant at least 24 hours' notice and will request and obtain Tenant's permission before entering, and Tenant will not unreasonably refuse permission. In an emergency, including fire, flood, or another threat of serious injury or death, Landlord may enter at any time.
notes: MI: Supersedes landlords-access for MI. Where the Housing Law of Michigan applies, 'Before entering a leasehold regulated by this act, the owner of the leasehold shall request and obtain permission to enter the leasehold. However, in the case of an emergency, including, but not limited to, fire, flood, or other threat of serious injury or death, the owner may enter at any time.' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 125.526(11)). The Housing Law covers cities, villages and townships of 10,000 or more by the last federal census, and private and 2-family dwellings only in those of 100,000 or more unless the local body adopts it (Mich. Comp. Laws § 125.401(2)). Rule 32: the clause is drafted to the stricter rule so it is lawful everywhere, so no municipality list was built. Outside Housing Law places no Michigan statute sets entry notice (MI batteries 11, 12); the 24-hour figure is the landlord's. Entry may not become unlawful interference with possession (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.2918(2)-(3)(b)). No published case construing Mich. Comp. Laws § 125.526(11), including whether a lease term can itself supply the permission it requires, was found (MI log §1.4), so the clause asks for permission each time. edu-entry-mi. Rule 15: written section-open. Pub. Acts 102 and 103, eff. Sept. 21, 2026) (MI log §1, MI log §17). | IA: Applies as written (tagged instead of the base `landlords-access`, independent check round 1). Iowa Code § 562A.19: tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent for listed purposes, including to inspect, repair and show the unit to purchasers, mortgagees and prospective tenants (1); entry without consent in an emergency (2); except in an emergency or where impracticable, at least 24 hours' notice and entry only at reasonable times (3); no other right of access except court order, Iowa Code §§ 562A.28, 562A.29, abandonment or surrender (4). This variant's 'request and obtain Tenant's permission ... Tenant will not unreasonably refuse permission' matches Iowa Code § 562A.19(1); its notice duty is stricter than Iowa's (no impracticability exception), which is lawful. The base `landlords-access` grants a 'right of reasonable access' on notice without the consent framing; an entry without consent is a common law trespass (Butter v Midwest Property Management IC, LLC, ___ N.W.3d ___ (Iowa 2025) (No. 24-1752, filed Dec. 31, 2025, amended Jan. 6, 2026): the lease there was 'subject to Resident's consent, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld', and consent is judged by what the tenant's conduct led the landlord to believe), so the base is not tagged for Iowa. Remedies, Iowa Code § 562A.35; see `edu-landlord-entry-ia`.

title: Smoking Policy
bodyText: Smoking of any kind, including smoking tobacco or marihuana, and vaping tobacco or nicotine products with an electronic cigarette or similar device, is not permitted anywhere on the property, including inside the dwelling, on porches or balconies, or in any common area. Tenant will be responsible for any cost Landlord incurs to remediate odor, staining or damage caused by smoking or vaping in violation of this Section, and a violation may be treated as a default under this Lease. As Michigan law requires, this Section does not prohibit Tenant from lawfully possessing marihuana or consuming it by means other than smoking.
notes: MI: Supersedes smoking-policy for MI. Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act (Initiated Law 1 of 2018), Mich. Comp. Laws § 333.27954(4): a person may prohibit or regulate the consumption and cultivation of marihuana on property the person owns, occupies or manages, 'except that a lease agreement may not prohibit a tenant from lawfully possessing and consuming marihuana by means other than smoking'; smoking where prohibited by the person who owns, occupies or manages the property is not authorized (Mich. Comp. Laws § 333.27954(1)(e)). The act does not define 'smoking' (MI battery 40), and no Michigan appellate decision on whether vaping marihuana is smoking was found (MI log §1.4); the clause bans vaping of tobacco and nicotine only and keeps the base's smoking ban (model smoking-policy-mo). Medical marihuana: an owner need not lease to a person who smokes or cultivates marihuana on the premises 'if the prohibition against smoking or cultivating marihuana is in the written lease' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 333.26427(c)(3)); this clause is that written prohibition for smoking; cultivation is cannabis-cultivation-mi. A lease term contrary to the act would be void (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(2)-(3)). edu-cannabis-mi. Rule 15: written section-open. title: Pets
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord: [list approved pets, or state that no pets are permitted]. Tenant will pay a pet deposit of {{pet_deposit}}, if applicable. Any refundable pet deposit is part of the Security Deposit for all purposes of Michigan law, including the limit on the total Security Deposit, and will be held, used and returned under this Lease's Security Deposit terms. Tenant will pay pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month, if applicable. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor and disturbance caused by a pet, and will reimburse Landlord for claims caused by Tenant's pet, except to the extent a claim arises from Landlord's failure to perform, or negligent performance of, a duty imposed by law. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern, and Tenant will then remove the pet within [number] days after Landlord's written notice; failure to do so is a default under this Lease. Landlord may enter the property in connection with a pet only as this Lease's Access & Entry terms permit, and will not seize or remove a pet without a court order. This Section does not limit animal control or law enforcement acting under their own authority. This Section does not apply to a service animal or assistance animal.
notes: MI: Supersedes pet-policy for MI (model pet-policy-mo). (1) A security deposit is 'a deposit, in any amount, paid by the tenant ... to be held for the term' and includes 'any other amount of money or property returnable to the tenant on condition of return of the rental unit' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.601(d)), so a refundable pet deposit is a security deposit and counts toward the 1 1/2-month cap (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.602) and the act's uses and return rules (Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 554.607-554.613); a nonrefundable pet fee or pet rent is not (edu-pet-deposit-mi). (2) The reimbursement sentence carves out the lessor's failure to perform or negligent performance of a duty imposed by law (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(e)). (3) Removal of a tenant's property is unlawful interference with possession (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.2918(2)(b)); entry follows landlords-access-mi (Mich. Comp. Laws § 125.526(11)). title: Parking & Vehicle Requirements
bodyText: Only operable, currently registered passenger vehicles may be parked at the property; commercial vehicles, recreational vehicles, trailers, and oversized vehicles are not permitted without Landlord's prior written consent. Landlord may require Tenant to provide vehicle registration information and may issue parking tags, decals, or access cards, the cost of which may be charged to Tenant. title: Returned Payments
bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes is returned or fails because of insufficient funds, a closed or nonexistent account, a stop-payment order or any other reason, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of [amount], and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. If more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term are returned or fail, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent to be made by cashier's check, certified check or money order; Landlord will not charge an additional fee for paying by at least one of those methods.
notes: MI: Supersedes returned-payments for MI (model returned-payments-ok). The base's 'not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' points at no general Michigan cap (rule 53): Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.2952 fixes a $25 processing fee (paid within 7 days, excluding weekends and holidays, after its statutory written demand is mailed) or $35 (within 30 days), with civil damages and costs only through that demand procedure (edu-dishonored-check-mi). The fee is a hand-filled landlord figure. Penalty test: Michigan courts enforce an agreed sum that is reasonable with relation to the possible injury suffered and not unconscionable or excessive, and decide enforceability as a question of law (Curran v Williams, 352 Mich 278, 282 (1958); UAW-GM Human Resource Ctr v KSL Recreation Corp, 228 Mich App 486, 508 (1998)); no published Michigan case applying the test to a residential lease fee was found (MI log §1.4). Laws § 554.633(1)(l)); acceptable-payment-methods-mi defers to it expressly so the two do not conflict, and the last clause keeps a fee-free method as Mich. Comp. title: Controlled Substances and Criminal Activity
bodyText: Tenant, members of Tenant's household and other persons under Tenant's control will not unlawfully manufacture, deliver, possess with intent to deliver, or possess a controlled substance on the property, and will not engage in other criminal activity on the property that threatens the health, safety or peaceful enjoyment of other residents, neighbors, Landlord or Landlord's agents. If any of them unlawfully manufactures, delivers, possesses with intent to deliver, or possesses a controlled substance on the property, Landlord may terminate this Lease, and if a formal police report has been filed alleging that conduct, Landlord may give Tenant a written 24-hour notice to quit. A breach of this Section is a material breach for which Landlord may end this Lease without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure, and this Section controls over any other provision of this Lease that would require one. This Section does not apply to the possession or use of marihuana that Michigan law permits, although this Lease's smoking and cultivation terms still apply, or to criminal activity of which Tenant or a member of Tenant's household is the victim or threatened victim.
notes: MI: Optional (rule 54, identification trigger). Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.134(4) and Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(b) give a 24-hour notice to quit or demand for possession only where the lease is terminated 'pursuant to a clause in the lease providing for termination because a tenant, a member of the tenant's household, or other person under the tenant's control has unlawfully manufactured, delivered, possessed with intent to deliver, or possessed a controlled substance on the leased premises' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(b); Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.134(4) reads 'because the tenant' and omits 'unlawfully'), and only if a formal police report has been filed; 'controlled substance' means a schedule 1, 2 or 3 substance under Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 333.7211-333.7216. Without this clause the 24-hour route is unavailable. Such a case is heard at the first appearance (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5735(7)) and a writ may issue immediately (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5744(3)(f)). The statute speaks of 'unlawfully' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(b)); lawful marihuana use under Mich. Comp. Laws § 333.27954 is carved out. The other-crime sentence is a lease covenant; ending the lease for it runs through the power-to-terminate route (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(c)(i)); the threatened-injury ground is statutory (Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714(1)(e)). Models criminal-activity-mo / -in; the RPOA lease has a crime-free policy and a drug clause (MI log §15). Federal subsidized housing: 24 C.F.R. § 966.4(l) (public housing lease grounds) and 24 C.F.R. § 982.310 (voucher owner grounds) read; in a covered housing program a tenant may not lose tenancy solely for criminal activity directly relating to domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking where the activity is engaged in by a household member, guest or other person under the tenant's control and the tenant or an affiliated individual is the victim or threatened victim (24 C.F.R. § 5.2005(b)(2)); the clause's carve-out covers victims and threatened victims in Tenant's household. title: Consent to Electronic Service of a Demand for Possession
bodyText: Tenant may, but is not required to, consent to receive a demand for possession or payment by electronic service. Landlord will not refuse to enter into this Lease because Tenant declines. If Tenant consents by initialing here [Tenant's initials] and providing the following e-mail address: [e-mail address], the consent takes effect only after Landlord or Tenant sends this consent, or a confirmation of it, to the other by e-mail and the other affirmatively replies by e-mail. The e-mail address remains Tenant's electronic service address until Tenant notifies Landlord in writing that Tenant no longer has an electronic service address, or the parties repeat this process with a different address.
notes: MI: Optional (rule 54). Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5718(1)(d): a demand for possession or payment may be served 'by electronic service, if the person in possession has in writing specifically consented to electronic service of the demand and if the consent or confirmation of the consent has been sent by 1 party and affirmatively replied to, by electronic transmission, by the other party'; Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5718(2): the address remains in effect until the process is repeated or the party gives written notice it no longer has one, and 'A landlord shall not refuse to enter a lease because the prospective tenant declines to consent to electronic service under this section.' Other methods remain (personal delivery, delivery to a household member, first-class mail, Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5718(1)(a)-(c)). Michigan's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act applies only between parties who agreed to transact electronically, and a party may refuse further electronic transactions (Mich. Comp. Laws § 450.835(2)-(3)). Builder: the e-mail confirmation and reply is a step after signing (MI log §10). The RPOA lease has an e-service consent paragraph (MI log §15). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Water and Sewer Bills
bodyText: Tenant will pay all water and sewage system charges for the property directly to the provider, with the service in Tenant's name where the provider allows. Landlord is the lessor for purposes of the following sentence. The lessor shall not be liable for payment of water or sewage system bills accruing subsequent to the filing of the affidavit provided by Mich. Comp. Laws § 123.165.
notes: MI: Optional (rule 54, identification trigger). Municipal water and sewer charges are a lien on the premises supplied, with priority over all other liens except taxes and special assessments (Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 123.162, 123.165), enforceable by shutoff or suit (Mich. Comp. Laws § 123.166). The Municipal Water Liens act 'shall not apply if a lease has been legally executed, containing a provision that the lessor shall not be liable for payment of water or sewage system bills accruing subsequent to the filing of the affidavit provided by this section' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 123.165); the second sentence quotes that provision verbatim except that 'this section' is replaced by its citation, since the lease is not that section (rule 59); the affidavit is filed 'with the board, commission, or other official in charge of the water works system or sewage system, or both'. The landlord must then file the affidavit (with the lease's expiration date) and give 20 days' notice of any cancellation, change or termination of the lease (edu-municipal-water-lien-mi). Where a municipality's charges run under a revenue-bond ordinance instead, written notice with a copy of the lease stops the lien and the municipality must then receive a cash deposit before giving further service (Mich. Comp. Laws § 141.121(3)). The RPOA 2024 lease cites Mich. Comp. Laws § 123.165 (MI log §15). Rule 15: written section-open. title: Holdover Charge
bodyText: If Tenant remains in possession after the end of the Term, and Landlord has not agreed in writing to a continued tenancy or accepted Rent for one under the Holdover section of this Lease, then, in place of the actual damages and reasonable rental value described in that section, Tenant will pay Landlord a holdover charge of {{holdover_daily_rate}} for each day Tenant remains in possession. Landlord and Tenant agree that Landlord's loss from a holdover, including delay in making the property available to a new tenant, is difficult to estimate accurately in advance, that this charge is a reasonable estimate of that loss, and that it is not a penalty. Landlord's acceptance of a holdover charge is not acceptance of Rent for a continued tenancy. This Section does not limit Landlord's right to recover possession, unpaid Rent and other amounts due for the period before the Term ended, or damages for harm to the property.

title: Fire or Casualty: Landlord Termination (Lease of 1 Year or More)
bodyText: This Section applies only if the Term of this Lease is at least one year, and does not apply to any month-to-month or other periodic continuation of this Lease. If the property is destroyed by fire, storm or other casualty, or is damaged by one so that it is unfit to live in and the repairs cannot reasonably be completed within [number] days after the casualty, Landlord may end this Lease by written notice to Tenant. If this Lease ends under this Section, Rent stops as of the date the property became unfit to live in, any Rent Tenant prepaid for the period after that date will be refunded, and the Security Deposit will be returned as this Lease and Michigan law provide. Tenant keeps any claim Tenant has for Landlord's failure to make repairs before this Lease ends. If the damage was caused by the wilful or irresponsible conduct, or lack of conduct, of Tenant, ending this Lease does not release Tenant from liability for the damage or for Landlord's resulting losses. Nothing in this Section limits Tenant's right under Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.201 to quit and surrender possession, and owe no Rent after surrender, if the damage occurred without Tenant's fault or neglect, or any other right Tenant has under Michigan law.
notes: MI: Optional, never a default (rule 54). Taylor, 2026-10-01 (MI log §6.2): narrow clause, for a Term of at least one year only, with the tenant's statutory surrender right expressly preserved, rent stopping from the date the home became unfit, no release for tenant-caused damage. Basis: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.201 gives the tenant, not the landlord, a surrender right where a building is destroyed or made untenantable without the tenant's fault or neglect 'and no express agreement to the contrary has been made in writing'; the preservation sentence keeps this clause from being read as such an agreement. The landlord's covenant to keep the premises in reasonable repair runs 'during the term of the lease' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(1)(b)) and may be modified only where the lease has a current term of at least 1 year (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(2)), hence the one-year condition written into the clause; a provision that 'Waives or alters a remedy available to the parties when the premises are in a condition that violates the covenants of fitness and habitability' is void (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(a)), which is why the tenant keeps any claim for the landlord's failure to repair before termination. No published Michigan case construing Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 554.201 and 554.633(1)(a), or a landlord casualty-termination clause, was found (MI log §1.4); Taylor's reading, recorded at his direction: Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.633(1)(e)'s carve-out for a release from liability for fire or other casualty covered by insurance shows the Legislature expected leases to address casualty (an inference from the text, not from a source read). Tenant fault: the repair covenant excepts disrepair 'caused by the tenants wilful or irresponsible conduct or lack of conduct' (Mich. Comp. Laws § 554.139(1)(b)); rule 54 tenant-caused-damage point. Shorter tenancies: edu-casualty-short-term-mi. The repair period is a hand-filled landlord figure. Model casualty-termination-in / -mo, narrowed. Rule 15: written section-open.
