title: Tenant Default
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due and does not pay all past-due Rent within 10 days after Landlord's written demand for it, or fails to comply with any other obligation under this Lease and does not cure the failure after receiving written notice. Landlord need not give Tenant an opportunity to cure before seeking possession for criminal activity, or in any other case where North Carolina law permits Landlord to proceed without one. Except as required by applicable law, Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate this Lease or pursue eviction. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may exercise all rights and remedies available under applicable law, including terminating this Lease, regaining possession of the property, and recovering unpaid Rent, late fees and Landlord's actual damages, less amounts obtained from the Security Deposit. Landlord will not charge Tenant any administrative fee, out-of-pocket expense or litigation cost for filing a complaint for summary ejectment or money owed except those N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-46 allows. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to mitigate damages resulting from Tenant's default to the extent required by applicable law.
notes: NC: NEW 2026-10-02 (SOP 1.21 retro, rules 49, 43 and 47; replaces `default-by-tenant-ks-ne` for NC, which is untagged). Text is `default-by-tenant-ks-ne`'s with three North Carolina changes. (1) RULE 49: 'recovering unpaid Rent, late fees, and reasonable costs and expenses' became 'unpaid Rent, late fees and Landlord's actual damages', plus a sentence limiting eviction filing charges to those N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-46 allows. It is 'contrary to public policy ... for a lease to provide for the payment of, any out-of-pocket expenses or litigation costs for filing a complaint for summary ejectment and/or money owed other than those expressly authorized under subsection (i)' (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-46(h)(3a)); administrative fees other than (e)-(g) likewise ((h)(3)); contrary provisions are void ((h)(4)). The shared 'reasonable costs and expenses', read literally, provides for litigation costs beyond (i), and 'available under applicable law' is self-limiting wording that hides the conflict (rule 53). Collecting a charge the landlord is not 'legally entitled to' also risks N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 75-55(2), 75-56(b) (rule 47). What (i) allows: court filing fees, service costs, and, under a written lease, attorneys' fees capped at 15% (the opt-in `eviction-fees-nc`, on by default per Taylor's 2026-09-28 decision). Damages that are not eviction filing costs (re-renting costs, repairs) remain recoverable as actual damages and from the deposit (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-51(a)(2), (5)). (2) RULE 43, RENT LIMB: summary ejectment always needs a 'demand made for its surrender' (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-26(a)), but no statute sets a cure period for nonpayment where the lease itself provides the forfeiture (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-26(a)(2)). title: Returned Payments (North Carolina)
bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes is returned or fails because of insufficient funds, because Tenant has no account, or for any other reason, Tenant will pay Landlord a returned-payment fee of [amount; North Carolina caps the processing fee for a check refused for insufficient funds or no account at $35.00 where the statute applies (checks taken in payment for goods or services), and no statute sets a fee for a failed electronic payment, so $35.00 or less is the safe figure for any returned payment], and Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check or money order. title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule for private houses and apartments. A fixed-term lease ends on its last day, and a periodic tenancy ends on the notice North Carolina law sets (seven days for month-to-month, two days for week-to-week, one month before the end of the year for year-to-year), with no reason required. The limits are situational. A tenant may defend an eviction as retaliatory if it is substantially in response to protected activity in the 12 months before filing, such as a good-faith repair request or code complaint, an attempt to enforce lease or legal rights, or involvement with a tenants' rights organization; the landlord still wins in listed cases, including a breach of the rent covenant or another substantial covenant, a holdover after a fixed term with no option to renew, a good-faith notice to quit given before the protected activity, and a good-faith recovery at the end of the term to live in the unit, to demolish it or make major alterations that require the household to move out completely, or to stop renting it for at least six months. A landlord may not end or refuse to renew a tenancy based substantially on a tenant's or household member's status as a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. When a building is converted to condominiums, tenants cannot be required to leave on less than 90 days' notice except for nonpayment, waste, disturbing other tenants or another breach giving a right to repossess, and the tenancy terms cannot change during that period. Public housing authorities and manufactured home communities have their own rules, which this library does not cover. North Carolina has no rent-escrow procedure that bars eviction: rent paid to the clerk during an appeal only stays the eviction while the appeal is pending. Fair housing law applies.

title: Fees and Rent
bodyText: No North Carolina statute says whether late fees, utility charges or other fees count as rent; that depends on the lease. Several statutes keep fees apart from rent. Unpaid landlord-billed water, sewer or electric charges can never be a ground to end the lease, and payments go to rent first unless the tenant directs otherwise. An eviction administrative fee cannot be deducted from a later rent payment or made a ground for a later eviction, and a late fee for one payment cannot be deducted from a later payment to put it in default. The eviction filing costs and fees the law allows may be included in the amount needed to cure a default. This library's clauses do not label fees as rent, and its default clause does not let an unpaid late fee alone end the lease.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix It and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Some states let a landlord give notice, do work the tenant failed to do, and add the cost to the rent. North Carolina has no such statute. Two narrower rules exist: after repairing an imminently dangerous condition that is the tenant's fault, the landlord may recover the actual and reasonable cost of the repair from the tenant; and a tenant who disables or damages a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm must reimburse the reasonable and actual cost of repairing or replacing it within 30 days of the landlord's written notice. Otherwise the landlord recovers the cost of tenant-caused damage as damages or from the security deposit. The landlord must give the tenant written notice of breaches of the tenant's maintenance duties, except in emergencies.

title: No Blank-Space or Lease-Copy Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be completed, treating a blank as a breach, or requiring the landlord to give the tenant a signed copy. Several North Carolina rules still turn on what the lease says: where the security deposit is held (the landlord must tell the tenant within 30 days after the term begins, and naming the bank or bond company in the lease is the simplest way), the late fee and the eviction fees and attorneys' fees (allowed only if the lease provides for them), and the emergency contact a landlord names in a tenant-death affidavit. A blank in one of those leaves a right lost or a duty unclear. Fill in every blank before signing and give the tenant a copy, as good practice rather than a statutory duty.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: No North Carolina statute states a landlord's covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession for residential leases. The closest statute is the policy statement behind the expedited criminal-activity eviction procedure, which recognizes residents' right to the peaceful, safe and quiet enjoyment of their homes and applies that procedure to every residential rental agreement. Possession is otherwise protected by the ban on self-help eviction: a residential tenant can be removed only through a court eviction. Whether a lease carries an implied covenant of quiet enjoyment is a question of case law that this library has not reviewed.

title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: North Carolina prescribes no form for a residential lease or for a landlord's demand for rent or notice to quit. The statutes do supply a few forms a landlord may meet. The small claims statute sets out a sufficient form of complaint in summary ejectment. A court form published by the Administrative Office of the Courts may not be modified in a way that keeps its official appearance, and anyone who modifies one must clearly note that it was modified and say what changed. A tenant who appeals an eviction may stay it with a bond and undertaking substantially in a statutory form. A landlord who sues on a knowingly bad check must first send demand letters substantially in the statutory forms. The notice to the State Bar about an attorney tenant's files has statutory contents but no set form.

title: Unfair Trade Practices Act and Rentals
bodyText: North Carolina's Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act declares unlawful unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce, and defines commerce to include all business activities. How far it reaches residential leasing is settled by court decisions this library has not reviewed, but several landlord-tenant statutes assume it can apply (for example, the statute allowing a partial-payment non-waiver clause says using one is not a violation of the Act). The Act has no list of unfair practices for leases, and nothing on blank spaces filled in after signing or on giving the tenant a copy. A person injured by a violation may recover three times their damages, and a court may award attorney's fees where the violation was willful and there was an unwarranted refusal to resolve the matter. Separately, the Act's debt-collection article bars anyone collecting a consumer debt from collecting any fee, charge or expense incidental to the debt unless legally entitled to it, or from falsely representing that the debt may be increased by attorney's fees or other fees; a violation carries actual damages plus a civil penalty of $500 to $4,000 for each violation. So collecting a fee that a void lease term provides for, such as a late fee above North Carolina's cap or an eviction cost the law does not allow, can create liability, not just an unenforceable term. A knowing violation of the North Carolina Servicemembers Civil Relief Act is also an unfair trade practice.

title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire, water, a vehicle or any other cause, and the damage results from the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, an Occupant, or a guest or invitee of Tenant, then: (1) as long as Landlord makes the repairs within a reasonable time, Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired, for as long as this Lease continues; and (2) if this Lease ends because of the damage, Tenant will be liable for Landlord's actual damages, including the Rent Landlord loses while the property is repaired, up to the end of the Term (for a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, up to the earliest date Tenant could have ended the tenancy by notice), less any Rent Landlord receives from re-renting the property. Landlord will make repairs as North Carolina law requires and will use reasonable efforts to re-rent the property. This Section is in addition to Tenant's liability for the cost of repairing the damage.
notes: NC: NEW 2026-10-02 (SOP 1.21 retro, rule 54t). OPTIONAL clause (CONDITIONAL, not a default), state version of `tenant-caused-damage-tn` (read; TN row not tagged), wording as `tenant-caused-damage-ga`. Each abatement or exit route checked for a tenant-fault exception. (i) Casualty: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-12 gives a surrender right only where the damage occurred 'without negligence on the part of the lessee or his agents or servants', and only if 'there is no agreement in the lease respecting repairs, or providing for such a case'; 'This section shall not apply if a contrary intention appear from the lease.' The right is displaceable, so part (1) waives no non-waivable right, and the opt-in `casualty-termination-nc` already excludes damage caused by Tenant, household members, guests or invitees. (ii) Essential services and landlord-breach termination: no North Carolina statute; the tenant's rent duty and the landlord's fitness duty are 'mutually dependent' (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-41), and rent abatement for a landlord's breach is case law, NOT read (rule 76 label: whether a court would abate rent for a condition the tenant caused while the landlord repairs within a reasonable time). (iii) Rent into court: only the appeal stay bond (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-34(b)), not an abatement route. Repair duty: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-42(a)(2) has no tenant-fault exception and cannot be waived (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-42(b)); for imminently dangerous conditions the landlord must repair even when the tenant is at fault and then 'may recover from the tenant the actual and reasonable costs of repairs that are the fault of the tenant' (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-42(a)(8)). Hence 'Landlord will make repairs as North Carolina law requires', which cannot be read as softening that duty. Part (1) is also NARROWED (rule 76, a drafting call; prompted by the independent check) to apply only 'as long as Landlord makes the repairs within a reasonable time', so it bars abatement only while the landlord is itself complying; any abatement claim for the landlord's own delay is untouched (N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 42-41, 42-42(b)). This narrowing departs from `tenant-caused-damage-ga` on purpose. Tenant duties: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-43(a)(4), (6); retaliation defense unavailable where the tenant's household or guests caused the condition (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-37.1(c)(3)). Part (2) fills a gap: no North Carolina statute measures lost rent when the lease ends because of tenant-caused damage. Periodic limb (rule 37): N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-14 notice periods. Deposit: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-51(a)(2), (3), (5). Accidental damage despite reasonable diligence is outside the clause (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-10; `edu-tenant-caused-damage-nc`). UNREAD RISK (rule 76 label): whether a North Carolina court measures damages as lost Rent to the end of the Term, and the mitigation standard, rest on case law not read. title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: North Carolina law leaves much of the cost of tenant-caused damage with the tenant. A tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or knowingly let anyone else do so, and is responsible for damage inside the unit under the tenant's exclusive control except ordinary wear and tear, acts of the landlord, defective products or repairs the landlord authorized, acts of third parties who are not the tenant's invitees, and natural forces. The landlord must still make the repairs needed to keep the home fit and habitable, and must fix an imminently dangerous condition within a reasonable time even when the tenant caused it, but may then recover the actual and reasonable repair cost from the tenant; the security deposit may also be applied to damage. The statutory right to surrender the lease after a fire or other casualty does not apply if the tenant's (or the tenant's agents' or servants') negligence caused the damage, or if the lease provides for repairs or casualty; the library's optional casualty clause excludes damage caused by the tenant, household members, guests or invitees. No North Carolina statute addresses rent during repairs or the landlord's lost rent if the lease ends because of tenant-caused damage; the library offers an optional clause for that. A tenant is not liable for damage that happens accidentally despite reasonable diligence unless the tenant agreed to be. That agreement is lawful, but the library does not offer it, because it would sit uneasily with the landlord's repair duty, which cannot be waived, and with the statute's list of damage the tenant is not responsible for; a landlord who wants one can add their own clause after taking legal advice. Willfully damaging the rented house is also a misdemeanor.
notes: NC: NEW 2026-10-02 (SOP 1.21 retro, rules 54t and 54). Controlling text, read section-open: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-43(a)(4), (6); N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-42(a)(2), (a)(8), (b); N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-51(a)(2); N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-12; N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-10 ('shall not be liable for damage occurring on the demised premises accidentally, and notwithstanding reasonable diligence on his part, unless he so contract': a lawful option the library declines, rule 54); N.C.
